preguntas.q: In immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), the autoantibodies against platelets are produced by plasma cells located primarily in which organ?

e.correcta: In ITP, autoantibodies (typically IgG against platelet glycoproteins like GPIIb/IIIa) are produced by plasma cells residing in the spleen, and these antibody-coated platelets are then also predominantly destroyed by splenic macrophages via Fc receptor-mediated phagocytosis — this dual splenic role (antibody production and platelet clearance) is exactly why splenectomy is an effective second-line treatment for refractory ITP. This distinguishes ITP mechanistically from platelet destruction processes that occur primarily through consumption (like DIC or TTP) rather than antibody-mediated clearance.

incorrectas.B: The liver's Kupffer cells contribute to some degree of antibody-coated platelet clearance, but it is not the primary site of autoantibody production against platelets, and it is not the organ targeted by splenectomy, the definitive treatment tied to the spleen's central role in ITP.
incorrectas.C: Bone marrow is the site of platelet production (from megakaryocytes) and can show compensatory megakaryocyte hyperplasia in ITP as the marrow attempts to replace destroyed platelets, but it is not where the autoantibodies against platelets are generated.
incorrectas.D: The thymus is the site of T-cell maturation and central tolerance, relevant to autoimmune diseases like myasthenia gravis (with thymoma) or in some T-cell mediated processes, but it is not the site of plasma cell antibody production implicated in ITP's platelet-directed humoral response.

preguntas.q: Which cause of pauci-immune glomerulonephritis is associated with c-ANCA (PR3-ANCA)?

e.correcta: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener) is a small-vessel vasculitis driven by antibodies against proteinase-3 (PR3-ANCA), which produce a cytoplasmic staining pattern on immunofluorescence (c-ANCA); it classically involves the upper respiratory tract (sinusitis, saddle-nose deformity), lungs (nodules/cavitation), and kidneys (pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis with necrotizing granulomatous inflammation). The PR3/c-ANCA association is a testable, specific serologic marker that distinguishes it from the other ANCA-associated vasculitides, which are linked instead to MPO/p-ANCA.

incorrectas.B: Microscopic polyangiitis is also a pauci-immune small-vessel vasculitis causing rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, but it is associated with MPO-ANCA (p-ANCA, perinuclear pattern) and characteristically lacks the granulomas and upper respiratory involvement seen in GPA.
incorrectas.C: Churg-Strauss syndrome (eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis) is associated with p-ANCA/MPO-ANCA (when ANCA is present at all) and is distinguished by asthma, eosinophilia, and granulomatous inflammation, not the c-ANCA/PR3 pattern.
incorrectas.D: Goodpasture syndrome causes pulmonary-renal syndrome via anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies producing linear IgG deposition on immunofluorescence, an entirely different (anti-GBM, immune-complex-mediated) mechanism rather than pauci-immune ANCA-associated vasculitis.

preguntas.q: Which causes of pauci-immune glomerulonephritis are associated with p-ANCA (MPO-ANCA)?

o.B: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis and Goodpasture syndrome

e.correcta: Microscopic polyangiitis and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss) are both associated with p-ANCA (perinuclear pattern), which targets myeloperoxidase (MPO) within neutrophil granules; these antibodies are thought to contribute to neutrophil activation and vessel wall injury in small-vessel pauci-immune vasculitis. Recognizing the p-ANCA/MPO-ANCA association is clinically useful because it helps distinguish these entities from granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener), which is instead linked to c-ANCA (cytoplasmic pattern) directed against proteinase-3 (PR3).

incorrectas.B: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is associated with c-ANCA (PR3-ANCA), not p-ANCA, and Goodpasture syndrome is an anti-GBM antibody disease (linear IF deposits), not a pauci-immune ANCA-associated vasculitis at all, so pairing them under p-ANCA is doubly incorrect.
incorrectas.C: IgA nephropathy and lupus nephritis are immune-complex-mediated glomerulonephritides with granular immunofluorescence deposits (IgA or full-house immunofluorescence, respectively), not pauci-immune diseases, and neither is defined by ANCA positivity.
incorrectas.D: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and membranous nephropathy are also immune-complex-mediated diseases with characteristic granular deposits (subepithelial humps or spikes), not pauci-immune ANCA-associated vasculitides.

preguntas.q: Decay accelerating factor (DAF/CD55) and membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis (MIRL/CD59) are anchored to the RBC membrane by which glycolipid anchor?

e.correcta: DAF (CD55) and MIRL (CD59) are complement regulatory proteins tethered to the outer leaflet of the RBC membrane via a glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor, which protects host cells from inappropriate complement-mediated lysis by inhibiting C3/C5 convertase formation (DAF) and blocking membrane attack complex assembly (MIRL). This GPI-anchoring mechanism is the key link to paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, where a PIGA gene mutation impairs GPI anchor synthesis, causing loss of these proteins and unchecked complement-mediated hemolysis.

incorrectas.B: Phosphatidylserine is normally kept on the inner leaflet of the membrane by flippases and is exposed on the outer leaflet as an 'eat-me' signal during apoptosis or platelet activation, not the anchor used to tether complement regulatory proteins like DAF and MIRL.
incorrectas.C: Sphingomyelin is a membrane phospholipid important for membrane rigidity and lipid raft structure, but it is not the anchoring molecule that attaches complement-regulatory proteins to the cell surface.
incorrectas.D: Cholesterol is a membrane component that modulates fluidity and is enriched in lipid rafts, but proteins like DAF and MIRL are attached via a GPI anchor (a glycolipid structure), not directly via cholesterol.

preguntas.q: Absence of GPI anchors on blood cells (with resulting loss of DAF and MIRL) renders cells susceptible to destruction mediated by which system?

e.correcta: GPI-anchored proteins DAF (CD55) and MIRL (CD59) normally protect host cells by inhibiting complement C3/C5 convertases and blocking membrane attack complex formation; when a somatic PIGA mutation (as in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria) prevents GPI anchor synthesis, these protective proteins are lost from the cell surface, leaving red cells vulnerable to unchecked complement-mediated lysis, especially during the relative acidosis of sleep.

incorrectas.B: NK cell-mediated cytotoxicity relies on recognizing missing/altered MHC class I or stress ligands on target cells, a mechanism unrelated to GPI-anchor loss or the DAF/MIRL complement regulators being described here.
incorrectas.C: Antibody-dependent phagocytosis requires opsonizing antibodies binding target cells and being recognized by Fc receptors on phagocytes — this is a distinct pathway from the direct complement membrane attack complex lysis caused by loss of DAF/MIRL.
incorrectas.D: Neutrophil oxidative burst is a mechanism neutrophils use to kill phagocytosed pathogens via reactive oxygen species, not a process that targets host red blood cells lacking GPI-anchored complement regulators.

preguntas.q: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) classically causes which type of anemia (based on red cell size)?

o.D: Anemia of chronic disease pattern only

e.correcta: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria results from an acquired PIGA gene mutation in a hematopoietic stem cell clone, causing loss of GPI-anchored complement regulatory proteins (CD55 and CD59) on blood cell membranes. Without these protective proteins, red blood cells are susceptible to complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis, producing a normocytic hemolytic anemia (since the red cells themselves are of normal size but are being destroyed, not underproduced or affected by a size-altering nutritional/maturation defect).

incorrectas.B: Macrocytic anemia results from impaired DNA synthesis (e.g., B12/folate deficiency) or accelerated erythropoiesis with reticulocytosis skewing cell size upward, but PNH's defining anemia is a hemolytic, normocytic process driven by complement-mediated destruction, not by red cell size-altering maturation defects.
incorrectas.C: Microcytic anemia is typically caused by defects in hemoglobin synthesis (iron deficiency, thalassemia, sideroblastic anemia), a fundamentally different mechanism from PNH's complement-mediated lysis of otherwise normally sized red blood cells.
incorrectas.D: PNH is a primary hemolytic disorder from a specific membrane defect (loss of CD55/CD59), not a nonspecific anemia of chronic disease pattern, which arises from hepcidin-mediated iron sequestration during chronic inflammation — a distinct and unrelated mechanism.

preguntas.q: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria is primarily characterized by which type of hemolysis?

o.C: Hemolysis confined to the spleen only
o.D: Hemolysis mediated exclusively by IgE antibodies

e.correcta: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria results from an acquired PIGA gene mutation that impairs GPI-anchor synthesis, leading to deficient CD55/CD59 (complement regulatory proteins) on red cell membranes; without these protective proteins, complement is free to assemble the membrane attack complex directly on the RBC surface, causing intravascular hemolysis with hemoglobinuria, especially noted in morning urine due to nocturnal complement activation during relative acidosis in sleep. This intravascular mechanism (versus destruction by splenic macrophages) is why free hemoglobin appears in the urine and plasma, and why patients are at increased risk of thrombosis.

incorrectas.B: Extravascular hemolysis, where macrophages in the spleen/liver phagocytose antibody- or complement-tagged RBCs, is the mechanism in conditions like warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia or hereditary spherocytosis, not PNH, where complement directly lyses cells within the vasculature itself.
incorrectas.C: PNH hemolysis is not confined to the spleen; it occurs throughout the intravascular space wherever complement can assemble the membrane attack complex on unprotected red cells, which is precisely why free hemoglobin appears in the urine.
incorrectas.D: PNH hemolysis is complement-mediated (via the alternative pathway attacking GPI-anchor-deficient cells), not IgE-mediated; IgE-driven mechanisms are characteristic of type I hypersensitivity reactions, an entirely different immunologic process.

preguntas.q: The intravascular hemolysis of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria occurs episodically, often during which activity/state?

e.correcta: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria results from an acquired PIGA gene mutation in a hematopoietic stem cell clone, leading to deficiency of GPI-anchored complement regulatory proteins (CD55 and CD59) on blood cells, which leaves red cells vulnerable to complement-mediated lysis. Hemolysis classically occurs during sleep because the relative respiratory acidosis that develops overnight (from reduced ventilation) lowers blood pH slightly, which activates the alternative complement pathway more readily, precipitating episodes of intravascular hemolysis noticed as dark urine upon waking. This nocturnal/early-morning hemoglobinuria pattern is the classic clinical clue pointing to PNH.

incorrectas.B: Exercise is not the classic trigger for PNH hemolysis; it is more relevant to conditions like myoglobinuria from rhabdomyolysis or G6PD-related oxidative hemolytic crises, whereas PNH's hallmark trigger relates to the mild nocturnal acidosis during sleep, not physical exertion.
incorrectas.C: Eating is not linked to complement activation or hemolysis in PNH; there is no established mechanism by which digestion or meal timing would trigger the alternative complement pathway the way relative nocturnal hypoventilation and acidosis do.
incorrectas.D: Sun exposure triggers hemolysis in conditions involving photosensitizing porphyrins (like erythropoietic protoporphyria) or exacerbates certain autoimmune conditions, but it is not the mechanism behind PNH's complement-mediated red cell lysis, which is tied to sleep-related pH changes.

preguntas.q: Which test is classically used to screen for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria?

o.D: Ham's acid hemolysis test as the initial screen only, never sucrose

e.correcta: The sucrose test (sugar water test) is the classic bedside screen for PNH: lowering the ionic strength of the solution promotes complement activation on the red cell surface, and cells that lack the GPI-anchored complement regulators CD55 (DAF) and CD59 (MIRL) — as occurs in PNH due to a somatic PIGA mutation — lyse. It's used as a rapid screen because it's simple to perform, though the more specific confirmatory test today is flow cytometry for CD55/CD59 expression (the Ham acid hemolysis test is the more specific historical confirmatory test).

incorrectas.B: The Coombs test detects antibody or complement bound to red cells, which is the mechanism of autoimmune hemolytic anemia, not PNH — PNH hemolysis is due to intrinsic complement hypersensitivity from a missing GPI anchor, not antibody-mediated destruction, so the direct antiglobulin test is classically negative in PNH.
incorrectas.C: The osmotic fragility test detects red cells that lyse in hypotonic saline due to a membrane defect that reduces surface-area-to-volume ratio, which is the hallmark of hereditary spherocytosis, not PNH — PNH cells are structurally normal but abnormally vulnerable to complement, a different mechanism entirely.
incorrectas.D: This option misstates test sequencing — Ham's test is a confirmatory/historical test for complement-mediated lysis under acidified conditions, but the classically cited initial screening test in this question stem is the sucrose test, not Ham's test used as a mandatory first step.

preguntas.q: Patients with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria can develop abdominal pain, dysphagia, and erectile dysfunction because free hemoglobin acts as a scavenger of which molecule?

e.correcta: In PNH, complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis releases large amounts of free hemoglobin into the plasma, which avidly binds and scavenges nitric oxide (forming methemoglobin and nitrate), depleting NO available for smooth muscle relaxation. Since NO is the key mediator of smooth muscle relaxation in the gut, esophagus, and corpus cavernosum, this scavenging produces smooth muscle dystonia manifesting as abdominal pain, dysphagia, and erectile dysfunction — a hallmark feature linking hemolysis to these seemingly unrelated symptoms.

incorrectas.B: Prostaglandin E2 is involved in pain and inflammatory signaling but is not the molecule classically scavenged by free plasma hemoglobin to produce the smooth muscle dystonia syndrome seen in PNH.
incorrectas.C: Serotonin affects vascular tone and gut motility through its own receptor systems, but it is not depleted by free hemoglobin scavenging in the mechanism responsible for PNH's characteristic symptom triad.
incorrectas.D: Acetylcholine mediates parasympathetic smooth muscle contraction (often opposing NO's relaxant effect) but is not bound or scavenged by free hemoglobin; the pathophysiology specifically implicates NO depletion, not disruption of cholinergic signaling.

preguntas.q: What is the main cause of death in patients with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria?

o.C: Acute renal failure from hemoglobin cast nephropathy

e.correcta: In PNH, free hemoglobin released by intravascular hemolysis scavenges nitric oxide, which promotes platelet activation and a hypercoagulable state; combined with complement-mediated activation of platelets and endothelium, this drives a strong predisposition to venous thrombosis, particularly in unusual sites like the hepatic (Budd-Chiari), portal, and cerebral veins — this thrombotic tendency is the leading cause of death in PNH, more so than the anemia itself.

incorrectas.B: While PNH can be associated with bone marrow failure/aplastic anemia and resultant cytopenias in some patients, sepsis from neutropenia is not the primary cause of mortality in PNH — the thrombotic complications from complement-driven hemolysis are the dominant clinical threat.
incorrectas.C: Hemoglobinuria and renal iron deposition can contribute to chronic kidney injury over time in PNH, but acute renal failure from cast nephropathy is not identified as the main cause of death; thrombosis at unusual venous sites remains the leading fatal complication.
incorrectas.D: Hemorrhagic stroke is not a typical feature of PNH; if anything, the hypercoagulable state predisposes to thrombotic (ischemic), not hemorrhagic, cerebrovascular events, consistent with the thrombosis-driven mortality pattern of the disease.

preguntas.q: Which type of anemia, characterized by microcytosis, may develop as a complication of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria?

e.correcta: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) arises from a somatic PIGA mutation causing loss of GPI-anchored complement regulatory proteins (CD55/CD59) on blood cells, leading to complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis and chronic hemoglobinuria. The chronic loss of hemoglobin (and thus iron) in the urine over time depletes total body iron stores, producing a superimposed iron deficiency anemia with microcytosis — distinct from the hemolysis itself, which is typically normocytic. Recognizing this secondary iron deficiency is key to understanding why PNH patients can have a microcytic picture despite a primarily hemolytic disease.

incorrectas.B: Thalassemia is an inherited defect in globin chain synthesis, unrelated to the acquired GPI-anchor defect and chronic urinary iron loss that characterizes PNH; it would not be described as a 'complication' arising from PNH.
incorrectas.C: Sideroblastic anemia results from defective heme synthesis (often mitochondrial, causing ringed sideroblasts) rather than iron loss, and is not the mechanism by which PNH produces microcytic anemia.
incorrectas.D: Anemia of chronic kidney disease is due to erythropoietin deficiency and is typically normocytic, not microcytic, and is unrelated to the complement-mediated hemolysis and iron wasting seen in PNH.

preguntas.q: Which hormone's secretion from the zona glomerulosa is under tonic, but not exclusive, control by ACTH?

e.correcta: Aldosterone secretion from the zona glomerulosa is primarily regulated by the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (angiotensin II) and by serum potassium, with ACTH providing only tonic, permissive support rather than the dominant drive. This is why aldosterone levels can remain largely independent of cortisol-driven ACTH fluctuations, distinguishing zona glomerulosa regulation from the zona fasciculata, which is tightly and primarily ACTH-dependent.

incorrectas.B: Cortisol is secreted by the zona fasciculata under direct and primary control of ACTH via the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, unlike aldosterone, whose main regulators are angiotensin II and potassium, with ACTH only playing a minor, tonic role.
incorrectas.C: Renin is secreted by the juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney, not the adrenal zona glomerulosa, in response to decreased renal perfusion, decreased Na+ delivery, or sympathetic stimulation — it is upstream of aldosterone, not the hormone being asked about.
incorrectas.D: Angiotensin II is generated in the circulation (from angiotensinogen via renin and ACE), not secreted by the adrenal zona glomerulosa; it is the stimulus that acts on the zona glomerulosa to induce aldosterone release, not the hormone secreted by that layer.

preguntas.q: Which hormone increases renal Na+ reabsorption, thereby restoring ECF volume and blood volume to normal?

e.correcta: Aldosterone, released from the adrenal zona glomerulosa in response to angiotensin II or hyperkalemia, acts on the principal cells of the renal collecting duct to upregulate ENaC and Na+/K+-ATPase activity, increasing sodium (and secondarily water) reabsorption. This expands extracellular fluid and blood volume back toward normal when volume has fallen, making aldosterone the key effector hormone of the RAAS for long-term volume homeostasis.

incorrectas.B: Atrial natriuretic peptide is released in response to atrial stretch from volume overload and does the opposite of aldosterone — it promotes natriuresis (sodium excretion) and vasodilation to reduce excess volume, not restore depleted volume.
incorrectas.C: Cortisol has some mineralocorticoid cross-reactivity at very high levels but its primary physiologic roles are metabolic (gluconeogenesis) and immunomodulatory; it is not the hormone whose main regulated function is restoring ECF volume via renal Na+ reabsorption.
incorrectas.D: Erythropoietin stimulates red blood cell production in the bone marrow in response to hypoxia; it has no direct effect on renal sodium handling or extracellular fluid volume.

preguntas.q: To which receptor does angiotensin II bind to exert its main physiologic effects?

e.correcta: Angiotensin II exerts its main physiologic effects (vasoconstriction, aldosterone secretion, increased sodium reabsorption, and stimulation of thirst/ADH release) primarily through the AT1 receptor, a G-protein coupled receptor that activates the Gq pathway to increase intracellular calcium and drive smooth muscle contraction. This is why ARBs (angiotensin receptor blockers) are specifically designed to block the AT1 receptor to blunt these pressor and sodium-retaining effects in the treatment of hypertension and heart failure.

incorrectas.B: The AT2 receptor is also activated by angiotensin II but generally mediates opposing effects such as vasodilation, antiproliferation, and apoptosis, and its physiologic role is much less prominent than AT1 in mediating the classic pressor and volume-retaining actions of the renin-angiotensin system.
incorrectas.C: The V1 receptor is a vasopressin (ADH) receptor found on vascular smooth muscle that mediates vasoconstriction in response to ADH, not angiotensin II, representing an entirely separate hormone-receptor system.
incorrectas.D: The V2 receptor is also a vasopressin (ADH) receptor, located on renal collecting duct principal cells, mediating water reabsorption via aquaporin-2 insertion in response to ADH, not angiotensin II, so it is unrelated to angiotensin II's primary receptor-mediated effects.

preguntas.q: Through which secondary messenger system does the angiotensin II-bound AT1 receptor propagate its signal?

e.correcta: The AT1 receptor is Gq-coupled, so when angiotensin II binds it, phospholipase C is activated to generate IP3 and DAG, raising intracellular calcium and causing vascular smooth muscle contraction (vasoconstriction) as well as aldosterone release from the adrenal cortex. This IP3/Ca2+ pathway is the same general mechanism used by other Gq-coupled vasoconstrictor receptors (like alpha-1 adrenergic and V1 receptors), which is a useful pattern to recognize across the vasoconstrictor hormone family.

incorrectas.B: cAMP signaling is characteristic of Gs-coupled receptors (like beta-adrenergic or V2 receptors), not the Gq-coupled AT1 receptor, which instead signals via IP3/Ca2+.
incorrectas.C: cGMP is the second messenger for nitric oxide/guanylate cyclase signaling (a vasodilatory pathway), the functional opposite of the vasoconstrictive AT1 receptor's IP3/Ca2+ mechanism.
incorrectas.D: Tyrosine kinase signaling is typical of growth factor and insulin receptors, not G-protein-coupled receptors like AT1, which signals through the Gq/PLC/IP3 pathway instead.

preguntas.q: How does hyperkalemia influence aldosterone secretion?

o.D: Increased renin secretion but no change in aldosterone

e.correcta: Hyperkalemia directly stimulates the zona glomerulosa cells of the adrenal cortex to secrete aldosterone, independent of the renin-angiotensin system — elevated extracellular potassium depolarizes glomerulosa cell membranes, opening voltage-gated calcium channels and triggering aldosterone synthesis and release. The resulting aldosterone then acts on the principal cells of the cortical collecting duct to increase Na+/K+-ATPase activity and open ENaC/ROMK channels, promoting renal potassium excretion — a direct feedback loop that helps correct the hyperkalemia.

incorrectas.B: Decreased aldosterone secretion in response to hyperkalemia would be counterproductive physiologically, since aldosterone is precisely the hormone the body needs to increase in order to excrete excess potassium; this is the opposite of the actual homeostatic feedback relationship.
incorrectas.C: No effect on aldosterone would ignore a well-established direct, angiotensin-II-independent pathway by which potassium itself acts on the adrenal zona glomerulosa; potassium is, in fact, one of the most potent direct stimulators of aldosterone secretion.
incorrectas.D: Increased renin without a change in aldosterone misrepresents the pathway — hyperkalemia does not primarily act through increased renin release (in fact, the direct adrenal potassium-sensing pathway operates independently of renin), and the end effect is a clear rise in aldosterone, not an isolated renin change.

preguntas.q: Aldosterone increases reabsorption of which ion (along with H2O) at the distal tubules and collecting duct?

e.correcta: Aldosterone acts on principal cells of the distal tubule and collecting duct, upregulating epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) and the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase to increase sodium reabsorption; water follows sodium osmotically (when ADH is present), which is why aldosterone increases both Na+ and water retention. This mechanism is central to volume and blood pressure regulation via the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, and it's coupled with aldosterone's reciprocal effect of promoting potassium and hydrogen ion secretion into the tubular lumen.

incorrectas.B: Aldosterone actually promotes potassium secretion (not reabsorption) into the tubular lumen in exchange for sodium reabsorption, which is why hyperaldosteronism causes hypokalemia rather than potassium retention.
incorrectas.C: Calcium reabsorption in the distal nephron is primarily regulated by parathyroid hormone and vitamin D, not by aldosterone, which centers its action on sodium (and secondarily potassium and hydrogen) handling.
incorrectas.D: Phosphate reabsorption is chiefly regulated in the proximal tubule by parathyroid hormone (which inhibits it) and FGF23, not by aldosterone's distal sodium-water reabsorption mechanism.

preguntas.q: Which system is a slow, hormonally mediated mechanism for regulating arterial pressure?

e.correcta: The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system is a slow, hormonally mediated mechanism that responds to decreased renal perfusion by releasing renin, generating angiotensin II (a vasoconstrictor) and stimulating aldosterone secretion (which promotes renal sodium and water retention) — because this cascade depends on enzymatic conversion steps and hormone synthesis/secretion, it acts over hours to days rather than seconds, making it well-suited for long-term blood pressure and volume regulation rather than rapid, moment-to-moment control.

incorrectas.B: The baroreceptor reflex is a fast, neurally mediated mechanism using stretch receptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch that adjusts blood pressure within seconds via the autonomic nervous system, the opposite time course of the hormonally mediated RAAS.
incorrectas.C: The chemoreceptor reflex responds to changes in blood oxygen, CO2, and pH via peripheral and central chemoreceptors, acting rapidly through neural pathways to adjust ventilation and, secondarily, blood pressure — it is not a slow hormonal system.
incorrectas.D: The Cushing reflex is an acute neural response to rising intracranial pressure, causing hypertension and bradycardia within minutes to preserve cerebral perfusion, which is a rapid protective reflex rather than a slow hormonal pathway.

preguntas.q: The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system regulates mean arterial pressure primarily by adjusting what parameter?

e.correcta: The RAAS regulates mean arterial pressure primarily by adjusting blood volume: aldosterone (stimulated by angiotensin II) increases renal sodium (and secondarily water) reabsorption in the collecting duct, expanding extracellular fluid and blood volume, which raises venous return and cardiac output over the long term. While angiotensin II also causes acute vasoconstriction, the RAAS's dominant long-term blood pressure control mechanism is this volume-based effect, which is why chronic RAAS activity (or RAAS blockade with ACE inhibitors/ARBs) has such profound effects on long-term blood pressure.

incorrectas.B: Heart rate is regulated primarily by the autonomic nervous system (baroreceptor reflex via sympathetic/parasympathetic tone), not primarily by RAAS, which acts mainly through volume and vascular tone rather than direct chronotropic effects.
incorrectas.C: Vascular compliance is a structural/passive property of vessel walls, not the primary lever the RAAS uses; RAAS instead primarily changes blood volume (via aldosterone-mediated sodium retention) and vascular tone (via angiotensin II).
incorrectas.D: Cardiac contractility is influenced mainly by sympathetic stimulation and intrinsic myocardial factors, not by RAAS directly — RAAS's main long-term blood pressure effect operates through blood volume expansion.

preguntas.q: The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system is activated in response to what change in mean arterial pressure?

o.C: No change, only changes in serum osmolarity

e.correcta: The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) is a compensatory response to a fall in effective circulating volume or pressure: a drop in renal perfusion pressure is sensed by the juxtaglomerular (JG) cells of the afferent arteriole (baroreceptor mechanism), and reduced NaCl delivery past the macula densa reinforces the signal, together triggering renin release. Renin cleaves angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, which ACE converts to angiotensin II, driving vasoconstriction and aldosterone release to restore blood pressure and volume. This is a negative-feedback loop, so a decrease — not an increase — in MAP is what turns the system on.

incorrectas.B: An increase in MAP would suppress renin release (reduced JG cell stretch-sensing of pressure and increased NaCl delivery to the macula densa), the opposite of what activates RAAS; the system is designed to correct low pressure, not respond to high pressure by activating further.
incorrectas.C: Serum osmolarity changes primarily drive ADH (vasopressin) release from the posterior pituitary via hypothalamic osmoreceptors, a distinct volume/tonicity-regulating axis; RAAS activation is fundamentally a pressure/volume-sensing response, not an osmolarity-sensing one, even though the two systems can act together.
incorrectas.D: Serum potassium does directly stimulate aldosterone secretion from the adrenal zona glomerulosa (independent of angiotensin II), but this is a separate trigger for aldosterone alone, not the renin-driven trigger for the whole RAAS cascade, which is fundamentally pressure-dependent.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II?

e.correcta: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), located predominantly on the luminal surface of pulmonary and renal vascular endothelium, cleaves the inactive decapeptide angiotensin I into the active octapeptide angiotensin II by removing two C-terminal amino acids. Angiotensin II then drives potent vasoconstriction and stimulates aldosterone release from the adrenal cortex, making ACE the key pharmacologic target of ACE inhibitors used to treat hypertension and heart failure.

incorrectas.B: Renin is the enzyme released by juxtaglomerular cells in response to low renal perfusion, and it acts earlier in the cascade — cleaving angiotensinogen (made by the liver) into angiotensin I, not converting angiotensin I to angiotensin II.
incorrectas.C: Chymase is an alternative, ACE-independent pathway (especially active in cardiac and vascular tissue) that can also convert angiotensin I to angiotensin II, which is clinically relevant as a reason ACE inhibitors don't fully suppress angiotensin II production, but it is not the primary/classic enzyme being asked about here.
incorrectas.D: Aldosterone synthase acts downstream in the adrenal cortex to produce aldosterone from corticosterone precursors in response to angiotensin II stimulation; it plays no role in converting angiotensin I to angiotensin II.

preguntas.q: In which organ does ACE primarily catalyze the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II?

e.correcta: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) is expressed abundantly on the luminal surface of pulmonary vascular endothelium, so as blood passes through the extensive capillary network of the lungs, angiotensin I is efficiently converted to angiotensin II. This pulmonary first-pass conversion is why ACE inhibitors, by blocking this specific site, reduce angiotensin II formation systemically and also cause the classic ACE-inhibitor side effect of dry cough, thought to result from accumulated bradykinin in the lung tissue.

incorrectas.B: The kidneys are the site of renin release (from juxtaglomerular cells) in response to decreased perfusion, which cleaves angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, but the subsequent conversion to angiotensin II by ACE occurs predominantly in the pulmonary vasculature, not the kidney itself.
incorrectas.C: The liver produces angiotensinogen, the precursor protein that renin acts upon, but it does not carry out the ACE-mediated conversion step; hepatic synthesis and pulmonary conversion are distinct steps in the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone pathway.
incorrectas.D: The adrenal glands respond to angiotensin II by secreting aldosterone from the zona glomerulosa, acting downstream of angiotensin II formation, but they are not the site where ACE converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II.

preguntas.q: Angiotensin II stimulates the synthesis and secretion of which hormone by the adrenal cortex?

e.correcta: Angiotensin II binds AT1 receptors on zona glomerulosa cells of the adrenal cortex, stimulating both the synthesis and secretion of aldosterone as part of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). Aldosterone then acts on the distal nephron to increase Na+ reabsorption and K+/H+ secretion, restoring blood volume and pressure — the physiologic endpoint of the RAAS cascade triggered by low renal perfusion or low Na+ delivery. This is the basis for why ACE inhibitors and ARBs blunt aldosterone release and are used in heart failure and hypertension.

incorrectas.B: Cortisol secretion is primarily driven by ACTH from the anterior pituitary acting on the zona fasciculata, a distinct axis (HPA axis) from angiotensin II's action on the zona glomerulosa.
incorrectas.C: DHEA is produced by the zona reticularis under ACTH stimulation as part of adrenal androgen synthesis, not by angiotensin II acting on the zona glomerulosa.
incorrectas.D: Epinephrine is synthesized and secreted by the adrenal medulla (chromaffin cells) in response to sympathetic stimulation, an entirely separate part of the adrenal gland and pathway from the angiotensin II-aldosterone axis.

preguntas.q: Angiotensin II increases which exchange process in the proximal convoluted tubule?

e.correcta: Angiotensin II enhances Na+-H+ exchange (via the NHE3 antiporter) on the apical membrane of proximal convoluted tubule cells, increasing Na+ (and secondarily water and HCO3−) reabsorption to help restore intravascular volume and blood pressure as part of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. This is one of angiotensin II's several volume-conserving actions, alongside efferent arteriolar constriction and stimulation of aldosterone release, all coordinated to counter states of low perfusion.

incorrectas.B: K+-H+ exchange is primarily relevant in the distal nephron/collecting duct (and stomach), not the dominant angiotensin II-driven mechanism in the proximal tubule, so it is not the process angiotensin II is classically described as upregulating there.
incorrectas.C: Cl−-HCO3− exchange occurs in other nephron segments (e.g., intercalated cells) for acid-base handling, but it is not the proximal tubule transporter angiotensin II is known to stimulate for volume reabsorption.
incorrectas.D: Na+-Ca2+ exchange is a mechanism more relevant to distal tubule calcium handling (e.g., under PTH influence) and cardiac/muscle physiology, not the proximal tubule sodium-reabsorption pathway that angiotensin II upregulates.

preguntas.q: Angiotensin II increases which sensation via its action on the hypothalamus?

e.correcta: Angiotensin II acts on the hypothalamus (specifically circumventricular organs like the subfornical organ and OVLT, which lack a complete blood-brain barrier, allowing circulating angiotensin II direct access) to stimulate the sensation of thirst, promoting water intake. This makes physiologic sense as part of the broader renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system's role in volume regulation: in states of hypovolemia or hypotension, angiotensin II simultaneously causes vasoconstriction, stimulates aldosterone (sodium/water retention), and drives thirst, all working together to restore intravascular volume.

incorrectas.B: Hunger is regulated by separate hypothalamic circuits (e.g., the arcuate nucleus responding to leptin, ghrelin, and insulin), not by angiotensin II, which is specifically tied to volume/osmotic regulation rather than energy balance.
incorrectas.C: Satiety, the sensation of fullness after eating, is likewise controlled by hypothalamic pathways responsive to metabolic and hormonal signals like leptin and CCK, not by the renin-angiotensin system.
incorrectas.D: Sleepiness is regulated by circadian and homeostatic sleep-drive mechanisms involving structures like the suprachiasmatic nucleus and adenosine accumulation, unrelated to angiotensin II's role in volume homeostasis.

preguntas.q: What effect does angiotensin II have on arterioles?

e.correcta: Angiotensin II is one of the body's most potent vasoconstrictors, acting on AT1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle (via Gq/IP3/Ca2+ signaling) to constrict both afferent and especially efferent renal arterioles as well as systemic arterioles, raising both renal filtration pressure and systemic blood pressure. This is central to the RAAS pathway's role in blood pressure homeostasis and explains why ACE inhibitors and ARBs are used as antihypertensives.

incorrectas.B: Dilation is the opposite of angiotensin II's actual effect; vasodilation is instead produced by substances like bradykinin, nitric oxide, or prostaglandins, not angiotensin II.
incorrectas.C: Angiotensin II clearly has a potent effect on arteriolar tone (vasoconstriction) — 'no effect' ignores its central role as an effector hormone of the RAAS system in blood pressure regulation.
incorrectas.D: Angiotensin II acts on arterioles broadly (both afferent and efferent), not selectively on veins, and its action is constriction, not dilation — so 'selective venodilation' misrepresents both the vessel type and the direction of effect.

preguntas.q: Decreased O2 delivery to the kidneys due to hypoxia causes increased production of which factor, which then stimulates EPO synthesis?

e.correcta: Under normoxic conditions, HIF-1α is continuously hydroxylated by prolyl hydroxylases (an O2-dependent reaction) and targeted for proteasomal degradation via the von Hippel-Lindau protein. When renal peritubular fibroblast-like cells sense hypoxia, this hydroxylation fails, HIF-1α accumulates and translocates to the nucleus, and it transactivates the EPO gene along with other hypoxia-response genes. This O2-sensing mechanism is why chronic kidney disease (loss of EPO-producing cells) causes anemia, and why HIF-stabilizing drugs (e.g., roxadustat) can be used to treat it.

incorrectas.B: Angiotensin II is generated in response to decreased renal perfusion pressure and sympathetic activation (via the renin-angiotensin system) and primarily causes vasoconstriction and aldosterone release; it is not the oxygen-sensing signal that directly drives EPO gene transcription.
incorrectas.C: VEGF is itself a downstream target gene of HIF-1α, promoting angiogenesis in hypoxic tissue, but it is not the upstream factor that stimulates EPO synthesis in this pathway.
incorrectas.D: Renin is released by juxtaglomerular cells in response to decreased afferent arteriolar pressure, decreased NaCl delivery to the macula densa, or sympathetic stimulation — it initiates the RAAS cascade, not the hypoxia-EPO axis.

preguntas.q: Erythropoietin (EPO) causes differentiation of which cell type, which undergoes further development into mature erythrocytes?

e.correcta: Erythropoietin, produced mainly by renal peritubular interstitial fibroblasts in response to hypoxia, binds its receptor on committed erythroid progenitors and drives their differentiation into proerythroblasts, the earliest morphologically recognizable red cell precursor in the bone marrow, which then matures through several stages (basophilic, polychromatophilic, orthochromatic normoblast) before enucleating into a reticulocyte and finally a mature erythrocyte. This EPO-proerythroblast link is why conditions of renal failure (reduced EPO) or EPO-secreting tumors directly affect the earliest committed step of red cell production.

incorrectas.B: Megakaryocytes are the precursor cells for platelets, driven primarily by thrombopoietin rather than erythropoietin, and represent an entirely separate hematopoietic lineage from red blood cell production.
incorrectas.C: Myeloblasts are the earliest precursors of the granulocytic (neutrophil/eosinophil/basophil) lineage, driven by factors like G-CSF and GM-CSF, not erythropoietin, and are unrelated to red cell differentiation.
incorrectas.D: Reticulocytes are a later stage in erythropoiesis — the immediate precursor of the mature erythrocyte after enucleation — but they arise downstream of the proerythroblast; EPO's direct differentiation-inducing action is on the earlier proerythroblast stage, not the reticulocyte.

preguntas.q: Aldosterone increases secretion of which two ions at the distal tubules and collecting duct?

e.correcta: Aldosterone acts on principal cells of the distal tubule and collecting duct to upregulate epithelial Na+ channels (ENaC) and the Na+-K+-ATPase, increasing Na+ reabsorption which creates a lumen-negative electrochemical gradient that drives K+ secretion into the tubule; it simultaneously stimulates H+-ATPase in intercalated cells, increasing H+ secretion as well. This dual K+ and H+ secretion explains why hyperaldosteronism causes hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis, while aldosterone deficiency causes hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis.

incorrectas.B: Aldosterone increases Na+ reabsorption (not secretion) rather than secreting it, and it has no significant direct effect on Ca2+ handling at this segment, making this pairing incorrect on both the ion identity and the direction of Na+ transport.
incorrectas.C: Aldosterone's principal ionic effects at the distal nephron are on Na+, K+, and H+ transport; Cl− follows Na+ passively but is not itself independently secreted by aldosterone, and HCO3− handling is primarily a proximal tubule and intercalated cell process not driven by aldosterone in this way.
incorrectas.D: Mg2+ and phosphate handling occur mainly in the proximal tubule and thick ascending limb (influenced by PTH for phosphate), not through aldosterone-driven secretion at the distal tubule and collecting duct.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme metabolizes sorbitol into fructose?

e.correcta: Sorbitol dehydrogenase catalyzes the conversion of sorbitol to fructose as the second step of the polyol pathway, following aldose reductase's initial conversion of glucose to sorbitol. Tissues with low or absent sorbitol dehydrogenase activity (such as the lens, retina, kidney, and Schwann cells) are vulnerable to sorbitol accumulation and osmotic damage in hyperglycemic states like diabetes, which contributes to diabetic cataracts, retinopathy, and neuropathy.

incorrectas.B: Aldose reductase catalyzes the first step of the polyol pathway, reducing glucose to sorbitol using NADPH — it acts upstream of the reaction in question and does not itself convert sorbitol into fructose.
incorrectas.C: Fructokinase phosphorylates fructose to fructose-1-phosphate as part of fructose metabolism (relevant to essential fructosuria and hereditary fructose intolerance), acting on fructose after it is formed, not catalyzing the sorbitol-to-fructose conversion itself.
incorrectas.D: Hexokinase phosphorylates glucose (and other hexoses) to initiate glycolysis, a different reaction entirely from the polyol pathway's conversion of sorbitol to fructose.

preguntas.q: Which stereoisomeric form of amino acids is found in mammalian proteins?

e.correcta: Mammalian ribosomal protein synthesis exclusively incorporates L-amino acids because the aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases and the ribosomal machinery are stereospecific for the L-configuration, reflecting the evolutionary "choice" of L-amino acids as the building blocks of life. This stereochemical uniformity allows proteins to fold into predictable, functional secondary and tertiary structures; D-amino acids, when they appear (e.g., in some bacterial cell walls or peptide antibiotics), are made by separate non-ribosomal pathways.

incorrectas.A: D-amino acids are found in certain bacterial cell wall peptidoglycans and some non-ribosomal peptide antibiotics, but they are not incorporated into mammalian proteins because the human translational machinery is stereospecific for L-amino acids.
incorrectas.C: Racemic mixtures (equal D and L forms) do not occur in mammalian protein synthesis because the process is enzymatically controlled and stereospecific, not a random chemical reaction that would produce equal proportions of both forms.
incorrectas.D: Meso forms refer to achiral molecules with internal symmetry (relevant to compounds like meso-tartaric acid), a concept that does not apply to the amino acids used in protein synthesis, which are chiral L-forms.

preguntas.q: Which amino acids are the branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs)?

e.correcta: The branched-chain amino acids — valine, leucine, and isoleucine — share a distinctive aliphatic side chain with a branch point, and unlike most amino acids, they are metabolized primarily in skeletal muscle (rather than the liver) via branched-chain aminotransferase and branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase, the latter being the enzyme deficient in maple syrup urine disease. Recognizing this trio matters clinically because BCAA metabolism defects cause a distinct toxic buildup pattern and characteristic sweet-smelling urine in MSUD.

incorrectas.B: Alanine, glycine, and serine are simple, non-branched amino acids involved in gluconeogenesis and one-carbon metabolism — they do not share the branched aliphatic side-chain structure that defines the BCAA group.
incorrectas.C: Lysine, arginine, and histidine are basic amino acids with charged side chains, important in urea cycle and protein modification (e.g., histone methylation for lysine/arginine) — they are chemically and metabolically distinct from BCAAs.
incorrectas.D: Phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan are aromatic amino acids, grouped together because of their ring-containing side chains and shared relevance to neurotransmitter synthesis (dopamine, serotonin) — this is a different classification entirely from the branched-chain group.

preguntas.q: Which amino acids serve as precursors to catecholamines and melanin?

e.correcta: Tyrosine is the direct precursor for catecholamine synthesis: tyrosine hydroxylase converts it to L-DOPA, which is then decarboxylated to dopamine and further hydroxylated/methylated to norepinephrine and epinephrine; tyrosine (via tyrosinase) is also the precursor for melanin in melanocytes. Phenylalanine is upstream of tyrosine, converted to it by phenylalanine hydroxylase, so it feeds into the same pathway (this is why phenylketonuria, a defect in this enzyme, can cause tyrosine deficiency and impaired catecholamine/melanin synthesis). Remembering 'tyrosine to catecholamines and melanin' is a high-yield biochemistry pathway link.

incorrectas.B: Tryptophan is the precursor for serotonin (via tryptophan hydroxylase) and niacin/NAD+, and histidine is the precursor for histamine (via histidine decarboxylase) — both are amino acid precursor pathways, but neither feeds into catecholamine or melanin synthesis, which is tyrosine-specific.
incorrectas.C: Glutamate and aspartate are excitatory neurotransmitters and also urea cycle/nucleotide synthesis intermediates (aspartate contributes nitrogen to the urea cycle and purine/pyrimidine rings), but they do not lie on the pathway to catecholamines or melanin.
incorrectas.D: Lysine and arginine are basic amino acids important for protein structure (e.g., histone lysine residues) and arginine specifically is the substrate for nitric oxide synthase and the urea cycle, but neither contributes to catecholamine or melanin biosynthesis.

preguntas.q: Which amino acid is the precursor to serotonin and niacin?

e.correcta: Tryptophan is converted via the kynurenine pathway partly into niacin (vitamin B3) and via hydroxylation and decarboxylation into serotonin, which is further converted to melatonin. This dual role explains why severe tryptophan or vitamin B6 (a required cofactor) deficiency can contribute to pellagra-like symptoms and mood disturbances, and why conditions like carcinoid syndrome (which divert tryptophan toward serotonin production) can precipitate niacin deficiency due to substrate diversion.

incorrectas.B: Tyrosine is the precursor to catecholamines (dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine) and thyroid hormone, not serotonin or niacin, reflecting a distinct biosynthetic pathway from tryptophan's.
incorrectas.C: Histidine is decarboxylated to histamine, a mediator of allergic and inflammatory responses, but it does not feed into serotonin or niacin synthesis pathways.
incorrectas.D: Glycine is used in porphyrin, purine, and glutathione synthesis among other roles, but it is not a precursor for either serotonin or niacin.

preguntas.q: Which amino acid is the precursor to histamine?

e.correcta: Histamine is synthesized from the amino acid histidine through decarboxylation by the enzyme histidine decarboxylase, a reaction that removes the carboxyl group to yield the biogenic amine histamine, which is then stored in mast cell and basophil granules for release during allergic and inflammatory responses. Recognizing this precursor-product relationship helps connect amino acid metabolism to clinically relevant mediators like histamine's role in type I hypersensitivity reactions.

incorrectas.B: Tryptophan is the precursor to serotonin (via tryptophan hydroxylase and decarboxylation) and subsequently to melatonin and niacin, a distinct biosynthetic pathway from histamine synthesis.
incorrectas.C: Tyrosine is the precursor to the catecholamines (dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine) via tyrosine hydroxylase and subsequent enzymatic steps, as well as to thyroid hormone, none of which involve histamine production.
incorrectas.D: Arginine is the precursor to nitric oxide (via nitric oxide synthase) as well as to creatine and polyamines through other pathways, none of which produce histamine.

preguntas.q: Which two amino acids are negatively charged (acidic) at body pH?

e.correcta: Aspartate and glutamate have side chains containing a carboxylic acid group that is deprotonated (negatively charged) at physiologic pH, making them the two acidic amino acids; they play key roles as excitatory neurotransmitters (glutamate) and in the urea cycle and transamination reactions (aspartate). Their negative charges make them important in forming ionic bonds/salt bridges in protein tertiary structure and in binding positively charged substrates or metal ions.

incorrectas.B: Lysine and arginine are basic (positively charged) amino acids at body pH due to their amine/guanidinium side chains, the opposite charge category from what the question asks about.
incorrectas.C: Serine and threonine are polar, uncharged amino acids with hydroxyl-containing side chains (important for phosphorylation sites), not charged acidic residues.
incorrectas.D: Cysteine and methionine are sulfur-containing amino acids that are nonpolar/neutral at physiologic pH (cysteine's thiol has a high pKa and is largely protonated), not negatively charged acidic residues.

preguntas.q: Which two amino acids are positively charged (basic) at body pH?

e.correcta: Lysine and arginine both carry side chains with amine groups (an epsilon-amino group on lysine and a guanidinium group on arginine) that are protonated and carry a net positive charge at physiologic pH (~7.4), making them basic amino acids (histidine is also basic but has a pKa near 6, so it's often only partially protonated at body pH). This positive charge is functionally important — for example, arginine and lysine residues in histone tails interact electrostatically with the negatively charged phosphate backbone of DNA, helping compact chromatin.

incorrectas.B: Aspartate and glutamate have carboxylic acid side chains that are deprotonated and negatively charged at body pH, making them acidic amino acids — essentially the electrochemical opposite of the basic amino acids the question asks about.
incorrectas.C: Valine and leucine are branched-chain, nonpolar aliphatic amino acids with hydrophobic side chains; they carry no ionizable charge at physiologic pH and are classified by hydrophobicity, not charge.
incorrectas.D: Serine and threonine have polar, uncharged hydroxyl-containing side chains (important for phosphorylation and O-linked glycosylation), but they do not ionize to carry a net charge at body pH the way lysine and arginine do.

preguntas.q: What is the charge of the amino acid histidine at body pH?

e.correcta: Histidine's imidazole side chain has a pKa (~6.0) close to physiologic pH (7.4), meaning at body pH the imidazole ring is predominantly deprotonated and the amino acid carries essentially no net charge, unlike the other basic amino acids (lysine, arginine) whose side chains remain protonated and positively charged at physiologic pH. This near-neutral pKa is exactly why histidine is such an effective physiologic buffer (e.g., in hemoglobin) and why it can act as a general acid/base catalyst in enzyme active sites (e.g., chymotrypsin's catalytic triad).

incorrectas.B: A strongly negative charge at body pH describes acidic amino acids like aspartate and glutamate, whose carboxylic acid side chains have low pKa values and are fully deprotonated (anionic) at physiologic pH — histidine's imidazole group behaves oppositely, being a weak base rather than an acid.
incorrectas.C: A strongly positive charge describes lysine and arginine, whose side chains (amine and guanidinium groups respectively) have pKa values well above 7.4 and are therefore fully protonated and cationic at body pH — histidine's side-chain pKa is much lower, close to neutral pH, so it is not consistently positively charged.
incorrectas.D: All amino acids are zwitterionic at physiologic pH by virtue of their backbone amino and carboxyl groups, but describing histidine's overall charge as 'net negative' is incorrect — the defining feature of histidine is that its side chain's pKa near 6 leaves the overall molecule close to charge-neutral, not net negative.

preguntas.q: Which amino acids are the target residues phosphorylated by protein kinase A and protein kinase C?

e.correcta: Protein kinase A and protein kinase C are serine/threonine kinases, meaning they transfer the gamma-phosphate of ATP onto the hydroxyl group present on the side chains of serine and threonine residues within target proteins. This phosphorylation induces a conformational change that can activate or inhibit the substrate protein's function (e.g., PKA phosphorylating and activating hormone-sensitive lipase in adipocytes, or CREB in gene transcription), forming the molecular basis of second-messenger signaling downstream of cAMP (PKA) and DAG/calcium (PKC).

incorrectas.B: Tyrosine is phosphorylated by a distinct class of enzymes, tyrosine kinases (e.g., receptor tyrosine kinases like the insulin receptor, or non-receptor kinases like JAK), not by PKA/PKC; histidine phosphorylation is a mechanism used mainly in bacterial two-component signaling systems, not typical mammalian PKA/PKC substrates.
incorrectas.C: Lysine and arginine are more commonly sites of other post-translational modifications such as acetylation, methylation, or ubiquitination (on lysine) rather than phosphorylation, since their side chains lack the hydroxyl group needed for a phosphoester bond.
incorrectas.D: Cysteine and methionine contain sulfur-based side chains that undergo modifications like disulfide bond formation or oxidation, not phosphorylation by serine/threonine kinases, since they lack the hydroxyl acceptor group required for this reaction.

preguntas.q: Which amino acids contain sulfur in their side chains?

e.correcta: Cysteine and methionine are the two proteinogenic amino acids containing sulfur: cysteine has a thiol (-SH) group that allows it to form disulfide bonds (critical for tertiary/quaternary protein structure, e.g., in immunoglobulins and keratin), while methionine contains a thioether sulfur and serves as the initiator amino acid for translation (via its role in the start codon AUG) and as a methyl group donor through S-adenosylmethionine (SAM).

incorrectas.B: Serine and threonine are hydroxyl-containing amino acids (not sulfur-containing) important as phosphorylation sites for kinases and in enzyme active sites (e.g., serine proteases), but their side chains contain oxygen, not sulfur.
incorrectas.C: Aspartate and glutamate are acidic amino acids with carboxylic acid side chains that carry a negative charge at physiologic pH, important for enzyme active sites and neurotransmission (glutamate), but they contain no sulfur.
incorrectas.D: Valine and isoleucine are branched-chain aliphatic amino acids with hydrocarbon side chains, important as essential amino acids and energy substrates in muscle, but they lack sulfur entirely.

preguntas.q: Which amino acids are considered essential/required during periods of rapid growth (e.g., in children)?

e.correcta: Arginine and histidine are classified as conditionally (or 'required') essential amino acids during periods of rapid growth, such as childhood, because the endogenous synthetic pathways for these amino acids cannot keep pace with the increased demand for protein synthesis needed for growth, even though adults can typically synthesize adequate amounts endogenously. This distinction matters clinically for pediatric nutrition, where dietary intake of these amino acids becomes necessary to support normal growth.

incorrectas.B: Alanine and glutamine are classic nonessential amino acids that the body readily synthesizes via transamination and glutamine synthetase reactions respectively, and they are not considered conditionally essential during growth.
incorrectas.C: Tyrosine and cysteine are conditionally essential in specific contexts (tyrosine when phenylalanine hydroxylase is deficient as in PKU, cysteine when methionine metabolism is impaired), but they are not the amino acids classically cited as becoming essential during rapid growth — that designation belongs to arginine and histidine.
incorrectas.D: Glycine and serine are nonessential amino acids that are readily interconverted and synthesized from other metabolic intermediates, and are not part of the growth-related conditionally essential amino acid group.

preguntas.q: Which amino acids are purely ketogenic (not glucogenic)?

e.correcta: Leucine and lysine are the only two amino acids that are purely ketogenic, meaning their carbon skeletons are degraded exclusively into acetyl-CoA and/or acetoacetate rather than any glucose precursor (like pyruvate or TCA cycle intermediates), so they cannot contribute to gluconeogenesis. This matters clinically because ketogenic amino acids can be converted to ketone bodies and fatty acids but never to glucose, which is relevant in disorders of amino acid metabolism and in understanding fasting/starvation physiology. A helpful mnemonic is that leucine and lysine are the 'purely ketogenic two' — all other amino acids are either purely glucogenic or mixed.

incorrectas.B: Valine and methionine are purely glucogenic amino acids, metabolized via propionyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA, a TCA cycle intermediate that can feed into gluconeogenesis, the opposite of ketogenic-only metabolism.
incorrectas.C: Alanine and glycine are classic purely glucogenic amino acids, converting directly to pyruvate, which is a major gluconeogenic substrate, making them the opposite category from what the question asks.
incorrectas.D: Aspartate and glutamate are purely glucogenic, entering the TCA cycle as oxaloacetate and α-ketoglutarate respectively, both of which are glucogenic intermediates rather than ketogenic dead-ends.

preguntas.q: Are the essential amino acids methionine, valine, and histidine ketogenic or glucogenic?

e.correcta: Methionine, valine, and histidine are catabolized through pathways that feed exclusively into gluconeogenic intermediates — for example, via propionyl-CoA to methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA (a TCA cycle intermediate that can be converted to oxaloacetate for glucose synthesis) — making them purely glucogenic amino acids. Recognizing which amino acids are purely glucogenic versus ketogenic versus both helps predict how the body manages carbon skeletons during prolonged fasting when amino acid catabolism is diverted toward glucose production.

incorrectas.B: Purely ketogenic describes only lysine and leucine, which generate exclusively acetyl-CoA/acetoacetyl-CoA with no route into gluconeogenesis — methionine, valine, and histidine, by contrast, feed into the TCA cycle for glucose synthesis and are not ketogenic.
incorrectas.C: Both ketogenic and glucogenic describes amino acids like phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan, isoleucine, and threonine, which have carbon skeletons that split into both pathways — methionine, valine, and histidine do not share this dual fate and are purely glucogenic.
incorrectas.D: These amino acids are actively catabolized into central carbon metabolism intermediates (not simply excreted as nitrogen waste); their carbon skeletons are used productively for gluconeogenesis, which is the entire point of classifying them as glucogenic.

preguntas.q: Are the amino acids phenylalanine, isoleucine, threonine, tryptophan, and tyrosine ketogenic, glucogenic, or both?

o.D: Neither, they are only used for protein synthesis

e.correcta: Phenylalanine, isoleucine, threonine, tryptophan, and tyrosine are degraded into intermediates that feed into both gluconeogenic pathways (e.g., via pyruvate or TCA cycle intermediates like fumarate/succinyl-CoA) and ketogenic pathways (via acetyl-CoA or acetoacetate), making them both glucogenic and ketogenic. This dual classification matters because their carbon skeletons can be shunted toward glucose synthesis during fasting or toward ketone body production, depending on the metabolic state, unlike amino acids that feed into only one of these pathways exclusively.

incorrectas.B: Purely ketogenic would mean only lysine and leucine, the only two amino acids that are exclusively ketogenic (yielding only acetyl-CoA/acetoacetyl-CoA with no gluconeogenic intermediates) — the amino acids in this question have mixed metabolic fates, not purely ketogenic ones.
incorrectas.C: Purely glucogenic would apply to amino acids like alanine or glycine, whose breakdown products feed only into gluconeogenesis; the amino acids named here also generate ketogenic intermediates, so classifying them as only glucogenic misses half their metabolic fate.
incorrectas.D: These amino acids are catabolized into central metabolic intermediates for either glucose or ketone body synthesis, not simply reserved for protein synthesis alone — describing them as having no catabolic fate ignores their essential role in intermediary metabolism.

preguntas.q: What happens to the insulin receptor upon insulin binding that leads to activation of its tyrosine kinase activity?

o.C: It is internalized into a coated vesicle immediately

e.correcta: The insulin receptor is a preformed tetramer of two alpha and two beta subunits, but insulin binding to the extracellular alpha subunits induces a conformational change that brings the two intracellular beta subunits (each containing a tyrosine kinase domain) into close proximity, allowing them to trans-autophosphorylate each other on tyrosine residues. This autophosphorylation activates the kinase domains, which then phosphorylate downstream substrates like IRS-1, triggering the PI3K/Akt and MAPK signaling cascades responsible for insulin's metabolic and growth effects. Note the receptor is technically already a dimer of dimers before ligand binding, but functionally the ligand-induced conformational shift that juxtaposes the kinase domains is often summarized as the 'dimerization' step that turns on kinase activity.

incorrectas.B: Proteolytic cleavage is not part of insulin receptor activation; the receptor is activated reversibly through phosphorylation, not through irreversible cleavage of the protein, which would be inconsistent with the receptor's ability to be recycled and reused.
incorrectas.C: Internalization into a coated vesicle does occur with the insulin receptor, but it happens after activation as a means of signal termination and receptor recycling/degradation, not as the initiating step that turns on tyrosine kinase activity.
incorrectas.D: Dissociation into monomeric subunits is the opposite of what happens; insulin binding promotes closer association and conformational coupling of the beta subunits so their kinase domains can trans-phosphorylate each other, not separation into monomers.

preguntas.q: Following binding of insulin receptor substrate 1 (IRS-1) to the insulin receptor, proteins with which domain bind to IRS-1?

e.correcta: Once IRS-1 is tyrosine-phosphorylated after insulin binds its receptor and activates the receptor's intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity, downstream signaling proteins containing SH2 (Src homology 2) domains recognize and bind these phosphotyrosine residues on IRS-1, propagating the signal (e.g., activating PI3K and the Ras/MAPK pathway). This SH2-domain-mediated docking is a general theme in receptor tyrosine kinase signaling, not unique to insulin, and underlies how a single phosphorylated adaptor protein can recruit multiple downstream effectors.

incorrectas.B: PDZ domains mediate protein-protein interactions typically involved in scaffolding proteins at cell junctions and ion channel/receptor clustering, not in binding phosphotyrosine residues on activated signaling adaptors like IRS-1.
incorrectas.C: Death domains are protein-interaction modules found in receptors and adaptors of apoptotic and inflammatory signaling pathways (e.g., TNF receptor, Fas), unrelated to the phosphotyrosine-recognition role needed to bind activated IRS-1.
incorrectas.D: Bromodomains are modules that recognize acetylated lysine residues on histones, relevant to chromatin regulation and gene transcription, not to binding phosphotyrosine sites on cytoplasmic signaling adaptors like IRS-1.

preguntas.q: Which SH2-domain protein, when activated by binding IRS-1, results in translocation of GLUT-4 to the membrane in adipose and muscle tissue?

e.correcta: When insulin binds its receptor, the receptor's tyrosine kinase activity phosphorylates IRS-1, which then recruits and activates PI3 kinase via its SH2 domains; PI3 kinase generates PIP3, activating Akt (PKB), which drives translocation of GLUT-4 transporters to the plasma membrane in adipose and skeletal muscle, allowing glucose uptake. This PI3K/Akt arm is the metabolic signaling branch of the insulin receptor, distinct from the Ras/MAP kinase arm that mediates insulin's growth-promoting effects.

incorrectas.B: Protein kinase A is activated downstream of cAMP-generating GPCRs (e.g., glucagon or epinephrine signaling) and generally opposes insulin's effects by promoting glycogenolysis/lipolysis; it is not part of the IRS-1/GLUT-4 pathway.
incorrectas.C: MAP kinase is activated by the Ras-dependent branch of insulin receptor signaling and mediates insulin's mitogenic/growth effects on gene transcription, not the acute metabolic effect of GLUT-4 translocation.
incorrectas.D: Adenylate cyclase generates cAMP in response to Gs-coupled receptor signaling (e.g., glucagon), which is part of a counter-regulatory pathway to insulin, and has no role in the IRS-1-PI3K-GLUT4 axis.

preguntas.q: Detection of a germline RET oncogene mutation (MEN 2A/2B) warrants which prophylactic procedure?

e.correcta: A germline RET proto-oncogene mutation causes constitutive activation of this receptor tyrosine kinase, driving medullary thyroid carcinoma (arising from calcitonin-secreting parafollicular C cells) with near-100% penetrance in MEN 2A/2B, so prophylactic thyroidectomy is performed—often in early childhood—before malignant transformation can occur. This is a key genotype-phenotype correlation in medicine: unlike most cancer syndromes where surveillance suffices, RET mutation carriers get preemptive organ removal because MTC is aggressive and the mutation's penetrance is so high.

incorrectas.B: Adrenalectomy is reserved for when a pheochromocytoma actually develops (a separate MEN 2 manifestation from adrenal medullary chromaffin cells) — it is not the prophylactic procedure tied directly to the RET mutation itself, since pheochromocytomas are treated when identified rather than removed preemptively in an unaffected gland.
incorrectas.C: Parathyroidectomy addresses the primary hyperparathyroidism seen in MEN 2A (from parathyroid hyperplasia), but this is again a reactive procedure for confirmed disease, not the preemptive, mutation-triggered prophylactic surgery that defines RET-positive management.
incorrectas.D: Pancreatectomy is not part of MEN 2 management at all — pancreatic islet cell tumors are a feature of MEN 1 (associated with MEN1/menin mutations), a genetically and clinically distinct syndrome from the RET-driven MEN 2A/2B.

preguntas.q: Amplification/overexpression of which oncogene is classically associated with neuroblastoma?

e.correcta: N-myc amplification, typically as double minutes or homogeneously staining regions on cytogenetics, is the classic molecular marker of neuroblastoma and correlates strongly with advanced stage and poor prognosis. Because N-myc drives proliferation of the neural crest-derived cells that give rise to neuroblastoma, the degree of amplification is used clinically to risk-stratify patients and guide treatment intensity.

incorrectas.B: C-myc amplification/translocation (t(8;14) placing MYC next to the IgH enhancer) is the hallmark of Burkitt lymphoma, not neuroblastoma — it drives a completely different cell lineage (B lymphocytes) via a different mechanism (chromosomal translocation rather than gene amplification).
incorrectas.C: L-myc overexpression is associated with small cell lung carcinoma, reflecting the tissue-specific expression pattern of myc family members rather than any role in neural crest tumors like neuroblastoma.
incorrectas.D: HER2/neu (ERBB2) amplification is the key oncogenic driver in a subset of breast (and gastric) adenocarcinomas, where it activates a tyrosine kinase growth-signaling pathway — it is unrelated to the myc-family amplification that characterizes neuroblastoma.

preguntas.q: HPV infection is an established risk factor for which subtype(s) of cervical carcinoma?

o.A: Both squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma

e.correcta: High-risk HPV subtypes (especially 16 and 18) produce the E6 and E7 oncoproteins, which inactivate the tumor suppressors p53 and Rb respectively, driving malignant transformation in both squamous epithelium and glandular (endocervical) epithelium of the cervix. Because HPV infects the transformation zone where squamous and columnar epithelium meet, it is causally linked to both squamous cell carcinoma (the more common subtype) and adenocarcinoma, which is why HPV vaccination and screening programs target both histologic types.

incorrectas.B: Restricting HPV's role to only squamous cell carcinoma ignores substantial evidence that the same E6/E7-driven oncogenic mechanism also transforms glandular endocervical cells, producing HPV-associated adenocarcinoma.
incorrectas.C: Restricting HPV's role to only adenocarcinoma is incorrect because squamous cell carcinoma is in fact the more common cervical cancer subtype and is strongly, if not more strongly, associated with high-risk HPV infection.
incorrectas.D: Describing both subtypes as HPV-independent is incorrect; HPV is the dominant driver of cervical carcinogenesis overall, unlike endometrial or ovarian cancers where distinct HPV-independent pathways predominate.

preguntas.q: Which histological finding is classically seen in serous papillary endometrial carcinoma (the sporadic, non-estrogen-driven pathway)?

e.correcta: Serous papillary endometrial carcinoma, the aggressive type II (non-estrogen-driven, p53-mutated) pathway, classically shows psammoma bodies — concentric, laminated calcifications that form within papillary structures, similar to those seen in papillary thyroid carcinoma and ovarian serous tumors. Recognizing psammoma bodies histologically is a classic board association that points toward serous (rather than endometrioid) histology and its typically worse prognosis.

incorrectas.B: Reinke crystals are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions found in Leydig cell tumors of the testis, an entirely different tumor type and organ system, not endometrial carcinoma.
incorrectas.C: Call-Exner bodies are small follicle-like structures containing eosinophilic material seen in granulosa cell tumors of the ovary, not in serous endometrial carcinoma.
incorrectas.D: Auer rods are eosinophilic, needle-shaped cytoplasmic inclusions found in myeloid blasts in acute myeloid leukemia, a hematologic malignancy completely unrelated to endometrial carcinoma histology.

preguntas.q: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is strongly associated with infection by which virus?

e.correcta: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma has one of the strongest associations with EBV of any human cancer, particularly the undifferentiated (non-keratinizing) subtype common in Southeast Asian and North African populations; EBV genome and gene products (like LMP1) are found in tumor cells, driving proliferation and immune evasion. This EBV link is a classic board association, alongside EBV's associations with Burkitt lymphoma and some Hodgkin lymphomas.

incorrectas.B: HPV is strongly associated with cervical, anal, and oropharyngeal (tonsillar/base-of-tongue) squamous cell carcinomas, not nasopharyngeal carcinoma, which has a distinct viral association with EBV.
incorrectas.C: HBV is linked to hepatocellular carcinoma through chronic liver inflammation and cirrhosis, an entirely different organ and mechanism than the EBV-driven lymphoepithelial process in nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
incorrectas.D: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma (and is linked to primary effusion lymphoma and multicentric Castleman disease), not nasopharyngeal carcinoma, which is the EBV-associated malignancy.

preguntas.q: Berylliosis results from prolonged occupational exposure to which agent?

e.correcta: Berylliosis is a granulomatous lung disease caused by chronic occupational inhalation of beryllium dust or fumes, encountered in industries like aerospace, electronics, and nuclear weapons manufacturing. Beryllium acts as a hapten, triggering a cell-mediated (type IV) hypersensitivity response with formation of non-caseating granulomas that closely mimics sarcoidosis both clinically and histologically, which is why occupational history is essential to distinguish the two.

incorrectas.B: Asbestos exposure causes asbestosis (pulmonary fibrosis), pleural plaques, and increased risk of mesothelioma and bronchogenic carcinoma, a distinct fibrotic/neoplastic pattern rather than the granulomatous disease specifically named berylliosis.
incorrectas.C: Silica exposure causes silicosis, characterized by nodular fibrosis predominantly in the upper lung lobes and increased tuberculosis risk, which is a different pneumoconiosis from the hypersensitivity-granuloma pattern of berylliosis.
incorrectas.D: Coal dust exposure causes coal workers' pneumoconiosis (black lung disease), marked by anthracotic pigment-laden macrophages and simple or complicated fibrosis, a separate entity from beryllium-induced granulomatous disease.

preguntas.q: Which radioactive gas is formed by the decay of uranium present in soil?

e.correcta: Radon is a radioactive noble gas produced by the natural decay of uranium-238 present in soil and rock, and it seeps into buildings (especially basements) where inhalation of its decay products deposits alpha-emitting particles in the lung epithelium, causing DNA damage that makes radon the second leading cause of lung cancer after smoking (and the leading cause in non-smokers). This is why home radon testing and mitigation systems are recommended, particularly in regions with uranium-rich soil.

incorrectas.B: Thoron is a related isotope (radon-220) arising from the thorium decay series rather than uranium, and while chemically similar to radon, the question specifically asks about the uranium decay product, which is radon (radon-222) from the uranium-238 series.
incorrectas.C: Argon is a stable, non-radioactive noble gas that makes up about 1% of the atmosphere; it is not a decay product of uranium and carries no radiological cancer risk.
incorrectas.D: Krypton is also a stable, essentially non-radioactive noble gas under normal conditions (aside from trace cosmogenic or fission-product isotopes) and is not the gas produced by uranium decay in soil that drives residential lung cancer risk.

preguntas.q: Radon gas tends to accumulate in which type of location?

e.correcta: Radon gas is a dense, colorless, radioactive noble gas produced by the decay of uranium in soil and rock, and because it is denser than air, it seeps up from the ground and accumulates in poorly ventilated, low-lying enclosed spaces like basements. Chronic radon exposure is the second leading cause of lung cancer after smoking (and the leading cause in nonsmokers), because inhaled radon daughters emit alpha particles that damage bronchial epithelial DNA.

incorrectas.B: Rooftops are open, well-ventilated, elevated spaces where radon (being denser than air and emanating from the ground) would readily dissipate rather than accumulate.
incorrectas.C: Open fields allow radon gas to disperse into the atmosphere due to ventilation and lack of enclosure, so concentrations do not build up to hazardous levels the way they do in enclosed basements.
