incorrectas.D: Kartagener syndrome (primary ciliary dyskinesia) causes chronic sinusitis and can be associated with nasal polyps due to impaired mucociliary clearance, but it is a less classic/common association than aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease in adults and typically also features situs inversus and infertility.

preguntas.q: Which condition is characterized by the triad of asthma, aspirin-induced bronchospasm, and nasal polyps?

e.correcta: Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (classically called Samter's triad) presents with the combination of asthma, aspirin/NSAID-induced bronchospasm, and chronic nasal polyps; the mechanism involves NSAID inhibition of the COX pathway, which shunts arachidonic acid metabolism toward the lipoxygenase pathway and overproduction of bronchoconstrictive, pro-inflammatory leukotrienes. Recognizing this triad matters clinically because these patients must avoid aspirin/NSAIDs and may benefit from leukotriene receptor antagonists.

incorrectas.B: Churg-Strauss syndrome (eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis) does feature asthma and sometimes sinus/nasal involvement, but it is a systemic ANCA-associated vasculitis with eosinophilia, pulmonary infiltrates, and multi-organ involvement (e.g., neuropathy, cardiac disease) — it is a distinct disease from the COX-inhibition-driven triad described, not simply another name for it.
incorrectas.C: This option's phrasing is essentially self-contradictory and non-standard — the eponym for this exact triad is Samter's triad (aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease), not a variant of 'allergic rhinitis,' which is a separate, IgE-mediated condition without the aspirin-sensitivity component.
incorrectas.D: Loeffler syndrome is a transient pulmonary eosinophilia typically triggered by parasitic larval migration (e.g., Ascaris) through the lungs, causing cough and eosinophilic infiltrates — it has no relationship to aspirin sensitivity, asthma, or nasal polyps.

preguntas.q: What are benign tumors of the nasal mucosa composed of large blood vessels and fibrous tissue called?

e.correcta: Angiofibromas of the nasal mucosa (juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibromas) are benign tumors composed of a proliferation of thin-walled blood vessels within a fibrous stroma, classically occurring in adolescent males and presenting with profuse epistaxis and nasal obstruction due to their vascularity and location. Their rich vascular supply (often from the internal maxillary artery) makes them prone to significant bleeding, which is why biopsy is generally avoided and imaging/embolization plus surgical excision are preferred. The name itself reflects the dual tissue composition: 'angio' for vessels and 'fibroma' for the fibrous tissue component.

incorrectas.B: Nasal polyps are inflammatory, edematous outgrowths of sinonasal mucosa (often associated with chronic rhinosinusitis, allergies, aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, or cystic fibrosis), composed of loose stroma with inflammatory cells, not a proliferation of blood vessels and fibrous tissue as described.
incorrectas.C: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a malignant epithelial tumor strongly associated with EBV infection, particularly in Southern Chinese populations, and is a cancer rather than a benign vascular/fibrous growth, making it histologically and biologically distinct from the tumor described.
incorrectas.D: Hemangiomas of the skin are benign vascular proliferations, but they occur in cutaneous tissue rather than the nasal mucosa and typically lack the significant fibrous stromal component that defines an angiofibroma, so they don't match the described histology or location.

preguntas.q: Which demographic is classically associated with angiofibroma?

e.correcta: Angiofibroma (nasopharyngeal angiofibroma) classically occurs in adolescent males, a demographic pattern thought to reflect hormonal influences (androgen receptor expression in the tumor stroma) on this highly vascular, benign but locally aggressive tumor arising near the sphenopalatine foramen. It classically presents with epistaxis and nasal obstruction in a teenage boy, and its marked vascularity means biopsy is generally avoided due to bleeding risk, with imaging and sometimes preoperative embolization guiding management instead.

incorrectas.B: Elderly females is not the demographic associated with angiofibroma; this age/sex pattern is more relevant to other head and neck conditions like giant cell arteritis, not to the hormonally-influenced, adolescent-male-predominant angiofibroma.
incorrectas.C: Young children of either sex is not the classic angiofibroma demographic — the tumor's association with pubertal hormonal changes specifically points to adolescent males rather than younger, prepubertal children of either sex.
incorrectas.D: Middle-aged smokers are the classic demographic for tobacco-related head and neck squamous cell carcinomas, a completely different tumor type and etiology from the benign, hormonally-associated vascular tumor of adolescent males.

preguntas.q: Nasopharyngeal angiofibromas often present with profuse occurrence of which symptom?

e.correcta: Nasopharyngeal angiofibromas are highly vascular benign tumors, classically occurring in adolescent males, and their dense network of thin-walled, poorly supported blood vessels within the tumor stroma makes them prone to profuse, often recurrent epistaxis, which is typically the presenting symptom that prompts imaging and diagnosis. This vascularity also makes biopsy risky (due to hemorrhage risk), so diagnosis is often made by characteristic imaging rather than tissue sampling.

incorrectas.B: Hemoptysis refers to coughing up blood from the lower respiratory tract, which is not the expected presentation of a nasopharyngeal mass — the bleeding source in angiofibroma is the nasal/nasopharyngeal vasculature, presenting as epistaxis, not hemoptysis.
incorrectas.C: Otorrhea (ear discharge) would suggest a middle ear or external auditory canal process, not a nasopharyngeal vascular tumor, which more directly involves the nasal cavity and produces nasal bleeding rather than ear symptoms.
incorrectas.D: Dysphagia can occur with large masses obstructing the nasopharynx/oropharynx, but it is not the hallmark presenting symptom of angiofibroma — the defining and most profuse symptom relates directly to the tumor's vascularity causing epistaxis.

preguntas.q: What is the malignant tumor arising from nasopharyngeal epithelium called?

e.correcta: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a malignant tumor of nasopharyngeal epithelial cells, strongly associated with EBV infection and endemic in Southern China and Southeast Asia; it classically presents with cervical lymphadenopathy, epistaxis, or nasal obstruction. Histologically it is typically a poorly differentiated (nonkeratinizing) squamous cell carcinoma, and biopsy showing EBV-positive tumor cells is a key diagnostic clue tested on exams.

incorrectas.B: Angiofibroma is a benign, highly vascular tumor arising in the nasopharynx of adolescent males, presenting with epistaxis, but it is benign (not malignant) and not epithelial-derived malignancy like NPC.
incorrectas.C: Nasal polyps are benign inflammatory growths of edematous mucosa, commonly linked to chronic rhinosinusitis, allergies, cystic fibrosis, or aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease — they are not neoplastic or malignant.
incorrectas.D: Laryngeal papilloma is a benign HPV-associated squamous papilloma of the larynx (vocal cords), not the nasopharynx, and is benign rather than malignant.

preguntas.q: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma often presents with involvement of which lymph nodes?

e.correcta: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma, strongly associated with EBV infection and common in Southeast Asian populations, frequently presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy because the nasopharynx drains lymphatically to the cervical (neck) lymph node chains — often the neck mass is the presenting complaint before the primary nasopharyngeal lesion itself is noticed. Recognizing this lymphatic drainage pattern is key to working up an EBV-associated neck mass and considering nasopharyngeal carcinoma in the differential.

incorrectas.B: Axillary lymph nodes drain the upper limb, breast, and thoracic wall, not the nasopharynx — this drainage territory is anatomically unrelated to the head and neck region where nasopharyngeal carcinoma arises.
incorrectas.C: Inguinal lymph nodes drain the lower limbs, external genitalia, and perineum, which have no lymphatic connection to the nasopharynx, making this an anatomically implausible presentation site for this cancer.
incorrectas.D: Mediastinal lymph nodes drain thoracic structures such as the lungs and esophagus; while some deep cervical nodes can communicate with the thoracic duct system, mediastinal nodes are not the classic first-echelon nodes for nasopharyngeal carcinoma the way cervical nodes are.

preguntas.q: What is the most common cause of acute epiglottitis, especially in non-immunized children?

e.correcta: Haemophilus influenzae type B is the classic cause of acute epiglottitis in unvaccinated children, producing a rapidly progressive, life-threatening cellulitis of the epiglottis and surrounding supraglottic structures that can cause airway obstruction — presenting with high fever, drooling, dysphagia, and a 'tripod' positioning to maximize airway patency. Widespread Hib vaccination has made this presentation rare in immunized populations, which is why exam questions specifically flag 'non-immunized' children as the at-risk group.

incorrectas.B: Streptococcus pyogenes can cause pharyngitis and other invasive infections but is not the classic causative organism of epiglottitis; it's more associated with strep throat, scarlet fever, and rheumatic complications.
incorrectas.C: Parainfluenza virus is the classic cause of croup (laryngotracheobronchitis), which produces a barky cough and stridor from subglottic narrowing (the 'steeple sign' on X-ray) — a distinct, generally less acutely dangerous condition than epiglottitis.
incorrectas.D: Staphylococcus aureus can occasionally cause epiglottitis or tracheitis, particularly bacterial tracheitis with a 'straight sign' and purulent secretions, but it is not the classic and most common cause in non-immunized children — that is H. influenzae type B.

preguntas.q: Acute epiglottitis may present with a muffled voice and what type of respiratory sound?

e.correcta: Acute epiglottitis, most classically caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b in unvaccinated children (though now also seen in adults), causes rapid inflammatory swelling of the epiglottis and supraglottic structures. Because the obstruction is at or above the larynx (an extrathoracic, upper airway lesion), turbulent airflow during inspiration produces a high-pitched inspiratory stridor, and the swollen supraglottic tissues muffle the voice, producing the classic 'hot potato voice.' This is a medical emergency because further swelling can completely occlude the airway, so the mnemonic '3 Ds' — drooling, dysphagia, distress — plus stridor should prompt immediate airway management rather than throat exam.

incorrectas.B: Expiratory wheeze is the hallmark of lower airway/intrathoracic obstruction (e.g., asthma, bronchiolitis) where airways narrow further during the forced expiratory phase, not a supraglottic process like epiglottitis, which obstructs during inspiration instead.
incorrectas.C: A pleural friction rub is heard with pleural inflammation (e.g., pleuritis from pneumonia or pulmonary embolism), a completely different anatomic location from the upper airway swelling seen in epiglottitis, and would not explain a muffled voice.
incorrectas.D: Crackles (rales) reflect fluid or secretions in the alveoli or small airways, as in pneumonia, pulmonary edema, or fibrosis, which is a parenchymal/alveolar finding rather than the upper-airway extrathoracic obstruction that characterizes epiglottitis.

preguntas.q: Acute epiglottitis carries a risk of which life-threatening acute complication?

e.correcta: Acute epiglottitis, classically caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b (though now more common from other organisms post-vaccination), causes rapid, severe swelling of the epiglottis and surrounding supraglottic tissue that can occlude the airway with little warning, especially in children who present with drooling, stridor, and a 'tripod' positioning. This risk of sudden complete airway obstruction is why epiglottitis is a medical emergency requiring careful airway management (often in a controlled setting like the OR) rather than direct visualization with a tongue depressor, which can precipitate laryngospasm and obstruction.

incorrectas.B: Pneumothorax results from air entering the pleural space (e.g., from trauma, bleb rupture, or barotrauma), a mechanically distinct process from the localized supraglottic swelling of epiglottitis, which threatens the airway lumen rather than the pleural space.
incorrectas.C: Pulmonary embolism arises from venous thromboembolism traveling to the pulmonary vasculature, an unrelated process to the local inflammatory swelling of the epiglottis, and is not the emergent complication classically linked to epiglottitis.
incorrectas.D: Cardiac tamponade results from fluid accumulation compressing the heart within the pericardium, a cardiovascular emergency with no direct relationship to epiglottic swelling narrowing the upper airway, which is the actual life-threatening mechanism in epiglottitis.

preguntas.q: What is the most common cause of laryngotracheobronchitis (croup)?

e.correcta: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) is most commonly caused by parainfluenza virus, which infects the upper airway and causes subglottic edema, producing the classic barking ('seal-like') cough, inspiratory stridor, and hoarseness typically seen in children 6 months to 3 years old. The 'steeple sign' on frontal neck X-ray reflects this subglottic narrowing and is a classically tested radiographic correlate of parainfluenza-driven airway inflammation.

incorrectas.B: Haemophilus influenzae type B is the classic cause of epiglottitis, a more rapidly progressive and dangerous condition involving supraglottic swelling with high fever and drooling, distinct from the more indolent, viral croup syndrome caused by parainfluenza.
incorrectas.C: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is the most common cause of bronchiolitis in infants, characterized by wheezing and lower airway obstruction, rather than the barking cough and subglottic narrowing typical of parainfluenza-driven croup.
incorrectas.D: Rhinovirus is the most frequent cause of the common cold (upper respiratory infection) and can trigger asthma exacerbations, but it is not the predominant etiologic agent identified in classic croup presentations.

preguntas.q: Combining dextromethorphan with other serotonergic agents (e.g., SSRIs, MAOIs) puts a patient at risk for which condition?

e.correcta: Dextromethorphan, despite being an over-the-counter antitussive, has significant serotonergic activity as a serotonin reuptake inhibitor at higher doses, so combining it with other serotonergic drugs like SSRIs or MAOIs can cause an excessive accumulation of serotonin at central and peripheral synapses. This produces serotonin syndrome, characterized by the classic triad of altered mental status, autonomic instability (hyperthermia, diaphoresis, tachycardia), and neuromuscular abnormalities (clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor), and it is a key reason patients on MAOIs are warned to avoid common cough medicines. Recognizing this interaction is important because serotonin syndrome can be life-threatening and requires prompt discontinuation of the offending agents plus supportive care (and cyproheptadine in severe cases).

incorrectas.B: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome results from dopamine receptor blockade (typically by antipsychotics) or abrupt dopaminergic withdrawal, a completely different mechanism from the serotonergic excess caused by combining dextromethorphan with SSRIs/MAOIs.
incorrectas.C: Malignant hyperthermia is a genetic disorder of the ryanodine receptor triggered by volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine, causing uncontrolled calcium release in skeletal muscle — unrelated to serotonergic drug combinations.
incorrectas.D: Anticholinergic toxicity arises from blockade of muscarinic receptors (e.g., by antihistamines, TCAs) producing dry mouth, mydriasis, urinary retention, and delirium, a distinct clinical picture from the serotonergic excess and neuromuscular findings of serotonin syndrome caused by this drug combination.

preguntas.q: What is the first-line treatment for nocturnal enuresis (bedwetting) in children?

e.correcta: Nocturnal enuresis in children is first managed with behavioral/motivational interventions such as star charts, bedwetting alarms, and reassurance, because most cases resolve spontaneously with maturation of bladder control and reinforcement of dry-night behavior carries no risk. This conservative approach also avoids exposing a child to medication side effects for a condition that is, in most cases, self-limited before treating it pharmacologically. Only when behavioral therapy fails after an adequate trial do clinicians move to pharmacologic options like desmopressin.

incorrectas.B: Desmopressin (a vasopressin analog that reduces nocturnal urine volume) is an effective second-line option once behavioral measures have failed or for short-term use (e.g., sleepovers), but it is not first-line because it doesn't address the underlying maturational delay and enuresis often recurs when the drug is stopped.
incorrectas.C: Imipramine, a tricyclic antidepressant, was historically used for enuresis and can reduce bedwetting, but its cardiotoxicity in overdose and side-effect profile make it a later-line option reserved for refractory cases, not initial therapy.
incorrectas.D: Bladder augmentation surgery is an invasive intervention reserved for severe, anatomically or neurologically driven bladder dysfunction (e.g., neurogenic bladder), and is never indicated for typical primary nocturnal enuresis, which is overwhelmingly a benign developmental issue.

preguntas.q: Long-term infant deprivation of affection classically results in failure to do what?

e.correcta: Chronic deprivation of affection and stimulation in infancy classically produces failure to thrive, characterized by poor weight gain, developmental delay, and sometimes a withdrawn, apathetic affect, as originally described in institutionalized infants with minimal caregiver interaction (e.g., Harlow's and Spitz's studies on maternal deprivation). This occurs even when caloric intake is adequate, underscoring that emotional and social stimulation is a biological necessity for normal growth, not simply nutrition. The concept underlies why attachment and consistent caregiving are considered essential developmental inputs, not just emotional nice-to-haves.

incorrectas.B: Failure to ambulate (delayed walking) can occur with severe global neglect, but the classic, most specific consequence taught for affective deprivation is failure to thrive (growth failure), not an isolated motor milestone delay.
incorrectas.C: Failure to wean is not the classic finding associated with deprivation; weaning delay is not typically the highlighted consequence in descriptions of maternal/affective deprivation syndromes.
incorrectas.D: Temperature regulation is a basic physiologic function not classically disrupted by emotional deprivation in the way growth and developmental trajectory are; this option does not match the well-described failure-to-thrive phenomenon.

preguntas.q: Long-term infant deprivation of affection may result in poor development of which skills?

e.correcta: Long-term affective deprivation impairs the social and linguistic stimulation infants need to develop normal language and socialization skills, since these domains depend heavily on reciprocal caregiver interaction (talking, responding to cues, modeling social behavior) rather than purely innate maturation. Classic studies of institutionalized children showed marked delays specifically in language acquisition and social engagement (e.g., poor eye contact, lack of stranger anxiety, delayed speech) when caregiver interaction was minimal, even when physical needs were met.

incorrectas.B: Fine motor skills (e.g., pincer grasp, using utensils) develop largely through physical practice and maturation of neuromuscular control, and are not the domain classically highlighted as most affected by emotional/social deprivation.
incorrectas.C: Gross motor skills (e.g., sitting, walking) also depend more on neuromuscular maturation than on social interaction, and while severe global neglect can delay them, the specific deficit emphasized in deprivation syndromes is language/social skill impairment.
incorrectas.D: Visual-spatial skills relate to parietal lobe function and are not the classic domain of impairment described in maternal/affective deprivation; the well-documented deficits are in language and social/emotional development.

preguntas.q: Long-term infant deprivation of affection may result in a lack of what fundamental psychological attribute?

e.correcta: According to Erikson's psychosocial stages, the earliest developmental task of infancy is establishing basic trust versus mistrust, which depends on consistent, responsive caregiving that teaches the infant the world is safe and their needs will be met. Chronic deprivation of affection and consistent caregiving during this critical period (as classically illustrated by studies of institutionalized/neglected infants) impairs the formation of this basic trust, predisposing to attachment disorders and difficulty forming secure relationships later in life.

incorrectas.B: Object permanence is a cognitive milestone from Piaget's sensorimotor stage (understanding that objects continue to exist when out of sight), a distinct cognitive-developmental concept from the socioemotional attachment deficit caused by affection deprivation.
incorrectas.C: Self-esteem develops later in childhood and adolescence through mastery experiences and social feedback (related to Erikson's later stages like industry vs. inferiority), not as the immediate consequence of infantile affection deprivation, which is specifically linked to trust formation.
incorrectas.D: Autonomy versus shame/doubt is Erikson's second stage, occurring in toddlerhood (roughly ages 1-3) around independence and self-control, which follows and depends on the more fundamental trust established in infancy — the stage actually impaired here.

preguntas.q: Severe, long-term infant deprivation of affection can lead to which named disorder, in which the infant is emotionally withdrawn and unresponsive to comfort?

e.correcta: Reactive attachment disorder arises from severe early neglect or deprivation of a consistent caregiver, and manifests as an inhibited, emotionally withdrawn child who rarely seeks or responds to comfort even when distressed, reflecting a failure to form a normal attachment bond during a critical developmental window. This distinguishes it from typical stranger anxiety or shyness, and the key diagnostic requirement is a documented history of grossly inadequate caregiving (e.g., institutionalization, repeated changes in caregivers, or neglect) alongside the persistent social/emotional withdrawal pattern.

incorrectas.B: Disinhibited social engagement disorder arises from the same kind of neglectful caregiving history, but the behavioral phenotype is the opposite of withdrawal: the child is indiscriminately, overly familiar with unfamiliar adults, showing no normal wariness of strangers, rather than being emotionally shut down and unresponsive to comfort.
incorrectas.C: Autism spectrum disorder involves impaired social communication and restricted/repetitive behaviors that are present from early development independent of caregiving quality (it is a neurodevelopmental disorder, not caused by deprivation), which is a fundamentally different etiology than the deprivation-driven attachment disorders.
incorrectas.D: Separation anxiety disorder is excessive fear or distress specifically about separation from an attachment figure, which actually implies the child HAS formed an attachment and is anxious about losing it, the opposite of the failure to form attachment seen in reactive attachment disorder.

preguntas.q: Infant deprivation lasting longer than approximately how long can lead to irreversible developmental changes?

e.correcta: Classic developmental teaching (based on studies of institutionalized and deprived infants) holds that deprivation of affection and stimulation lasting longer than about 6 months can produce irreversible cognitive, social, and emotional deficits, reflecting a critical/sensitive period in early brain development during which attachment and environmental input shape neural circuitry. Shorter periods of deprivation are more likely to be followed by recovery if a nurturing environment is subsequently provided, which is why early identification and intervention in cases of neglect are emphasized clinically.

incorrectas.B: Two weeks is far shorter than the threshold associated with irreversible changes; brief separations of this duration are generally followed by recovery once normal caregiving resumes, unlike prolonged deprivation.
incorrectas.C: One month, like two weeks, falls below the roughly 6-month threshold classically cited for irreversible developmental damage, so deprivation of this duration is more consistent with reversible effects.
incorrectas.D: Two years substantially overshoots the classically cited 6-month threshold; while longer deprivation certainly worsens prognosis, the teaching point is that irreversibility risk begins around 6 months, not that it requires two full years.

preguntas.q: What is the most severe possible outcome of severe infant deprivation?

e.correcta: Severe infant deprivation (profound neglect of physical, emotional, and social needs) can produce a syndrome sometimes called 'failure to thrive' or reactive attachment issues, and in its most extreme, prolonged form can lead to death — historically documented in institutionalized infants deprived of caregiving (as in Rene Spitz's studies of 'hospitalism'), where mortality rates were markedly elevated due to a combination of failure to thrive, susceptibility to infection, and lack of stimulation necessary for basic physiologic and psychological development. This illustrates why early attachment and caregiving are considered essential, not just for emotional development, but for basic survival in infancy.

incorrectas.B: Chronic constipation is not the severe, life-threatening endpoint associated with profound infant deprivation — while gastrointestinal dysfunction can occur with severe neglect, it is not the 'most severe possible outcome' this question is testing.
incorrectas.C: Precocious puberty is an endocrine disorder of early pubertal onset, unrelated to the failure-to-thrive/mortality risk described in classic studies of infant deprivation and is not a recognized consequence of caregiver neglect in this context.
incorrectas.D: Hyperactivity disorder describes a behavioral/attentional condition that can be associated with various developmental disruptions, but it is not the most severe, potentially fatal outcome historically linked to profound early deprivation, which is death.

preguntas.q: Which finding on physical exam, especially rib fractures or spiral long-bone fractures in different stages of healing, is classic evidence of child physical abuse?

e.correcta: Rib fractures (especially posterior ones, which require significant direct force rarely caused by accidental trauma) and spiral long-bone fractures (caused by twisting forces inconsistent with a young child's own mobility) occurring in multiple stages of healing indicate repeated episodes of trauma over time rather than a single accidental event. This pattern — injuries of different ages that don't match the reported mechanism or the child's developmental ability — is the classic radiographic red flag prompting mandatory reporting for suspected non-accidental trauma.

incorrectas.B: Dislocations are less specific for abuse and are not the classic finding cited in this context; the teaching point centers on fracture patterns and healing stages, not joint dislocations.
incorrectas.C: Osteoporosis is a condition of reduced bone density typically seen in the elderly or with chronic disease/steroid use, and is not a mechanism or finding associated with child abuse; it would actually be an alternative explanation to rule out before diagnosing abuse (e.g., osteogenesis imperfecta mimics).
incorrectas.D: Growth plate widening suggests a metabolic or nutritional process such as rickets, not trauma, and is a distractor that should prompt consideration of a differential rather than supporting a diagnosis of abuse.

preguntas.q: Which skin finding, especially on the trunk, ears, or neck, or in a pattern resembling an implement, suggests child physical abuse?

e.correcta: Bruises in unusual locations such as the trunk, ears, buttocks, or neck — areas not typically injured during normal childhood play (which usually produces bruises over bony prominences like shins and knees) — or bruises that reproduce the shape of an object (a belt buckle, cord loop, or hand print) are highly suspicious for inflicted trauma. Recognizing these patterned or atypically located injuries is a core skill for identifying non-accidental trauma, since accidental bruising in mobile children clusters over bony, exposed areas rather than protected soft-tissue regions.

incorrectas.B: Petechiae are pinpoint hemorrhages from thrombocytopenia, vasculitis, or increased venous pressure (e.g., from strangulation or severe coughing); while petechiae from strangulation can indicate abuse, the classic patterned/implement-shaped, atypically located finding described here is bruising, not petechiae as a general category.
incorrectas.C: Vitiligo is an autoimmune depigmentation disorder with a well-demarcated, patchy loss of melanocytes, entirely unrelated to trauma and not a marker of abuse.
incorrectas.D: Café-au-lait spots are congenital pigmented macules associated with neurofibromatosis and McCune-Albright syndrome; they are present from a benign genetic/developmental cause and have no relationship to inflicted injury.

preguntas.q: Which type of skin injury, such as from a cigarette or located on the buttocks/thighs, is classic evidence of child physical abuse?

e.correcta: Burns with patterned shapes (such as circular cigarette burns) or in unusual, non-accidental locations (buttocks, thighs, or stocking/glove-distribution immersion burns) are classic red flags for physical abuse because these areas are not typically exposed to accidental burn mechanisms during normal childhood activity, and patterned or sharply demarcated burns suggest deliberate contact with a hot object or forced immersion. Recognizing these patterns is a key clinical skill for identifying non-accidental trauma and triggering mandatory reporting.

incorrectas.B: Lacerations can occur in abuse but are not the classic pattern-specific finding highlighted in child abuse teaching the way patterned burns are; lacerations lack the same diagnostic specificity of shape and location that make burns so recognizable as abuse indicators.
incorrectas.C: Abrasions are common accidental injuries in active children (scraped knees, elbows) and, without a distinctive pattern or unusual location, do not carry the same specific association with abuse that patterned burns do.
incorrectas.D: Ulcers are typically associated with chronic conditions like pressure injuries, vascular insufficiency, or infection rather than acute inflicted trauma, so they are not the classic abuse indicator being tested here.

preguntas.q: Children who are victims of physical abuse often display what behavior on exam?

o.D: Increased physical affection toward the examiner

e.correcta: Children who have suffered physical abuse frequently exhibit avoidance of eye contact along with other signs of hypervigilance, withdrawal, or fearfulness around caregivers and examiners, reflecting a learned association between adult proximity and threat or unpredictable punishment. Recognizing these behavioral cues alongside physical findings (bruising in unusual locations, fractures inconsistent with the stated mechanism, or injuries at different healing stages) is part of the clinical gestalt that should prompt further evaluation for abuse. This behavioral withdrawal is a well-documented marker used in child abuse screening and forensic interviewing.

incorrectas.B: Excessive eye contact is not the classic abuse-related behavior; abused children more typically avoid direct gaze as a protective, hypervigilant response rather than seeking it out.
incorrectas.C: Hyperverbal speech is not a recognized behavioral marker of physical abuse; abused children are more often withdrawn or guarded in their communication rather than unusually talkative.
incorrectas.D: Increased physical affection toward an unfamiliar examiner is atypical and more consistent with indiscriminate attachment behaviors seen in some neglect or institutionalization scenarios, not the guarded avoidance typical of physical abuse victims.

preguntas.q: In cases of child physical abuse, the abuser is usually which individual?

e.correcta: In cases of child physical abuse, the perpetrator is most commonly a biological parent, and specifically the biological mother is statistically the most frequent abuser, often reflecting that mothers are frequently the primary caregiver and spend the most unsupervised time with the child, compounded by risk factors such as caregiver stress, mental illness, substance abuse, or lack of social support. This epidemiologic pattern is clinically important because it reminds physicians that abuse is far more often perpetrated by a trusted caregiver within the home than by an unfamiliar outsider, which shapes how child abuse is screened for and reported.

incorrectas.B: A stranger is actually an uncommon perpetrator of child physical abuse; the epidemiology consistently shows that abuse is overwhelmingly committed by a familiar caregiver in the home rather than an unrelated outsider.
incorrectas.C: A teacher is not the typical perpetrator profile in child physical abuse statistics; while abuse by non-family caregivers or authority figures does occur, it is far less common than abuse by a parent within the household.
incorrectas.D: An older sibling can occasionally be involved in child maltreatment, but this is not the demographic most classically and statistically identified as the primary abuser in child physical abuse, which points instead to a parent, especially the mother.

preguntas.q: Approximately 40% of deaths related to child abuse or neglect occur in children younger than what age?

e.correcta: Approximately 40% of fatal child abuse and neglect cases occur in children younger than 1 year old, reflecting the profound vulnerability of infants who cannot escape or report abuse, combined with their fragility to trauma (e.g., abusive head trauma/shaken baby syndrome causing fatal intracranial hemorrhage). This statistic underscores why clinicians maintain a particularly high index of suspicion for non-accidental trauma in infants presenting with unexplained injuries or altered mental status.

incorrectas.B: 3 years old is an older age group with a lower proportion of abuse-related fatalities compared to infants under 1 year, since mobility and non-verbal reporting capacity, while still limited, are somewhat improved.
incorrectas.C: 5 years old represents an even lower-risk age bracket for abuse fatality compared to infancy — most fatal abuse cases cluster in the youngest, most vulnerable, pre-verbal children.
incorrectas.D: 10 years old is well outside the age range where the highest proportion of fatal child abuse occurs; children this age are more able to seek help, and fatal abuse incidence drops substantially compared to infancy.

preguntas.q: Genital, anal, or oral trauma in a child is evidence of which type of abuse?

e.correcta: Physical findings such as trauma to the genital, anal, or oral regions in a child are classic red flags for sexual abuse, since these areas do not sustain trauma through normal childhood activity or accidental injury. Clinicians are trained to recognize such findings (along with STIs in a prepubertal child, or precocious sexualized behavior) as indications requiring further evaluation and mandatory reporting.

incorrectas.B: Physical abuse typically presents with bruises in various stages of healing, fractures inconsistent with the reported mechanism (e.g., spiral fractures in a non-ambulatory infant), or patterned injuries (belt marks, cigarette burns) rather than genital/anal/oral trauma specifically.
incorrectas.C: Emotional abuse involves verbal degradation, rejection, or terrorizing a child and leaves no physical findings at all, so it cannot be diagnosed from genital, anal, or oral trauma.
incorrectas.D: Medical neglect refers to failure to provide necessary medical care (e.g., withholding needed treatment or vaccinations), which presents as untreated illness or missed care, not as localized trauma to the genital or oral regions.

preguntas.q: The perpetrator of child sexual abuse is usually which of the following?

o.A: A male known to the victim
o.D: A female known to the victim

e.correcta: Child sexual abuse is most commonly perpetrated by a male who is known to the victim — such as a family member, family friend, or other trusted acquaintance — rather than a stranger, which reflects the reality that abuse typically exploits a position of trust and access rather than opportunistic contact with an unknown assailant. This epidemiologic pattern is clinically important because it shapes screening and prevention strategies, emphasizing that 'stranger danger' education addresses a much less common scenario than abuse by someone already inside the child's circle of trust.

incorrectas.B: A female stranger is a rare profile for child sexual abuse; perpetrators are overwhelmingly male, and the relationship to the victim is typically one of familiarity and trust rather than an anonymous encounter.
incorrectas.C: A male stranger, while possible, is far less common than a male known to the victim; most abuse occurs within existing relationships (family, family friends, caregivers) where the perpetrator has ongoing access to the child.
incorrectas.D: A female known to the victim describes a real but statistically much less frequent perpetrator profile compared to a male known to the victim, who represents the overwhelming majority of documented cases.

preguntas.q: What is the peak age incidence for child sexual abuse?

e.correcta: Epidemiologic data on child sexual abuse show the peak incidence occurs between roughly 9 and 12 years of age, a period when children may be more accessible to and less able to resist or report abuse by a trusted adult, but are still developmentally naive; recognizing this peak age helps guide screening and index of suspicion in clinical and forensic evaluation of at-risk children.

incorrectas.B: Ages 0-2 years are actually the peak age range for child physical abuse and abusive head trauma (shaken baby syndrome), not sexual abuse, reflecting the vulnerability of infants to caregiver frustration rather than the pattern seen with sexual abuse.
incorrectas.C: Ages 3-5 years, while a period during which some sexual abuse does occur and disclosure can be complicated by limited verbal ability, is not the epidemiologically identified peak incidence window, which occurs later in the 9-12 year range.
incorrectas.D: Ages 15-17 years fall outside the documented peak incidence window for child sexual abuse; abuse in older adolescents does occur but the epidemiologic peak specifically clusters earlier, around 9-12 years.

preguntas.q: Failure to provide a child with adequate food, shelter, supervision, education, and/or affection is defined as what?

e.correcta: Child neglect is defined as the failure to provide a child's basic needs — adequate food, shelter, supervision, education, medical care, and/or emotional affection — regardless of whether this is due to intentional withholding or parental incapacity (e.g., poverty, mental illness, substance use). It is actually the most common form of child maltreatment reported in the US, and recognizing it matters clinically because it often presents subtly (failure to thrive, poor hygiene, missed vaccinations/appointments) rather than with the overt physical signs seen in abuse.

incorrectas.B: Child physical abuse involves the intentional infliction of physical injury (bruises in unusual patterns/locations, fractures inconsistent with the reported mechanism, burns), which is an act of commission rather than the omission of basic needs described in this question.
incorrectas.C: Child sexual abuse involves engaging a child in sexual activity that the child cannot legally or developmentally consent to, which is a distinct category of maltreatment unrelated to failure to provide food, shelter, or supervision.
incorrectas.D: Munchausen syndrome by proxy (factitious disorder imposed on another) is a specific and rarer form of abuse in which a caregiver fabricates or induces illness in a child for attention, which is a different mechanism entirely from simply failing to meet the child's basic needs.

preguntas.q: What is the mathematical relationship expressed by prevalence / (1 - prevalence)?

o.D: Positive predictive value / negative predictive value

e.correcta: The expression prevalence / (1 - prevalence) mathematically equals incidence multiplied by the average duration of disease, a relationship that holds in steady-state populations where the disease is neither rapidly increasing nor decreasing in frequency. This formula highlights that prevalence is a function of both how many new cases arise (incidence) and how long people remain diseased (duration) — a chronic, slowly fatal disease can have high prevalence despite modest incidence, while a highly lethal but short-duration illness may have low prevalence despite substantial incidence.

incorrectas.B: Sensitivity and specificity are properties of a diagnostic test's ability to correctly identify true positives and true negatives, respectively; their product has no established equivalence to the prevalence odds formula, which instead relates to disease frequency and duration.
incorrectas.C: Relative risk and attributable risk are measures used in cohort studies to quantify the strength of association and excess risk attributable to an exposure; their product is not the mathematical identity represented by prevalence/(1-prevalence).
incorrectas.D: Positive predictive value and negative predictive value are test performance measures that depend on prevalence and test characteristics, but their ratio is not equivalent to the prevalence odds expression, which specifically decomposes into incidence times disease duration.

preguntas.q: For a short-duration disease such as the common cold, how does prevalence compare to incidence?

o.B: Prevalence is much greater than incidence
o.D: Prevalence cannot be measured for short-duration disease

e.correcta: Prevalence approximates incidence multiplied by average disease duration; for a short-duration disease like the common cold, since duration is brief, prevalence stays close to the incidence rate because cases resolve quickly and don't accumulate in the population. This contrasts with chronic diseases (like diabetes or hypertension), where long duration causes prevalence to substantially exceed incidence because affected individuals remain 'prevalent cases' for years.

incorrectas.B: Prevalence being much greater than incidence is characteristic of chronic, long-duration diseases where cases accumulate over time, not short-duration illnesses like the common cold that resolve quickly.
incorrectas.C: Prevalence cannot be zero for a disease that is actively occurring in the population — the common cold has measurable prevalence at any given time, it's just close in magnitude to incidence rather than zero.
incorrectas.D: Prevalence absolutely can be measured for short-duration diseases (as point prevalence or period prevalence); the key concept being tested is the relationship between prevalence and incidence based on disease duration, not measurability.

preguntas.q: For a chronic disease such as diabetes, how does prevalence compare to incidence?

o.D: Prevalence equals incidence divided by duration

e.correcta: Prevalence reflects the total number of existing cases in a population at a point in time, while incidence reflects only new cases arising over a period; for a chronic disease like diabetes, patients survive for years after diagnosis and accumulate in the population, so prevalence (existing + new cases) becomes much greater than incidence (new cases only). This relationship — prevalence approximately equals incidence multiplied by average disease duration — explains why chronic, non-fatal diseases have high prevalence relative to their incidence, whereas acute, rapidly resolving or rapidly fatal diseases have prevalence closer to incidence.

incorrectas.B: Prevalence and incidence are similar only for acute conditions with very short duration (rapid recovery or rapid death), which is the opposite pattern from a chronic disease like diabetes where affected individuals remain in the prevalence pool for years.
incorrectas.C: Prevalence being less than incidence does not occur under steady-state conditions for a chronic disease, since existing chronic cases persist and add to new cases rather than disappearing quickly; this pattern would require an implausibly short disease duration for a chronic illness.
incorrectas.D: The correct relationship is prevalence approximately equals incidence multiplied by average duration, not incidence divided by duration — dividing by duration would make prevalence smaller as duration increases, which is backwards for a chronic disease.

preguntas.q: What happens to incidence and prevalence when an effective treatment for a disease is developed (without a cure)?

o.A: No change in incidence; decreased prevalence
o.C: No change in incidence; increased prevalence
o.D: Decreased incidence; no change in prevalence

e.correcta: An effective treatment (without a cure) prolongs survival and duration of disease without reducing the rate of new cases, so incidence — the rate of new cases arising — remains unchanged, while prevalence — the total number of existing cases at a point in time — decreases only if people are cured or die faster; but since the treatment is not curative and prolongs life, prevalence actually tends to rise, not fall (people live longer with the disease, accumulating in the population). The correct framework is: incidence reflects new-case rate (unaffected by treating existing cases), while prevalence = incidence × average disease duration, so an effective but non-curative treatment that extends survival increases prevalence, not decreases it — making close attention to this incidence/prevalence relationship essential.

incorrectas.B: Decreased incidence would require reducing new cases (e.g., via prevention or vaccination), not treatment of existing disease; an effective treatment for existing cases does not by itself change the rate of new cases occurring.
incorrectas.C: No change in incidence is correct, but prevalence would increase (not stay the same) if treatment prolongs disease duration/survival without curing it, since prevalence depends on both incidence and duration of disease.
incorrectas.D: Decreased incidence with no change in prevalence reverses the actual relationship — treatment does not reduce new case rates, and by prolonging disease duration without cure, it would increase, not leave unchanged, disease prevalence.

preguntas.q: What happens to incidence and prevalence when an effective vaccine for a disease is developed?

o.B: No change in incidence; decreased prevalence
o.C: Decreased incidence; no change in prevalence

e.correcta: An effective vaccine prevents new infections, which directly lowers incidence (the rate of new cases arising over time). Because prevalence is a function of incidence and disease duration (prevalence ≈ incidence × duration), fewer new cases feeding into the pool of existing disease causes prevalence to fall as well, assuming duration of illness is unchanged.

incorrectas.B: This choice incorrectly assumes incidence stays flat while prevalence drops — but a vaccine's entire mechanism of benefit is blocking new infections, so incidence must fall; prevalence then falls as a downstream consequence, not independently of incidence.
incorrectas.C: This choice would only hold if the disease became more chronic (longer duration) even as new cases declined, which is not what an effective vaccine does — vaccines don't change disease duration in existing cases, so prevalence falls in parallel with incidence.
incorrectas.D: An effective vaccine cannot increase incidence — that would mean it is not preventing infection, which contradicts the premise of an 'effective vaccine'; this pattern would instead describe something like improved detection/screening increasing apparent case counts while treatment shortens illness duration.

preguntas.q: If people with a chronic disease live longer (without a change in new case detection), what happens to incidence and prevalence?

o.A: No change in incidence; increased prevalence
o.C: No change in incidence; decreased prevalence
o.D: Increased incidence; no change in prevalence

e.correcta: Incidence measures new cases over time, so it remains unchanged if disease detection rates are unchanged — but prevalence (which reflects both new and existing cases at a point in time) rises when people live longer with the disease, since they remain counted as prevalent cases for a longer duration. This distinction, prevalence approximately equals incidence times duration, is a classic epidemiology concept: interventions that improve survival (without preventing new cases) increase prevalence without altering incidence.

incorrectas.B: Decreased incidence would require a change in the rate of new cases being diagnosed, which the question specifies has not changed — only survival duration has changed, so incidence stays the same.
incorrectas.C: Decreased prevalence would occur if duration of disease shortened (e.g., faster deaths or cures), which is the opposite of the scenario described where patients are living longer with the disease.
incorrectas.D: Increased incidence would imply more new cases are being diagnosed, which contradicts the premise that only survival (not new case detection) has changed.

preguntas.q: Which type of prevalence refers to the amount of an existing condition present in a population at a single point in time?

e.correcta: Point prevalence measures the proportion of a population that has a given condition at one specific moment in time (a 'snapshot'), calculated as the number of existing cases at that instant divided by the total population at that instant. This measure is useful for understanding disease burden at a fixed point (e.g., prevalence of diabetes on a specific survey date) but does not capture new cases that develop or resolve before or after that moment, unlike period prevalence which spans an interval.

incorrectas.B: Period prevalence measures existing cases over a defined span of time (not a single instant), combining point prevalence with new cases arising during that interval, which is a related but distinct concept from the single-moment measure the question describes.
incorrectas.C: Cumulative incidence measures the proportion of a population that develops a new case of disease over a specified time period, which reflects risk of developing disease, not the burden of existing cases at one point in time.
incorrectas.D: Attack rate is a form of cumulative incidence used typically in outbreak settings over a short, defined time period, measuring new cases, not the point-in-time snapshot of existing disease burden described here.

preguntas.q: Which type of prevalence refers to the amount of an existing condition present in a population during a particular time period?

e.correcta: Period prevalence is the proportion of a population that has a given condition at any point during a specified time interval — it captures cases that existed at the start of the period plus any new cases that arise during it. It's distinct from a single-moment snapshot because it accumulates cases over a duration, which is why the question's phrasing ('during a particular time period') maps to period rather than point prevalence.

incorrectas.B: Point prevalence measures the proportion of a population with a condition at one specific instant in time (a single point), not summed over a duration — it would be used for a question asking about a survey done on a single day, not 'during a time period.'
incorrectas.C: Incidence rate measures the rate of NEW cases arising in a population over time, not the total existing burden of disease; prevalence and incidence answer different questions (existing cases vs. new cases) and are often conflated by test-takers.
incorrectas.D: Case fatality rate is the proportion of people with a disease who die from it — a measure of disease severity/lethality, unrelated to how many people currently have the condition in the population.

preguntas.q: Which study design is an observational study that compares a group of people with a disease to a group without the disease?

e.correcta: A case-control study is an observational design that starts by identifying a group with the disease (cases) and a group without it (controls), then looks backward in time to compare the frequency of prior exposures between the two groups, allowing calculation of an odds ratio as an estimate of association. This retrospective, outcome-based sampling makes case-control studies efficient for studying rare diseases, since you can deliberately enroll enough diseased individuals rather than waiting for disease to develop in a large cohort.

incorrectas.B: A cohort study instead starts with groups defined by exposure status (exposed vs. unexposed) and follows them forward in time to see who develops disease, calculating relative risk — this is the opposite direction of inquiry from a case-control study.
incorrectas.C: A cross-sectional study measures exposure and disease status simultaneously at a single point in time in a population, providing prevalence data, but it does not specifically select subjects based on disease status the way a case-control study does.
incorrectas.D: A randomized controlled trial is an experimental (not observational) design in which the investigator actively assigns exposure/intervention, which is fundamentally different from a case-control study's observational, retrospective comparison of pre-existing groups.

preguntas.q: Case-control studies are almost always which type of design with respect to time?

e.correcta: Case-control studies start by identifying subjects who already have the outcome/disease (cases) and those without it (controls), then look backward in time to compare prior exposures between the two groups — this backward-looking design is what makes them retrospective. This structure makes case-control studies efficient for studying rare diseases (you don't have to wait for the outcome to occur) and allows calculation of odds ratios, but it is inherently susceptible to recall bias since exposure data is gathered after the outcome is known.

incorrectas.B: Prospective design (following subjects forward in time from exposure to eventual outcome) describes cohort studies, not case-control studies, which instead select subjects based on outcome status and look backward at exposure.
incorrectas.C: Cross-sectional studies measure exposure and outcome simultaneously at a single point in time (a "snapshot"), which is a fundamentally different temporal structure from case-control studies that require establishing outcome status first, then tracing exposure history.
incorrectas.D: Ambispective designs combine retrospective and prospective components (e.g., some data collected historically, then subjects followed forward), which is not the typical structure of a standard case-control study.

preguntas.q: Are case-control studies useful for directly measuring incidence and/or prevalence?

e.correcta: Case-control studies start by selecting participants based on outcome status (cases with disease vs. controls without) and then look backward to compare exposure history, so the investigator is not sampling from a defined population followed over time. Because the proportion of cases and controls is set by the study design rather than reflecting how common the disease actually is in the population, you cannot calculate incidence (new cases over time) or prevalence (existing cases at a point in time) from this design. What case-control studies can estimate is the odds ratio, which approximates relative risk when the disease is rare.

incorrectas.B: Incidence requires following a population forward in time to count new cases, which is the domain of cohort studies, not case-control studies where the outcome has already occurred before subjects are even enrolled.
incorrectas.C: Prevalence requires a snapshot of an entire representative population to determine what proportion has the disease at a given moment, which is the province of cross-sectional studies; case-control studies enroll a fixed, disproportionate number of cases and controls that does not reflect true population prevalence.
incorrectas.D: Case-control studies cannot measure either incidence or prevalence because their sampling is anchored to outcome status rather than to a population followed over time or sampled cross-sectionally, so this option overstates their capability in both directions.

preguntas.q: Which type of study is an observational study that compares the frequency of disease and frequency of risk-related factors at one time point?

e.correcta: A cross-sectional study captures a snapshot of a population at a single point in time, simultaneously measuring both disease status and exposure/risk factor status in each subject, which allows calculation of prevalence but not incidence, and cannot establish temporal (cause-effect) relationships since exposure and outcome are assessed together. This design is useful for quickly estimating how common a disease or risk factor is in a population, such as national health surveys, but is vulnerable to reverse causality since you cannot tell whether the exposure preceded the disease. Recognizing the 'single time point, look at both variables at once' pattern is the key distinguishing feature tested here.

incorrectas.B: A case-control study is retrospective, starting with subjects already classified as having the disease (cases) versus not (controls), then looking backward for prior exposures — it does not evaluate disease and risk factors simultaneously at one time point the way a cross-sectional study does.
incorrectas.C: A cohort study follows exposed and unexposed groups forward over time to see who develops disease, directly measuring incidence — this longitudinal design contrasts with the single-time-point structure of a cross-sectional study.
incorrectas.D: A twin concordance study compares disease concordance rates between monozygotic and dizygotic twins to estimate heritability, a specialized design for assessing genetic contribution to disease, not a general one-time-point observational comparison of disease and risk factor frequency.

preguntas.q: Are cross-sectional surveys useful for measuring incidence and/or prevalence?

e.correcta: Cross-sectional surveys capture a snapshot of a population at a single point in time, measuring how many existing cases of disease are present at that moment, which is precisely the definition of prevalence. Because they only observe disease status once rather than following subjects over time to detect new cases arising, cross-sectional studies cannot capture incidence, which requires longitudinal follow-up of an at-risk population.

incorrectas.B: Incidence measures the rate of new cases developing over a defined period, which requires tracking a population longitudinally (as in cohort studies) — a single-timepoint cross-sectional survey cannot distinguish new from pre-existing cases, so it cannot measure incidence.
incorrectas.C: Both incidence and prevalence would require the study design to include follow-up over time to detect new cases, but the defining feature of a cross-sectional study is a single point-in-time measurement, which limits it to prevalence only.
incorrectas.D: Neither incidence nor prevalence is incorrect because cross-sectional surveys are, in fact, the classic tool for measuring prevalence; they are only limited in their ability to capture incidence, not both measures.

preguntas.q: Which type of study is an observational study that compares groups with a given exposure or risk factor to a group without such exposure?

e.correcta: A cohort study is an observational design that starts by identifying groups based on exposure status (exposed vs. unexposed) and then follows them forward in time to compare the incidence of an outcome between the groups. This design allows direct calculation of relative risk and is well suited for studying common outcomes and multiple effects of a single exposure, though it can be time- and resource-intensive, especially for rare outcomes.

incorrectas.B: A case-control study works in the opposite direction — it starts by selecting groups based on outcome/disease status (cases vs. controls) and looks backward to compare prior exposure rates, calculating an odds ratio rather than starting from exposure status as cohort studies do.
incorrectas.C: A cross-sectional study measures exposure and outcome simultaneously at a single point in time in a population, providing a prevalence snapshot rather than following exposed and unexposed groups forward to observe incident outcomes.
incorrectas.D: A case series simply describes the clinical features of a group of patients with a particular condition, without a comparison group of any kind, so it cannot compare an exposed group to an unexposed group at all.

preguntas.q: Which type of observational study can be designed as either retrospective or prospective?

e.correcta: Cohort studies follow a defined group based on exposure status and observe outcomes over time, and this design can be conducted prospectively (following subjects forward from exposure to future outcome) or retrospectively (using existing historical records to look backward from exposure to outcomes that already occurred). This flexibility makes cohort studies useful when researchers want to calculate relative risk and incidence directly, unlike designs whose timing structure is fixed by definition.

incorrectas.B: Case-control studies are inherently retrospective by design — they start with cases (disease present) and controls (disease absent) and look backward for prior exposures, calculating odds ratios rather than being adaptable to a prospective format.
incorrectas.C: Cross-sectional studies capture exposure and outcome simultaneously at a single point in time, providing prevalence data; by definition they lack the temporal dimension needed to be classified as prospective or retrospective longitudinal designs.
incorrectas.D: Ecological studies analyze population-level (not individual-level) data to correlate group exposure rates with group outcome rates at a point or period in time, and are typically discussed as a distinct level-of-analysis issue (ecological fallacy) rather than being characterized by a retrospective/prospective cohort framework.

preguntas.q: Which type of study design is useful for calculating relative risk (RR)?

e.correcta: Cohort studies follow exposed and unexposed groups forward in time and directly measure the incidence of disease in each group, so relative risk (incidence in exposed / incidence in unexposed) can be calculated directly. This prospective (or retrospective cohort) design is what makes RR computable, whereas designs that start by selecting on outcome status cannot generate true incidence rates.

incorrectas.B: Case-control studies start with people who already have the disease (cases) and compare their exposure history to controls, so the true incidence of disease in exposed versus unexposed groups is unknown — this design yields an odds ratio, which approximates RR only when the disease is rare, but does not calculate RR directly.
incorrectas.C: Cross-sectional studies capture exposure and disease status at a single point in time, allowing calculation of prevalence rather than incidence, so relative risk (which requires tracking new cases over time) cannot be determined from this design.
incorrectas.D: Case series simply describe a group of patients with a given condition without a comparison group at all, so there is no way to compute any relative measure of risk like RR.

preguntas.q: Are cohort studies useful for measuring incidence and/or prevalence?

o.D: Both incidence and prevalence equally well

e.correcta: Cohort studies follow a group of individuals without the disease over time, tracking new cases as they arise, which makes them well suited to directly measure incidence (the rate of new disease occurrence). Because subjects are enrolled before disease onset and followed longitudinally, cohort studies can also calculate relative risk, but their design's core strength is capturing new-onset disease over a defined follow-up period — prevalence is better captured by cross-sectional studies that survey a population at a single point in time.

incorrectas.B: Prevalence describes the proportion of a population with disease at a single time point and is best measured with cross-sectional studies; cohort studies are designed around following people forward in time to detect new cases, not snapshotting existing disease burden.
incorrectas.C: Cohort studies are in fact very useful for incidence, so 'neither' is incorrect — their prospective, longitudinal structure is precisely what allows calculation of incidence rates and relative risk.
incorrectas.D: Cohort studies do not measure prevalence and incidence equally well; their strength is specifically incidence (and measures derived from it like relative risk), while prevalence is a cross-sectional measure better suited to a different study design.

preguntas.q: Which type of study is an observational study that compares the frequency with which monozygotic and dizygotic twins develop the same disease?

e.correcta: A twin concordance study compares how often monozygotic (genetically identical) twins both develop a disease versus how often dizygotic (fraternal) twins both develop it; a higher concordance rate in monozygotic pairs suggests a stronger genetic contribution to the disease, while similar concordance rates in both groups suggest environmental factors dominate. This design is a classic way to estimate heritability without the confounding of a shared family environment being different between the two twin types, since both MZ and DZ twins are typically raised in similar environments.

incorrectas.B: A cohort study follows a defined group of individuals (exposed vs. unexposed) forward in time to see who develops disease, calculating incidence and relative risk — it is not structured around comparing genetic relatedness (MZ vs DZ) as its defining feature, unlike a twin study.
incorrectas.C: A case-control study starts with people who already have the disease (cases) and compares their past exposures to disease-free controls, calculating an odds ratio — this retrospective, exposure-comparison design is unrelated to the twin-based genetic comparison described in the question.
incorrectas.D: An adoption study compares outcomes between biological and adoptive relatives to separate genetic from environmental contributions to a trait, which is a related but distinct design from a twin study — the question specifically describes comparing MZ versus DZ twin concordance, which defines the twin study, not the adoption study.

preguntas.q: The E6 protein of Human Papillomavirus (HPV) binds to and inhibits which tumor suppressor gene product?

e.correcta: The HPV E6 oncoprotein binds p53 and targets it for ubiquitin-mediated proteasomal degradation, removing this critical tumor suppressor's ability to halt the cell cycle or trigger apoptosis in response to DNA damage; loss of p53 function allows cells with accumulating mutations (including those from high-risk HPV integration) to survive and proliferate, driving cervical and oropharyngeal carcinogenesis. This E6-p53 interaction, alongside E7's inactivation of Rb, is the core molecular mechanism by which high-risk HPV types (16, 18) cause malignant transformation.

incorrectas.B: Rb (retinoblastoma protein) is the target of the HPV E7 protein, not E6 — E7 binding releases E2F transcription factors from Rb inhibition, driving unchecked cell cycle progression, a distinct mechanism from E6's degradation of p53.
incorrectas.C: BRCA1 is a tumor suppressor involved in DNA double-strand break repair via homologous recombination; it is not a target of HPV E6, and its loss is linked instead to hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndromes.
incorrectas.D: p16 (p16INK4a) is actually upregulated as a surrogate marker of HPV-driven Rb pathway inactivation (used diagnostically as p16 immunostaining), not degraded by E6 — its increased expression, rather than loss, is the clinically useful HPV signature.

preguntas.q: The E7 protein of Human Papillomavirus (HPV) binds to and inhibits which tumor suppressor?

e.correcta: The HPV E7 oncoprotein binds and promotes degradation of the retinoblastoma protein (Rb), which normally sequesters the E2F transcription factor to prevent unchecked progression through the cell cycle; by inactivating Rb, E7 releases E2F to drive cells into S phase uncontrollably, contributing to the oncogenic transformation seen in HPV-associated cervical and oropharyngeal cancers. This action works together with the E6 oncoprotein (which degrades p53) to disable both major tumor suppressor checkpoints, explaining why high-risk HPV strains are so strongly carcinogenic.

incorrectas.A: p53 is the tumor suppressor targeted by the HPV E6 protein (not E7), which promotes its degradation via ubiquitination, impairing apoptosis and DNA damage response — a distinct oncoprotein-target pairing from E7's action on Rb.
incorrectas.C: PTEN is a tumor suppressor phosphatase that antagonizes the PI3K/AKT pathway and is implicated in cancers like endometrial carcinoma and Cowden syndrome, but it is not the direct target of HPV E7.
incorrectas.D: APC is the tumor suppressor inactivated in the adenoma-carcinoma sequence of colorectal cancer (as in familial adenomatous polyposis), functioning in the Wnt/beta-catenin pathway, and is unrelated to HPV E7's mechanism of action on Rb.

preguntas.q: What benign tumor of the squamous mucosa of the sinuses is thought to be caused by HPV infection?

e.correcta: Sinonasal (Schneiderian) papilloma is a benign tumor arising from the squamous/respiratory epithelium lining the sinonasal tract, and HPV infection (particularly certain low-risk and some high-risk types) is implicated in its pathogenesis, especially in the exophytic/fungiform subtype. Recognizing the HPV association is clinically relevant because inverted-type sinonasal papillomas carry a risk of local recurrence and, less commonly, malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma, warranting complete surgical excision and surveillance.

incorrectas.B: Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a benign but locally aggressive vascular tumor arising in the nasopharynx of adolescent males, driven by hormonal factors rather than HPV infection, and is a mesenchymal/vascular lesion rather than a squamous epithelial one.
incorrectas.C: Esthesioneuroblastoma (olfactory neuroblastoma) arises from olfactory neuroepithelium at the cribriform plate and is a neuroectodermal/neuroendocrine tumor, not a squamous mucosal papilloma, and has no established HPV etiology.
incorrectas.D: Antrochoanal polyp is an inflammatory, non-neoplastic polypoid growth arising from the maxillary sinus that prolapses into the nasal cavity/choana, related to chronic inflammation rather than HPV-driven epithelial proliferation.

preguntas.q: What is the most common cause of Condyloma acuminata?

e.correcta: Condyloma acuminata (genital warts) are caused overwhelmingly by the low-risk HPV serotypes 6 and 11, which infect squamous epithelium and produce benign exophytic, cauliflower-like papillomas through episomal viral replication without significant oncogenic potential. This is a key distinction tested repeatedly: low-risk types 6/11 cause warts, while high-risk types like 16/18 integrate viral DNA into the host genome and drive cervical and other anogenital cancers via E6/E7 oncoprotein inactivation of p53 and Rb.

incorrectas.B: HPV16 and HPV18 are the high-risk oncogenic serotypes responsible for the vast majority of cervical, anal, and oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinomas, but they are not the typical cause of visible genital warts, which are driven by low-risk types 6 and 11.
incorrectas.C: Herpes simplex virus 2 causes painful genital vesicles and ulcers (genital herpes), a clinically distinct presentation from the painless warty lesions of condyloma acuminata caused by HPV.
incorrectas.D: Molluscum contagiosum virus, a poxvirus, causes small, umbilicated flesh-colored papules, which are morphologically and etiologically distinct from the cauliflower-like condyloma acuminata caused by HPV.

preguntas.q: Which condition, caused by HPV (typically types 6 and 11), presents as genital warts?

e.correcta: Condyloma acuminatum refers to genital warts caused by low-risk HPV types 6 and 11, which infect squamous epithelium and drive keratinocyte proliferation, producing raised, cauliflower-like papillomatous lesions on the genital or perianal skin. These HPV types are considered low-risk because the E6/E7 viral oncoproteins they express are much less efficient at inactivating p53 and Rb than high-risk types like 16 and 18, so condyloma acuminatum carries minimal malignant potential compared to cervical dysplasia-associated HPV infections.

incorrectas.B: Condyloma latum refers to the flat, wart-like lesions of secondary syphilis caused by Treponema pallidum, a bacterial infection entirely distinct from the HPV-driven epithelial proliferation that produces condyloma acuminatum.
incorrectas.C: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by a poxvirus (not HPV) and produces small, umbilicated, flesh-colored papules through a different viral replication mechanism, distinguishing it clinically and etiologically from genital warts.
incorrectas.D: Bowenoid papulosis is associated with high-risk HPV types (like 16) and represents a form of squamous intraepithelial neoplasia with malignant potential, unlike the benign, low-risk HPV 6/11-driven warts of condyloma acuminatum.

preguntas.q: Which histological feature, characterized by raisin-like nuclei with perinuclear halos, is a hallmark of HPV infection?

e.correcta: Koilocytes are squamous epithelial cells infected by HPV that show a characteristic raisin-like, wrinkled, hyperchromatic nucleus surrounded by a clear perinuclear halo, reflecting cytopathic changes induced by viral E6/E7 protein activity disrupting normal cell cycle regulation. Identifying koilocytes on Pap smear or biopsy is a key histologic clue for HPV infection and is used in cervical cytology screening to flag squamous intraepithelial lesions.

incorrectas.B: Councilman bodies are eosinophilic apoptotic hepatocyte remnants seen in viral hepatitis (e.g., yellow fever, other hepatitides), reflecting programmed cell death in the liver, not the koilocytic nuclear change associated with HPV in squamous epithelium.
incorrectas.C: Negri bodies are cytoplasmic inclusions found in neurons infected with rabies virus, representing sites of viral replication in the CNS, and have no relationship to the nuclear halo changes seen with HPV.
incorrectas.D: Owl's eye inclusions describe the large intranuclear inclusions seen in cells infected with cytomegalovirus (CMV), a distinct viral cytopathic pattern from the perinuclear cytoplasmic halo and raisin-like nucleus that defines koilocytes in HPV infection.

preguntas.q: What is the carcinoma risk associated with HPV types 6 and 11?

o.D: No risk at all, they are never oncogenic

e.correcta: HPV types 6 and 11 are classified as low-risk strains because they predominantly cause condyloma acuminata (genital warts) and laryngeal papillomas rather than integrating their genome in a way that drives malignant transformation; unlike high-risk types, their E6 and E7 oncoproteins are much weaker inhibitors of the p53 and Rb tumor suppressor pathways, so they rarely progress to carcinoma. This risk stratification (low-risk 6/11 vs. high-risk 16/18) is a foundational virology fact tied directly to cervical cancer screening and HPV vaccine design.

incorrectas.B: High carcinoma risk is characteristic of HPV types 16 and 18, whose E6 and E7 oncoproteins potently degrade p53 and Rb respectively, driving cervical, anal, and oropharyngeal carcinogenesis — this is the opposite risk category from types 6 and 11, which cause benign warts rather than driving malignant transformation.
incorrectas.C: There is no clinically meaningful 'intermediate' risk category in the standard low-risk/high-risk HPV classification used on exams and in clinical guidelines — HPV types are binned as low-risk (6, 11, and others causing warts) or high-risk (16, 18, and others associated with cancer).
incorrectas.D: While types 6 and 11 are low-risk, saying they are 'never oncogenic' overstates the point — they are simply much less likely to cause malignant transformation compared to high-risk types, and the standard classification is 'low risk,' not a claim of zero oncogenic potential in any circumstance.

preguntas.q: Which HPV types are the cause of HPV-related vulvar carcinoma?

e.correcta: High-risk HPV types 16, 18, 31, and 33 (with 16 and 18 accounting for the majority of cases) produce the E6 and E7 oncoproteins, which inactivate the tumor suppressors p53 and Rb respectively, driving uncontrolled cellular proliferation in genital squamous epithelium including the vulva. This same oncogenic mechanism underlies HPV-related cervical, anal, and oropharyngeal carcinomas, which is why these types are targeted by the HPV vaccine.

incorrectas.B: Low-risk HPV 6 and 11 cause benign condyloma acuminata (genital warts) rather than malignancy; they do not produce the potent E6/E7 oncoproteins at levels sufficient to reliably transform cells into carcinoma.
incorrectas.C: HPV 2 and 4 cause common cutaneous warts (verruca vulgaris) on skin such as the hands, an entirely different clinical entity from genital/mucosal high-risk HPV disease and carrying no meaningful oncogenic potential.
incorrectas.D: HPV 5 and 8 are associated with epidermodysplasia verruciformis, a rare genetic susceptibility to widespread cutaneous HPV infection and skin cancer, not with vulvar carcinoma.
