incorrectas.D: Peptic ulcer disease is not related to negative inotropy; disopyramide's other notable side effects are actually anticholinergic (dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation) rather than any effect that would worsen ulcer disease via a contractility mechanism.

preguntas.q: Class IA antiarrhythmics have what relative binding affinity for the Na+ channel?

o.D: Variable and unrelated to channel state

e.correcta: Class IA antiarrhythmics (e.g., quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide) have an intermediate affinity and dissociation rate for the fast Na+ channel — faster-dissociating than class IC drugs but slower than class IB. This intermediate kinetic profile lets them block sodium channels enough to slow phase 0 depolarization and widen the QRS, while also prolonging the action potential duration (via K+ channel effects) and thus the QT interval, which is why they carry torsades risk.

incorrectas.B: Very low/negligible affinity would essentially mean no clinically meaningful sodium channel blockade, which contradicts the defining mechanism of class I antiarrhythmics — all class I drugs, including IA, act specifically by blocking fast Na+ channels.
incorrectas.C: Extremely strong/irreversible binding describes neither class IA nor any clinically used antiarrhythmic; irreversible channel blockade would be markedly proarrhythmic and pharmacologically impractical, unlike the reversible, use-dependent blockade seen with class I drugs.
incorrectas.D: Class I antiarrhythmics are use-dependent, meaning their binding is state-dependent (preferring open/inactivated channels) and reproducible, not 'variable and unrelated to channel state' — this description misrepresents the basic pharmacology of the class.

preguntas.q: In addition to Na+ channels, Class IA antiarrhythmics also block which other channel?

e.correcta: Class IA antiarrhythmics (quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide) block fast Na+ channels with intermediate kinetics to slow phase 0 depolarization, but they also block K+ channels, which prolongs repolarization and increases the action potential duration and effective refractory period. This combined Na+/K+ blockade widens the QRS complex and prolongs the QT interval, which is clinically important because it also predisposes patients to torsades de pointes. Remembering 'Class IA = slows conduction AND prolongs repolarization' via K+ block is key to anticipating its proarrhythmic risk.

incorrectas.B: Ca2+ channel blockade is the hallmark of Class IV antiarrhythmics (verapamil, diltiazem), which act mainly on the AV node to slow conduction there; Class IA drugs do not significantly block calcium channels as part of their classic mechanism.
incorrectas.C: Cl- channels are not a target of any major antiarrhythmic drug class; chloride conductance is not part of the cardiac action potential phases that antiarrhythmics are designed to modulate.
incorrectas.D: HCN (funny) channels, which generate the pacemaker current in the SA node, are specifically blocked by ivabradine, a distinct rate-control agent — this is not a mechanism shared by Class IA antiarrhythmics.

preguntas.q: What effect do Class IA antiarrhythmics have on action potential duration?

e.correcta: Class IA antiarrhythmics (e.g., quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide) block fast sodium channels with intermediate kinetics and also block potassium channels, which prolongs the action potential duration in addition to slowing phase 0 depolarization. This combined sodium and potassium channel blockade is what distinguishes class IA from IB (which shortens action potential duration) and IC (which has minimal effect on duration), and it underlies the QT-prolonging risk associated with these drugs.

incorrectas.B: Decreased action potential duration is characteristic of class IB agents like lidocaine and mexiletine, which preferentially block sodium channels in ischemic or depolarized tissue without significantly affecting potassium channels, the opposite effect from class IA.
incorrectas.C: No change in action potential duration is more characteristic of class IC agents like flecainide and propafenone, which strongly slow phase 0 conduction velocity but have minimal effect on repolarization/duration compared to class IA.
incorrectas.D: A biphasic effect on duration is not the defining pharmacologic profile taught for any major antiarrhythmic class; class IA's effect on action potential duration is a straightforward prolongation due to concurrent potassium channel blockade, not a biphasic pattern.

preguntas.q: What effect do Class IA antiarrhythmics have on the effective refractory period (ERP) in ventricular tissue?

e.correcta: Class IA antiarrhythmics increase the effective refractory period (ERP) in ventricular tissue as a direct consequence of prolonging the action potential duration through combined sodium and potassium channel blockade — a longer action potential means the myocardium takes longer before it can be excited again. This ERP prolongation is part of their antiarrhythmic mechanism, making it harder for reentrant circuits to sustain themselves, but it also underlies the risk of torsades de pointes from excessive QT prolongation.

incorrectas.B: A decreased ERP would be expected with an agent that shortens action potential duration, such as class IB antiarrhythmics (lidocaine, mexiletine), which is the opposite of class IA's potassium-channel-blocking, duration-prolonging mechanism.
incorrectas.C: No change in ERP does not fit the pharmacology of class IA drugs, since their added potassium channel blockade (beyond sodium channel blockade alone) specifically extends the time tissue remains refractory, distinguishing them from agents with minimal repolarization effects.
incorrectas.D: ERP becoming 'unmeasurable' is not a real pharmacologic concept — ERP remains a measurable electrophysiologic property under drug effect; class IA drugs simply lengthen it rather than eliminating its measurability.

preguntas.q: Class IA antiarrhythmics are used to treat which type(s) of arrhythmia?

e.correcta: Class IA antiarrhythmics (quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide) block sodium channels with intermediate kinetics and also prolong the action potential duration via some potassium channel blockade, giving them efficacy against both supraventricular arrhythmias (like atrial fibrillation/flutter) and ventricular arrhythmias. This broad spectrum of action, spanning atrial and ventricular tissue, is what distinguishes Class IA from the more selective Class IB (ventricular-predominant) and helps explain their historical use across a wide range of arrhythmia types.

incorrectas.B: Class IA agents are not restricted to supraventricular arrhythmias alone — their sodium and potassium channel blocking effects also make them effective against ventricular arrhythmias, so this option describes only half of their actual clinical spectrum.
incorrectas.C: Class IA agents are not restricted to ventricular arrhythmias alone — they are also used for supraventricular arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation, which is why their broad efficacy across both types is the defining feature tested here.
incorrectas.D: Class IA antiarrhythmics do not treat bradyarrhythmias; by blocking sodium channels they slow conduction and can even cause or worsen bradyarrhythmias/heart block as an adverse effect, rather than treating them.

preguntas.q: Which subclass of Class I antiarrhythmics may be used to treat Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome, a type of SVT?

e.correcta: Class IA antiarrhythmics (e.g., quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide) block fast sodium channels with intermediate kinetics and also prolong the action potential/refractory period by blocking potassium channels, which slows conduction through both the atria/ventricles and, importantly, through the accessory bypass tract in WPW. This dual property makes Class IA useful for both the ectopic reentrant circuit and the accessory pathway itself, unlike drugs that act mainly on the AV node.

incorrectas.B: Class IB agents (lidocaine, mexiletine) bind rapidly to sodium channels in depolarized/ischemic tissue and are primarily used for ventricular arrhythmias, especially post-MI; they have minimal effect on atrial or accessory pathway tissue, so they are not the drug of choice for WPW-associated SVT.
incorrectas.C: Class IC agents (flecainide, propafenone) strongly slow conduction via sodium channel blockade and are used for supraventricular arrhythmias including WPW in some contexts, but in this class hierarchy question, Class IA is specifically identified as the classic answer because of its added potassium channel blocking effect on the bypass tract's refractoriness.
incorrectas.D: Class II antiarrhythmics are beta-blockers, which slow conduction through the AV node by reducing sympathetic tone, not through the accessory pathway; in WPW, blocking the AV node preferentially can be dangerous because it shifts conduction entirely onto the unprotected bypass tract during atrial fibrillation.

preguntas.q: Class IB antiarrhythmics have what relative binding affinity for the Na+ channel?

e.correcta: Class IB antiarrhythmics (lidocaine, mexiletine) have a low affinity for Na+ channels combined with fast dissociation kinetics, meaning they bind and unbind quickly and preferentially affect ischemic or rapidly depolarizing (already partially depolarized) tissue rather than normal myocardium. This selectivity for diseased/ischemic tissue with minimal effect on normal conduction is why Class IB drugs are classically used to treat ventricular arrhythmias occurring after a myocardial infarction, where they suppress abnormal automaticity without excessively slowing conduction in healthy tissue.

incorrectas.B: Intermediate Na+ channel binding affinity describes Class IA antiarrhythmics (like procainamide and quinidine), which sit between IB's low affinity and IC's high affinity in the classic potency/kinetics spectrum.
incorrectas.C: Very strong Na+ channel binding with slow dissociation is characteristic of Class IC antiarrhythmics (flecainide, propafenone), which markedly slow conduction in normal tissue and carry a higher proarrhythmic risk (e.g., post-MI), the opposite kinetic profile from Class IB.
incorrectas.D: Class IC agents, not Class IB, have the strongest/highest Na+ channel binding affinity among the sodium channel blocker subclasses; Class IB is specifically noted for its low affinity and rapid kinetics.

preguntas.q: What effect do Class IB antiarrhythmics have on action potential duration?

o.D: Duration becomes prolonged only in ischemic tissue

e.correcta: Class IB antiarrhythmics (e.g., lidocaine, mexiletine) block fast sodium channels with rapid on/off kinetics and preferentially bind inactivated channels, which are more abundant in depolarized/ischemic tissue; this selective action shortens the action potential duration by decreasing the sodium current's contribution to the plateau phase, which is particularly useful for suppressing reentrant arrhythmias in ischemic myocardium without significantly widening the QRS in normal tissue.

incorrectas.B: Increased action potential duration is characteristic of Class IA (e.g., quinidine, procainamide) and Class III agents (e.g., amiodarone, sotalol), which block potassium channels or have mixed channel effects prolonging repolarization — this is the opposite of the IB mechanism.
incorrectas.C: Class IC agents (e.g., flecainide, propafenone) have minimal effect on action potential duration because they bind and unbind sodium channels slowly without much associated potassium channel blockade, but this 'no change' profile is characteristic of class IC, not class IB, which does shorten duration.
incorrectas.D: Class IB drugs shorten action potential duration throughout affected tissue via their kinetics, not only in ischemic tissue; ischemic/depolarized tissue is simply where they preferentially bind and act, but the class-defining electrophysiologic effect (APD shortening) is a general property of the drug class.

preguntas.q: Which subclass of Class I antiarrhythmics may be used to treat digitalis (digoxin)-induced arrhythmias?

e.correcta: Class IB antiarrhythmics (e.g., lidocaine, mexiletine) are useful in digoxin-induced arrhythmias because they preferentially bind depolarized/ischemic tissue with fast dissociation kinetics, shortening the action potential and effectively reducing the ectopic automaticity that digoxin toxicity causes via increased intracellular calcium and delayed afterdepolarizations. Their relatively selective action on abnormal, rapidly firing tissue (as opposed to healthy conducting tissue) makes them well-suited to treat toxicity-induced ventricular arrhythmias without further impairing normal conduction.

incorrectas.B: Class IA agents (e.g., quinidine, procainamide) prolong the action potential duration and QT interval, and quinidine in particular can actually increase digoxin levels by displacing it from tissue binding sites and reducing its renal clearance, making Class IA a poor and potentially dangerous choice in digoxin toxicity.
incorrectas.C: Class IC agents (e.g., flecainide, propafenone) markedly slow conduction velocity with minimal effect on action potential duration and are proarrhythmic in structurally abnormal hearts; they are not the preferred choice for digoxin-induced arrhythmias and are generally avoided post-MI or with structural heart disease.
incorrectas.D: Class III agents (e.g., amiodarone) block potassium channels and prolong repolarization; amiodarone can also increase serum digoxin levels by reducing its clearance, similar to quinidine, making it a poor choice to treat digoxin toxicity rather than a preferred treatment.

preguntas.q: Class IC antiarrhythmics have what relative binding affinity for the Na+ channel?

e.correcta: Class IC agents (flecainide, propafenone) have the strongest binding affinity for the fast Na+ channel among class I antiarrhythmics and dissociate very slowly from the channel, producing the most pronounced slowing of phase 0 upstroke velocity and the greatest widening of the QRS complex. This strong, slow-off binding is why IC drugs are avoided post-MI (CAST trial showed increased mortality) — in structurally abnormal or ischemic myocardium, this profound conduction slowing promotes reentrant ventricular arrhythmias.

incorrectas.B: Low Na+ channel affinity is characteristic of class IB agents (lidocaine, mexiletine), which bind and dissociate rapidly, explaining why they have minimal effect on normal tissue and act preferentially on rapidly firing/ischemic tissue rather than causing the marked QRS widening seen with IC.
incorrectas.C: Intermediate affinity describes class IA agents (quinidine, procainamide), which fall between IB and IC in their kinetics and also block K+ channels, prolonging the action potential and QT interval, a feature not shared by IC drugs.
incorrectas.D: Having no appreciable Na+ channel affinity would place a drug outside the class I category altogether (e.g., class III agents primarily block K+ channels), which does not describe any class I subtype including IC.

preguntas.q: Blood flows from the left atrium to the left ventricle through which valve?

e.correcta: The mitral (bicuspid) valve separates the left atrium from the left ventricle and opens during ventricular diastole to allow oxygenated blood to flow from the atrium into the ventricle, then closes during systole to prevent backflow. Its two-leaflet structure (compared to the tricuspid valve's three leaflets) is a classic anatomic distinguishing feature and is clinically relevant in conditions like mitral stenosis and regurgitation, which are heard best at the cardiac apex.

incorrectas.B: The tricuspid valve is the atrioventricular valve on the right side of the heart, controlling flow from the right atrium to the right ventricle, not the left-sided chambers described in the question.
incorrectas.C: The pulmonic valve is a semilunar valve that regulates outflow from the right ventricle into the pulmonary artery, functioning during ventricular ejection rather than atrioventricular flow on the left side.
incorrectas.D: The aortic valve is the semilunar valve through which blood exits the left ventricle into the aorta during systole; it is downstream of the mitral valve and governs ventricular outflow, not atrial-to-ventricular filling.

preguntas.q: Blood flows from which structure to the systemic arteries and tissues?

e.correcta: The aorta is the final chamber-adjacent great vessel through which oxygenated blood leaves the left ventricle to be distributed to the systemic arteries and peripheral tissues, following the sequence: pulmonary veins to left atrium to left ventricle to aorta to systemic circulation. Its thick, elastic wall allows it to withstand high systolic pressures and to recoil during diastole (Windkessel effect), helping maintain continuous forward flow to tissues between heartbeats.

incorrectas.B: The pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood from the lungs into the left atrium, an earlier step in the circuit that precedes the aorta rather than directly supplying the systemic arteries and tissues.
incorrectas.C: The vena cava (superior and inferior) returns deoxygenated blood from the systemic circulation back to the right atrium, moving in the opposite direction of blood flow described in the question.
incorrectas.D: The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood into the pulmonary artery toward the lungs for oxygenation, which is part of the pulmonary circuit and not the vessel that supplies oxygenated blood to systemic tissues.

preguntas.q: Blood flows from the tissues to the systemic veins and ultimately to which structure before returning to the right atrium?

e.correcta: Deoxygenated blood from the tissues drains into progressively larger systemic veins that ultimately converge into the superior and inferior vena cava, which empty directly into the right atrium — this is the final common venous conduit before blood enters the heart on the right side.

incorrectas.B: The aorta carries oxygenated blood away from the left ventricle to the systemic tissues — it is the starting point of systemic arterial flow, not the endpoint of systemic venous return.
incorrectas.C: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs for oxygenation — it comes after the right atrium/ventricle in the circuit, not before, and isn't part of the systemic venous return pathway.
incorrectas.D: The coronary sinus collects venous blood specifically from the heart muscle itself (cardiac veins) and drains it into the right atrium, but it is not where systemic (body-wide) venous blood collects before reaching the heart.

preguntas.q: Deoxygenated blood flows from the vena cava into which chamber of the heart?

e.correcta: The superior and inferior vena cavae drain deoxygenated systemic venous blood directly into the right atrium, which then passes it through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle for pumping to the lungs via the pulmonary arteries. This is the first chamber in the normal deoxygenated blood flow pathway: vena cava to right atrium to right ventricle to pulmonary artery to lungs.

incorrectas.B: The left atrium receives oxygenated blood returning from the lungs via the pulmonary veins, not deoxygenated blood from the vena cava — mixing these up reverses the fundamental right-sided (deoxygenated) versus left-sided (oxygenated) circulation.
incorrectas.C: The right ventricle does receive this deoxygenated blood, but only after it has first passed through the right atrium and tricuspid valve — the vena cava empties directly into the right atrium, not directly into the ventricle.
incorrectas.D: The left ventricle receives oxygenated blood from the left atrium (via the mitral valve) to pump into the systemic circulation via the aorta, which is the opposite (oxygenated, left-sided) side of the circulation from what the vena cava supplies.

preguntas.q: Blood flows from the right atrium to the right ventricle through which valve?

e.correcta: The tricuspid valve, named for its three cusps, sits between the right atrium and right ventricle and opens during ventricular diastole to allow deoxygenated blood to flow from the atrium into the ventricle before it is pumped to the lungs via the pulmonary artery. Its right-sided position (as opposed to the mitral valve on the left) is a key anatomic landmark for understanding right heart pathology, such as tricuspid regurgitation seen with right heart failure or endocarditis in IV drug users.

incorrectas.B: The mitral valve is the left-sided atrioventricular valve, controlling flow from the left atrium into the left ventricle, not from the right atrium to right ventricle as asked in this question.
incorrectas.C: The pulmonic valve is a semilunar valve located between the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery, regulating outflow from the ventricle into the pulmonary circulation, not the inflow from atrium to ventricle described here.
incorrectas.D: The aortic valve is a semilunar valve between the left ventricle and the aorta, governing systemic outflow on the left side of the heart, unrelated to the right atrium-to-right ventricle flow path being asked about.

preguntas.q: Blood flows from the right ventricle to the pulmonary artery through which valve?

e.correcta: Deoxygenated blood exits the right ventricle through the pulmonic (pulmonary) valve, a semilunar valve that opens during ventricular systole to allow ejection into the pulmonary trunk and prevents backflow into the ventricle during diastole. This valve, along with the aortic valve, is a semilunar valve with three cusps and no chordae tendineae, unlike the atrioventricular valves. Its competence is essential for unidirectional flow into the pulmonary circulation for gas exchange.

incorrectas.B: The tricuspid valve is the atrioventricular valve between the right atrium and right ventricle, controlling flow into the ventricle during diastole — it is not involved in the ventricle's outflow to the pulmonary artery.
incorrectas.C: The mitral valve is the atrioventricular valve on the left side of the heart, regulating flow from the left atrium into the left ventricle, and has no anatomic relationship to the right ventricular outflow tract.
incorrectas.D: The aortic valve is the semilunar valve through which the left ventricle ejects oxygenated blood into the systemic circulation via the aorta, not the pathway used by the right ventricle to reach the lungs.

preguntas.q: Blood flows from the pulmonary artery to which structure for oxygenation?

e.correcta: Deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle travels through the pulmonary artery to the lungs, where it passes through the pulmonary capillary bed alongside alveoli for gas exchange — carbon dioxide diffuses out and oxygen diffuses in. This is the only arterial vessel in the body that carries deoxygenated blood, a classic exception worth memorizing because it inverts the usual artery/vein oxygenation rule. After oxygenation, the blood returns via the pulmonary veins to the left atrium.

incorrectas.B: The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs via the pulmonary veins, not from the pulmonary artery — it is downstream of the gas exchange step described in the question, not the site where oxygenation happens.
incorrectas.C: The aorta carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle out to the systemic circulation; it is on the opposite (left-sided, post-oxygenation) side of the circuit from the pulmonary artery, which feeds the right-sided, pre-oxygenation pathway.
incorrectas.D: The liver receives blood via the hepatic artery and portal vein for metabolic processing, not gas exchange, and has no role in the pulmonary circuit that oxygenates blood returning from the right heart.

preguntas.q: Which type of blood vessel has extensive elastic tissue and smooth muscle?

e.correcta: Arteries, particularly the larger elastic and muscular arteries, contain extensive elastic tissue (especially in the tunica media of elastic arteries like the aorta) that allows them to stretch during systole and recoil during diastole, smoothing pulsatile flow into a steadier stream (Windkessel effect), combined with abundant smooth muscle for regulating vessel tone and blood pressure. This structural combination is essential for withstanding high pulsatile pressures directly from the heart, which is why arteries have much thicker walls relative to their lumen than veins carrying the same volume of blood at lower pressure.

incorrectas.B: Veins have thinner walls with less elastic tissue and smooth muscle relative to their lumen size, since they operate under low pressure; they instead rely on valves and skeletal muscle pump action to return blood to the heart.
incorrectas.C: Capillaries consist of a single layer of endothelium with no smooth muscle or elastic tissue at all, which is what permits efficient diffusion of gases and nutrients across their thin walls.
incorrectas.D: Venules, like veins, have thin walls with minimal smooth muscle and elastic tissue compared to arteries, reflecting their role as low-pressure collecting vessels rather than pressure-regulating ones.

preguntas.q: Arteries are under what type of pressure?

e.correcta: Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure generated directly by ventricular contraction, so their walls are built thick with abundant smooth muscle and elastic tissue (especially in elastic arteries near the heart, which recoil during diastole to maintain flow) to withstand and buffer these pressures. This structural adaptation is why arterial pressure is measured (e.g., 120/80 mmHg) and why arterial injury causes brisk, pulsatile bleeding compared to venous bleeding.

incorrectas.B: Low pressure describes the venous system, which returns blood to the heart after it has passed through the high-resistance arterioles and capillary beds; veins have thinner walls and rely on valves and skeletal muscle pumps rather than high intrinsic pressure to move blood.
incorrectas.C: Negative pressure is not a feature of the systemic arterial or venous circuits under normal physiology; it is more relevant to specialized contexts like intrathoracic pressure during respiration, not arterial hemodynamics.
incorrectas.D: Isobaric (constant) pressure is incorrect because arterial pressure is pulsatile, fluctuating between systolic and diastolic values with each cardiac cycle rather than remaining constant.

preguntas.q: What is the term for the blood volume contained in the arteries?

e.correcta: Stressed volume refers to the blood volume in the arterial (and to a lesser extent venous) system that actively distends the vessel wall above its unstressed baseline, generating wall tension and thus arterial pressure per the law of Laplace; it is the blood volume that directly contributes to mean arterial pressure. Because arteries have thick, muscular, low-compliance walls, most of the blood volume within them is stressed volume, in contrast to the high-compliance venous system, which mostly holds unstressed volume.

incorrectas.B: Unstressed volume is the volume that fills a vessel without generating wall tension or significant pressure, and it predominates in the highly compliant venous system (the blood reservoir) rather than in the arteries, which are described in this question.
incorrectas.C: Central venous volume refers to blood volume in the great veins/right atrium relevant to venous return and preload, a distinct physiologic concept from the arterial stressed volume being asked about here.
incorrectas.D: Residual volume is a pulmonary physiology term describing the air remaining in the lungs after maximal expiration, and has no relationship to arterial blood volume or vascular wall tension.

preguntas.q: What are the smallest branches of arteries called?

e.correcta: Arterioles are the smallest branches derived from arteries, formed as the arterial tree progressively divides into ever-smaller vessels before ultimately transitioning into capillaries. They possess a thick relative layer of smooth muscle compared to their small lumen diameter, which allows them to act as the primary site of resistance regulation in the circulation — vasoconstriction and vasodilation of arterioles is what chiefly controls total peripheral resistance and blood pressure. This structural-functional link is why arterioles, not capillaries or venules, are often called "resistance vessels."

incorrectas.B: Capillaries are the smallest vessels overall but are not classified as arterial branches — they are the exchange vessels connecting the arterial and venous systems, consisting of a single endothelial layer with no smooth muscle.
incorrectas.C: Venules are the smallest branches of the venous system, receiving blood from capillaries, not the smallest branches of arteries; they belong to the opposite (return) side of the circulation.
incorrectas.D: Metarterioles are an intermediate vessel between arterioles and capillaries with a discontinuous smooth muscle coat (precapillary sphincters), but they are not what is classically defined as the smallest arterial branch — arterioles are smaller and more numerous overall.

preguntas.q: Arteriolar resistance is regulated primarily by which division of the nervous system?

e.correcta: Arteriolar smooth muscle tone, and thus systemic vascular resistance, is regulated primarily by the sympathetic nervous system through norepinephrine acting on alpha-1 adrenergic receptors to cause vasoconstriction (and to a lesser extent beta-2 receptors causing vasodilation in certain vascular beds like skeletal muscle). This continuous sympathetic tone allows rapid, widespread adjustments in resistance to maintain blood pressure and redistribute blood flow during stress, exercise, or hemorrhage.

incorrectas.B: The parasympathetic nervous system has minimal direct innervation of most arterioles (with limited exceptions like erectile tissue and some cranial vasculature) and is not the primary regulator of systemic arteriolar resistance.
incorrectas.C: The somatic nervous system innervates skeletal muscle via motor neurons for voluntary movement and has no direct role in regulating smooth muscle tone in arteriolar walls.
incorrectas.D: The enteric nervous system governs gastrointestinal motility and secretion semi-autonomously within the gut wall; while it can influence local splanchnic blood flow, it is not the primary system regulating systemic arteriolar resistance overall.

preguntas.q: What type of receptor is found on the arterioles of skin, splanchnic, and renal circulation?

e.correcta: Arterioles in the skin, splanchnic bed, and kidney are richly supplied with α1-adrenergic receptors, which when activated by norepinephrine cause Gq-mediated smooth muscle contraction and vasoconstriction. This allows the sympathetic nervous system to shunt blood away from these "non-essential" beds during stress, exercise, or hemorrhage, preserving perfusion to the heart and brain, which have different receptor profiles (predominantly β2 and autoregulation, respectively).

incorrectas.B: β1-adrenergic receptors are located predominantly on cardiac tissue (increasing heart rate and contractility) and on the juxtaglomerular apparatus (stimulating renin release), not diffusely on peripheral arterioles controlling vascular tone in these beds.
incorrectas.C: β2-adrenergic receptors mediate vasodilation (and bronchodilation) and are found on arterioles of skeletal muscle and coronary circulation, which needs increased blood flow during the fight-or-flight response — the opposite distribution from the vasoconstricting α1 receptors of skin/gut/kidney.
incorrectas.D: M3 muscarinic receptors mediate parasympathetic vasodilation via nitric oxide release from endothelium and are not the primary determinant of sympathetic tone in skin, splanchnic, or renal arterioles.

preguntas.q: What types of receptors are found on the arterioles of skeletal muscle?

e.correcta: Skeletal muscle arterioles express both α1-adrenergic receptors (mediating vasoconstriction, dominant at rest and during baseline sympathetic tone) and β2-adrenergic receptors (mediating vasodilation in response to circulating epinephrine, which becomes more prominent during exercise or the fight-or-flight response to redirect blood flow toward working muscle). This dual receptor expression allows skeletal muscle vasculature to shift from constriction to dilation depending on physiologic demand, unlike organs with only one dominant receptor type.

incorrectas.B: α1-adrenergic receptors alone would only account for vasoconstriction and would not explain the well-documented epinephrine-mediated vasodilation seen in skeletal muscle during exercise, which requires β2 receptor activity as well.
incorrectas.C: β1-adrenergic receptors are found predominantly in cardiac tissue (increasing heart rate and contractility) and the kidney (renin release), not as the receptor mediating vascular tone changes in skeletal muscle arterioles.
incorrectas.D: M2 muscarinic receptors are primarily found in cardiac tissue mediating parasympathetic slowing of heart rate, not on skeletal muscle arterioles, which lack significant direct parasympathetic innervation.

preguntas.q: When activated, α1-adrenergic receptors cause what effect on vascular smooth muscle?

e.correcta: Alpha-1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle couple to Gq proteins, activating phospholipase C to generate IP3 and DAG, which raises intracellular calcium and triggers actin-myosin cross-bridge formation, producing smooth muscle contraction (vasoconstriction). This is the mechanism behind alpha-1 agonists like phenylephrine being used clinically to raise blood pressure, and why alpha-1 blockers (e.g., prazosin) are used to lower peripheral vascular resistance in hypertension.

incorrectas.B: Relaxation of vascular smooth muscle is instead produced by beta-2 receptor activation (via Gs/cAMP) or by nitric oxide-mediated cGMP pathways, not by alpha-1 stimulation, which drives the opposite effect (contraction).
incorrectas.C: Hyperplasia (increased cell number) is a chronic structural/proliferative response that can occur with sustained trophic stimulation over time in certain pathologic states, but it is not the acute, direct functional effect of alpha-1 receptor activation on smooth muscle tone.
incorrectas.D: Apoptosis (programmed cell death) is not a consequence of alpha-1 adrenergic signaling; alpha-1 activation produces an acute contractile response through calcium-dependent mechanisms, not a cell-death pathway.

preguntas.q: When activated, β2-adrenergic receptors cause what effect on vascular smooth muscle?

e.correcta: Beta-2 adrenergic receptors on vascular smooth muscle are Gs-coupled, so activation raises cAMP, which activates protein kinase A to ultimately reduce intracellular calcium available for the myosin light chain kinase-driven contraction, producing smooth muscle relaxation and vasodilation. This is why beta-2 agonists preferentially dilate the vasculature of skeletal muscle and other beds during sympathetic 'fight or flight' activation, redirecting blood flow to where it's needed, in contrast to the vasoconstriction produced by alpha-1 receptor activation elsewhere.

incorrectas.B: Contraction of vascular smooth muscle is mediated by alpha-1 adrenergic receptors (via Gq, IP3, and calcium release), the opposite Gs-versus-Gq signaling pathway from the relaxation produced by beta-2 receptor activation.
incorrectas.C: Hypertrophy is a longer-term structural adaptation (seen for example in cardiac myocytes with chronic beta-1 stimulation or pressure overload), not the acute functional effect of beta-2 receptor activation on vascular smooth muscle tone.
incorrectas.D: Increased vascular permeability is mediated by mediators like histamine and bradykinin acting on endothelial cells (causing gap formation), not by beta-2 adrenergic receptor signaling on smooth muscle, which instead relaxes the vessel.

preguntas.q: Which type of blood vessel has the largest total cross-sectional and surface area?

e.correcta: Although individual capillaries are the smallest vessels, there are billions of them running in parallel throughout the body, and this enormous number gives capillaries the largest total cross-sectional area and surface area of any vessel type in the circulation. This large aggregate cross-sectional area causes blood flow velocity to slow dramatically as blood passes through the capillary bed (since velocity is inversely related to total cross-sectional area at constant flow), which is physiologically important because it maximizes the time available for diffusion of oxygen, nutrients, and waste products across the capillary wall.

incorrectas.B: Arteries have a relatively small total cross-sectional area compared to capillaries because there are far fewer of them and they are organized as a converging (proximal) rather than maximally branching network, so blood flow velocity through arteries is much faster than through capillaries.
incorrectas.C: Veins do have a larger cross-sectional area than arteries (contributing to their role as a blood volume reservoir), but their combined area is still smaller than the vast capillary bed, since veins represent the converging, not the maximally divergent, part of the circulation.
incorrectas.D: Arterioles have a smaller total cross-sectional area than capillaries; they are fewer and larger-caliber than the capillaries they feed into, and their primary function is regulating resistance and pressure rather than providing the massive surface area capillaries provide for exchange.

preguntas.q: Which type of blood vessel is the primary site of exchange of nutrients, water, and gases?

e.correcta: Capillaries are the primary site of exchange because their walls are only a single layer of endothelial cells with no smooth muscle or elastic tissue, minimizing diffusion distance, and their extensive branching creates a huge total cross-sectional area that slows blood flow velocity, giving nutrients, gases, and water time to diffuse across via pores, fenestrations, or pinocytosis depending on the capillary type. This structural specialization is why capillary density (and the presence of continuous, fenestrated, or sinusoidal types) varies by tissue metabolic demand.

incorrectas.B: Arteries have thick, muscular, elastic walls built to withstand high pressure and conduct blood away from the heart — their walls are far too thick for efficient diffusion, since their job is pressure regulation and distribution, not exchange.
incorrectas.C: Veins have thinner walls than arteries and function mainly as capacitance vessels that return blood to the heart, often against gravity (aided by valves) — their structure is suited for blood storage and return, not for gas/nutrient exchange.
incorrectas.D: Arterioles are the primary site of vascular resistance regulation, using smooth muscle to control blood flow into capillary beds — they play a critical role in regulating pressure and flow distribution but their walls are still too thick and muscular to serve as the main exchange surface.

preguntas.q: Which layer of the epidermis serves as the regenerative (stem cell) layer?

e.correcta: The stratum basale (basalis) is the deepest epidermal layer, sitting on the basement membrane, and contains the mitotically active keratinocyte stem cells that continuously divide to replenish the epidermis as cells migrate upward and differentiate into the more superficial layers. This regenerative property is why basal cell carcinoma arises from this layer and why the basal layer is critical for wound healing and epidermal turnover.

incorrectas.B: The stratum spinosum lies above the basal layer and is composed of keratinocytes connected by desmosomes ('spines' seen histologically), providing structural cohesion, but it is not the primary site of stem cell proliferation.
incorrectas.C: The stratum granulosum is where keratinocytes accumulate keratohyalin granules as part of terminal differentiation into corneocytes; these cells are already committed to dying and shedding, not dividing to regenerate the epidermis.
incorrectas.D: The stratum corneum is the outermost layer made of dead, anucleate, keratin-filled corneocytes that form the skin's protective barrier; being terminally differentiated and dead, it has no regenerative or stem cell capacity.

preguntas.q: Which epidermal layer is characterized by prominent desmosomes connecting keratinocytes (giving a 'spiny' appearance)?

e.correcta: The stratum spinosum owes its 'spiny' histologic appearance to numerous desmosomes, intercellular junctions that anchor adjacent keratinocytes together via intermediate filament attachments, which retract slightly during tissue fixation and create the characteristic spine-like intercellular bridges seen microscopically. This layer is also where keratinocytes begin synthesizing keratin filaments as they migrate outward toward the skin surface, making it structurally important for epidermal cohesion.

incorrectas.B: Stratum basalis is the deepest epidermal layer, containing mitotically active basal keratinocytes and melanocytes responsible for continual epidermal renewal, but it is not defined by the prominent desmosomal 'spiny' appearance seen in the layer above it.
incorrectas.C: Stratum lucidum is a thin, translucent layer found only in thick skin (palms and soles), composed of flattened, densely packed eleidin-containing cells without visible nuclei, distinct from the spiny desmosomal appearance of the stratum spinosum.
incorrectas.D: Stratum corneum is the outermost layer made of anucleate, fully keratinized corneocytes embedded in a lipid matrix that forms the skin's barrier, structurally very different from the desmosome-rich spinous layer beneath it.

preguntas.q: Which epidermal layer is characterized by keratohyalin granules within keratinocytes?

e.correcta: The stratum granulosum is the epidermal layer where keratinocytes accumulate keratohyalin granules, which contain profilaggrin and other proteins that aggregate keratin filaments and contribute to formation of the impermeable cornified envelope. This layer marks the transition point where cells begin the terminal differentiation process that ultimately produces the dead, keratin-packed corneocytes of the stratum corneum. Recognizing keratohyalin granules histologically is a classic way to identify this layer on skin biopsy.

incorrectas.B: The stratum basalis is the deepest layer, composed of mitotically active cuboidal/columnar stem cells that continuously regenerate the epidermis; it lacks keratohyalin granules since these cells have not yet begun terminal differentiation.
incorrectas.C: The stratum spinosum sits above the basal layer and is characterized by desmosome-rich 'prickly' intercellular connections and ongoing keratin synthesis, but keratohyalin granules have not yet formed at this stage of differentiation.
incorrectas.D: The stratum corneum is the outermost layer of dead, anucleate corneocytes filled with keratin and surrounded by lipid, representing the end product of differentiation — keratohyalin granules have already been degraded/incorporated by this point, not the defining feature of this layer.

preguntas.q: Which epidermal layer consists of keratin-filled, anucleate cells?

e.correcta: The stratum corneum is the outermost epidermal layer, composed of terminally differentiated keratinocytes that have lost their nuclei and organelles and become flattened, keratin-filled squames; this anucleate, keratin-packed structure forms a durable, water-resistant barrier that protects against desiccation, friction, and microbial entry. This layer is the end product of the keratinocyte maturation process that begins in the stratum basalis, making it the natural 'final stage' to associate with anucleate, keratinized cells.

incorrectas.B: Stratum basalis is the deepest epidermal layer, containing mitotically active, nucleated keratinocyte stem cells that continuously divide to replenish the epidermis — the opposite end of differentiation from the anucleate corneum cells.
incorrectas.C: Stratum granulosum cells are still nucleated (though the nuclei are beginning to degrade) and contain keratohyalin granules that contribute to keratin formation, but they have not yet lost their nuclei or become fully keratin-filled squames.
incorrectas.D: Stratum spinosum cells are nucleated, living keratinocytes connected by desmosomes ('spiny' appearance on histology), actively synthesizing keratin precursors, well before reaching the anucleate terminal state of the stratum corneum.

preguntas.q: Which skin layers contain nerve endings, blood vessels, lymphatics, and adnexal structures such as hair follicles and glands?

e.correcta: The dermis contains the vascular and neural supply of the skin along with adnexal (accessory) structures like hair follicles, sebaceous and sweat glands, while the underlying hypodermis (subcutaneous fat) houses larger vessels and nerves along with adipose tissue for insulation and energy storage. The epidermis above, by contrast, is avascular and depends on diffusion from the dermal papillae for nutrients, which is why it contains no vessels, nerves, or glands itself.

incorrectas.B: Epidermis and stratum corneum are avascular, keratinized epithelial layers that provide the physical barrier of the skin; they lack blood vessels, nerve endings, and adnexal structures, all of which are functionally dependent on the dermis beneath them.
incorrectas.C: Stratum basalis and stratum spinosum are sublayers of the epidermis responsible for keratinocyte proliferation and structural cohesion via desmosomes, not for housing vasculature or glands.
incorrectas.D: Stratum granulosum and stratum lucidum are epidermal layers involved in keratinization (granulosum forms keratohyalin granules; lucidum is seen in thick skin), and like all epidermal layers they are avascular and gland-free.

preguntas.q: Which epithelial cell junction prevents paracellular movement of solutes between cells?

e.correcta: Tight junctions (zonula occludens) seal the apical intercellular space between adjacent epithelial cells using claudin and occludin proteins that fuse the outer leaflets of neighboring cell membranes, physically blocking paracellular diffusion of solutes and maintaining apical-basal polarity. This barrier function is critical in epithelia like the gut lining and blood-brain barrier, where selective transcellular transport (rather than uncontrolled leakage between cells) is required for proper regulation of what crosses the epithelium.

incorrectas.B: Adherens junctions use cadherin proteins linked to the actin cytoskeleton to provide mechanical adhesion between cells, helping maintain tissue integrity and shape, but they do not seal the intercellular space against solute passage the way tight junctions do.
incorrectas.C: Desmosomes are spot-like adhesion structures that anchor intermediate filaments (like keratin) between cells, providing mechanical strength against shearing forces — important in tissues like epidermis, but they do not form a paracellular diffusion barrier.
incorrectas.D: Gap junctions are channels made of connexons that allow direct cytoplasmic communication and passage of ions and small molecules between adjacent cells, enabling electrical and metabolic coupling — the opposite function of sealing off the paracellular space.

preguntas.q: What proteins compose tight junctions?

e.correcta: Tight junctions are composed of transmembrane proteins claudins and occludins, which interlock between adjacent epithelial cells to seal the paracellular space, preventing free passage of ions and molecules and enforcing apical-basal cell polarity. This barrier function is essential in tissues like the intestinal epithelium and blood-brain barrier, and disruption of claudins/occludins (e.g., by certain bacterial toxins) can increase paracellular permeability and contribute to disease processes like secretory diarrhea.

incorrectas.B: Cadherins and catenins are the proteins that compose adherens junctions and desmosomes, providing mechanical adhesion between cells via calcium-dependent interactions, not the paracellular seal formed by tight junctions.
incorrectas.C: Connexins (which form connexons/gap junctions) create channels that allow direct cytoplasmic communication and ion/small-molecule passage between adjacent cells, the opposite function of the sealing barrier formed by tight junctions.
incorrectas.D: Integrins and laminins mediate cell adhesion to the extracellular matrix (as in hemidesmosomes), not cell-to-cell paracellular sealing, which is the specific role of claudins and occludins in tight junctions.

preguntas.q: Which epithelial cell junction connects the actin cytoskeletons of adjacent cells?

e.correcta: Adherens junctions (zonula adherens) use transmembrane cadherin proteins linked intracellularly to catenins, which in turn anchor to the actin cytoskeleton, forming a continuous adhesive belt just below the tight junctions that helps maintain epithelial sheet integrity and coordinate cell shape changes. This actin linkage is what distinguishes adherens junctions functionally from desmosomes, which perform an analogous adhesive role but anchor to intermediate filaments (keratin) instead.

incorrectas.B: Tight junctions (zonula occludens) use claudins and occludins to seal the paracellular space and regulate barrier permeability between cells, but they are linked to actin filaments too in some models — critically, their defining function is barrier sealing, not actin-linked adhesion, which is the specific role of adherens junctions in this question.
incorrectas.C: Desmosomes (macula adherens) are punctate adhesive junctions using cadherins (desmoglein/desmocollin) linked to intermediate (keratin) filaments, not actin, providing strong mechanical resistance to shearing forces — this intermediate filament linkage is the key distinguishing feature from adherens junctions.
incorrectas.D: Hemidesmosomes anchor the basal surface of epithelial cells to the underlying basement membrane using integrins linked to intermediate filaments, a cell-to-matrix (not cell-to-cell) attachment, and like desmosomes connect to keratin filaments rather than actin.

preguntas.q: Which epithelial cell junction connects the intermediate filaments of adjacent cells?

e.correcta: Desmosomes (macula adherens) are spot-like junctions where cadherin proteins (desmogleins and desmocollins) span the intercellular space and anchor to intracellular plaques that connect to keratin intermediate filaments, creating a mechanically strong network that resists shearing forces across the epidermis. This is why autoantibodies against desmogleins (as in pemphigus vulgaris) cause intraepidermal blistering — the intermediate filament-linked adhesion is lost. This link to intermediate filaments specifically (as opposed to actin) is the distinguishing structural feature of desmosomes.

incorrectas.B: Adherens junctions connect adjacent cells via cadherins linked intracellularly to the actin cytoskeleton (via catenins), not intermediate filaments, forming a continuous adhesion belt rather than discrete spot connections.
incorrectas.C: Tight junctions (zonula occludens) use claudins and occludins to seal the paracellular space and prevent molecule passage between cells; they do not connect to intermediate filaments and function in barrier formation, not filament anchoring.
incorrectas.D: Gap junctions are made of connexin proteins forming channels (connexons) that allow direct cytoplasmic communication and ion/small molecule passage between cells, unrelated to intermediate filament anchoring.

preguntas.q: What ion is required by cadherin proteins in epithelial cell junctions for their adhesive function?

e.correcta: Cadherins are calcium-dependent adhesion molecules — their extracellular cadherin repeat domains require bound Ca2+ ions to adopt the rigid, rod-like conformation needed for homophilic binding between cadherins on adjacent cells, which is essential for forming stable adherens junctions and desmosomes. Without calcium, cadherin extracellular domains become flexible and lose their adhesive capacity, which is exploited experimentally (e.g., calcium chelation with EDTA) to dissociate epithelial cell layers.

incorrectas.B: Sodium ions are central to processes like the resting membrane potential and secondary active transport (e.g., Na+/glucose cotransport), but they are not the ion required for cadherin-mediated adhesion, which specifically depends on calcium binding.
incorrectas.C: Potassium ions are critical for setting resting membrane potential and cardiac/neuronal action potentials, but they play no direct role in stabilizing the cadherin extracellular domain conformation needed for cell-cell adhesion.
incorrectas.D: Magnesium is an important cofactor for many enzymes (e.g., ATP-utilizing enzymes, kinases) and nucleic acid stability, but it is not the ion cadherins specifically require for their adhesive conformation — that role belongs to calcium, as reflected in the name 'cadherin' (calcium + adherin).

preguntas.q: Which epithelial cell junction permits electrical and chemical communication between adjacent cells?

e.correcta: Gap junctions are made of connexon channels that directly connect the cytoplasm of adjacent cells, allowing ions and small molecules to pass through — this permits electrical coupling (as in cardiac myocytes and smooth muscle) and metabolic/chemical communication between cells, unlike the purely mechanical junctions in skin.

incorrectas.B: Tight junctions seal the space between adjacent epithelial cells to prevent paracellular movement of molecules and establish apical-basal polarity — they block passage between cells rather than enabling communication through them.
incorrectas.C: Desmosomes are spot-weld-like adhesion structures that anchor intermediate filaments (keratin) between adjacent cells to resist mechanical stress — they provide structural strength, not a channel for electrical or chemical exchange.
incorrectas.D: Hemidesmosomes anchor the basal surface of epithelial cells to the underlying basement membrane, providing structural attachment to the extracellular matrix rather than a cell-to-cell communication channel.

preguntas.q: Gap junctions contain channel proteins called what, which allow communication between cells?

e.correcta: Gap junctions are formed by connexons, hexameric assemblies of connexin protein subunits, that align between adjacent cell membranes to create a direct channel allowing ions and small molecules (like second messengers) to pass between the cytoplasms of neighboring cells. This direct cytoplasmic continuity enables rapid electrical coupling and metabolic cooperation, which is why gap junctions/connexons are essential for coordinated contraction in cardiac and smooth muscle (allowing action potentials to spread cell-to-cell) as well as in tissues like the lens and skin.

incorrectas.B: Cadherins are transmembrane proteins that mediate calcium-dependent cell-cell adhesion at adherens junctions and desmosomes, providing mechanical strength between cells rather than forming a channel for direct cytoplasmic communication.
incorrectas.C: Integrins are transmembrane receptors that mediate cell-extracellular matrix adhesion (e.g., at hemidesmosomes and focal adhesions), not cell-cell communication channels like gap junctions.
incorrectas.D: Claudins (along with occludins) are the key structural proteins of tight junctions, which seal the space between adjacent cells to prevent paracellular movement of molecules — functionally the opposite role of gap junctions, which permit direct intercellular communication.

preguntas.q: Which epithelial cell junction connects keratin in basal cells to the underlying basement membrane?

e.correcta: Hemidesmosomes use integrins to anchor the keratin intermediate filament network of basal keratinocytes to the underlying basement membrane (via laminin in the lamina lucida), providing the structural link that keeps the epidermis attached to the dermis. Autoantibodies against hemidesmosomal proteins (as in bullous pemphigoid) cause subepidermal blistering because this basal attachment is disrupted, unlike desmosomal diseases which cause intraepidermal splitting.

incorrectas.B: Desmosomes connect keratin filaments between adjacent keratinocytes (cell-to-cell), not keratinocytes to the basement membrane — their disruption (e.g., in pemphigus vulgaris) causes intraepidermal, not subepidermal, blistering.
incorrectas.C: Adherens junctions link the actin cytoskeleton (via cadherins) between adjacent cells to provide mechanical continuity at the lateral cell membrane, not a connection between keratin and the basement membrane.
incorrectas.D: Gap junctions form channels for direct cytoplasmic communication between adjacent cells and have no structural role anchoring cells to the basement membrane.

preguntas.q: What protein in hemidesmosomes binds to fibronectin, laminin, or collagen in the basement membrane (and is not calcium-dependent)?

e.correcta: Integrins are transmembrane heterodimeric proteins in hemidesmosomes that anchor basal keratinocytes to the underlying basement membrane by binding extracellular matrix components such as laminin, fibronectin, and type IV collagen, and this binding is calcium-independent (unlike cadherins). This anchoring function is critical for epidermal-dermal adhesion, and its disruption (as in autoimmune attack on integrin/BP180 complexes in bullous pemphigoid) produces subepidermal blistering, distinguishing hemidesmosome pathology from intraepidermal blistering diseases.

incorrectas.B: Cadherins are calcium-dependent adhesion molecules found in desmosomes and adherens junctions, mediating cell-to-cell adhesion (e.g., desmoglein, a cadherin family member, in pemphigus vulgaris) — this is fundamentally different from hemidesmosomes, which attach cells to the basement membrane and do so independent of calcium.
incorrectas.C: Connexins form the subunits of gap junctions, which create channels for direct ion and small molecule passage between adjacent cells — an entirely different structural and functional role from the basement membrane anchoring performed by integrins.
incorrectas.D: Desmoglein is a cadherin-family adhesion protein found in desmosomes (cell-cell junctions targeted in pemphigus vulgaris), not hemidesmosomes, and like other cadherins it requires calcium for its adhesive function, unlike the integrin described here.

preguntas.q: What dermatologic lesion is described as a flat, well-circumscribed color change in the skin measuring less than 1 cm?

e.correcta: A macule is a flat, non-palpable, well-circumscribed area of color change in the skin measuring less than 1 cm, with the color change arising from pigment alteration (melanin), vascular changes, or hemorrhage without any change in skin texture or elevation. This 'flat and small' definition is what distinguishes macules from other primary lesions on exam and in dermatologic description, and freckles or petechiae are classic examples.

incorrectas.B: A patch is essentially a larger macule — a flat, non-palpable color change but measuring greater than 1 cm — so size is the key distinguishing feature from a macule, not the flatness (both are flat).
incorrectas.C: A papule is elevated and palpable due to solid tissue increase, which is the opposite of the flat, non-palpable character that defines a macule; papules represent a change in skin contour, macules do not.
incorrectas.D: A plaque is an elevated, flat-topped lesion generally larger than 1 cm, combining palpable elevation with substantial surface area — this contrasts with a macule, which by definition has no elevation at all.

preguntas.q: What dermatologic lesion is a macule that is larger than 1 cm?

e.correcta: A patch is defined as a flat, non-palpable area of skin color change greater than 1 cm in diameter, essentially a larger version of a macule — the size threshold (1 cm) is the key distinguishing criterion tested here, analogous to how a nodule is a larger papule. Examples include vitiligo patches or café-au-lait spots, which are flat but span a larger surface area than a macule.

incorrectas.B: A macule is by definition a flat lesion measuring less than 1 cm; once it exceeds 1 cm while remaining flat, it is reclassified as a patch, so 'macule' cannot be the answer to a lesion described as larger than 1 cm.
incorrectas.C: A papule is a raised, palpable lesion less than 1 cm, distinguished from a macule/patch by being elevated above the skin surface, not simply by size — this question is about a flat lesion's size threshold, not elevation.
incorrectas.D: A nodule is a raised, palpable lesion greater than 1 cm (larger version of a papule), so it shares the size criterion but not the flatness — nodules are elevated, whereas the lesion in the question (an enlarged macule) remains flat, making 'patch' the correct term.

preguntas.q: What dermatologic lesion is an elevated, solid skin lesion measuring less than 1 cm?

e.correcta: A papule is defined as a small, elevated, solid skin lesion less than 1 cm in diameter, with elevation coming from a localized increase in cells or deposited material within the epidermis or superficial dermis (as in acne, warts, or insect bites). The key distinguishing features tested are 'solid' (not fluid-filled) and 'elevated' (palpable), which separate it from flat color changes and from larger or fluid-containing lesions.

incorrectas.B: A macule is a flat, non-palpable area of color change less than 1 cm — it lacks any elevation, which is the opposite of the defining feature of a papule (freckles and flat pigmented spots are classic macules).
incorrectas.C: A plaque is also elevated and solid, but by definition it is a larger, flat-topped lesion typically greater than 1 cm (often described as a confluence of papules, as in psoriasis), so size is what separates it from a papule.
incorrectas.D: A nodule shares the 'elevated and solid' quality of a papule but is deeper and larger, generally exceeding 1 cm and often palpable within the dermis or subcutaneous tissue, so nodules are essentially larger, deeper papules rather than the correct answer here.

preguntas.q: What dermatologic lesion is a papule that is larger than 1 cm?

e.correcta: A plaque is defined as a flat-topped, elevated lesion greater than 1 cm in diameter, essentially a large papule or confluence of papules with a broad surface area — classic examples include psoriatic plaques. The size cutoff of 1 cm is the key distinguishing feature examiners test, since the underlying morphology (elevated, palpable) is otherwise similar to a papule.

incorrectas.B: A patch is a flat, non-palpable lesion greater than 1 cm — it is the macular (flat) counterpart to a plaque, differing by lacking elevation, whereas the question specifies a larger papule, which is by definition elevated.
incorrectas.C: A papule itself is defined as an elevated lesion less than 1 cm in diameter, so once it exceeds 1 cm it is reclassified as a plaque, making the term 'papule' technically excluded once size increases.
incorrectas.D: A nodule is a larger, deeper, more solid palpable lesion (often extending into the dermis or subcutis) rather than the superficial broadening described for a plaque; nodules are distinguished by depth and firmness, not just surface diameter.

preguntas.q: The ventral horn of the spinal cord contains two types of motor neurons: one that makes muscles contract and another that regulates muscle spindle sensitivity. What are these two types, respectively?

e.correcta: Alpha motor neurons in the ventral horn have large-diameter axons that innervate extrafusal skeletal muscle fibers directly, producing the force that causes muscle contraction. Gamma motor neurons are smaller neurons that innervate the intrafusal fibers of the muscle spindle, adjusting spindle sensitivity so the spindle continues to accurately signal stretch even as the muscle shortens during alpha-driven contraction (alpha-gamma coactivation). This dual system lets the nervous system maintain proprioceptive feedback across the full range of muscle length, which is essential for smooth, coordinated movement.

incorrectas.B: Beta and delta are not the names of ventral horn motor neuron types; beta fibers refer to touch/pressure afferents and delta fibers to fast pain afferents in sensory nerve classification, not motor neuron subtypes controlling contraction or spindle sensitivity.
incorrectas.C: Ia and Ib are sensory afferent fiber types (Ia from muscle spindles, Ib from Golgi tendon organs) that carry information into the spinal cord, not efferent motor neurons in the ventral horn that drive muscle contraction or regulate spindle sensitivity.
incorrectas.D: Upper and lower motor neuron is a clinical/anatomical distinction referring to corticospinal neurons versus the neurons that directly innervate muscle, not the specific alpha/gamma division within the lower motor neuron pool that governs contraction versus spindle sensitivity.

preguntas.q: Which type of motor neuron directly makes skeletal muscle contract?

e.correcta: Alpha motor neurons originate in the anterior horn of the spinal cord (or cranial nerve motor nuclei) and directly innervate extrafusal skeletal muscle fibers via the neuromuscular junction, releasing acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors to trigger the muscle action potential and contraction. As the final common pathway for all voluntary and reflexive movement, their loss (as in ALS or poliovirus infection) produces classic lower motor neuron signs: flaccid paralysis, hyporeflexia, fasciculations, and atrophy.

incorrectas.B: Gamma motor neurons innervate intrafusal fibers within the muscle spindle, adjusting spindle sensitivity to stretch so the stretch reflex remains accurate as the muscle shortens — they modulate sensory feedback rather than directly generating the force of contraction in the working (extrafusal) muscle fibers.
incorrectas.C: Preganglionic sympathetic neurons are autonomic neurons that originate in the spinal cord's intermediolateral column and synapse on postganglionic neurons in sympathetic ganglia — they regulate involuntary functions like heart rate and vasoconstriction, not the direct innervation of skeletal muscle.
incorrectas.D: Postganglionic parasympathetic neurons innervate smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands as part of the autonomic nervous system, using mostly muscarinic acetylcholine receptors — this is a completely separate system from the somatic motor pathway that makes skeletal muscle contract.

preguntas.q: Which type of motor neuron increases the sensitivity of muscle spindles to stretch?

e.correcta: Gamma motor neurons innervate the contractile polar ends of intrafusal muscle fibers within the muscle spindle, causing those ends to contract and take up slack in the spindle's central sensory region; this keeps the spindle taut and sensitive to stretch even as the whole muscle (via extrafusal fibers driven by alpha motor neurons) shortens during a contraction, a mechanism called alpha-gamma coactivation that preserves the stretch reflex's sensitivity across the full range of muscle length.

incorrectas.B: Alpha motor neurons innervate extrafusal muscle fibers, the main contractile fibers responsible for generating force and movement, but they do not adjust the sensitivity of the muscle spindle itself; without gamma coactivation, spindle sensitivity would actually be lost (go slack) during alpha-driven muscle shortening.
incorrectas.C: Ib afferent fibers carry sensory information FROM Golgi tendon organs (sensing muscle tension) TO the spinal cord, providing input rather than motor output, and they play no role in adjusting muscle spindle sensitivity, which is a gamma motor neuron function.
incorrectas.D: Renshaw cells are inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord that provide recurrent inhibition of alpha motor neurons (negative feedback to limit motor neuron firing), a completely different circuit from the gamma motor neuron system that tunes muscle spindle sensitivity.

preguntas.q: How many neurons are required in the lateral corticospinal tract pathway for voluntary muscle movement?

o.A: Two (upper motor neuron and lower motor neuron)
o.C: Three (including an interneuron in the thalamus)
o.D: Four (including two interneurons in the spinal cord)

e.correcta: The lateral corticospinal tract uses a two-neuron pathway for voluntary movement: the upper motor neuron (UMN) has its cell body in the primary motor cortex and descends through the internal capsule, crossing at the pyramidal decussation in the medulla, to synapse onto the lower motor neuron (LMN) in the anterior horn of the spinal cord; the LMN then exits via the ventral root to directly innervate skeletal muscle. This two-neuron chain is a foundational concept for localizing lesions (UMN vs LMN signs) in neurologic exams.

incorrectas.B: A single continuous neuron running from cortex to muscle does not exist in this pathway — there is an obligatory synapse between the UMN and LMN in the spinal cord anterior horn, which is exactly why UMN and LMN lesions produce distinguishable clinical signs.
incorrectas.C: Adding a third neuron with a thalamic interneuron describes sensory (ascending) pathways like the dorsal column-medial lemniscus system, which does relay through the thalamus, not the descending motor corticospinal pathway, which has no thalamic relay.
incorrectas.D: Four neurons with two spinal interneurons overcomplicates the classic two-neuron corticospinal architecture; while spinal interneurons do modulate motor output in various reflex circuits, the direct voluntary corticospinal pathway itself is described as UMN-to-LMN, a two-neuron chain.

preguntas.q: Where are the cell bodies of upper motor neurons primarily found?

o.B: Ventral horn of the spinal cord

e.correcta: Upper motor neurons originate in the primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus, Brodmann area 4) as well as premotor and supplementary motor areas, and their axons descend as the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts to synapse on lower motor neurons in the spinal cord ventral horn or brainstem motor nuclei. This anatomic distinction is the basis for localizing lesions clinically: UMN lesions (cortex/tract) produce spasticity and hyperreflexia, while LMN lesions produce flaccidity and hyporeflexia.

incorrectas.B: The ventral horn of the spinal cord houses the cell bodies of lower motor neurons, which directly innervate skeletal muscle, not upper motor neurons, which instead originate in the cortex and synapse onto these ventral horn cells.
incorrectas.C: The dorsal root ganglion contains cell bodies of primary sensory (afferent) neurons, not motor neurons, and is unrelated to either the upper or lower motor neuron pathways.
incorrectas.D: The cerebellar cortex modulates and coordinates motor output (timing, precision) via connections to motor pathways but does not contain the cell bodies of the corticospinal upper motor neurons themselves.

preguntas.q: The axons of upper motor neurons destined for peripheral nerves travel in which tract?

e.correcta: The corticospinal tract carries upper motor neuron axons from the primary motor cortex through the internal capsule and brainstem, decussating at the pyramids in the medulla, to ultimately synapse on lower motor neurons in the spinal cord that innervate peripheral nerves to skeletal muscle. This tract is the principal pathway for voluntary control of limb and trunk musculature, and its lesions produce the classic upper motor neuron signs of spasticity, hyperreflexia, and a positive Babinski sign.

incorrectas.B: The corticobulbar tract also carries upper motor neuron axons, but it terminates on cranial nerve motor nuclei in the brainstem to control facial, head, and neck muscles — not on the peripheral nerves of the limbs and trunk.
incorrectas.C: The spinothalamic tract is an ascending sensory pathway carrying pain and temperature information from the periphery to the thalamus, not a descending motor pathway.
incorrectas.D: The dorsal column-medial lemniscus tract is also an ascending sensory pathway, carrying fine touch, vibration, and proprioception, and has nothing to do with upper motor neuron output.

preguntas.q: Upper motor neurons synapse with the cell bodies of lower motor neurons in which part of the spinal cord?

e.correcta: Upper motor neuron axons descending in the corticospinal tract synapse onto lower motor neuron cell bodies located in the ventral (anterior) horn of the spinal cord gray matter, from which the lower motor neuron axons exit via the ventral root to innervate skeletal muscle. This anatomic arrangement explains the classic UMN versus LMN lesion patterns: a lesion above this synapse produces UMN signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia), while damage to the anterior horn cells themselves or their axons produces LMN signs (flaccid weakness, fasciculations, atrophy), as seen in diseases like ALS.

incorrectas.B: The dorsal (posterior) horn receives incoming sensory afferent fibers carrying information like pain, temperature, and touch from primary sensory neurons — it is part of the sensory relay pathway, not the location of motor neuron synapses.
incorrectas.C: The lateral horn, present at spinal cord levels T1-L2/L3, contains preganglionic sympathetic autonomic neurons, not the somatic lower motor neurons targeted by corticospinal upper motor neuron input.
incorrectas.D: The central canal region is a fluid-filled channel continuous with the ventricular system that contains cerebrospinal fluid, not neuronal cell bodies serving as synaptic targets for descending motor pathways.

preguntas.q: Lower motor neurons leave the spinal cord and synapse with skeletal muscle at which structure?

e.correcta: Lower motor neurons exit the spinal cord via the ventral horn and ventral root, travel through peripheral nerves, and synapse with skeletal muscle fibers at the neuromuscular junction, where acetylcholine released from the motor neuron terminal binds nicotinic receptors on the muscle membrane to trigger depolarization and contraction. This synapse is the final common pathway for all voluntary movement and is the target of diseases like myasthenia gravis and toxins like botulinum toxin.

incorrectas.B: The Golgi tendon organ is a sensory receptor located at the muscle-tendon junction that detects muscle tension and provides afferent (not motor efferent) feedback to the spinal cord, the opposite direction of information flow from a motor neuron synapse.
incorrectas.C: The muscle spindle capsule houses intrafusal fibers and sensory afferents that detect muscle length and stretch, again a sensory structure providing afferent input rather than a site of lower motor neuron synapse onto skeletal muscle.
incorrectas.D: The dorsal root ganglion contains the cell bodies of sensory (afferent) neurons, not motor neurons, and is unrelated to where lower motor neurons synapse with muscle.

preguntas.q: Upper motor neurons initially descend in which position relative to the lower motor neurons they will eventually innervate (before decussation)?

e.correcta: Upper motor neurons of the corticospinal tract originate in the motor cortex and descend ipsilaterally through the internal capsule, cerebral peduncles, and pons before the majority decussate at the pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla to then synapse on contralateral lower motor neurons in the spinal cord. This anatomical arrangement explains why a lesion above the decussation (e.g., cortical stroke) causes contralateral weakness, while a lesion below the decussation (e.g., spinal cord injury) causes ipsilateral weakness — a key localizing principle in neurology.

incorrectas.B: Contralateral would describe the relationship only after decussation has occurred; before crossing in the medulla, upper motor neurons remain on the same side as their cortical origin, so 'contralateral' mischaracterizes the pre-decussation anatomy.
incorrectas.C: Bilateral descent would imply simultaneous innervation on both sides before any crossing occurs, which is not how the corticospinal tract is organized — each tract descends on one side only until the discrete point of decussation in the medulla.
incorrectas.D: Dorsal position describes a spatial location within the spinal cord white matter (as with dorsal column sensory tracts), not the laterality relationship between upper motor neurons and their eventual lower motor neuron targets, which is what this question addresses.

preguntas.q: Is the lateral corticospinal tract classified as an ascending or descending tract?

o.D: Neither; it is a commissural tract

e.correcta: The lateral corticospinal tract carries voluntary motor commands from the primary motor cortex down through the internal capsule, crossing (decussating) at the pyramids of the medulla, and descending in the lateral funiculus of the spinal cord to synapse on lower motor neurons. Because it conveys signals from the brain down to the periphery, it is classified as a descending tract — this is the principal pathway for voluntary limb movement and its lesions produce upper motor neuron signs.

incorrectas.B: Ascending tracts, like the dorsal columns or spinothalamic tract, carry sensory information from the periphery up to the brain; the corticospinal tract runs in the opposite direction (motor output from cortex to muscle), so it cannot be classified as ascending.
incorrectas.C: A single tract has one direction of information flow; the lateral corticospinal tract is purely efferent (motor), carrying no ascending sensory information, so it cannot be both ascending and descending.
incorrectas.D: Commissural tracts (like the corpus callosum) connect corresponding areas across the two cerebral hemispheres; the corticospinal tract instead runs longitudinally from cortex to spinal cord and does decussate, but that crossing at the pyramids does not make it a commissural tract.

preguntas.q: The motor component of skeletal muscle reflexes (such as the muscle stretch reflex) is mediated by which type of motor neuron?

e.correcta: The efferent (motor) limb of skeletal muscle reflexes, including the muscle stretch reflex, is carried by lower motor neurons — the alpha motor neurons whose cell bodies reside in the ventral horn of the spinal cord and whose axons directly innervate extrafusal skeletal muscle fibers via the neuromuscular junction. This is why a lesion of the lower motor neuron itself (as opposed to descending upper motor neuron pathways) abolishes the reflex (hyporeflexia/areflexia) along with flaccid paralysis and fasciculations.

incorrectas.B: Upper motor neurons originate in the cortex or brainstem and descend to influence and modulate lower motor neuron activity, but they do not directly synapse on skeletal muscle; their lesions classically cause hyperreflexia (loss of inhibitory modulation) rather than mediating the basic reflex arc itself.
incorrectas.C: Postganglionic sympathetic neurons are part of the autonomic nervous system and innervate smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands, not skeletal muscle, so they have no role in the somatic muscle stretch reflex.
