incorrectas.C: The diaphragm is the primary muscle of inspiration (it contracts and flattens to increase thoracic volume); it does not act during expiration, whose passive nature at rest depends on the diaphragm relaxing, not contracting.
incorrectas.D: Sternocleidomastoid and scalene muscles are accessory muscles of inspiration, recruited during heavy breathing to elevate the rib cage further; they play no role in expiration at any level of exertion.

preguntas.q: Which respiratory center, located in the reticular formation and containing inspiratory and expiratory centers, coordinates the basic rhythm of breathing?

e.correcta: The medullary respiratory center, located in the reticular formation of the medulla, contains the dorsal respiratory group (mainly inspiratory, setting the basic rhythm via inspiratory ramp signals) and the ventral respiratory group (containing both inspiratory and expiratory neurons, more active during increased ventilatory demand like exercise), together generating the fundamental automatic rhythm of breathing that occurs even without conscious input. This basic rhythm is then modulated by the pontine respiratory centers (apneustic and pneumotaxic centers), which fine-tune the timing and depth of breaths, but the actual rhythm-generating pacemaker activity originates in the medulla.

incorrectas.B: The pontine respiratory center (including the pneumotaxic center) modulates and fine-tunes the rate and depth of breathing by inhibiting inspiration at the right moment, but it does not itself generate the basic automatic rhythm; that pacemaker function resides in the medulla.
incorrectas.C: The cortex allows voluntary control over breathing (e.g., holding your breath, speaking), but this voluntary pathway can be overridden by the automatic medullary rhythm when CO2/pH drive becomes strong enough, showing the cortex is not the site of basic rhythm generation.
incorrectas.D: The hypothalamus integrates autonomic and endocrine responses to things like temperature and emotion, which can influence breathing indirectly (e.g., panting, hyperventilation with anxiety), but it is not the anatomic site that generates the basic inspiratory/expiratory rhythm.

preguntas.q: The dorsal and ventral respiratory groups are located in which part of the brainstem?

e.correcta: The dorsal respiratory group (primarily inspiration) and ventral respiratory group (both inspiration and active expiration) are medullary nuclei that generate the basic automatic rhythm of breathing, receiving input from chemoreceptors and higher centers to adjust rate and depth. This medullary rhythm generator works together with the pontine respiratory centers (apneustic and pneumotaxic centers), which fine-tune and smooth the transition between inspiration and expiration but do not generate the basic rhythm themselves.

incorrectas.B: The pons contains the pneumotaxic and apneustic centers, which modulate and refine the pattern/timing of breathing (e.g., inhibiting inspiration to prevent overinflation), but the basic rhythmic generation resides in the dorsal and ventral respiratory groups of the medulla, not the pons.
incorrectas.C: The midbrain is not involved in generating or directly controlling the basic respiratory rhythm; it contains structures like the superior/inferior colliculi and substantia nigra, unrelated to the dorsal/ventral respiratory groups.
incorrectas.D: The cerebellum coordinates movement, balance, and motor learning, and while it may have some subtle roles in respiratory pattern adjustment during voluntary movements, it is not the location of the core dorsal/ventral respiratory groups that generate breathing rhythm.

preguntas.q: The dorsal respiratory group receives sensory input from peripheral chemoreceptors via which two cranial nerves?

e.correcta: The dorsal respiratory group in the medulla receives afferent input from peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid and aortic bodies) via the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX, from the carotid bodies) and the vagus nerve (CN X, from the aortic bodies), allowing the respiratory center to adjust ventilation in response to changes in arterial PO2, PCO2, and pH detected peripherally. This is the same CN IX/X pairing responsible for carrying baroreceptor information to the medulla, making it a high-yield combination to remember for autonomic reflex arcs.

incorrectas.B: Trigeminal (CN V) and facial (CN VII) nerves carry sensory information from the face and taste, respectively, and are not involved in relaying peripheral chemoreceptor signals to the respiratory centers.
incorrectas.C: Vagus (CN X) is correct for the aortic bodies, but hypoglossal (CN XII) is a purely motor nerve to the tongue muscles and carries no chemoreceptor sensory information, so this pairing is incorrect.
incorrectas.D: Glossopharyngeal (CN IX) is correct for the carotid bodies, but accessory nerve (CN XI) is a motor nerve to the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles and does not carry chemoreceptor afferents.

preguntas.q: Which lecithin:sphingomyelin (L/S) ratio, measured by amniocentesis, indicates a mature fetal lung?

e.correcta: An L/S ratio greater than 2 indicates that lecithin (phosphatidylcholine) production by maturing type II pneumocytes has sufficiently outpaced sphingomyelin, signaling adequate surfactant production and low risk of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome if delivery occurs. This ratio is used clinically via amniocentesis to help time delivery or decide whether antenatal corticosteroids are needed to accelerate fetal lung maturity.

incorrectas.B: An L/S ratio less than 1 indicates immature lungs with insufficient surfactant, placing the neonate at high risk for respiratory distress syndrome — the opposite conclusion from the maturity indicated by a ratio greater than 2.
incorrectas.C: An L/S ratio of exactly 1 reflects a transitional period around 32 weeks gestation where lecithin and sphingomyelin are roughly equal, still considered inadequate evidence of full lung maturity compared to the greater-than-2 threshold.
incorrectas.D: A ratio between 1 and 1.5 falls in an intermediate zone still associated with a meaningful risk of surfactant deficiency and is not the established cutoff clinicians use to confirm fetal lung maturity.

preguntas.q: Which two phospholipids are the most abundant components of pulmonary surfactant?

e.correcta: Pulmonary surfactant is primarily composed of phospholipids, with dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (lecithin) being the major surface-tension-reducing component and sphingomyelin present as well (its relatively stable level is why it is used as the denominator in the L/S ratio to track lecithin's rise). Lecithin's amphipathic structure allows it to line the air-liquid interface of alveoli and disrupt the cohesive forces of water molecules, dramatically lowering surface tension and preventing alveolar collapse per the law of Laplace.

incorrectas.B: Cholesterol and phosphatidylserine are present in cell membranes generally but are not the principal or defining components of pulmonary surfactant measured clinically for fetal lung maturity.
incorrectas.C: Phosphatidylethanolamine and phosphatidylinositol are minor phospholipid components found in surfactant and other membranes but are not the two most abundant, clinically tracked components (lecithin and sphingomyelin) used in maturity assessment.
incorrectas.D: Sphingosine and ceramide are sphingolipid metabolic intermediates/backbone molecules, not the major structural phospholipids of surfactant; they are more relevant to sphingolipid signaling and storage diseases than to surfactant function.

preguntas.q: The alveolar walls are lined by which two types of epithelial cells?

o.A: Type I and type II pneumocytes
o.B: Goblet cells and ciliated columnar cells

e.correcta: The alveolar wall is lined by type I pneumocytes, which are thin, squamous cells that make up about 97% of the alveolar surface area and are optimized for efficient gas diffusion, and type II pneumocytes, which are cuboidal cells that secrete pulmonary surfactant to reduce alveolar surface tension and also serve as the progenitor cells that can regenerate type I cells after lung injury. This division of labor — thin cells for diffusion, specialized cells for surfactant production and regeneration — is central to understanding both normal gas exchange physiology and pathologies like ARDS, where type I cell damage impairs diffusion and surfactant dysfunction promotes alveolar collapse.

incorrectas.B: Goblet cells and ciliated columnar cells line the conducting airways (trachea, bronchi) to produce and clear mucus, not the alveolar walls, which lack cilia and goblet cells entirely since these structures would interfere with gas exchange.
incorrectas.C: Club (Clara) cells line the bronchioles, where they secrete a protective surfactant-like substance and detoxify inhaled toxins, while basal cells serve as an epithelial stem cell population in the conducting airways — neither of these forms the epithelial lining of the alveolar wall itself.
incorrectas.D: Alveolar macrophages and mast cells are immune cells that reside within the alveolar space and interstitium performing surveillance and defense functions, but they are not the epithelial cells that structurally form the alveolar wall lining.

preguntas.q: Which type of pneumocyte has the capacity to regenerate into both type I and type II pneumocytes?

e.correcta: Type II pneumocytes are the alveolar stem/progenitor cells: in addition to producing surfactant, they retain the capacity to proliferate and differentiate into both new type II cells and terminally differentiated type I pneumocytes after alveolar injury (e.g., in ARDS or diffuse alveolar damage). Type I cells themselves are thin, squamous, and terminally differentiated for optimal gas exchange, so they cannot divide or regenerate the epithelium — repair depends entirely on the type II cell pool. This regenerative role is why type II hyperplasia is a classic histologic finding during the proliferative phase of lung injury.

incorrectas.B: Type I pneumocytes are terminally differentiated, flattened cells optimized for gas diffusion across a thin membrane; they lack the proliferative capacity and organelle machinery (cuboidal shape, lamellar bodies) needed to regenerate the alveolar lining.
incorrectas.C: Club (Clara) cells are progenitor cells for the bronchiolar epithelium, giving rise to ciliated and secretory cells in the terminal bronchioles, but they are not the reserve/stem cell population for the alveolar epithelium itself.
incorrectas.D: Alveolar macrophages are phagocytic immune cells derived from circulating monocytes; they clear debris and pathogens in the alveolar space but have no epithelial regenerative capacity.

preguntas.q: What substance, a mixture of phospholipids lining the alveoli, functions to reduce alveolar surface tension?

e.correcta: Surfactant, produced by type II pneumocytes and composed mainly of dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC) along with surfactant proteins, reduces alveolar surface tension by disrupting the cohesive forces between water molecules lining the alveoli. This prevents smaller alveoli (which would otherwise have higher collapsing pressure per LaPlace's law) from collapsing into larger ones and reduces the work of breathing — its deficiency in premature infants (due to immature type II pneumocytes) causes neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

incorrectas.B: Mucus is secreted by goblet cells and submucosal glands in the conducting airways to trap particles and pathogens as part of mucociliary clearance, but it does not line the alveoli or reduce surface tension there.
incorrectas.C: Elastin is a structural connective tissue protein that provides elastic recoil to lung parenchyma, allowing passive exhalation, but it does not function as a surface-tension-reducing phospholipid mixture.
incorrectas.D: Collagen provides tensile strength and structural support within the lung interstitium and alveolar walls, but like elastin, it is a structural protein rather than a surface-tension-lowering phospholipid layer.

preguntas.q: Surfactant reduces alveolar surface tension by disrupting the intermolecular forces between molecules of what substance?

e.correcta: Surface tension in the alveoli arises from the strong cohesive hydrogen bonding between water molecules at the air-liquid interface, which would otherwise pull the alveolar walls inward and promote collapse (per LaPlace's law, smaller alveoli are at greater risk). Surfactant, a phospholipid mixture rich in dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC) secreted by type II pneumocytes, inserts itself between these water molecules and disrupts their intermolecular attraction, thereby lowering surface tension and stabilizing alveoli — especially smaller ones, where surfactant molecules become more concentrated as the alveolus shrinks.

incorrectas.B: Oxygen is a dissolved gas in the alveolar space and does not generate the surface tension problem being addressed; surfactant's job is not related to intermolecular forces among O2 molecules.
incorrectas.C: Carbon dioxide is likewise a gas being exchanged across the alveolar membrane, not the source of surface tension; surfactant's mechanism targets the water lining, not gas molecules.
incorrectas.D: Surfactant reduces tension by acting on water's intermolecular forces, not by disrupting bonds among surfactant molecules themselves — the therapeutic/physiologic target is the air-water interface, not surfactant-surfactant interactions.

preguntas.q: What is the term for the collapse of small alveoli that occurs in the absence of adequate surfactant?

e.correcta: Atelectasis refers to collapse of previously expanded lung tissue, and when small alveoli lack adequate surfactant, the law of Laplace (P = 2T/r) means smaller alveoli generate higher collapsing pressure for a given surface tension, so without surfactant to lower tension preferentially in small alveoli, they collapse into larger ones. This is the pathophysiology behind neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, where insufficient surfactant from immature type II pneumocytes leads to widespread microatelectasis and poor gas exchange.

incorrectas.B: Pneumothorax is air in the pleural space causing lung collapse from an external mechanical cause (trauma, rupture of a bleb), not the intrinsic alveolar instability from high surface tension that occurs with surfactant deficiency.
incorrectas.C: Emphysema is permanent enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchiole due to destruction of alveolar walls (often from protease-antiprotease imbalance), which is essentially the opposite process of alveolar collapse.
incorrectas.D: Bronchiectasis is permanent dilation of bronchi from chronic infection/inflammation destroying the airway wall, an airway-level structural problem rather than an alveolar surface-tension problem caused by surfactant deficiency.

preguntas.q: Which lecithin is the most important component of pulmonary surfactant?

e.correcta: Dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine (DPPC) is the principal phospholipid component of pulmonary surfactant, produced by type II pneumocytes; its two saturated palmitic acid tails pack tightly at the air-liquid interface, allowing it to dramatically lower surface tension (via the Laplace relationship, P = 2T/r) and prevent alveolar collapse at end-expiration, especially in smaller alveoli that would otherwise be most prone to collapse. A relative deficiency of DPPC (as in preterm infants with immature type II pneumocytes) causes neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, which is why the lecithin:sphingomyelin ratio is used clinically to assess fetal lung maturity.

incorrectas.B: Sphingomyelin is used as a stable reference lipid in the lecithin:sphingomyelin (L:S) ratio precisely because its concentration in amniotic fluid stays relatively constant while lecithin (DPPC) rises with maturity — it is not itself a functional surface-tension-reducing component of surfactant.
incorrectas.C: Phosphatidylserine is a minor membrane phospholipid better known for its externalization as an 'eat-me' signal on apoptotic cells; it is not a major structural or functional component of pulmonary surfactant.
incorrectas.D: Phosphatidylinositol is present in small amounts in surfactant and can be used as a secondary marker of fetal lung maturity in some contexts, but it is not the dominant, most important surfactant lipid — that role belongs to DPPC.

preguntas.q: In fetal development, surfactant synthesis begins as early as which gestational week?

e.correcta: Surfactant synthesis by type II pneumocytes begins as early as week 20 of gestation, during the canalicular stage of lung development when respiratory bronchioles and future alveolar ducts start forming, though levels remain low and clinically insufficient until a marked surge occurs around weeks 34-36. Knowing that synthesis starts this early (even though adequate surfactant for extrauterine survival isn't reliably present until much later) helps explain why extremely preterm infants can occasionally survive with intensive support and antenatal corticosteroids, which accelerate type II pneumocyte maturation.

incorrectas.B: Week 8 falls within the embryonic/early pseudoglandular stage, when the lung is still forming its bronchial tree and far too immature for any surfactant-producing type II pneumocytes to exist yet.
incorrectas.C: Week 28 is well after surfactant synthesis has already begun (week 20) and is more relevant as a viability milestone than the actual onset of surfactant production.
incorrectas.D: Week 35 is near when surfactant levels become abundant enough to reliably prevent respiratory distress syndrome, but this is long after the initial onset of synthesis at week 20, not the starting point the question asks about.

preguntas.q: Mature levels of pulmonary surfactant are typically not achieved until around which gestational week?

e.correcta: Type II pneumocytes begin producing surfactant around week 26 but do not reach mature, adequate levels until approximately week 35, which is why infants born before this point are at significant risk for neonatal respiratory distress syndrome due to high alveolar surface tension and atelectasis. This timeline is clinically important because it guides decisions about antenatal corticosteroid administration to accelerate fetal lung maturity in anticipated preterm delivery.

incorrectas.B: Week 20 is too early — surfactant production by type II pneumocytes has not even significantly begun at this stage, as it typically starts around week 26 and doesn't mature until much later.
incorrectas.C: Week 24 marks roughly the beginning of measurable surfactant production (and viability threshold), not the point of mature surfactant levels, which is why infants born around this gestational age remain at very high risk for RDS.
incorrectas.D: Week 40 is full term, well beyond when mature surfactant levels are reached (around week 35); using week 40 as the maturation threshold would incorrectly suggest that infants born from 35-39 weeks lack adequate surfactant, which is not the case.

preguntas.q: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (NRDS) is most strongly associated with which type of birth?

e.correcta: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome results from insufficient surfactant production by type II pneumocytes, which normally begin producing adequate surfactant later in gestation (surfactant levels rise sharply after about 34-36 weeks, reflected clinically by a lecithin-to-sphingomyelin ratio ≥2). Premature infants are born before this maturation is complete, so their alveoli have high surface tension and collapse at end-expiration (atelectasis), causing hypoxemia and increased work of breathing. This is why antenatal corticosteroids are given to mothers at risk of preterm delivery — they accelerate fetal type II pneumocyte surfactant production to reduce NRDS risk.

incorrectas.B: Post-term birth means the fetus has had extra time for lung maturation, including surfactant production, so NRDS is not a concern; if anything, post-term pregnancies raise concerns about placental insufficiency and meconium aspiration, not surfactant deficiency.
incorrectas.C: Cesarean birth at term does not itself cause surfactant deficiency (the lungs have already matured normally by term); elective term C-section is more classically associated with transient tachypnea of the newborn from delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid, a distinct and milder condition than NRDS.
incorrectas.D: Twin birth at term does not inherently cause NRDS since gestational age (lung maturity), not twin status, drives surfactant sufficiency; twins are at higher risk mainly when they are born prematurely, in which case the risk comes from prematurity itself, not from being a twin.

preguntas.q: What lecithin:sphingomyelin (L/S) ratio is considered indicative of adequate surfactant production?

e.correcta: An L/S ratio greater than 2 in amniotic fluid indicates that fetal type II pneumocytes are producing adequate lecithin (phosphatidylcholine, the major component of surfactant) relative to sphingomyelin, signaling sufficient pulmonary maturity to reduce the risk of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome after birth. This ratio is used clinically to help decide timing of delivery when preterm birth is being considered, since surfactant deficiency causes high alveolar surface tension, alveolar collapse, and the characteristic 'ground-glass' appearance and diffuse atelectasis of RDS.

incorrectas.B: An L/S ratio less than 1 indicates poor surfactant production and a high risk of respiratory distress syndrome, essentially the opposite finding from adequate maturity, since lecithin production has not yet outpaced sphingomyelin.
incorrectas.C: An L/S ratio equal to 1 reflects an intermediate, transitional stage in lung maturation (roughly corresponding to the crossover point around 32 weeks) and does not yet indicate adequate surfactant for reduced RDS risk.
incorrectas.D: An L/S ratio less than 1.5 still falls short of the greater-than-2 threshold used to indicate reduced RDS risk, and would instead suggest an intermediate-to-immature surfactant status.

preguntas.q: What lecithin:sphingomyelin (L/S) ratio is predictive of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (NRDS)?

e.correcta: An L/S ratio less than 1.5 in amniotic fluid indicates insufficient surfactant (lecithin/phosphatidylcholine) production relative to sphingomyelin, predicting inadequate alveolar surface tension reduction after birth and thus a high risk of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, most classically seen in premature infants whose type II pneumocytes have not yet matured enough to produce adequate surfactant. This ratio is clinically used (via amniocentesis) to assess fetal lung maturity before elective preterm delivery, guiding decisions about administering antenatal corticosteroids to accelerate surfactant production.

incorrectas.B: An L/S ratio greater than 2 is generally considered reassuring for fetal lung maturity, indicating adequate surfactant production and a low risk of respiratory distress syndrome, the opposite of the risk profile described in the question.
incorrectas.C: A ratio greater than 3 is not the threshold used in standard clinical practice for lung maturity assessment; ratios above 2 are already considered mature, so this value does not reflect the recognized clinical cutoff.
incorrectas.D: A ratio equal to 2 sits at or near the boundary typically considered indicative of adequate (not high-risk) lung maturity in most clinical references, rather than representing the risk threshold for NRDS.

preguntas.q: In neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, how does respiratory effort change after birth?

e.correcta: In neonatal (infant) respiratory distress syndrome, insufficient surfactant (from immature type II pneumocytes, typically in preterm infants) leads to high alveolar surface tension and progressive alveolar collapse (atelectasis); as compliance worsens, the infant's respiratory effort increases in an attempt to compensate, producing tachypnea, grunting, nasal flaring, and intercostal/subcostal retractions. Recognizing that respiratory effort increases (rather than the infant simply becoming apneic) is key to identifying the compensatory phase before eventual respiratory fatigue and failure if untreated.

incorrectas.B: A decrease in respiratory effort would suggest the infant is fatiguing or entering respiratory failure/apnea, which is a late, ominous finding rather than the expected initial physiologic response to surfactant deficiency — the classic early presentation is increased work of breathing as the infant compensates for poor lung compliance.
incorrectas.C: Respiratory effort does not remain unchanged in RDS — the loss of surfactant and resulting alveolar collapse forces the infant to generate substantially more inspiratory effort to keep alveoli open, producing visible signs of distress like retractions and grunting.
incorrectas.D: Effort ceasing entirely would represent respiratory arrest, an end-stage and life-threatening event, not the expected clinical course early in surfactant-deficient RDS, where the hallmark is increased compensatory work of breathing rather than immediate cessation.

preguntas.q: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome may present with which abnormal respiratory rate finding, along with use of accessory muscles and grunting?

e.correcta: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (NRDS) results from surfactant deficiency (most often due to prematurity, before type II pneumocytes mature around 35 weeks), causing high alveolar surface tension and diffuse alveolar collapse. The infant compensates for the resulting hypoxia and reduced compliance by breathing faster (tachypnea), while also recruiting accessory muscles (retractions) and grunting (expiring against a partially closed glottis to generate auto-PEEP and keep alveoli open).

incorrectas.B: Bradypnea (abnormally slow breathing) would worsen hypoxia and is not the physiologic response to surfactant deficiency; a distressed neonate compensates by breathing faster, not slower, so bradypnea would instead suggest fatigue or impending respiratory failure.
incorrectas.C: Apnea (cessation of breathing) can occur in extremely premature infants but is a distinct, more severe finding, not the classic accompanying sign of NRDS alongside grunting and retractions — NRDS is characterized by increased respiratory effort, not absence of it.
incorrectas.D: A normal respiratory rate would not fit a neonate in visible distress with grunting and accessory muscle use; the whole point of these compensatory findings is that the infant is working hard to breathe faster than normal to offset poor gas exchange.

preguntas.q: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome classically shows diffuse granularity of the lungs with what descriptive appearance on chest X-ray?

e.correcta: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome results from surfactant deficiency (often due to prematurity, before adequate type II pneumocyte surfactant production), causing widespread alveolar collapse (atelectasis) that on chest X-ray produces a diffuse 'ground-glass' appearance along with air bronchograms, reflecting innumerable microatelectatic alveoli against aerated bronchi. Recognizing this ground-glass pattern helps distinguish NRDS from other neonatal lung pathologies and underscores why antenatal corticosteroids (to accelerate fetal lung maturity) and postnatal surfactant replacement are the mainstays of prevention/treatment.

incorrectas.B: A honeycomb appearance describes end-stage pulmonary fibrosis with cystic airspaces, a chronic adult lung disease pattern (e.g., usual interstitial pneumonia), not the acute surfactant-deficient atelectasis of neonatal RDS.
incorrectas.C: A water-bottle appearance on chest X-ray describes cardiomegaly from a large pericardial effusion, an unrelated cardiac silhouette finding rather than a lung parenchymal pattern seen in RDS.
incorrectas.D: A cannonball appearance refers to multiple round pulmonary metastases (classically from renal cell carcinoma or choriocarcinoma), a pattern of discrete nodules entirely different from the diffuse ground-glass haziness of surfactant-deficient neonatal lungs.

preguntas.q: Which gastrointestinal pathology is associated with neonatal respiratory distress syndrome due to hypoxemia?

e.correcta: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (surfactant deficiency, typically in preterm infants) causes hypoxemia and reduced mesenteric perfusion as blood flow is redistributed away from the gut to protect vital organs; this ischemia predisposes the immature bowel mucosa to necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), where bacterial invasion of the ischemic bowel wall causes necrosis, pneumatosis intestinalis, and risk of perforation. This link between prematurity, hypoxemia, and gut ischemia is why NEC is a feared complication in preemies with RDS. Recognizing this connection helps explain why sick, hypoxic preterm infants are watched closely for feeding intolerance and abdominal distension.

incorrectas.B: Hirschsprung disease is a congenital absence of ganglion cells (failure of neural crest cell migration) in the distal colon causing functional obstruction; it's a developmental/neurocristopathy issue present from birth, not something caused by postnatal hypoxemia from respiratory distress.
incorrectas.C: Pyloric stenosis is hypertrophy of the pyloric sphincter muscle causing projectile vomiting, typically presenting in the first few weeks of life; its etiology involves genetic and environmental factors affecting muscle hypertrophy, not ischemia from neonatal hypoxemia.
incorrectas.D: Intussusception is telescoping of one bowel segment into another, most classically triggered by a lead point such as a Meckel diverticulum or lymphoid hyperplasia (often post-viral) in older infants; it is not a recognized ischemic consequence of neonatal RDS-related hypoxemia.

preguntas.q: What treatment may be administered to the mother before birth to help prevent neonatal respiratory distress syndrome?

e.correcta: Maternal corticosteroids (e.g., betamethasone) given before an anticipated preterm birth cross the placenta and accelerate fetal type II pneumocyte maturation, boosting surfactant production and lung structural development, which reduces the incidence and severity of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome caused by surfactant deficiency in premature infants. This intervention works by essentially speeding up the natural glucocorticoid-driven surge in surfactant synthesis that normally occurs late in gestation.

incorrectas.B: Maternal antibiotics are used to treat or prevent infection (e.g., for preterm premature rupture of membranes or Group B strep prophylaxis), but they do not stimulate fetal lung maturation or surfactant production.
incorrectas.C: Maternal insulin is used to manage maternal diabetes, and poorly controlled maternal hyperglycemia actually delays fetal lung maturation (fetal hyperinsulinemia inhibits surfactant production) — insulin administration itself does not prevent neonatal RDS.
incorrectas.D: Maternal anticoagulants are used for thromboembolic disease or certain cardiac conditions and have no role in promoting fetal surfactant synthesis or lung maturity.

preguntas.q: Systemic amyloidosis is a recognized cause of which renal disease presentation?

e.correcta: In systemic amyloidosis, misfolded protein fibrils (e.g., AL or AA amyloid) deposit in the glomerular basement membrane and mesangium, thickening and disrupting the filtration barrier so that large amounts of protein leak into the urine, producing nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, and hyperlipidemia — the classic nephrotic syndrome picture. Amyloid deposits classically show apple-green birefringence under polarized light after Congo red staining, and renal involvement is one of the most common and clinically significant manifestations of systemic amyloidosis.

incorrectas.B: Acute interstitial nephritis is typically a hypersensitivity reaction to drugs (e.g., NSAIDs, penicillins) causing tubulointerstitial inflammation with fever, rash, and eosinophiluria — a mechanism unrelated to extracellular fibril deposition in glomeruli.
incorrectas.C: Renal artery stenosis results from atherosclerosis or fibromuscular dysplasia narrowing the renal artery lumen, causing renin-mediated hypertension, not from amyloid infiltrating the glomerular filtration apparatus.
incorrectas.D: Diabetes insipidus reflects a defect in ADH production or renal responsiveness to ADH, causing inability to concentrate urine — this is a tubular/collecting duct water-handling problem, distinct from the glomerular protein-leak mechanism of amyloid nephropathy.

preguntas.q: In systemic amyloidosis, which organ is most commonly involved?

e.correcta: The kidney is the most commonly involved organ in systemic amyloidosis because its highly permeable glomerular capillaries and large filtration surface area make it especially susceptible to amyloid fibril deposition, and renal dysfunction (proteinuria progressing to nephrotic syndrome and renal failure) is frequently the presenting and most clinically significant manifestation. This is why renal biopsy with Congo red staining is a key diagnostic step when amyloidosis is suspected.

incorrectas.B: The liver can be involved in systemic amyloidosis (hepatomegaly, deposition in space of Disse), but it is not the most commonly or clinically dominant organ affected compared to the kidney.
incorrectas.C: The spleen is a classic site of amyloid deposition (producing 'sago' or 'lardaceous' spleen patterns), but splenic involvement is typically less clinically significant than renal involvement and is not the most commonly affected organ overall.
incorrectas.D: The heart is importantly involved in systemic amyloidosis (particularly AL and transthyretin amyloidosis, causing restrictive cardiomyopathy), and cardiac involvement often determines prognosis, but renal involvement remains more common across systemic amyloidosis broadly.

preguntas.q: Deposition of free immunoglobulin light chains in tissue, as seen in multiple myeloma, produces which type of amyloidosis?

e.correcta: In multiple myeloma, malignant plasma cells overproduce monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains (kappa or lambda), and when these misfolded light chain fragments deposit in tissues in a beta-pleated sheet configuration, they form primary (AL) amyloid — the "L" standing for light chain — which can infiltrate the heart, kidneys, and other organs causing restrictive cardiomyopathy, nephrotic syndrome, and macroglossia. This link between a plasma cell dyscrasia and the resulting amyloid subtype is a key biochemistry-to-clinical-pathology connection tested on exams.

incorrectas.B: Secondary (AA) amyloidosis arises from chronic inflammatory conditions (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, chronic infections, familial Mediterranean fever) where sustained elevation of serum amyloid A protein (an acute-phase reactant) leads to its deposition as amyloid — this is driven by chronic inflammation, not by a plasma cell clone producing light chains.
incorrectas.C: Dialysis-related amyloidosis results from accumulation of beta-2 microglobulin in patients on long-term hemodialysis, since this protein is normally cleared by the kidneys and dialysis membranes don't filter it efficiently — it has no relationship to immunoglobulin light chain overproduction from myeloma.
incorrectas.D: Senile systemic amyloidosis results from deposition of normal (wild-type) transthyretin protein, typically affecting the heart in elderly patients, and is unrelated to any clonal plasma cell process — the protein involved (transthyretin) is entirely different from the immunoglobulin light chains implicated in myeloma-associated amyloid.

preguntas.q: Deposition of amyloid-beta around cerebral vessels in Alzheimer's disease causes which condition?

e.correcta: In Alzheimer disease, amyloid-beta peptide (cleaved from amyloid precursor protein) is deposited not only in neuritic plaques within the brain parenchyma but also within the walls of small-to-medium cerebral vessels, producing cerebral amyloid angiopathy. This vascular amyloid deposition weakens vessel walls, making them prone to rupture, which is why cerebral amyloid angiopathy is a leading cause of lobar (as opposed to deep, hypertensive) intracerebral hemorrhage in older adults. It's a useful concept linking Alzheimer pathology to a distinct hemorrhagic stroke pattern.

incorrectas.B: Vasculitis is inflammatory damage to vessel walls (immune-mediated, e.g., by ANCA or immune complexes) causing luminal narrowing or aneurysm formation; amyloid deposition around vessels is a passive protein accumulation process, not an inflammatory vasculitic one.
incorrectas.C: Atherosclerosis is lipid-driven plaque formation within the intima of large and medium arteries via endothelial injury, LDL infiltration, and foam cell formation; it is a distinct process from amyloid protein deposition in small cerebral vessel walls and typically affects different vessel types.
incorrectas.D: Moyamoya disease is a progressive stenosis of the internal carotid arteries and their branches leading to compensatory fragile collateral vessel formation ('puff of smoke' appearance on angiography); it is an idiopathic vasculopathy unrelated to amyloid-beta deposition.

preguntas.q: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy most significantly increases the risk of which complication?

o.B: Ischemic stroke from large vessel occlusion

e.correcta: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) is caused by deposition of beta-amyloid protein within the walls of small-to-medium cortical and leptomeningeal arteries, which weakens the vessel wall (replacing normal smooth muscle with amyloid, causing fibrinoid necrosis and microaneurysm formation) and predisposes to spontaneous rupture. This classically produces recurrent, lobar (cortical/subcortical, sparing deep structures like the basal ganglia) intracranial hemorrhages in normotensive elderly patients, distinguishing it from hypertensive hemorrhage, which favors deep structures like the basal ganglia, thalamus, and pons.

incorrectas.B: Ischemic stroke from large vessel occlusion is typically due to atherosclerotic thromboembolism or cardioembolism affecting large arteries, not the small-vessel amyloid deposition of CAA, which weakens vessel walls to cause hemorrhage rather than occluding vessels to cause ischemia.
incorrectas.C: Subarachnoid hemorrhage from aneurysm rupture is usually due to berry (saccular) aneurysms at the circle of Willis, associated with conditions like ADPKD or connective tissue disorders — a distinct pathology from CAA's diffuse amyloid-weakened small cortical vessels causing lobar intraparenchymal bleeds.
incorrectas.D: Venous sinus thrombosis results from a prothrombotic or hypercoagulable state causing clot within the dural venous sinuses, an entirely different vascular compartment and mechanism from the arterial-wall amyloid deposition that defines CAA.

preguntas.q: Which yellow-brown "wear and tear" pigment accumulates with normal aging?

e.correcta: Lipofuscin is a yellow-brown, insoluble pigment composed of oxidized lipid-protein complexes derived from lysosomal breakdown of damaged organelles and membranes, and it accumulates within cells (especially cardiac myocytes, neurons, and hepatocytes) as a normal byproduct of aging and free radical-mediated lipid peroxidation over a lifetime. It is generally considered an innocent marker of cellular 'wear and tear' rather than a cause of cellular dysfunction itself.

incorrectas.B: Hemosiderin is an iron-storage pigment derived from ferritin aggregates, seen after hemorrhage or in iron overload states (e.g., hemosiderosis, hemochromatosis), reflecting iron handling rather than normal age-related lipid oxidation.
incorrectas.C: Melanin is the brown-black pigment produced by melanocytes via tyrosinase-mediated synthesis, responsible for skin/hair pigmentation, not the aging-related intracellular accumulation product described in the question.
incorrectas.D: Bilirubin is the yellow breakdown product of heme catabolism, relevant to jaundice and liver/biliary disease, not an intracellular 'wear and tear' pigment that accumulates with normal aging.

preguntas.q: Lipofuscin pigment characteristically accumulates within which cellular compartment?

e.correcta: Lipofuscin is a yellow-brown "wear-and-tear" pigment composed of oxidized, cross-linked lipid-protein complexes derived from the peroxidation of polyunsaturated lipids in cell membranes; these indigestible remnants accumulate within lysosomes because lysosomal enzymes cannot fully degrade the oxidized, cross-linked material. It is commonly seen in aging cells (e.g., cardiac myocytes, neurons, hepatocytes) and, while itself harmless, serves as a histologic marker of chronic oxidative stress and free radical injury over a cell's lifetime.

incorrectas.B: Mitochondria are the site of oxidative phosphorylation and a major source of the reactive oxygen species that initiate lipid peroxidation, but lipofuscin itself accumulates as an end-product within lysosomes (via autophagy of damaged organelles/membranes), not stored within the mitochondria themselves.
incorrectas.C: The endoplasmic reticulum is involved in protein synthesis/folding and lipid synthesis, and can show stress changes (e.g., dilation in reversible injury), but it is not the site where lipofuscin granules accumulate.
incorrectas.D: The nucleus houses genetic material and is not a site of lipofuscin deposition; nuclear changes in aging/injury involve chromatin condensation or pyknosis, a distinct process from cytoplasmic lysosomal pigment accumulation.

preguntas.q: Which cellular adaptation is defined by an increase in the number of cells in a tissue?

e.correcta: Hyperplasia is defined as an increase in the number of cells in a tissue or organ, typically driven by increased cell division in response to hormonal stimulation or a growth-promoting stimulus (e.g., endometrial hyperplasia from unopposed estrogen, or compensatory hyperplasia of the liver after partial resection). It occurs only in tissues capable of mitotic division and can be physiologic or pathologic, and importantly it can regress if the stimulus is removed, distinguishing it from neoplastic proliferation.

incorrectas.B: Hypertrophy is an increase in the SIZE of individual cells (via increased protein synthesis and organelle content), not an increase in cell number — classically seen in cardiac myocytes or skeletal muscle, which are largely incapable of dividing.
incorrectas.C: Metaplasia is a reversible change in which one differentiated cell type is replaced by another differentiated cell type better suited to a new stressor (e.g., squamous metaplasia in the bronchus from smoking), not an increase in overall cell number.
incorrectas.D: Dysplasia refers to disordered, atypical cellular growth with loss of normal maturation and architecture, representing a preneoplastic change, rather than simply an increase in the number of normal-appearing cells.

preguntas.q: Which cellular adaptation is defined by an increase in the size of individual cells?

e.correcta: Hypertrophy is defined as an increase in the size of individual cells (without cell division), typically driven by increased synthesis of structural proteins and organelles in response to increased functional demand or hormonal stimulation — classic examples include cardiac myocyte hypertrophy in hypertension and skeletal muscle hypertrophy with resistance training, both occurring in permanent, non-dividing cell populations that must adapt by growing larger rather than proliferating.

incorrectas.B: Hyperplasia is an increase in the number of cells via mitotic division, seen in tissues capable of proliferation (e.g., endometrial hyperplasia from estrogen stimulation), which is a distinct adaptation from hypertrophy's increase in individual cell size without added cell number.
incorrectas.C: Metaplasia is the reversible replacement of one differentiated cell type by another better suited to a new stressor (e.g., squamous metaplasia in the bronchus from chronic smoking), a change in cell type/identity rather than a change in cell size.
incorrectas.D: Atrophy is a decrease in cell size and/or number due to decreased functional demand, denervation, or nutrient deprivation — the direct opposite of the size increase seen in hypertrophy.

preguntas.q: Gene activation, increased protein synthesis, and increased organelle production are hallmarks of which cellular adaptation?

e.correcta: Hypertrophy is an increase in the size of individual cells achieved through activation of specific genes, increased synthesis of structural proteins, and an increase in the number of organelles (e.g., mitochondria, sarcomeres) — mechanisms classically seen in cardiac myocytes responding to chronic pressure overload (e.g., hypertension causing left ventricular hypertrophy) or skeletal muscle responding to resistance training. This adaptation occurs in permanent, non-dividing cells that cannot compensate for increased workload by proliferating, so they instead grow larger and more metabolically robust.

incorrectas.B: Hyperplasia is an increase in the NUMBER of cells through cell division, which requires a tissue capable of mitosis; it is a distinct adaptation from hypertrophy's cell enlargement via increased protein/organelle synthesis and occurs in different tissue types (e.g., epithelium versus cardiac muscle).
incorrectas.C: Apoptosis is programmed cell death involving caspase-mediated cellular disassembly, representing the opposite of a growth adaptation — it is a mechanism of cell number reduction, not gene activation for cellular enlargement.
incorrectas.D: Autophagy is a catabolic process in which cells degrade their own organelles and proteins via lysosomes, typically to survive stress or nutrient deprivation — this represents a decrease, not increase, in cellular protein and organelle content.

preguntas.q: Controlled proliferation of stem cells and differentiated cells, increasing cell number in a tissue, describes which process?

e.correcta: Hyperplasia is the controlled, regulated increase in the number of cells in a tissue or organ, arising from proliferation of stem cells and/or existing differentiated cells that retain mitotic capacity, typically in response to a physiologic or compensatory stimulus (e.g., hormonal stimulation of endometrial hyperplasia, or compensatory liver hyperplasia after partial hepatectomy). Because it is a controlled adaptive response (unlike neoplasia), hyperplasia is generally reversible if the stimulus is removed, distinguishing it from dysregulated, autonomous proliferation seen in cancer.

incorrectas.B: Hypertrophy is an increase in the size of individual cells (not their number), typically occurring in cells with limited or no capacity to divide (such as cardiac or skeletal muscle), driven by increased synthesis of structural proteins/organelles rather than by cellular proliferation.
incorrectas.C: Metaplasia is the reversible replacement of one differentiated cell type with another, more suited to a new physiologic stress (e.g., squamous metaplasia of the bronchial epithelium in smokers), which involves a change in cell type/identity rather than an increase in overall cell number.
incorrectas.D: Necrosis is a form of pathologic, uncontrolled cell death typically due to ischemia, toxins, or trauma, resulting in cell loss and tissue damage — the opposite of the proliferative increase in cell number that defines hyperplasia.

preguntas.q: Permanent tissues such as cardiac muscle, skeletal muscle, and nerve respond to increased demand through which adaptation(s)?

e.correcta: Permanent (terminally differentiated) tissues like cardiac muscle, skeletal muscle, and neurons have exited the cell cycle and lost meaningful capacity to divide (hyperplasia), so their only means of responding to increased functional demand is hypertrophy — an increase in individual cell size through increased synthesis of structural proteins and organelles. This is why chronic pressure overload (e.g., hypertension) causes the heart to enlarge via myocyte hypertrophy rather than by generating new cardiac myocytes, in contrast to labile or stable tissues that retain proliferative capacity.

incorrectas.B: Hyperplasia requires cells capable of re-entering the cell cycle to divide; permanent tissues like cardiac and skeletal muscle and neurons are terminally differentiated and essentially cannot undergo clinically significant hyperplasia in response to demand.
incorrectas.C: Both hypertrophy and hyperplasia would apply to labile or stable tissues (like liver or skin) that retain regenerative/proliferative capacity, but permanent tissues are specifically defined by their inability to proliferate, limiting them to hypertrophy alone.
incorrectas.D: Metaplasia is the reversible replacement of one differentiated cell type with another (e.g., squamous metaplasia in the bronchus from smoking), typically an adaptation to chronic irritation, not a response to increased functional demand in permanent tissues.

preguntas.q: A decrease in tissue mass due to a reduction in cell size or number describes which cellular change?

e.correcta: Atrophy is the reduction in tissue mass that results from a decrease in the size and/or number of existing cells, often due to disuse, denervation, decreased hormonal stimulation, reduced blood supply, or aging — the cells shrink and downregulate organelles (autophagy of components) to lower their metabolic demand rather than dying outright. This is a reversible adaptive response (e.g., muscle atrophy after limb immobilization) distinguishing it from cell death processes.

incorrectas.B: Hypoplasia refers to underdevelopment or incomplete development of an organ or tissue during growth, resulting in fewer cells than normal from the outset (a developmental/congenital process), rather than a previously normal tissue shrinking afterward as in atrophy.
incorrectas.C: Necrosis is pathologic, uncontrolled cell death due to injury (ischemia, toxins, trauma) with cell swelling, membrane rupture, and an inflammatory response — it destroys cells rather than describing a controlled, adaptive reduction in cell size or number.
incorrectas.D: Aplasia is the complete failure of an organ or tissue to develop at all during embryogenesis (absence of the primordial cells), a much more extreme and congenital condition than the gradual size/number reduction described in atrophy.

preguntas.q: Atrophy occurring through a decrease in cell number is mediated by which process?

e.correcta: Atrophy is a decrease in cell size and/or number in response to decreased workload, denervation, diminished blood supply, or nutrient deprivation; when it proceeds through a reduction in cell number, the mechanism is apoptosis, a regulated, energy-dependent process involving caspase activation, chromatin condensation, and cell shrinkage without eliciting inflammation. This programmed removal of cells is distinct from the shrinkage of individual surviving cells (decreased organelles and cytoplasm), which is the other component of atrophy.

incorrectas.B: Necrosis is an unregulated, pathologic form of cell death characterized by cell swelling, membrane rupture, and release of intracellular contents that provokes an inflammatory response — this is not the controlled mechanism underlying physiologic atrophy.
incorrectas.C: Autophagy is the process by which a cell degrades its own organelles and cytoplasmic components via lysosomes to survive nutrient deprivation; it contributes to the shrinkage of individual atrophic cells but is not itself the mechanism that reduces cell number.
incorrectas.D: Pyknosis (nuclear condensation) is one morphologic feature seen during apoptosis and necrosis, but it is a descriptive nuclear change, not a standalone mechanism that accounts for the loss of cells in atrophy.

preguntas.q: Atrophy via decreased cell size can occur through degradation of the cytoskeleton by which system?

e.correcta: In atrophy, cells shrink in size (not necessarily number) by degrading their own structural components, and the ubiquitin-proteasome system is a major pathway for this: cytoskeletal and other cytosolic proteins are tagged with ubiquitin chains and then fed into the proteasome for ATP-dependent proteolytic destruction. This pathway is upregulated in states like disuse atrophy (immobilized limbs) and cachexia, where muscle fibers actively dismantle their own contractile and cytoskeletal proteins to reduce cell mass. It works alongside autophagy (which degrades organelles) as the two principal mechanisms underlying atrophic cell shrinkage.

incorrectas.B: The caspase cascade is the executioner pathway of apoptosis, causing controlled cell death via DNA fragmentation and cell dismantling — this is a distinct process from atrophy, which is reversible shrinkage of a living cell rather than programmed death of the cell.
incorrectas.C: The complement system is part of innate immunity, driving opsonization, inflammation, and membrane attack complex formation to kill pathogens or abnormal cells — it is not a mechanism cells use internally to degrade their own cytoskeleton during atrophy.
incorrectas.D: Autophagolysosomal fusion does contribute to atrophy, but it targets organelles (like mitochondria) broadly via lysosomal digestion, not specifically the cytoskeleton, and restricting it to 'mitochondria only' misdescribes the pathway responsible for cytoskeletal breakdown.

preguntas.q: Atrophy via decreased cell size may also occur through degradation of cellular organelles by which process?

e.correcta: Autophagy is the process by which a cell forms double-membraned autophagosomes around its own damaged or excess organelles, which then fuse with lysosomes for enzymatic digestion, recycling the resulting materials for cellular metabolism — this organelle turnover reduces cell mass and contributes to the size reduction seen in atrophy. This mechanism is a protective, adaptive response that lets a stressed or nutrient-deprived cell shrink and survive rather than die, and it complements the ubiquitin-proteasome system, which handles individual cytosolic and cytoskeletal proteins rather than whole organelles.

incorrectas.B: The ubiquitin-proteasome system degrades individually tagged cytosolic proteins (like cytoskeletal components) via the proteasome, but it is not the pathway responsible for degrading whole organelles, which require the lysosomal, autophagic route instead.
incorrectas.C: Phagocytosis by macrophages refers to external immune cells engulfing material from outside a cell (like dead cells, debris, or pathogens), which is a distinct process from a living cell using its own internal autophagic machinery to self-degrade its organelles during atrophy.
incorrectas.D: Complement-mediated lysis is an immune mechanism that punches holes in target cell membranes via the membrane attack complex, causing cell death — this is unrelated to the internal, adaptive organelle degradation process of autophagy that underlies atrophic shrinkage.

preguntas.q: Replacement of one differentiated cell type by another describes which process?

e.correcta: Metaplasia is an adaptive, reversible change in which one differentiated cell type is replaced by another differentiated cell type better suited to withstand a chronic stressor (e.g., squamous metaplasia of respiratory epithelium in smokers, or Barrett esophagus where squamous epithelium becomes columnar due to acid reflux). It occurs through reprogramming of stem cell differentiation pathways rather than through malignant change, and it is reversible if the inciting stimulus is removed, though persistent metaplasia can progress toward dysplasia.

incorrectas.B: Dysplasia refers to disordered, atypical growth of cells that are still of the same lineage but show loss of uniformity in size, shape, and organization — it is a step toward neoplasia, not a like-for-like swap of one differentiated cell type for another.
incorrectas.C: Hyperplasia is an increase in the number of cells of the same type in a tissue (e.g., endometrial hyperplasia), driven by increased cell division, not a change in the identity of the cell type present.
incorrectas.D: Anaplasia describes a loss of differentiation seen in malignant cells, where cells revert to a primitive, undifferentiated appearance — this is a hallmark of cancer, not an adaptive replacement of one mature cell type with another.

preguntas.q: Chronic exposure to an irritant such as gastric acid or cigarette smoke typically induces which cellular adaptation?

e.correcta: Metaplasia is the reversible replacement of one differentiated cell type with another that is better suited to withstand a chronic stressor — e.g., esophageal squamous epithelium converting to columnar epithelium in GERD (Barrett esophagus) or respiratory pseudostratified columnar epithelium converting to squamous epithelium with chronic smoke exposure. It is an adaptive response that trades away some specialized function (like mucociliary clearance) for greater durability, but it also carries increased malignant potential if the irritant persists.

incorrectas.B: Hypertrophy is an increase in individual cell size (e.g., cardiac myocytes in hypertension) in response to increased workload, not a change in cell type in response to chemical/mechanical irritation of an epithelial surface.
incorrectas.C: Hyperplasia is an increase in cell number due to increased proliferation of the same cell type (e.g., endometrial hyperplasia from estrogen excess), which is a different adaptive mechanism from swapping to a more resistant cell type.
incorrectas.D: Necrosis is irreversible cell death with membrane rupture and an inflammatory response, representing injury rather than adaptation — chronic low-grade irritants that the tissue can accommodate typically produce metaplasia, not outright cell death.

preguntas.q: What are the effects of histamine on arterioles and venules during acute inflammation?

e.correcta: Histamine released from mast cells during acute inflammation acts on vascular smooth muscle to cause arteriolar dilation (increasing blood flow into the area, contributing to redness and heat) while simultaneously causing venular constriction and increased venular permeability (via endothelial cell contraction), which together raise hydrostatic pressure in the capillary bed and promote fluid/protein exudation into tissue, producing edema. This combination of increased inflow and impaired outflow is a classic mechanism behind the swelling seen in acute inflammatory responses.

incorrectas.B: This reverses histamine's actual effects — histamine dilates arterioles (increasing inflow) rather than constricting them, and constricts (not dilates) venules, so this option describes an effect opposite to the real vascular response.
incorrectas.C: Constriction of both arterioles and venules would reduce blood flow into the area and is not consistent with the hyperemia (redness, warmth) and edema characteristic of histamine-mediated acute inflammation.
incorrectas.D: Dilation of both arterioles and venules is not accurate; histamine's differential effect — dilating arterioles but constricting venules — is what raises intravascular pressure and drives the transudation/exudation seen in the inflammatory response.

preguntas.q: What are the effects of bradykinin on arterioles and venules?

e.correcta: Bradykinin, generated via the kallikrein-kinin cascade, acts on B2 receptors on vascular endothelium to stimulate nitric oxide and prostacyclin release, causing arteriolar dilation, while it also increases venous permeability and promotes venous constriction, together raising local hydrostatic pressure and vascular leakage — contributing to the classic signs of inflammation (redness, warmth, swelling, pain). This dual arteriolar-dilation/venous-constriction pattern mirrors histamine's action and is central to how acute inflammatory mediators produce edema.

incorrectas.A: Pure arteriolar and venous dilation would increase blood flow into the area without efficiently raising venous outflow resistance, understating bradykinin's actual role in promoting venous constriction that helps trap fluid and increase local pressure/edema.
incorrectas.C: Arteriolar constriction would reduce blood flow into the tissue, which is the opposite of bradykinin's vasodilatory effect on arterioles mediated through B2-receptor-triggered nitric oxide release.
incorrectas.D: Constriction of both arterioles and venules would restrict blood flow into and out of the area, which does not match bradykinin's known pro-inflammatory, edema-promoting vascular actions of arteriolar dilation paired with venous constriction.

preguntas.q: How does the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) typically change in a patient with giant cell (temporal) arteritis?

e.correcta: Giant cell (temporal) arteritis produces a marked systemic inflammatory response, with granulomatous inflammation of medium/large arteries driving a very high ESR, often exceeding 100 mm/hr — this dramatic elevation is a key diagnostic clue (alongside jaw claudication and risk of irreversible vision loss) and is part of why clinicians treat empirically with corticosteroids before biopsy confirmation to prevent blindness.

incorrectas.B: ESR reflects the degree of inflammation-driven fibrinogen/acute-phase protein elevation causing red cell rouleaux formation; an active vasculitis like GCA increases, not decreases, this value, since there is ongoing systemic inflammation rather than its absence.
incorrectas.C: A normal ESR would be atypical and should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis, since GCA is a systemic granulomatous inflammatory disease that classically produces a markedly elevated, not normal, ESR.
incorrectas.D: While chronic disease can cause anemia, ESR elevation in GCA is driven by inflammatory acute-phase proteins, not by anemia itself, and the anemia of chronic disease does not mildly decrease the ESR — inflammation still drives it markedly upward.

preguntas.q: How does the ESR typically change in a patient with Takayasu arteritis?

e.correcta: Takayasu arteritis is a granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches, producing a systemic inflammatory state that elevates acute-phase reactants, so the ESR is characteristically increased, often markedly. This elevated ESR (along with CRP) serves as a useful marker for tracking disease activity and response to immunosuppressive treatment (typically corticosteroids), alongside the classic clinical findings of diminished pulses ('pulseless disease') and limb claudication in young women.

incorrectas.B: A decreased ESR would be atypical for an active granulomatous vasculitis, since inflammatory conditions generally raise rather than lower ESR through increased fibrinogen and other acute-phase proteins.
incorrectas.C: An unchanged ESR would not fit the systemic inflammatory nature of Takayasu arteritis, which, like other vasculitides, is expected to elevate inflammatory markers during active disease.
incorrectas.D: An undetectable ESR is not a physiologically meaningful description of disease activity and does not correspond to the expected acute-phase response seen in an inflammatory vasculitis like Takayasu arteritis.

preguntas.q: Which leukocyte is most involved in the acute inflammatory response?

e.correcta: Neutrophils are the first and most numerous leukocytes recruited to a site of acute inflammation (typically arriving within the first 6-24 hours), guided there by chemotactic factors like IL-8, C5a, and LTB4, where they phagocytose pathogens and debris and release granule contents/reactive oxygen species to kill microbes. Their predominance early in inflammation — visible histologically as neutrophilic infiltrate — is a defining feature that distinguishes acute inflammation from the mononuclear cell (lymphocyte/macrophage) predominance of chronic inflammation.

incorrectas.B: Lymphocytes are more characteristic of chronic inflammation and adaptive immune responses, arriving later than neutrophils and mediating antigen-specific responses (T cells) or antibody production (via differentiation into plasma cells) rather than the rapid, nonspecific response that defines the acute phase.
incorrectas.C: Plasma cells are terminally differentiated B cells that secrete antibodies, and their presence in tissue is a hallmark of chronic inflammation or an established humoral immune response — they are not part of the rapid initial acute inflammatory infiltrate.
incorrectas.D: Eosinophils are prominently recruited in allergic reactions and parasitic infections, releasing major basic protein and other granule contents, but they are not the dominant or first-responding cell type in the general acute inflammatory response the way neutrophils are.

preguntas.q: What is the primary function of macrophages with respect to bacteria, cellular debris, and RBCs?

o.C: They lyse them via complement activation
o.D: They sequester them within granulomas only

e.correcta: Macrophages are professional phagocytes that engulf and digest bacteria, dead cell debris, and senescent or damaged red blood cells, using lysosomal enzymes to break down the ingested material — this is their principal role in both innate immune defense and tissue cleanup/remodeling. This phagocytic activity is why macrophages are found removing effete RBCs in the spleen and liver, and why they are central to resolving inflammation by clearing debris after neutrophils have handled the initial acute response. Their versatility (classified as M1 pro-inflammatory or M2 reparative) all still centers on this core engulfment function.

incorrectas.B: Opsonization with antibody is performed by B cells/plasma cells producing immunoglobulin, and antibodies coat targets to enhance recognition by Fc receptors — macrophages are the cells that respond to opsonization by phagocytosing, not the cells that produce the opsonizing antibody themselves.
incorrectas.C: Complement-mediated lysis occurs via the membrane attack complex (C5b-9) generated by the complement cascade, a distinct humoral pathway from macrophage phagocytosis, and macrophages are not the effectors of this lytic mechanism.
incorrectas.D: Granuloma formation is a specialized, chronic response macrophages mount against material they cannot fully degrade (e.g., mycobacteria), walling it off rather than clearing it — this is a narrow exception, not the primary, everyday function of macrophages toward bacteria, debris, and RBCs.

preguntas.q: Acute inflammation in tissue is characterized by edema and the presence of which cell type?

e.correcta: Acute inflammation is defined by the rapid recruitment of neutrophils, which are the first responders drawn out of the vasculature by chemotactic signals (e.g., C5a, LTB4, IL-8) within hours of tissue injury or infection. Vasodilation and increased vascular permeability at the same time cause fluid and protein to leak into the interstitium, producing the edema classically seen alongside the neutrophilic infiltrate. This combination — neutrophils plus edema — is the histologic hallmark that separates acute from chronic inflammation.

incorrectas.B: Lymphocytes are the predominant cell of chronic inflammation and adaptive immune responses, arriving days to weeks after the initial insult once antigen presentation has occurred, not within the acute (hours) phase.
incorrectas.C: Fibroblasts proliferate during the repair/organization phase of inflammation, laying down collagen and granulation tissue well after the acute neutrophilic response has begun to resolve.
incorrectas.D: Plasma cells are terminally differentiated B cells that secrete antibody and are a marker of chronic inflammation or an established humoral response, not the acute phase.

preguntas.q: Toll-like receptor (TLR) activation results in upregulation of which nuclear transcription factor that activates immune response genes?

e.correcta: Toll-like receptors recognize pathogen-associated molecular patterns (like LPS via TLR4) and signal through adaptor proteins (MyD88 or TRIF) to activate IRAK and TRAF6, which ultimately triggers the IκB kinase complex to phosphorylate and degrade IκB, freeing NF-κB to translocate into the nucleus. There, NF-κB drives transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6) and other immune response genes, making it the central transcription factor linking innate immune pattern recognition to the inflammatory gene expression program.

incorrectas.B: STAT3 is activated by cytokine receptor signaling (e.g., IL-6 binding its receptor activates JAK kinases that phosphorylate STAT3), a distinct JAK-STAT pathway used downstream of cytokine receptors rather than the MyD88/TRIF-NF-κB axis specifically triggered by TLR activation.
incorrectas.C: AP-1 is indeed activated downstream of TLR signaling (via MAPK cascades), but it works in conjunction with NF-κB rather than acting 'alone' as the primary or sole transcription factor; NF-κB is the classic, most emphasized transcription factor for TLR-driven immune gene activation.
incorrectas.D: HIF-1α is a transcription factor activated primarily by hypoxia (stabilized when prolyl hydroxylases are inactive under low oxygen), driving genes for angiogenesis and metabolic adaptation, not the pattern-recognition-triggered inflammatory transcriptional response associated with TLR signaling.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme converts arachidonic acid into prostaglandins?

e.correcta: Cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2) converts arachidonic acid into prostaglandin H2, the common precursor that is then converted into various prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2/prostacyclin) and thromboxane A2 by downstream synthases. This is the enzyme targeted by NSAIDs and aspirin, which block COX to reduce prostaglandin-mediated pain, fever, and inflammation — understanding this pathway explains why NSAIDs also reduce thromboxane-driven platelet aggregation and can cause GI ulceration (loss of protective prostaglandins).

incorrectas.B: 5-lipoxygenase acts on arachidonic acid through a separate branch of the pathway to produce leukotrienes (LTB4, LTC4/D4/E4), which mediate neutrophil chemotaxis and bronchoconstriction respectively — a distinct product line from the prostaglandins made via the COX pathway.
incorrectas.C: Phospholipase A2 acts upstream of COX, cleaving membrane phospholipids to liberate arachidonic acid itself from the cell membrane; it does not convert arachidonic acid into prostaglandins, but rather generates the substrate that COX then acts upon.
incorrectas.D: Thromboxane synthase acts downstream of COX, converting the COX-generated intermediate prostaglandin H2 specifically into thromboxane A2 in platelets, rather than directly converting arachidonic acid into prostaglandins.

preguntas.q: Which prostaglandins mediate vasodilation and increased vascular permeability?

e.correcta: PGE2, PGD2, and PGI2 (prostacyclin) act on vascular smooth muscle and endothelium to cause vasodilation and increase vascular permeability, which is why they are central mediators of the redness, warmth, and edema seen in acute inflammation — PGE2 additionally sensitizes nociceptors, contributing to pain and fever.

incorrectas.B: Thromboxane A2 actually causes vasoconstriction and platelet aggregation (opposite effects to vasodilation), and PGF2 causes smooth muscle contraction (e.g., uterine) — neither drives the vasodilation/permeability changes described.
incorrectas.C: Leukotrienes C4, D4, and E4 are potent mediators of bronchoconstriction and increased vascular permeability (relevant in asthma and anaphylaxis) but they are not the classic vasodilatory prostaglandins being asked about here, and they act via different receptors (cysteinyl leukotriene receptors) than the PGE2/D2/I2 pathway.
incorrectas.D: Leukotriene B4 is primarily a potent chemotactic agent for neutrophils, recruiting them to sites of inflammation — it does not cause vasodilation or increased permeability, which are the properties being tested.

preguntas.q: Which prostaglandin is the principal mediator of pain and fever?

e.correcta: PGE2 is the prostaglandin most responsible for sensitizing peripheral nociceptors to painful stimuli and for raising the hypothalamic thermoregulatory set point during infection or inflammation, producing fever. This is precisely why NSAIDs and aspirin, which inhibit cyclooxygenase and thus PGE2 synthesis, are effective analgesics and antipyretics.

incorrectas.B: PGD2 is the predominant prostaglandin released by mast cells during allergic and anaphylactic reactions, contributing to bronchoconstriction and vasodilation, but it is not the principal mediator of pain and fever in the way PGE2 is.
incorrectas.C: PGI2 (prostacyclin), produced mainly by vascular endothelium, promotes vasodilation and inhibits platelet aggregation to counterbalance thromboxane, a cardiovascular regulatory role distinct from the pain/fever mediation attributed to PGE2.
incorrectas.D: Thromboxane A2, produced by platelets, promotes vasoconstriction and platelet aggregation to facilitate clot formation, a hemostatic function unrelated to the central pain and fever pathways driven by PGE2.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme converts arachidonic acid into leukotrienes?

e.correcta: 5-lipoxygenase acts on arachidonic acid (released from membrane phospholipids by phospholipase A2) to produce 5-HPETE, which is then converted into leukotrienes such as LTB4 (a potent neutrophil chemoattractant) and the cysteinyl leukotrienes LTC4/D4/E4 (mediators of bronchoconstriction and vascular permeability in asthma and anaphylaxis). This lipoxygenase pathway runs parallel to, but is biochemically distinct from, the cyclooxygenase pathway that produces prostaglandins and thromboxane.

incorrectas.B: Cyclooxygenase (COX) acts on the same arachidonic acid substrate but converts it into prostaglandins and thromboxane A2, not leukotrienes — this is why NSAIDs, which inhibit COX, can shunt substrate toward the lipoxygenase pathway and sometimes worsen leukotriene-mediated bronchospasm (aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease).
incorrectas.C: Phospholipase A2 acts upstream of leukotriene synthesis, cleaving membrane phospholipids to liberate arachidonic acid itself, rather than converting arachidonic acid into leukotrienes — it is the substrate-generating step, not the lipoxygenase step.
incorrectas.D: Prostacyclin synthase acts downstream in the cyclooxygenase pathway to convert prostaglandin endoperoxides into prostacyclin (PGI2), a vasodilator and antiplatelet mediator produced by endothelium, entirely separate from leukotriene production.

preguntas.q: Which leukotriene is primarily responsible for attracting and activating neutrophils?

e.correcta: Leukotriene B4 (LTB4) is the primary chemotactic leukotriene, acting as a potent chemoattractant that recruits neutrophils to sites of inflammation and also activates them (promoting adhesion to endothelium and degranulation), which is why it is grouped functionally with other neutrophil-recruiting mediators like C5a and IL-8 in the '5-HETE, LTB4, C5a, IL-8' mnemonic for neutrophil chemotactic factors. This distinguishes LTB4 from the cysteinyl leukotrienes, which act mainly on smooth muscle and vasculature rather than as chemoattractants.

incorrectas.B: Leukotriene C4 is one of the cysteinyl leukotrienes that mediates bronchoconstriction, increased vascular permeability, and mucus secretion (important in asthma pathophysiology) rather than acting as the primary neutrophil chemoattractant.
incorrectas.C: Leukotriene D4, also a cysteinyl leukotriene, similarly causes smooth muscle contraction (bronchoconstriction) and increased vascular permeability, part of the '(cysteinyl) LTC4, D4, E4 cause bronchoconstriction' grouping, not neutrophil chemotaxis.
incorrectas.D: Leukotriene E4 completes the cysteinyl leukotriene group (C4, D4, E4) responsible for the slow-reacting substance of anaphylaxis effects like bronchoconstriction and vascular leakage, distinct from LTB4's role in attracting and activating neutrophils.

preguntas.q: Which leukotrienes mediate vasoconstriction, bronchospasm, and increased vascular permeability?

e.correcta: Leukotrienes C4, D4, and E4 (the cysteinyl leukotrienes) are produced from arachidonic acid via the 5-lipoxygenase pathway and act on smooth muscle and vascular endothelium to cause bronchoconstriction, increased vascular permeability, and vasoconstriction — this is the mechanistic basis for their major role in asthma and anaphylaxis, and why leukotriene receptor antagonists like montelukast are used therapeutically to block these effects.

incorrectas.B: Leukotriene B4 is also a 5-lipoxygenase product, but it functions as a potent chemotactic factor for neutrophils rather than causing bronchospasm or vascular permeability changes, making it mechanistically distinct from the cysteinyl leukotrienes.
incorrectas.C: PGE2 and PGD2 are cyclooxygenase pathway products (prostaglandins), not leukotrienes; PGE2 causes vasodilation and pain sensitization while PGD2 causes bronchoconstriction and vasodilation, but neither is a leukotriene by definition.
incorrectas.D: Thromboxane A2 is also a cyclooxygenase product, produced mainly by platelets, and promotes platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction — it is not a leukotriene and its role centers on hemostasis, not the bronchospasm/permeability triad described.

preguntas.q: In general, prostaglandins cause which vascular effect?

e.correcta: Most prostaglandins (particularly PGE2 and PGI2/prostacyclin) cause vasodilation by increasing cAMP in vascular smooth muscle, contributing to the redness and warmth seen in acute inflammation and to the hypotension that can occur with excess prostaglandin release (e.g., in sepsis). This vasodilatory action also explains why NSAIDs, which inhibit cyclooxygenase and thus prostaglandin synthesis, can reduce inflammatory vasodilation and edema, but at the cost of effects like reduced renal blood flow when protective renal prostaglandins are also blocked.

incorrectas.B: Vasoconstriction is the characteristic action of thromboxane A2 (TXA2), a related eicosanoid made by a different enzymatic pathway (thromboxane synthase in platelets), which acts in functional opposition to vasodilatory prostaglandins like prostacyclin.
incorrectas.C: Prostaglandins have well-documented, clinically significant effects on vascular tone (vasodilation), so 'no change' does not reflect their known pharmacologic and physiologic role in the vasculature.
incorrectas.D: Prostaglandins act broadly on both arterial and venous smooth muscle rather than being restricted to selective venous dilation, so limiting the effect to veins only misrepresents their general vasodilatory action throughout the vascular tree.

preguntas.q: In general, prostaglandins have what effect on vascular permeability?

e.correcta: Prostaglandins generally increase vascular permeability by promoting vasodilation and potentiating the effects of other mediators like histamine and bradykinin on postcapillary venules, contributing to the exudation of fluid and proteins characteristic of acute inflammation.
