incorrectas.C: The defect in secondary insufficiency is precisely at the pituitary level (or above), not the adrenal cortex — that's the definition that separates it from primary insufficiency.
incorrectas.D: An ACTH-secreting pituitary tumor causing increased ACTH describes Cushing disease, the opposite hormonal problem (excess, not deficiency) at the pituitary.

preguntas.q: How do blood glucose levels change in secondary adrenocortical insufficiency, and why?

o.B: Hypoglycemia, due to decreased cortisol levels
o.C: No change, since aldosterone is unaffected
o.D: Hypoglycemia, due to elevated insulin secretion

e.correcta: Regardless of whether the defect is at the pituitary (secondary) or the adrenal gland (primary), the end result is the same: low cortisol. Since cortisol is essential for maintaining blood glucose during fasting and stress by promoting gluconeogenesis and antagonizing insulin, its deficiency in secondary insufficiency produces hypoglycemia just as it does in Addison disease.

incorrectas.A: ACTH is low, not elevated, in secondary insufficiency (that's the defining feature), and even if it were elevated, ACTH itself doesn't directly raise glucose — cortisol does, and cortisol is deficient here.
incorrectas.C: Aldosterone being unaffected is true in secondary insufficiency, but that fact is about sodium/potassium handling, not about glucose regulation, which depends on cortisol and is impaired.
incorrectas.D: Insulin secretion is not increased in this condition; the hypoglycemia results from loss of cortisol's counter-regulatory, glucose-raising effects, not from a primary insulin excess.

preguntas.q: Does secondary adrenocortical insufficiency present with hyperpigmentation? Why or why not?

o.A: Yes, because low cortisol directly darkens the skin
o.B: No, because ACTH levels are low, so there is no increased melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH) co-production
o.C: Yes, to the same degree as Addison disease
o.D: No, because aldosterone directly suppresses melanocyte activity

e.correcta: Hyperpigmentation in Addison disease occurs because ACTH is cleaved from the POMC precursor, which also yields melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH); high ACTH therefore comes bundled with increased MSH-like activity that darkens the skin. In secondary insufficiency, ACTH is low (the problem is at the pituitary), so there is no excess POMC-derived MSH activity and no hyperpigmentation, which is a useful bedside way to distinguish the two.

incorrectas.A: Cortisol itself does not directly pigment the skin; the pigmentation in adrenal insufficiency is mediated by elevated ACTH/MSH from the POMC precursor, which is specifically absent when ACTH is low.
incorrectas.C: Hyperpigmentation to the same degree as Addison disease would require the same elevated ACTH driving MSH production, which is exactly what's missing in secondary insufficiency.
incorrectas.D: Aldosterone has no role in melanocyte regulation; the pigmentation mechanism runs through ACTH/MSH from POMC, not through mineralocorticoid activity.

preguntas.q: Why does secondary adrenocortical insufficiency typically NOT present with hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, or hypotension?

o.A: Because ACTH levels remain elevated and compensate
o.B: Because aldosterone levels are normal in this condition
o.C: Because cortisol levels are actually normal in secondary insufficiency
o.D: Because the renin-angiotensin system is inactivated

e.correcta: Aldosterone secretion is regulated primarily by the renin-angiotensin system and serum potassium, not by ACTH, so when the defect in secondary insufficiency is confined to reduced pituitary ACTH, the zona glomerulosa keeps producing aldosterone relatively normally. Because aldosterone-driven sodium retention and potassium/hydrogen excretion remain largely intact, these patients don't develop the hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, and hypotension seen when aldosterone itself is deficient, as in Addison disease.

incorrectas.A: ACTH is actually low in secondary insufficiency (that is the core problem), not elevated, so it cannot be compensating for anything.
incorrectas.C: Cortisol levels are low, not normal, in secondary insufficiency — the ACTH deficiency directly causes reduced glucocorticoid output; what's preserved is aldosterone, not cortisol.
incorrectas.D: The renin-angiotensin system is not inactivated; it continues to drive aldosterone secretion independent of the pituitary defect, which is precisely why mineralocorticoid function is preserved.

preguntas.q: Which classes of steroid hormones are increased in Cushing syndrome/disease?

o.D: All three classes equally, including marked aldosterone excess

e.correcta: Cushing syndrome/disease is caused by excess ACTH (Cushing disease) or a cortisol-producing adrenal process, and since ACTH drives both the zona fasciculata and zona reticularis, patients have elevated cortisol and often elevated adrenal androgens as well. Aldosterone (zona glomerulosa) is largely ACTH-independent, so it's typically not significantly elevated, which is why the syndrome is defined mainly by glucocorticoid excess rather than a mineralocorticoid picture.

incorrectas.A: Mineralocorticoids alone being elevated would describe primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome), a distinct entity with hypertension and hypokalemia but normal cortisol, not Cushing syndrome.
incorrectas.C: Androgens alone with normal cortisol doesn't fit Cushing syndrome, which is defined by cortisol excess; isolated androgen excess with normal cortisol would suggest a different process, like an androgen-secreting tumor.
incorrectas.D: Marked aldosterone excess is not a feature of Cushing syndrome; aldosterone is regulated separately from ACTH, so it typically remains near normal even while cortisol is markedly elevated.

preguntas.q: What is the level of ACTH in Cushing disease, and why?

o.A: Decreased, due to negative feedback from high cortisol
o.B: Increased, because the disease is caused by an ACTH-secreting pituitary tumor
o.C: Normal, because Cushing disease is ACTH-independent
o.D: Increased, due to an adrenal cortisol-secreting adenoma

e.correcta: Cushing disease specifically refers to a pituitary corticotroph adenoma that autonomously secretes excess ACTH, which then drives the adrenal cortex to overproduce cortisol. Because the ACTH excess is the primary abnormality rather than a response to low cortisol, high-dose dexamethasone can still partially suppress it (distinguishing Cushing disease from ectopic ACTH-secreting tumors, which usually don't suppress).

incorrectas.A: ACTH is elevated because a pituitary tumor is autonomously overproducing it, not decreased — high cortisol would normally suppress a healthy pituitary, but the tumor cells escape most feedback control.
incorrectas.C: ACTH is not normal in Cushing disease; the whole disease process is defined by pathologic overproduction of ACTH from the pituitary adenoma.
incorrectas.D: An adrenal cortisol-secreting adenoma would produce a Cushing syndrome picture with LOW ACTH (due to feedback suppression of the normal pituitary), which is the opposite pattern from Cushing disease, where the tumor itself is in the pituitary.

preguntas.q: Which clinical feature in women with Cushing syndrome/disease results from increased adrenal androgen levels?

e.correcta: In Cushing disease, ACTH excess stimulates not just cortisol but also adrenal androgen production from the zona reticularis; in women, this androgen excess produces virilizing features such as hirsutism, temporal balding, clitoromegaly, and acne. This is the clinical clue that points specifically to androgen involvement rather than the glucocorticoid or mineralocorticoid effects of cortisol excess.

incorrectas.A: Osteoporosis in Cushing syndrome results from cortisol's catabolic effects on bone (inhibiting osteoblasts and promoting bone resorption), a glucocorticoid effect, not an androgen-driven one.
incorrectas.C: Moon facies results from cortisol-induced central fat redistribution, a classic glucocorticoid effect of hypercortisolism, unrelated to androgen excess.
incorrectas.D: Purple striae occur because cortisol impairs collagen synthesis, thinning the skin so that underlying vasculature shows through when stretched — again a direct glucocorticoid effect, not androgen-mediated.

preguntas.q: What is the expected result of a high-dose dexamethasone suppression test in a patient with Cushing disease (pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma)?

o.A: Cortisol response would NOT be suppressed at any dexamethasone dose
o.B: Cortisol response WOULD BE suppressed by high-dose dexamethasone
o.C: ACTH would rise paradoxically regardless of dose
o.D: Cortisol would be suppressed equally by both low and high doses

e.correcta: In Cushing disease, the pituitary corticotroph adenoma retains at least partial responsiveness to negative feedback, just with a higher set point than normal — so while low-dose dexamethasone fails to suppress cortisol, a high enough dose of dexamethasone can still override the tumor's resistance and suppress cortisol production. This pattern (suppression only at high dose) is what distinguishes a pituitary source from an ectopic ACTH-secreting tumor, which typically shows no suppression even at high doses.

incorrectas.A: No suppression at any dose is the pattern expected with an ectopic ACTH-secreting tumor (e.g., small cell lung cancer), which lacks the residual feedback sensitivity of a pituitary adenoma, not Cushing disease itself.
incorrectas.C: ACTH rising paradoxically regardless of dose isn't the physiologic response being tested; the point of the high-dose test is that ACTH (and downstream cortisol) actually falls with high-dose dexamethasone in pituitary disease.
incorrectas.D: Equal suppression at both low and high doses would suggest a normal or nearly normal feedback set point, which doesn't fit Cushing disease — the defining feature is that only high-dose dexamethasone succeeds where low-dose fails.

preguntas.q: Which medications are used as pharmacologic treatment for Cushing syndrome by blocking steroid hormone biosynthesis?

e.correcta: Ketoconazole and metyrapone are both steroidogenesis inhibitors: ketoconazole blocks several cytochrome P450 enzymes involved in cortisol synthesis, and metyrapone blocks 11β-hydroxylase, the enzyme that converts 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol. Both are used to rapidly lower cortisol levels in Cushing syndrome, whether as a bridge to definitive surgery or in patients who aren't surgical candidates.

incorrectas.A: Spironolactone and eplerenone are mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists used for conditions like hyperaldosteronism or heart failure; they block aldosterone's effects rather than inhibiting cortisol biosynthesis.
incorrectas.C: Hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone are replacement hormones used to treat adrenal insufficiency (a deficiency state) — giving them to a patient with cortisol excess would worsen Cushing syndrome, not treat it.
incorrectas.D: Cabergoline and pasireotide work by suppressing ACTH secretion at the pituitary (dopamine agonist and somatostatin analog, respectively) rather than by blocking adrenal steroid biosynthesis directly, which is a different mechanism than the question asks about.

preguntas.q: What is the definitive treatment for Cushing disease (ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma)?

e.correcta: Because Cushing disease is caused by an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma driving cortisol excess, the definitive and curative treatment is surgical resection of that tumor (typically via transsphenoidal surgery), which removes the source of excess ACTH and allows cortisol levels to normalize. Medical therapy and adrenalectomy are reserved for cases where surgery fails or isn't feasible, since they don't address the underlying pituitary lesion.

incorrectas.A: Lifelong ketoconazole controls cortisol levels pharmacologically but doesn't remove the tumor causing the disease, so it's a medical bridge or fallback, not the definitive cure.
incorrectas.B: Bilateral adrenalectomy removes the target organ rather than the source tumor, leaving the pituitary adenoma in place (which can even lead to Nelson syndrome from unchecked ACTH growth), so it is not first-line for Cushing disease.
incorrectas.D: High-dose glucocorticoid replacement would add more cortisol-like activity, which is the opposite of what's needed in a cortisol-excess state, and would never be an appropriate treatment for Cushing disease.

preguntas.q: Conn syndrome presents with hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis due to which hormonal abnormality?

e.correcta: Conn syndrome is primary hyperaldosteronism, usually from an aldosterone-producing adrenal adenoma, so aldosterone acts on the renal collecting duct to increase sodium (and water) reabsorption while increasing potassium and hydrogen ion excretion. This produces the classic triad of hypertension (from volume expansion), hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis, with suppressed renin due to the autonomous aldosterone excess (unlike secondary hyperaldosteronism, where renin is elevated).

incorrectas.B: Increased cortisol would produce a Cushing syndrome picture (weight gain, striae, hyperglycemia), and while very high cortisol can have some mineralocorticoid-like activity, the classic Conn syndrome triad is driven specifically by aldosterone excess, not cortisol.
incorrectas.C: Increased renin would describe secondary hyperaldosteronism (e.g., from renal artery stenosis or heart failure), where aldosterone rises in response to renin, the opposite of Conn syndrome, in which renin is actually suppressed by the autonomous aldosterone excess.
incorrectas.D: Decreased ACTH doesn't fit this picture at all; ACTH mainly drives cortisol and androgens, not aldosterone, and has no direct link to the hypertension/hypokalemia/alkalosis triad described.

preguntas.q: Which classes of adrenal steroid hormones are decreased in 21-hydroxylase deficiency (a cause of congenital adrenal hyperplasia)?

o.D: None; all steroid classes are increased

e.correcta: 21-hydroxylase converts progesterone and 17-hydroxyprogesterone into precursors of both aldosterone and cortisol, so its deficiency blocks synthesis of both glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids while shunting the accumulated precursors toward androgen synthesis (which doesn't require 21-hydroxylase). This is why classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency causes salt-wasting (low aldosterone), cortisol deficiency, and androgen excess all at once.

incorrectas.A: Androgens are actually increased, not decreased, in 21-hydroxylase deficiency, because the enzyme block shunts precursors away from the cortisol/aldosterone pathway and into androgen synthesis, which doesn't need 21-hydroxylase.
incorrectas.C: Androgens are elevated rather than decreased in this condition; only glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids are reduced because 21-hydroxylase is required for their synthesis but not for androgen production.
incorrectas.D: All steroid classes are not increased; glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids fall due to the enzyme block, while only androgens rise from the diverted precursors.

preguntas.q: Deficiency of which enzyme is the most common cause of congenital adrenal hyperplasia?

e.correcta: 21-hydroxylase deficiency accounts for roughly 90-95% of congenital adrenal hyperplasia cases, making it by far the most common enzyme defect in this disease. It causes decreased cortisol and aldosterone with increased androgens, producing ambiguous genitalia in females, salt-wasting crises in severe forms, and elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone, which is the diagnostic screening marker.

incorrectas.A: 17α-hydroxylase deficiency is a much rarer cause of CAH, and it produces a very different picture — decreased cortisol and androgens but increased mineralocorticoid precursors, causing hypertension and hypokalemia rather than the classic salt-wasting/virilizing presentation.
incorrectas.C: 11β-hydroxylase deficiency is the second most common cause of CAH but is much less frequent than 21-hydroxylase deficiency, and it causes hypertension (from mineralocorticoid precursor buildup) rather than salt-wasting.
incorrectas.D: 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency is a rare cause of CAH that affects all three steroid pathways early in synthesis, but it is far less common than 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

preguntas.q: In 21β-hydroxylase deficiency, what happens to ACTH levels and why?

o.A: Decreased, due to increased negative feedback from mineralocorticoids
o.B: Unchanged, because ACTH is independent of cortisol
o.C: Increased, due to decreased negative feedback from cortisol
o.D: Decreased, due to direct enzyme inhibition of the pituitary

e.correcta: In 21β-hydroxylase deficiency, the enzyme block prevents adequate cortisol synthesis, so cortisol's normal negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary is lost, and ACTH rises in compensation. This elevated ACTH further stimulates the adrenal cortex, driving even more precursor accumulation into the androgen pathway, which is why patients develop virilization alongside the cortisol/aldosterone deficiency.

incorrectas.A: Mineralocorticoids are decreased, not increased, in 21-hydroxylase deficiency, so there is no extra mineralocorticoid-driven feedback — the feedback loss comes specifically from low cortisol.
incorrectas.B: ACTH is very much dependent on cortisol feedback; it's the loss of cortisol's suppressive effect that causes ACTH to rise, so this option misrepresents the physiology of the HPA axis.
incorrectas.D: The enzyme defect is in the adrenal cortex (steroidogenesis), not in the pituitary itself; ACTH rises because of lost feedback, not because of any direct inhibitory effect on pituitary corticotrophs.

preguntas.q: A female infant with 21β-hydroxylase deficiency presents with clitoral enlargement and early pubic/axillary hair. These findings result from excess of which hormone class?

e.correcta: In 21β-hydroxylase deficiency, precursors that can't proceed down the blocked cortisol/aldosterone pathway are shunted into androgen synthesis, so affected female infants are exposed to excess adrenal androgens in utero and after birth. This androgen excess causes virilization of the external genitalia (clitoromegaly, labial fusion) and precocious pubic/axillary hair, which is the classic presenting picture of a virilized female infant with CAH.

incorrectas.A: Mineralocorticoids are actually decreased in this disorder (contributing to salt-wasting), so they cannot be the cause of virilizing signs like clitoromegaly and early pubic hair.
incorrectas.B: Glucocorticoids are decreased, not the cause of virilization; cortisol deficiency drives the compensatory ACTH rise, but it is the resulting androgen excess, not cortisol itself, that produces these findings.
incorrectas.D: Estrogens are not increased in this condition and do not cause virilizing signs like clitoral enlargement; these findings are specifically androgen-mediated.

preguntas.q: In 21β-hydroxylase deficiency, urinary excretion of which substance is increased, reflecting excess adrenal androgen production?

e.correcta: 21β-hydroxylase deficiency blocks cortisol and aldosterone synthesis, shunting the accumulated precursors (like 17-hydroxyprogesterone) down the androgen synthesis pathway, producing excess DHEA and androstenedione. These adrenal androgens are metabolized and excreted in urine as 17-ketosteroids, so elevated urinary 17-ketosteroids reflect the androgen excess driving virilization in these patients.

incorrectas.A: Vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) is a breakdown product of catecholamines (epinephrine/norepinephrine), classically elevated in pheochromocytoma, and has no relationship to adrenal androgen production or 21-hydroxylase deficiency.
incorrectas.C: 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) is the metabolite of serotonin, used to diagnose carcinoid syndrome, and is unrelated to adrenal steroidogenesis or CAH.
incorrectas.D: Metanephrines are also catecholamine metabolites (like VMA), used to screen for pheochromocytoma, not a marker of androgen excess from a blocked steroidogenic pathway.

preguntas.q: What is the appropriate treatment for classic 21β-hydroxylase deficiency (congenital adrenal hyperplasia)?

o.C: Replacement of both glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids
o.D: ACTH analog therapy to stimulate residual enzyme activity

e.correcta: Classic 21β-hydroxylase deficiency causes deficiencies of both cortisol and aldosterone, so treatment requires replacing both — glucocorticoids (e.g., hydrocortisone) to restore cortisol and suppress the excess ACTH driving androgen overproduction, and mineralocorticoids (e.g., fludrocortisone) to correct salt-wasting. Adequate glucocorticoid dosing is especially important because it indirectly controls virilization by lowering ACTH-driven androgen synthesis.

incorrectas.A: Mineralocorticoid replacement alone would help with salt-wasting but would leave cortisol deficient and ACTH elevated, so androgen overproduction and virilization would continue unchecked.
incorrectas.B: Androgen receptor blockade doesn't address the root enzymatic defect or the cortisol/aldosterone deficiencies; the mainstay is hormone replacement that also suppresses the ACTH drive causing androgen excess.
incorrectas.D: Giving ACTH analogs would be counterproductive, since ACTH is already elevated and driving the disease process (excess androgen production) — the goal of treatment is to suppress ACTH via glucocorticoid replacement, not stimulate it further.

preguntas.q: 17α-hydroxylase deficiency causes decreased production of which two classes of steroid hormones?

e.correcta: 17α-hydroxylase is required to convert pregnenolone/progesterone into precursors of cortisol and sex steroids (androgens and estrogens), but it is not needed for mineralocorticoid synthesis. Deficiency therefore causes decreased cortisol and decreased androgens/estrogens, while precursors are shunted into the mineralocorticoid pathway, causing mineralocorticoid excess (hypertension, hypokalemia) rather than deficiency.

incorrectas.A: Mineralocorticoids are actually increased, not decreased, in 17α-hydroxylase deficiency, because precursor steroids are shunted toward the mineralocorticoid pathway when the 17α-hydroxylation step is blocked.
incorrectas.C: Androgens are indeed decreased, but mineralocorticoids are increased (not decreased) in this disorder, which is the opposite of what this option states.
incorrectas.D: Glucocorticoids and estrogens are both decreased, but so are androgens (since 17α-hydroxylase is needed for the sex steroid pathway generally), so limiting the deficiency to "estrogens only" alongside glucocorticoids is incomplete.

preguntas.q: A phenotypic female with 17α-hydroxylase deficiency fails to develop pubic and axillary hair at puberty. This is due to decreased levels of which hormone class?

e.correcta: 17α-hydroxylase deficiency blocks the pathway needed to produce androgens (and downstream estrogens) from steroid precursors, so both androgen and estrogen levels are low. Because pubic and axillary hair growth at puberty is driven primarily by adrenal and gonadal androgens (not estrogens), the resulting androgen deficiency explains the failure to develop this sexual hair in an affected phenotypic female.

incorrectas.A: Mineralocorticoids are actually increased (not decreased) in 17α-hydroxylase deficiency, since precursors are shunted into that pathway, and mineralocorticoids have no role in triggering pubic/axillary hair growth anyway.
incorrectas.B: Glucocorticoids are decreased in this condition too, but glucocorticoid deficiency does not explain failure of pubic/axillary hair development — that is specifically an androgen-dependent process.
incorrectas.C: Estrogens are also decreased in this disorder, but pubic and axillary hair growth at puberty is driven by androgens, not estrogens, so estrogen deficiency isn't the mechanistic explanation being tested here.

preguntas.q: In 17α-hydroxylase deficiency, aldosterone levels are typically which of the following, despite mineralocorticoid excess symptoms?

e.correcta: In 17α-hydroxylase deficiency, the enzyme block occurs before the split into glucocorticoid/androgen and mineralocorticoid pathways, but only the branch requiring 17-hydroxylation (cortisol and sex steroids) is affected — the mineralocorticoid pathway (progesterone to DOC to corticosterone) does not require 17α-hydroxylase and is instead overdriven by the shunted precursors. This causes markedly elevated corticosterone and DOC (a weak but real mineralocorticoid), which produces hypertension and hypokalemia (mineralocorticoid excess symptoms), while aldosterone itself is actually suppressed because the resulting volume expansion and elevated DOC/corticosterone shut down renin-angiotensin activity. So the paradox is: mineralocorticoid excess symptoms are driven by DOC and corticosterone, not aldosterone, and feedback suppression makes true aldosterone low.

incorrectas.A: Aldosterone is not markedly increased in this disorder — the enzyme block does not increase flux specifically into the aldosterone synthase pathway, and the resulting volume expansion actually suppresses renin and thus aldosterone.
incorrectas.C: Aldosterone is not simply unchanged; the hypertension and volume expansion caused by excess DOC and corticosterone actively suppress the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis, driving aldosterone below normal, not leaving it neutral.
incorrectas.D: There is no stress-limited increase in aldosterone in this condition — the defect chronically suppresses renin-driven aldosterone production regardless of stress state, since the mineralocorticoid effects come from DOC/corticosterone, not from stress-triggered aldosterone release.

preguntas.q: Which adrenal enzyme deficiency causes shunting of steroid precursors toward the aldosterone (mineralocorticoid) synthesis pathway?

e.correcta: 17α-hydroxylase converts pregnenolone/progesterone into the 17-hydroxylated precursors required for cortisol and androgen synthesis; when this enzyme is deficient, precursors cannot proceed down those branches and accumulate proximal to the block, where they are instead shunted through the mineralocorticoid pathway (progesterone to DOC to corticosterone). This is why 17α-hydroxylase deficiency classically presents with hypertension and hypokalemia from mineralocorticoid excess (DOC, corticosterone) alongside absent sex steroid production, causing ambiguous or absent secondary sexual characteristics.

incorrectas.A: 21β-hydroxylase deficiency blocks conversion to both cortisol and aldosterone precursors (11-deoxycortisol and DOC), shunting precursors toward androgens instead, which is the opposite pattern — it causes virilization and often salt-wasting, not mineralocorticoid excess.
incorrectas.B: 11β-hydroxylase deficiency blocks the final step converting 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol and DOC to corticosterone, so precursors (including DOC itself) accumulate and cause mineralocorticoid excess along with virilization from shunted androgens — but it is not the enzyme that shunts precursors specifically into the aldosterone branch as its defining mechanism.
incorrectas.D: Aromatase converts androgens to estrogens peripherally and in the placenta/ovary; it has no role in adrenal steroidogenesis branch point regulation, so its deficiency does not shunt cortisol precursors toward mineralocorticoids.

preguntas.q: Which adrenal enzyme deficiency results in shunting of steroid precursors toward the androgen synthesis pathway?

e.correcta: 21β-hydroxylase normally converts 17-hydroxyprogesterone to 11-deoxycortisol (cortisol pathway) and progesterone to DOC (aldosterone pathway); when it is deficient, both of these routes are blocked, and the accumulating 17-hydroxyprogesterone is instead shunted into the androgen synthesis pathway, producing excess testosterone and virilization. This is the most common cause of congenital adrenal hyperplasia and classically causes ambiguous genitalia in females along with salt-wasting (due to low aldosterone) in the severe form.

incorrectas.A: 17α-hydroxylase deficiency blocks the pathway toward cortisol and androgens, shunting precursors toward mineralocorticoids (DOC, corticosterone) instead — this is the reverse pattern of shunting toward androgens.
incorrectas.C: Aromatase deficiency prevents peripheral/placental conversion of androgens to estrogens, causing androgen excess symptoms in the mother and virilization of a female fetus, but it does not act at the adrenal steroidogenic branch point that shunts precursors into androgen synthesis.
incorrectas.D: 5α-reductase deficiency impairs conversion of testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone in peripheral tissues, causing undervirilized external genitalia in 46,XY individuals, but it has nothing to do with adrenal precursor shunting toward the androgen pathway.

preguntas.q: The endocrine cells of the pancreas, comprising only 1-2% of pancreatic mass, are organized into which structures?

e.correcta: The islets of Langerhans are the endocrine (hormone-secreting) portion of the pancreas, small clusters of cells (alpha, beta, delta, PP cells) scattered throughout the much larger exocrine pancreas, making up only 1-2% of total pancreatic mass while the exocrine acinar tissue does the bulk digestive enzyme secretion. These islets are richly vascularized to allow rapid hormone (insulin, glucagon, somatostatin) release directly into the bloodstream, distinguishing their function from the duct-draining exocrine acini.

incorrectas.B: Crypts of Lieberkühn are intestinal glands found in the small and large intestine mucosa, involved in secretion and epithelial renewal, not an endocrine structure of the pancreas at all.
incorrectas.C: Peyer's patches are lymphoid follicles found in the ileum, part of gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) for immune surveillance, unrelated to pancreatic endocrine architecture.
incorrectas.D: Zona glomerulosa is a layer of the adrenal cortex (not the pancreas) responsible for aldosterone production; 'nodules' of it is not a real structure, and this option confuses adrenal with pancreatic endocrine anatomy.

preguntas.q: Besides alpha, beta, and delta cells, the remaining cells of the islets of Langerhans mainly secrete which substance?

e.correcta: The islets of Langerhans contain a minority population of PP cells (gamma cells) that secrete pancreatic polypeptide, which inhibits pancreatic exocrine secretion, gallbladder contraction, and gut motility, helping to regulate digestive processes after a meal. PP cells are typically concentrated in islets located in the head of the pancreas (derived from the ventral pancreatic bud), distinguishing their distribution from the more uniformly distributed alpha, beta, and delta cells.

incorrectas.A: Gastrin is secreted by G cells, which are found in the antrum of the stomach and duodenum (and rarely in gastrinoma-forming pancreatic tissue), not as a normal secretory product of the islets of Langerhans' fourth cell type.
incorrectas.B: Vasoactive intestinal peptide is produced by neurons and some rare pancreatic tumor cells (VIPomas), but it is not the physiologic secretory product of the normal fourth islet cell population, which is pancreatic polypeptide from PP cells.
incorrectas.D: Secretin is secreted by S cells of the duodenal mucosa in response to acidic chyme, stimulating pancreatic bicarbonate secretion — it is not produced by islet cells, which secrete pancreatic polypeptide instead.

preguntas.q: What structures link beta-cells to each other, alpha-cells to each other, and beta-cells to alpha-cells within the islets of Langerhans, enabling rapid intercellular communication?

e.correcta: Gap junctions are channels made of connexin proteins that directly connect the cytoplasm of adjacent cells, allowing ions and small signaling molecules to pass between them without crossing the plasma membrane — this permits electrical coupling and rapid coordination of secretory responses between beta-beta, alpha-alpha, and beta-alpha cell pairs within the islet. This rapid intercellular communication helps synchronize insulin and glucagon release across the islet in response to changing glucose levels, ensuring a coordinated hormonal response rather than isolated single-cell secretion.

incorrectas.A: Tight junctions seal the paracellular space between epithelial cells to control permeability (as in gut or renal tubule epithelium), but they do not create cytoplasmic channels for direct ion/molecule passage, so they cannot mediate the rapid electrical coupling described.
incorrectas.B: Desmosomes are mechanical anchoring junctions that link intermediate filaments between cells (important in tissues under mechanical stress, like skin), providing structural adhesion, not a conduit for intercellular communication.
incorrectas.D: Hemidesmosomes anchor epithelial cells to the underlying basement membrane, not to adjacent cells, so they play no role in cell-to-cell communication within the islet.

preguntas.q: The portal blood supply within the islets of Langerhans allows insulin-rich venous blood from which cells to bathe the alpha and delta cells, promoting paracrine communication?

e.correcta: Beta cells form the core of the islet, and their venous effluent (which is high in insulin) drains outward through a portal-like microcirculation to bathe the surrounding alpha and delta cells before leaving the islet — this anatomic arrangement lets insulin directly inhibit glucagon secretion from alpha cells in a paracrine fashion. This insulin-first, glucagon-second sequence of perfusion is a key mechanism ensuring that glucagon release is appropriately suppressed when insulin (and by extension glucose) is high.

incorrectas.A: Delta cells are downstream in this portal circulation (bathed by insulin from beta cells) and are not the source of the insulin-rich blood that perfuses other islet cells.
incorrectas.B: PP cells are a minor population typically located in islets of the pancreatic head and are not the source of the central insulin-rich blood flow that perfuses alpha and delta cells.
incorrectas.C: Alpha cells are recipients of the beta-cell-derived insulin-rich blood in this portal system (that's how insulin suppresses their glucagon secretion) — they are not the source of the perfusing blood themselves.

preguntas.q: Where are the somatostatin-secreting delta cells located within the islets of Langerhans?

o.A: Confined to the outermost periphery of the islet
o.B: Interspersed between alpha and beta cells
o.C: Clustered exclusively in the islet core
o.D: Located only in islets near the pancreatic tail

e.correcta: Delta cells are scattered throughout the islet, interspersed between the more centrally located beta cells and the peripheral alpha cells, which places them in an ideal position to exert paracrine inhibitory effects (via somatostatin) on both insulin secretion from beta cells and glucagon secretion from alpha cells. This intermediate, distributed location reflects somatostatin's role as a general dampener of islet hormone secretion rather than a cell type restricted to one anatomic zone.

incorrectas.A: Alpha cells, not delta cells, are classically described as occupying the peripheral rim of the islet — delta cells are interspersed more centrally between alpha and beta cells to allow paracrine signaling to both.
incorrectas.C: Delta cells are not clustered exclusively in the islet core; beta cells occupy the central core, while delta cells are distributed at the interface between the beta cell core and the alpha cell periphery.
incorrectas.D: Delta cells are present throughout islets across the pancreas (head, body, and tail), not restricted only to islets near the tail, so this description does not reflect their actual distribution.

preguntas.q: The gene directing insulin synthesis is located on which chromosome?

e.correcta: The insulin gene (INS) is located on the short arm of chromosome 11, and its expression in pancreatic beta cells produces preproinsulin, which is processed into proinsulin and then cleaved into mature insulin plus C-peptide within secretory granules. Knowing the chromosomal location is tested because chromosome 11 also harbors the beta-globin gene cluster, so questions often use insulin's location as a landmark or contrast point in genetics-focused vignettes. Mutations affecting this locus can contribute to certain familial forms of hyperproinsulinemia due to impaired proteolytic processing.

incorrectas.A: Chromosome 6 harbors the HLA gene complex (MHC class I and II genes), which is relevant to autoimmune associations like type 1 diabetes susceptibility, but it is not the chromosomal location of the insulin gene itself.
incorrectas.C: Chromosome 17 contains genes such as BRCA1 and TP53, which are important in oncology contexts, but has no relation to insulin gene location.
incorrectas.D: Chromosome 21 is most notable for its association with Down syndrome (trisomy 21) and genes like APP, but it does not carry the insulin gene.

preguntas.q: Ribosomal translation of insulin mRNA in the rough endoplasmic reticulum initially produces which precursor molecule, containing a signal peptide, the A and B chains, and a connecting peptide?

e.correcta: Translation of insulin mRNA on the rough ER ribosomes produces preproinsulin, the full-length primary product containing an N-terminal signal peptide (which directs translocation into the ER lumen) plus the B chain, C-peptide (connecting peptide), and A chain in sequence. Once inside the ER, the signal peptide is cleaved to yield proinsulin, which then folds and forms disulfide bonds before being transported to the Golgi for further processing — this progression (preproinsulin to proinsulin to insulin) is a classic example of sequential proteolytic maturation of a secreted peptide hormone.

incorrectas.A: Proinsulin is the product after the signal peptide has already been cleaved off preproinsulin in the ER — it still contains the A chain, B chain, and C-peptide, but it is not the very first translation product, which is preproinsulin.
incorrectas.C: Mature insulin (A and B chains joined by disulfide bonds, with C-peptide removed) is the final secretory product formed only after proteolytic cleavage in secretory granules, not the initial ribosomal translation product.
incorrectas.D: C-peptide alone is only one fragment released after cleavage of proinsulin in the secretory granule; it is not the full initial translation product, which includes the signal peptide and both A and B chains as well.

preguntas.q: After being formed in the rough endoplasmic reticulum, proinsulin is packaged into secretory granules within which organelle?

e.correcta: After proinsulin is synthesized and folded in the rough ER, it is transported via vesicles to the Golgi apparatus, where it is packaged into immature secretory granules; the Golgi is the sorting and packaging hub of the secretory pathway responsible for directing proteins into the regulated secretory granules that will eventually be released by exocytosis. Within these granules (which bud off from the trans-Golgi network), proinsulin is subsequently cleaved by prohormone convertases into mature insulin and C-peptide as the granule matures.

incorrectas.A: Mitochondria are the site of oxidative ATP production and are not involved in protein packaging or secretory granule formation for exported hormones like insulin.
incorrectas.C: Lysosomes are degradative organelles that break down proteins and cellular debris via acid hydrolases; they are not part of the normal biosynthetic/secretory packaging pathway that produces insulin granules.
incorrectas.D: Peroxisomes handle fatty acid oxidation and reactive oxygen species detoxification; they play no role in the packaging of secretory proteins like proinsulin into granules.

preguntas.q: During packaging into secretory granules, proteases cleave which peptide from proinsulin to yield mature insulin?

e.correcta: Within the maturing secretory granules, prohormone convertases and carboxypeptidase E cleave proinsulin at two internal sites, excising the connecting peptide (C-peptide) and leaving the A and B chains linked together by disulfide bonds as mature, biologically active insulin. This cleavage step is what converts the relatively inactive proinsulin into functional insulin, and because C-peptide is released in equimolar amounts, it serves as a useful clinical marker of endogenous insulin production.

incorrectas.A: The signal peptide is cleaved much earlier, in the rough ER, immediately after translation of preproinsulin — it is not the peptide removed during granule packaging to form mature insulin.
incorrectas.C: The A chain is retained as part of mature insulin (linked to the B chain via disulfide bonds); it is not cleaved away, so it cannot be the peptide removed to generate active insulin.
incorrectas.D: The B chain, like the A chain, is retained as part of mature insulin rather than being excised — cleavage removes the connecting peptide between the B and A chains, not the B chain itself.

preguntas.q: Insulin is packaged into secretory granules of the Golgi apparatus alongside which co-secreted peptide?

o.D: Amylin only, with no other peptide

e.correcta: When prohormone convertases cleave proinsulin within the secretory granule, they release mature insulin and C-peptide as two separate molecules in equimolar amounts, and both are co-packaged in the same granules and co-secreted together into the bloodstream upon beta-cell stimulation. Because C-peptide has a longer half-life and is not extracted by the liver the way insulin is, measuring C-peptide is a more stable proxy for endogenous insulin secretion, especially useful in patients on exogenous insulin.

incorrectas.A: Proinsulin is the uncleaved precursor that gives rise to insulin and C-peptide — a small amount of intact proinsulin is co-secreted, but the classically tested, clinically relevant co-secreted peptide alongside mature insulin is C-peptide, not proinsulin itself as the primary answer.
incorrectas.B: The signal peptide is cleaved off in the rough ER, long before granule packaging, and is degraded rather than co-packaged and co-secreted with mature insulin in the Golgi-derived granules.
incorrectas.D: Amylin (islet amyloid polypeptide) is indeed co-secreted with insulin, but describing it as the only co-secreted peptide is incorrect because C-peptide is the classic, equimolar, clinically measured co-secreted product of proinsulin cleavage.

preguntas.q: When a pancreatic beta cell is stimulated to release insulin, in what ratio are insulin and C-peptide released?

o.A: Insulin in a 2:1 excess over C-peptide
o.B: C-peptide in a 2:1 excess over insulin
o.D: A variable ratio depending on glucose concentration

e.correcta: Because proinsulin is cleaved into one molecule of insulin and one molecule of C-peptide in a 1:1 stoichiometric reaction, beta cells release insulin and C-peptide in equimolar amounts whenever they are stimulated to secrete. This equimolar relationship is exactly why C-peptide is used clinically as a surrogate marker for endogenous insulin secretion — its level reflects how much insulin the pancreas itself is producing, independent of any exogenous insulin the patient may be receiving.

incorrectas.A: Insulin is not released in excess over C-peptide; the cleavage of proinsulin produces one insulin molecule for every one C-peptide molecule, not a skewed 2:1 ratio favoring insulin.
incorrectas.B: C-peptide is not released in excess over insulin either — both are generated from a single proteolytic cleavage event of proinsulin, so their molar ratio is 1:1, not 2:1 favoring C-peptide.
incorrectas.D: The insulin:C-peptide ratio does not vary with glucose concentration; regardless of how much total secretion is stimulated, each cleaved proinsulin molecule always yields exactly one insulin and one C-peptide molecule.

preguntas.q: Which peptide, co-packaged and co-secreted with insulin, can be measured to monitor endogenous beta-cell function in patients receiving exogenous insulin therapy?

e.correcta: C-peptide is cleaved from proinsulin in equimolar amounts with insulin and is co-secreted with it, but unlike therapeutic insulin preparations, C-peptide is not present in exogenous insulin formulations — so measuring serum C-peptide reflects only the patient's own endogenous beta-cell insulin production, unaffected by injected insulin. This makes it clinically useful for distinguishing factitious hypoglycemia (exogenous insulin use, low C-peptide) from endogenous hyperinsulinemic states like insulinoma or sulfonylurea use (elevated C-peptide) in a patient already on insulin therapy.

incorrectas.A: Glucagon is secreted by alpha cells and physiologically opposes insulin's effects on glucose; it is not co-packaged with insulin in beta cell granules and does not serve as a marker of endogenous insulin secretion.
incorrectas.B: Amylin is co-secreted with insulin by beta cells and plays a role in glucose regulation (slowing gastric emptying), but it is not the classic marker used clinically to assess endogenous beta-cell insulin output — that role belongs specifically to C-peptide.
incorrectas.D: Somatostatin is secreted by delta cells (not beta cells) and inhibits insulin and glucagon secretion in a paracrine fashion; it is not co-packaged with insulin and is not used as a marker of endogenous beta-cell insulin production.

preguntas.q: A patient with a suspected insulinoma has elevated insulin along with elevated C-peptide. What is the most likely explanation for concurrently elevated levels of both insulin and C-peptide?

e.correcta: Insulinomas are beta-cell tumors that autonomously oversecrete both insulin and C-peptide together (since they still process proinsulin through the normal secretory pathway), and sulfonylureas act by closing beta-cell ATP-sensitive K+ channels to stimulate the patient's own beta cells to release more endogenous insulin and C-peptide — in both cases, the source is endogenous beta-cell secretion, so both insulin and C-peptide rise together. This pairing (elevated insulin AND elevated C-peptide) is the key lab pattern that identifies an endogenous cause of hyperinsulinemia, and a sulfonylurea screen is typically needed to distinguish factitious sulfonylurea use from a true insulinoma.

incorrectas.A: Exogenous insulin injection would elevate serum insulin but suppress endogenous beta-cell secretion (via negative feedback on glucose-stimulated insulin release), resulting in low or normal C-peptide, not concurrently elevated C-peptide as seen here.
incorrectas.C: Type 1 diabetes mellitus is characterized by beta-cell destruction and insulin deficiency, so both endogenous insulin and C-peptide would be low or absent, not elevated — this is essentially the opposite lab pattern.
incorrectas.D: Insulin receptor antibody-mediated resistance causes impaired insulin action at the receptor, often with compensatory hyperinsulinemia and elevated C-peptide from the pancreas trying to overcome resistance, but this is a distinct mechanism from a discrete insulin-secreting tumor or sulfonylurea stimulation and doesn't match the classic insulinoma-associated presentation being tested here.

preguntas.q: A patient has elevated serum insulin but normal or decreased C-peptide levels. What is the most likely cause?

e.correcta: Exogenous insulin injections (whether therapeutic or surreptitious) raise serum insulin levels directly without involving the patient's own beta cells, and since commercial insulin preparations do not contain C-peptide, the high circulating insulin suppresses endogenous insulin secretion via negative feedback on glucose sensing, driving down the patient's own proinsulin processing and thus C-peptide. The resulting pattern — high insulin with normal or low C-peptide — is the classic biochemical signature used to diagnose factitious hypoglycemia from surreptitious insulin use.

incorrectas.A: Insulinoma causes autonomous secretion of endogenous insulin via the normal beta-cell processing pathway, so it produces elevated C-peptide alongside elevated insulin, not the low/normal C-peptide pattern described here.
incorrectas.B: Sulfonylurea overdose stimulates the patient's own beta cells to secrete more endogenous insulin, which is co-released with C-peptide, so it would raise C-peptide along with insulin rather than causing a discordantly low C-peptide.
incorrectas.D: Glucagonoma causes excess glucagon secretion from alpha cells, leading to hyperglycemia and catabolic symptoms, not primarily elevated insulin with discordant C-peptide — it does not fit this insulin/C-peptide dissociation pattern at all.

preguntas.q: What is the major physiological regulator of insulin release from pancreatic beta cells?

e.correcta: Glucose is the dominant physiologic trigger for insulin secretion: rising blood glucose is taken up into beta cells via GLUT2, metabolized to generate ATP, which closes ATP-sensitive K+ channels, depolarizes the cell membrane, opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, and triggers exocytosis of insulin-containing granules. While amino acids, fatty acids, and incretin hormones can modulate insulin release, glucose is the primary, most tightly coupled signal that beta cells sense to match insulin output to circulating fuel levels.

incorrectas.A: Serum calcium plays an intracellular signaling role downstream in the beta cell (triggering granule exocytosis after depolarization), but extracellular serum calcium is not the primary physiologic sensor that beta cells use to detect the need for insulin release — glucose is.
incorrectas.C: Serum sodium has no established direct physiologic role in triggering insulin secretion from beta cells; the beta cell's glucose-sensing machinery (GLUT2, glucokinase, ATP-sensitive K+ channels) responds to glucose, not sodium concentration.
incorrectas.D: Cortisol generally opposes insulin action (promoting gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance) and is not the physiologic trigger for insulin secretion — it is more of a counter-regulatory, stress hormone rather than the primary driver of beta-cell insulin release.

preguntas.q: Glucose enters the pancreatic beta cell from the blood via which transporter, characterized by low affinity and high capacity facilitated diffusion?

e.correcta: GLUT2 is the glucose transporter expressed on pancreatic beta cells (and hepatocytes) that has a high Km (low affinity) but high Vmax (high capacity), allowing glucose to enter the cell via facilitated diffusion at a rate roughly proportional to blood glucose concentration across a wide physiologic range. This property lets the beta cell accurately sense and respond to changes in serum glucose without transporter saturation, which is essential for glucose-stimulated insulin secretion to properly track blood glucose levels.

incorrectas.A: GLUT1 is a high-affinity, low-capacity transporter found in red blood cells and the blood-brain barrier that ensures constant basal glucose uptake for these glucose-dependent tissues, not the beta-cell transporter responsible for glucose sensing.
incorrectas.C: GLUT4 is the insulin-responsive glucose transporter found in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue, translocating to the membrane in response to insulin signaling — it mediates glucose uptake in response to insulin, rather than functioning as the beta cell's glucose sensor for insulin secretion.
incorrectas.D: SGLT1 is a sodium-glucose cotransporter found in the intestinal brush border (and SGLT2 in the renal proximal tubule) that performs active, secondary transport against a concentration gradient, unlike the low-affinity facilitated diffusion mechanism used by beta cells.

preguntas.q: In the pancreatic beta cell, metabolism of glucose generates which molecule that causes closure of specific K+ channels and subsequent membrane depolarization?

e.correcta: Once glucose enters the beta cell via GLUT2, it is phosphorylated by glucokinase and metabolized through glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation to generate ATP; the resulting rise in the intracellular ATP:ADP ratio binds to and closes ATP-sensitive K+ (KATP) channels, preventing K+ efflux and causing the membrane to depolarize. This depolarization then opens voltage-gated calcium channels, and the resulting calcium influx triggers exocytosis of insulin granules — making ATP the critical metabolic signal that couples glucose sensing to electrical excitability in the beta cell.

incorrectas.A: NADH is generated during glycolysis and the TCA cycle and feeds into the electron transport chain to help generate ATP, but it is ATP itself (not NADH directly) that binds the KATP channel's regulatory subunit (SUR1) to trigger channel closure.
incorrectas.C: Acetyl-CoA is an intermediate that enters the TCA cycle to ultimately generate ATP via oxidative phosphorylation, but it does not itself act on the KATP channel — the final signaling molecule that closes the channel is ATP.
incorrectas.D: Pyruvate is the end product of glycolysis that enters mitochondria to be converted to acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle, but pyruvate itself does not directly close KATP channels — this action requires the downstream ATP generated from its oxidation.

preguntas.q: In the pancreatic beta cell, an increase in intracellular Ca2+ following membrane depolarization directly triggers which process, releasing insulin-containing granules?

e.correcta: Membrane depolarization from KATP channel closure opens voltage-gated L-type calcium channels, and the resulting influx of extracellular Ca2+ raises intracellular calcium, which binds proteins involved in vesicle docking and fusion (like synaptotagmin) to trigger exocytosis of insulin-containing secretory granules at the plasma membrane. This calcium-triggered exocytosis is the final common step by which the beta cell converts a glucose-sensing electrical signal into the physical release of insulin into the bloodstream.

incorrectas.A: Autophagy is a cellular self-degradation process for recycling organelles and proteins, unrelated to calcium-triggered granule release; it does not describe how insulin granules are released from the cell.
incorrectas.C: Pinocytosis is a form of endocytosis where cells take up extracellular fluid, the functional opposite of exocytosis, so it does not describe the calcium-triggered process by which insulin granules are released.
incorrectas.D: Apoptosis is programmed cell death and is not a secretory mechanism; rising intracellular calcium after depolarization triggers granule release (exocytosis), not death of the beta cell.

preguntas.q: Which class of drugs increases insulin secretion by closing ATP-sensitive K+ channels in pancreatic beta cells?

e.correcta: Sulfonylureas (like tolbutamide and glyburide) bind directly to the SUR1 regulatory subunit of the beta-cell ATP-sensitive K+ channel, causing it to close independent of the cell's actual glucose or ATP levels — this mimics the normal glucose-induced depolarization signal, opening voltage-gated Ca2+ channels and triggering insulin exocytosis even without a corresponding rise in blood glucose. Because this mechanism works regardless of ambient glucose, sulfonylureas carry an inherent risk of hypoglycemia, unlike drugs that only potentiate glucose-dependent insulin release.

incorrectas.A: Biguanides (metformin) work primarily by decreasing hepatic gluconeogenesis and improving peripheral insulin sensitivity via AMPK activation; they do not act on beta-cell KATP channels or directly increase insulin secretion.
incorrectas.B: Thiazolidinediones act on PPAR-gamma receptors to increase insulin sensitivity in adipose and muscle tissue, not by closing beta-cell KATP channels — they improve insulin action rather than directly stimulating its secretion.
incorrectas.D: GLP-1 receptor agonists enhance glucose-dependent insulin secretion by binding GLP-1 receptors on beta cells and raising intracellular cAMP, which potentiates but does not directly close KATP channels the way sulfonylureas do — their glucose-dependence also makes them lower risk for hypoglycemia.

preguntas.q: Why is an oral glucose load a more powerful stimulant of insulin secretion than an equivalent intravenous glucose infusion?

o.A: Oral glucose is absorbed faster into the bloodstream than IV glucose
o.B: Oral glucose stimulates secretion of GIP and GLP-1 from the gut
o.C: Oral glucose bypasses first-pass hepatic metabolism
o.D: Oral glucose directly activates beta-cell GLUT2 transporters more efficiently

e.correcta: Oral glucose triggers release of incretin hormones — GIP from K cells of the duodenum and GLP-1 from L cells of the ileum — in response to nutrients in the gut lumen, and these incretins act on pancreatic beta cells to amplify glucose-stimulated insulin secretion above what glucose alone would produce. This phenomenon, known as the incretin effect, explains why an oral glucose load produces a much greater insulin response than an IV glucose infusion that raises blood glucose to the same level, since IV glucose bypasses the gut entirely and never triggers incretin release.

incorrectas.A: The speed of absorption into the bloodstream is not the key mechanism — in fact IV glucose delivery is more rapid and direct, yet it produces a smaller insulin response, precisely because it bypasses the gut-derived incretin signal that amplifies secretion.
incorrectas.C: Oral glucose does not bypass first-pass hepatic metabolism — it is actually the opposite, since glucose absorbed from the gut travels through the portal vein to the liver first, whereas IV glucose bypasses the gut and portal circulation.
incorrectas.D: There is no evidence that oral glucose activates beta-cell GLUT2 transporters more efficiently than glucose delivered intravenously — the transporter's response depends on blood glucose concentration, not the route by which that glucose arrived, so this doesn't explain the incretin effect.

preguntas.q: By what mechanism do sulfonylurea drugs such as tolbutamide and glyburide increase insulin secretion?

o.A: By increasing beta-cell sensitivity to GLP-1
o.B: By closing ATP-dependent K+ channels, causing depolarization and insulin release
o.C: By inhibiting insulin degradation in the liver
o.D: By blocking glucagon receptors on beta cells

e.correcta: Sulfonylureas bind to the SUR1 subunit of the ATP-sensitive K+ channel on pancreatic beta cells, forcing the channel closed independent of the cell's actual metabolic (ATP) state; this closure prevents K+ efflux, depolarizes the membrane, opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, and triggers calcium-dependent exocytosis of insulin granules. Because this action occurs regardless of ambient glucose levels, sulfonylureas can provoke insulin release (and hypoglycemia) even when glucose is not elevated, distinguishing their mechanism from glucose-dependent insulin secretagogues.

incorrectas.A: Sulfonylureas do not act by sensitizing beta cells to GLP-1; their mechanism is a direct pharmacologic closure of the KATP channel, independent of incretin signaling pathways.
incorrectas.C: Sulfonylureas do not inhibit hepatic insulin degradation; insulin clearance in the liver is a separate process from beta-cell insulin secretion, and the drugs' therapeutic effect comes from directly stimulating release, not from slowing insulin breakdown.
incorrectas.D: Sulfonylureas do not act as glucagon receptor antagonists; their effect is entirely on the beta cell's own KATP channel/insulin secretion machinery, not on glucagon signaling.

preguntas.q: What effect does glucagon have on insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells?

o.D: Biphasic: initial decrease followed by suppression

e.correcta: Glucagon acts on pancreatic beta cells (in a paracrine fashion within the islet) to stimulate insulin secretion, which helps limit the rise in blood glucose that glucagon itself promotes via hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. This is a physiologic feedback loop: as glucagon raises glucose, the resulting insulin release helps drive glucose into cells and modulates the overall glycemic response, illustrating the tightly coupled cross-talk between alpha and beta cells within the islet.

incorrectas.A: Glucagon does not decrease insulin secretion — it actually stimulates it via cAMP-mediated signaling in beta cells, so pairing 'decreases' with glucagon reverses the true paracrine relationship between alpha and beta cells.
incorrectas.C: Glucagon is not neutral on insulin release; islet cells communicate via paracrine signaling, and glucagon has a clear stimulatory effect on beta cells, so 'no effect' ignores this well-established islet cross-talk.
incorrectas.D: There is no evidence for a biphasic decrease-then-suppression pattern; glucagon's effect on beta cells is stimulatory (increasing insulin secretion), not a suppressive or biphasic negative pattern.

preguntas.q: What effect does somatostatin, secreted by pancreatic delta cells, have on insulin secretion?

o.D: Converts insulin to its inactive precursor

e.correcta: Somatostatin, secreted by pancreatic islet delta cells, decreases insulin secretion (as well as glucagon secretion) through paracrine inhibitory signaling within the islet, acting via Gi-coupled somatostatin receptors that reduce cAMP and calcium influx in beta cells — this is part of a broader regulatory network where somatostatin serves as a general 'brake' on endocrine pancreatic secretion, helping fine-tune insulin/glucagon release rather than driving it. This inhibitory role is exploited clinically with somatostatin analogs (e.g., octreotide) used to suppress hormone hypersecretion in various endocrine tumors.

incorrectas.A: Somatostatin does not increase insulin secretion; its physiologic role within the islet is inhibitory (paracrine suppression) on neighboring beta cells, opposite to what stimulatory hormones like GLP-1 or glucose itself would do.
incorrectas.C: Somatostatin has a well-documented and significant inhibitory effect on insulin release, so 'no significant effect' understates its established paracrine role in dampening islet hormone secretion.
incorrectas.D: Somatostatin does not chemically convert insulin into an inactive precursor form; insulin's own precursor processing (proinsulin to insulin and C-peptide) occurs via prohormone convertases within beta cells, unrelated to somatostatin's inhibitory signaling action.

preguntas.q: The insulin receptor is a tetrameric structure composed of which subunits?

o.B: Two alpha and two beta subunits
o.D: One alpha and three beta subunits

e.correcta: The insulin receptor is a disulfide-linked tetramer composed of two extracellular alpha subunits (which bind insulin) and two transmembrane beta subunits (which contain intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity), arranged as an α2β2 heterotetramer. Insulin binding to the alpha subunits induces a conformational change that activates the beta subunits' tyrosine kinase domains, leading to receptor autophosphorylation and downstream phosphorylation of substrates like IRS-1, which propagate the insulin signal into the cell.

incorrectas.A: The receptor is not composed of four identical alpha subunits — it contains two distinct subunit types (alpha and beta) with different functions (ligand binding versus kinase signaling), not a homotetramer of a single subunit.
incorrectas.C: The receptor is not composed of four identical beta subunits either; it requires the extracellular alpha subunits specifically to bind insulin, since the beta subunits alone (being purely transmembrane/kinase domains) cannot perform ligand recognition.
incorrectas.D: The receptor does not have an asymmetric 1:3 alpha:beta subunit ratio — it is a symmetric heterotetramer with exactly two alpha and two beta subunits.

preguntas.q: Which subunits of the insulin receptor are connected by a disulfide bond and lie entirely within the extracellular domain?

e.correcta: The insulin receptor is a tetrameric transmembrane glycoprotein composed of two extracellular alpha subunits, which bind insulin, and two transmembrane beta subunits, which contain intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity; the two alpha subunits are linked to each other and to the beta subunits by disulfide bonds, and because they lie entirely outside the cell membrane, they form the insulin-binding pocket accessible from the extracellular space. Insulin binding to the alpha subunits triggers a conformational change that activates the intracellular beta subunit kinase domains, initiating downstream signaling (e.g., IRS-1 phosphorylation).

incorrectas.A: Beta subunits span the membrane and contain the intracellular tyrosine kinase domain that becomes autophosphorylated upon insulin binding; they are not the disulfide-linked, purely extracellular component described in the question.
incorrectas.C: The insulin receptor does not have gamma subunits; it is composed only of alpha and beta subunit pairs, so this option describes a component that does not exist in this receptor's structure.
incorrectas.D: Similarly, there are no delta subunits in the insulin receptor — its structure is limited to two alpha and two beta subunits linked by disulfide bonds.

preguntas.q: Which subunit of the insulin receptor is a transmembrane protein connected to the extracellular alpha subunit by a disulfide bond?

e.correcta: The beta subunit of the insulin receptor spans the plasma membrane and is linked to the extracellular alpha subunit via disulfide bonds, positioning it to transmit the signal generated by insulin binding on the alpha subunit into an intracellular response; its cytoplasmic tail contains the tyrosine kinase domain that autophosphorylates and phosphorylates downstream substrates like IRS-1 once insulin binds. This transmembrane architecture — extracellular ligand-binding alpha linked to transmembrane signal-transducing beta — is the defining structural feature that allows the receptor to convert an extracellular hormonal signal into an intracellular kinase cascade.

incorrectas.A: The alpha subunit is entirely extracellular and responsible for binding insulin; it does not span the membrane and lacks the kinase domain that transduces the signal intracellularly, which is instead the role of the beta subunit.
incorrectas.C: GLUT4 is a separate glucose transporter protein that translocates to the membrane downstream of insulin receptor signaling; it is not a subunit of the insulin receptor itself and is not connected to the alpha subunit by a disulfide bond.
incorrectas.D: IRS-1 is a cytoplasmic adaptor protein that gets phosphorylated by the activated beta subunit's kinase domain, propagating the signal further downstream; it is a separate signaling molecule, not a structural subunit of the receptor connected via disulfide bonds to the alpha subunit.

preguntas.q: The β subunits of the insulin receptor possess which intrinsic enzymatic activity?

e.correcta: The intracellular portion of the insulin receptor's beta subunit possesses intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity, meaning that upon insulin binding to the alpha subunits, the beta subunits autophosphorylate specific tyrosine residues on each other and then phosphorylate tyrosines on downstream substrates such as IRS-1 and IRS-2. This tyrosine phosphorylation cascade recruits and activates downstream effectors (like PI3K and the Ras/MAPK pathway), ultimately driving GLUT4 translocation, glycogen synthesis, and cell growth effects — making tyrosine kinase activity the essential catalytic step that initiates all insulin signaling.

incorrectas.A: Guanylate cyclase activity generates cGMP and is characteristic of receptors like the ANP receptor, not the insulin receptor, which instead relies on tyrosine phosphorylation to initiate its signaling cascade.
incorrectas.B: Serine/threonine kinase activity characterizes receptors like the TGF-beta receptor family; the insulin receptor's catalytic activity specifically phosphorylates tyrosine residues, not serine/threonine residues, which is a key distinguishing feature of the receptor tyrosine kinase family it belongs to.
incorrectas.D: Phospholipase C activity, which generates IP3 and DAG, is associated with certain G-protein coupled receptor pathways, not the insulin receptor, whose primary catalytic function is tyrosine phosphorylation of itself and downstream substrates.

preguntas.q: When insulin binds its receptor, which enzyme becomes activated and autophosphorylates the receptor's β-subunits, subsequently phosphorylating intracellular proteins?

e.correcta: The insulin receptor is a receptor tyrosine kinase: insulin binding to the extracellular α-subunits induces a conformational change that activates the intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity of the β-subunits, causing them to autophosphorylate each other on tyrosine residues. This activated kinase then phosphorylates downstream substrates like IRS-1, which recruits signaling complexes (PI3K/Akt for metabolic effects, Ras/MAPK for growth effects) that mediate GLUT4 translocation, glycogen synthesis, and other insulin actions. This is the same receptor tyrosine kinase mechanism used by growth factor receptors like EGFR and IGF-1R.

incorrectas.A: Adenylate cyclase generates cAMP downstream of Gs-coupled GPCRs like glucagon and epinephrine receptors, not the insulin receptor, which has no G-protein coupling and instead signals through intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity.
incorrectas.C: Protein kinase A is activated by cAMP downstream of Gs-coupled receptors and mediates catabolic hormone signaling (e.g., glucagon), the opposite of insulin's tyrosine kinase-driven anabolic signaling cascade.
incorrectas.D: Phosphodiesterase degrades cyclic nucleotides (cAMP/cGMP) and is actually stimulated by insulin signaling in some tissues to lower cAMP, but it is not the enzyme activated at the receptor itself upon insulin binding.

preguntas.q: After the insulin receptor phosphorylates intracellular proteins, what happens to the receptor itself?

o.A: It remains permanently on the cell surface
o.B: It is cleaved and released into the bloodstream
o.C: It is internalized via endocytosis and then degraded, stored, or recycled

e.correcta: After signaling, the insulin-receptor complex is internalized via receptor-mediated endocytosis, a process common to many activated receptor tyrosine kinases that both terminates the signal and allows the cell to process the receptor. Once internalized, the receptor can be degraded in lysosomes (down-regulating the response), or recycled back to the membrane depending on the insulin concentration and duration of exposure. This internalization-degradation cycle is part of why chronically high insulin levels (as in insulin resistance) lead to fewer surface receptors over time.

incorrectas.A: The receptor does not remain permanently on the surface; internalization is a normal, physiologic step in terminating and regulating receptor tyrosine kinase signaling, distinguishing it from receptors that recycle without turnover.
incorrectas.B: The receptor is not cleaved and released into the bloodstream; it stays membrane/vesicle-associated throughout endocytosis, unlike some ectodomain-shedding receptors, and functions intracellularly rather than being secreted.
incorrectas.D: GLUT4 translocation to the membrane is a downstream effect of insulin signaling (via the PI3K/Akt pathway), but the insulin receptor does not dimerize with GLUT4 — they are separate proteins acting at different steps of the pathway.

preguntas.q: Chronic elevation of insulin levels, such as occurs in obesity, has what effect on insulin receptors in target tissues?

o.C: Down-regulation, potentially contributing to insulin resistance
o.D: Conversion of receptors to a high-affinity state

e.correcta: Chronic hyperinsulinemia, as seen in obesity and early type 2 diabetes, triggers down-regulation of insulin receptors on target tissues (liver, muscle, fat) through receptor internalization and reduced receptor synthesis, a negative feedback response to sustained high ligand exposure; this receptor down-regulation contributes to the insulin resistance that characterizes these states, creating a vicious cycle where more insulin is needed to achieve the same glucose-lowering effect, further perpetuating hyperinsulinemia. This receptor-level mechanism works alongside post-receptor signaling defects (e.g., impaired GLUT4 translocation) to produce the overall insulin-resistant phenotype.

incorrectas.A: Upregulation with increased sensitivity is the opposite of what chronic hyperinsulinemia produces — sustained high hormone levels typically drive receptor down-regulation as a homeostatic response, not increased receptor number or sensitivity.
incorrectas.B: There is a well-documented change in receptor number in chronic hyperinsulinemic states — receptors decrease rather than staying constant, which is part of the mechanistic explanation for insulin resistance in obesity.
incorrectas.D: Chronic insulin excess does not convert receptors to a higher-affinity state; if anything, the functional coupling and number of receptors decline, which lowers rather than raises effective sensitivity to insulin.

preguntas.q: How does the number of insulin receptors change in starvation compared to obesity?

o.A: Increased in both starvation and obesity
o.B: Decreased in both starvation and obesity
o.C: Decreased in starvation, increased in obesity
o.D: Increased in starvation, decreased in obesity

e.correcta: Receptor number is regulated by ambient hormone levels through down-regulation: chronically high insulin (as in obesity, where hyperinsulinemia compensates for insulin resistance) drives more receptor internalization and degradation, reducing surface receptor density and worsening insulin resistance. Conversely, starvation is a low-insulin state, so cells up-regulate (increase) insulin receptor number to maximize sensitivity to the little insulin present, helping preserve glucose uptake in critical tissues. This receptor up/down-regulation is a general principle across hormone systems, not unique to insulin.

incorrectas.A: Receptors do not increase in both states — obesity is a hyperinsulinemic state that down-regulates receptors, the opposite of the up-regulation seen in the low-insulin state of starvation.
incorrectas.B: Receptors do not decrease in both states — starvation, with low ambient insulin, triggers compensatory up-regulation of receptors rather than a decrease.
incorrectas.C: This reverses the actual relationship: starvation (low insulin) leads to receptor up-regulation, while obesity (high insulin, insulin resistance) leads to receptor down-regulation, not the other way around.

preguntas.q: Which three tissues are the primary targets of insulin action?

e.correcta: Liver, skeletal muscle, and adipose tissue are the classic insulin-dependent tissues where insulin drives glucose uptake (via GLUT4 in muscle/fat) and anabolic storage — glycogen synthesis in liver and muscle, and triglyceride synthesis in adipose tissue. These tissues are central to whole-body fuel storage after a meal, which is why insulin resistance in these three sites underlies the pathophysiology of type 2 diabetes. Other tissues like brain and RBCs take up glucose via insulin-independent GLUT1/GLUT3 transporters, which is why the brain can still access glucose during insulin deficiency.

incorrectas.A: Brain glucose uptake is insulin-independent (via GLUT1/GLUT3), and the kidney and pancreas are not classified among the primary insulin target tissues for glucose disposal and storage.
incorrectas.C: Lung, heart, and skin are not the primary insulin-responsive tissues for glucose metabolism; cardiac muscle does use GLUT4 to some extent, but the classic triad tested is liver, skeletal muscle, and adipose tissue.
incorrectas.D: Bone, intestine, and thyroid are not major sites of insulin-mediated glucose uptake and storage; intestinal enterocytes absorb glucose via SGLT1/GLUT2, transporters independent of insulin action.

preguntas.q: Insulin lowers blood glucose in part by decreasing which hepatic process, mediated by increased fructose-2,6-bisphosphate?

e.correcta: Insulin raises hepatic fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (F2,6BP) by activating PFK-2, and F2,6BP is a potent activator of PFK-1 (glycolysis) and an inhibitor of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (gluconeogenesis). By pushing this reciprocal regulation, insulin favors glycolysis and suppresses gluconeogenesis, reducing hepatic glucose output — a key mechanism by which insulin lowers blood glucose beyond just promoting peripheral uptake. This F2,6BP switch is the same regulatory node that glucagon manipulates in the opposite direction during fasting.

incorrectas.A: Glycogenolysis is suppressed by insulin, but this occurs mainly through inhibition of glycogen phosphorylase (via dephosphorylation), not primarily through the F2,6BP-mediated glycolysis/gluconeogenesis switch described here.
incorrectas.B: Glycolysis is actually increased, not decreased, by the rise in F2,6BP under insulin's influence, since F2,6BP is an allosteric activator of PFK-1, the key glycolytic control enzyme.
incorrectas.D: Ketogenesis is reduced by insulin, but this happens via decreased lipolysis and malonyl-CoA-mediated inhibition of CPT-1, not through the hepatic F2,6BP/gluconeogenesis pathway being asked about here.

preguntas.q: In adipose tissue, insulin stimulates fat deposition while inhibiting which catabolic process?

e.correcta: Insulin inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase in adipocytes, directly suppressing lipolysis (breakdown of stored triglycerides into free fatty acids and glycerol). This shifts adipose tissue metabolism toward net fat storage, complementing insulin's simultaneous stimulation of glucose uptake and triglyceride synthesis, so less fatty acid substrate reaches the liver to drive ketogenesis and gluconeogenesis. This is why untreated diabetes (insulin deficiency) causes unchecked lipolysis, elevated free fatty acids, and ketoacidosis.

incorrectas.B: Fatty acid synthesis is actually stimulated (not inhibited) by insulin as part of its anabolic, fat-storing program, the opposite direction from the catabolic process (lipolysis) the question is asking about.
incorrectas.C: Glucose uptake into adipocytes is stimulated by insulin via GLUT4 translocation; it is an anabolic process insulin promotes, not the catabolic process being inhibited that the question asks for.
incorrectas.D: Triglyceride synthesis is increased by insulin, not inhibited — insulin promotes esterification of fatty acids into triglycerides for storage, which is the anabolic counterpart to the lipolysis it suppresses.

preguntas.q: Insulin inhibits hepatic formation of which compound by decreasing fatty acid degradation and thus limiting available acetyl-CoA substrate?

e.correcta: Ketoacids (acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate) are produced in the liver from acetyl-CoA generated by beta-oxidation of fatty acids. Insulin inhibits lipolysis in adipose tissue, cutting off the supply of free fatty acids to the liver, and also inhibits carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1 (CPT-1) via malonyl-CoA, so less fatty acid enters mitochondria for oxidation. With less fatty acid degradation, less acetyl-CoA is available to be shunted into ketogenesis, explaining why ketoacidosis is a hallmark of insulin deficiency (type 1 diabetes) rather than insulin excess.
