In males, this peripheral aromatization — occurring mainly in adipose tissue and the testis — is the primary source of circulating estrogen, which plays roles in bone maturation, epiphyseal closure, and feedback regulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis; this is why aromatase inhibitors or aromatase deficiency lead to tall stature and delayed bone age in men.

incorrectas.A: Glucocorticoids (like cortisol) are synthesized from cholesterol via a distinct adrenal cortex pathway involving 11-beta-hydroxylase and other enzymes, not via aromatase acting on androgens.
incorrectas.C: Mineralocorticoids (like aldosterone) arise from a separate adrenal zona glomerulosa pathway using aldosterone synthase, unrelated to the aromatization of androgens into estrogens.
incorrectas.D: Progestins (like progesterone) are made directly from pregnenolone via 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase earlier in steroidogenesis, not by aromatizing androgens, so aromatase is not involved in their production.

preguntas.q: In males, aromatization of androgens to estrogen occurs primarily in which two tissues?

e.correcta: In males, aromatase is expressed at meaningful levels in adipose tissue (peripheral conversion of adrenal and gonadal androgens) and in the testis itself (Leydig and Sertoli cells producing local estradiol important for spermatogenesis and feedback regulation). This dual site of aromatization explains both why obesity (increased adipose mass) is associated with relative estrogen excess and gynecomastia in men, and why testicular pathology can alter the androgen-to-estrogen balance.

incorrectas.A: The liver and kidney metabolize and clear steroid hormones and participate in conjugation/excretion, but they are not the primary sites of aromatase-mediated conversion of androgens to estrogens in males.
incorrectas.B: The adrenal cortex produces androgen precursors like DHEA and androstenedione, and skin has some steroidogenic capacity, but neither is the principal site of aromatization in males compared to adipose tissue and testis.
incorrectas.D: Skeletal muscle and bone are targets of androgen and estrogen action (e.g., bone mineralization, epiphyseal closure) but are not the major tissues where aromatase converts androgens into estrogens in males.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme is the key catalyst converting androgens (testosterone and androstenedione) into estrogens?

e.correcta: Aromatase (cytochrome P-450 aromatase, CYP19A1) catalyzes the rate-limiting aromatization reaction that converts the A ring of testosterone and androstenedione into the aromatic A ring characteristic of estradiol and estrone, respectively. This single enzymatic step is the sole route by which the body generates estrogens from androgen precursors, which is why aromatase inhibitors (e.g., anastrozole, letrozole) are used clinically to block estrogen synthesis in hormone-sensitive breast cancer.

incorrectas.A: 5-alpha-reductase converts testosterone into the more potent androgen DHT — a different, non-aromatizing reduction reaction — and plays no role in estrogen synthesis.
incorrectas.C: 17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase interconverts weaker and stronger forms of androgens and estrogens (e.g., androstenedione to testosterone, or estrone to estradiol) but does not perform the aromatization step itself.
incorrectas.D: 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase acts earlier in steroidogenesis, converting pregnenolone to progesterone and DHEA to androstenedione, and is unrelated to the aromatization of the steroid A ring.

preguntas.q: Ranking androgens by potency at the androgen receptor from most to least potent, which order is correct?

e.correcta: DHT has the highest affinity and slowest dissociation rate from the androgen receptor, making it the most potent androgen, followed by testosterone (which binds the same receptor but less avidly and can also be aromatized to estrogen), and finally androstenedione, a weak precursor androgen with low intrinsic receptor activity that mainly serves as a substrate for conversion to testosterone or estrone. This potency ranking (DHT > testosterone > androstenedione) explains why peripheral conversion of testosterone to DHT amplifies androgenic effects in tissues like the prostate, skin, and hair follicles.

incorrectas.A: This ordering incorrectly places testosterone above DHT, but DHT actually binds the androgen receptor with higher affinity and greater potency than testosterone due to a more stable receptor-ligand complex.
incorrectas.B: This ordering incorrectly places androstenedione above testosterone and DHT, but androstenedione is the weakest of the three, serving as a precursor rather than a potent direct androgen receptor agonist.
incorrectas.D: This ordering incorrectly places androstenedione above testosterone, but androstenedione is the least potent of the three androgens, well below both DHT and testosterone in receptor binding strength.

preguntas.q: The outer and largest layer of the ovary, which contains all the oocytes enclosed within follicles, is called the?

e.correcta: The ovarian cortex is the outer, denser connective tissue layer containing all the oocytes at various stages of follicular development (primordial, primary, secondary, and Graafian follicles), and it is this layer that undergoes cyclical changes throughout the menstrual cycle and is progressively depleted with age. The cortex surrounds the inner medulla, which contains the vasculature, nerves, and loose connective tissue supplying the ovary.

incorrectas.A: The medulla is the inner, more vascular core of the ovary that supports the organ with blood vessels, lymphatics, and nerves, but it does not contain the oocyte-bearing follicles.
incorrectas.B: The hilum is the point of attachment where vessels, nerves, and lymphatics enter and exit the ovary via the mesovarium — it is not the layer housing the oocytes.
incorrectas.D: The tunica albuginea is a dense fibrous capsule underlying the germinal (surface) epithelium of the ovary, but the follicles containing oocytes reside within the cortex deep to this capsule, not within the capsule itself.

preguntas.q: The middle layer of the ovary, containing a mixture of cell types including connective tissue, vessels, and nerves, is called the?

e.correcta: The ovarian medulla is the central layer of the ovary containing loose connective tissue along with the blood vessels, lymphatics, and nerves that enter and exit through the hilum, providing the vascular and neural supply to the more peripheral cortex where oocytes and follicles reside. This division into an outer functional cortex and inner supportive medulla mirrors the general organizational pattern seen in other organs (e.g., adrenal gland, kidney) and is tested as a basic ovarian histology landmark.

incorrectas.A: The cortex is the outer layer of the ovary containing the follicles at various stages of development (primordial, primary, secondary, Graafian) — it is the site of oogenesis and follicular maturation, not the vascular/connective tissue-rich middle layer described here.
incorrectas.C: The hilum is the specific point where vessels, nerves, and lymphatics enter and exit the ovary, continuous with the mesovarium, but it is a focal attachment site rather than the diffuse middle layer of ovarian tissue itself.
incorrectas.D: The germinal epithelium is the single layer of surface mesothelium covering the ovary externally, which is the site of origin for most epithelial ovarian tumors — it is the outermost covering, not the internal vascular medulla.

preguntas.q: The inner layer of the ovary, through which blood vessels and lymphatics pass, is called the?

e.correcta: The hilum of the ovary is the point of attachment to the broad ligament (via the mesovarium) and serves as the entry/exit site for the ovarian vessels, lymphatics, and nerves — functionally analogous to the hilum of other organs like the kidney or lung. This is distinct from the ovary's histologic layers (cortex containing follicles, medulla of loose connective tissue), since the hilum specifically denotes the vascular pedicle region rather than a general tissue zone.

incorrectas.A: The cortex is the outer region of the ovary containing the follicles at various stages of development (primordial through Graafian) — it is where oogenesis and folliculogenesis occur, not where the major vessels pass through.
incorrectas.B: The medulla is the central, loosely arranged connective tissue core of the ovary containing some vasculature, but the specific site of vessel and lymphatic entry/exit — the structure the question is describing — is the hilum.
incorrectas.D: The tunica albuginea is a dense fibrous connective tissue capsule underlying the surface epithelium of the ovary, providing structural support — it is not a vascular conduit or an 'inner layer' through which vessels pass.

preguntas.q: The functional unit of the ovaries, comprising a single germ cell surrounded by endocrine (granulosa and theca) cells, is called the?

e.correcta: The ovarian follicle is the basic functional and structural unit of the ovary, consisting of a single oocyte surrounded by supporting granulosa cells (which nurture the oocyte and later produce estrogen) and an outer layer of theca cells (which supply androgen precursors for estrogen synthesis). This unit undergoes sequential maturation stages (primordial, primary, secondary/antral, and Graafian) but at every stage the defining feature is the one oocyte plus its endocrine support cells, distinguishing it from later or degenerated structures like the corpus luteum or corpus albicans.

incorrectas.A: The corpus luteum is the structure that forms after ovulation from the ruptured follicle's remaining granulosa and theca cells; it no longer contains an oocyte and thus is not the basic follicular unit being described.
incorrectas.B: The Graafian follicle is simply the mature, pre-ovulatory stage of follicular development — one specific stage of the ovarian follicle's life cycle — not the general term for the fundamental oocyte-plus-endocrine-cell unit.
incorrectas.D: The corpus albicans is the fibrotic, scarred remnant left after the corpus luteum degenerates; it is hormonally inactive and contains no oocyte, making it the opposite of the functional unit described in the question.

preguntas.q: Primary oocytes remain arrested in which phase of the cell cycle from fetal life until ovulation?

e.correcta: Primary oocytes complete DNA replication and enter meiosis I during fetal development but arrest in prophase I (specifically the diplotene stage) due to oocyte maturation inhibitor produced by granulosa cells, remaining suspended there for years to decades until the LH surge triggers resumption of meiosis just before ovulation. This prolonged arrest explains the increasing risk of meiotic nondisjunction errors (e.g., trisomy 21) with advancing maternal age, since oocytes ovulated later in life have been arrested in prophase I for a much longer time.

incorrectas.A: Metaphase II of meiosis II is where the secondary oocyte (not the primary oocyte) arrests, after completing meiosis I; this later arrest point is distinct from the much longer prophase I arrest of the primary oocyte described here.
incorrectas.C: Metaphase I of meiosis I is a transient stage during the resumption of meiosis around the time of the LH surge, not the site of the long-term arrest that primary oocytes maintain from fetal life onward.
incorrectas.D: Anaphase II of meiosis II occurs only after fertilization triggers completion of the second meiotic division; it has nothing to do with the pre-ovulatory arrest state of the primary oocyte.

preguntas.q: Secondary oocytes are arrested in which phase of the cell cycle until fertilization occurs?

e.correcta: Secondary oocytes are arrested in metaphase II of meiosis II, having completed meiosis I (which produced the secondary oocyte and first polar body) but pausing again before anaphase II due to cytostatic factor (including Mos and cyclin B stabilization) that maintains high MPF activity — this second arrest is only released when a sperm triggers a calcium influx at fertilization, allowing anaphase II to proceed and the second polar body to be extruded. This double-arrest system (first at prophase I for years/decades, then again at metaphase II until fertilization) is a key distinguishing feature of oogenesis compared to the continuous, non-arrested progression of spermatogenesis.

incorrectas.A: Prophase I arrest describes the primary oocyte, which is held in this state (dictyotene) from fetal life until the LH surge triggers resumption of meiosis I at ovulation — this is an earlier arrest point than the metaphase II arrest of the already-ovulated secondary oocyte.
incorrectas.B: Anaphase I is a transient, actively progressing phase of chromosome segregation during meiosis I completion around ovulation, not a stable arrest point — the oocyte moves through this quickly on its way to becoming a secondary oocyte.
incorrectas.D: Telophase II would represent completion of meiosis II, which only happens after fertilization triggers the release from metaphase II arrest — an oocyte does not sit arrested in telophase II while waiting for a sperm.

preguntas.q: Primary oocytes are held in prophase I of meiosis I for years until which event triggers resumption of meiosis?

e.correcta: The LH surge that precedes ovulation triggers resumption of meiosis I in the primary oocyte, allowing it to complete the first meiotic division and extrude the first polar body, becoming a secondary oocyte that is then released from the follicle. This tight coupling between the LH surge and meiotic resumption ensures that oocyte maturation is synchronized with ovulation, so a mature, fertilizable oocyte is released precisely when it can be picked up by the fallopian tube.

incorrectas.A: Fertilization is the trigger that completes meiosis II (releasing the second polar body), not meiosis I; by the time fertilization occurs, the oocyte has already resumed and completed the first meiotic division at ovulation.
incorrectas.B: Menarche marks the onset of the first menstrual cycle and reproductive capability broadly, but it is not the specific trigger for resumption of meiosis in an individual oocyte during a given cycle — that is driven by the LH surge each cycle.
incorrectas.D: Implantation occurs days after fertilization, once a blastocyst embeds in the endometrium; it is far downstream of meiotic resumption and has no role in triggering the primary oocyte to exit prophase I arrest.

preguntas.q: Secondary oocytes remain arrested in metaphase II of meiosis II until which event occurs?

e.correcta: After ovulation, the secondary oocyte arrests again, this time in metaphase II, held in place by cytostatic factor until a sperm penetrates the oocyte at fertilization; the resulting calcium influx degrades cytostatic factor and allows completion of meiosis II with extrusion of the second polar body. This second arrest point ensures that the final reductional division and formation of a haploid, genetically complete egg pronucleus occurs only once fertilization is confirmed, preventing wasteful completion of meiosis in unfertilized eggs.

incorrectas.A: Ovulation is the event that releases the secondary oocyte already arrested in metaphase II — it does not resolve that arrest, since the oocyte remains stuck in metaphase II until fertilization occurs afterward.
incorrectas.B: The LH surge is what triggers ovulation and the earlier resumption of meiosis I (producing the secondary oocyte in the first place), but it does not release the metaphase II arrest, which requires the calcium signal from sperm entry at fertilization.
incorrectas.D: Menstruation reflects shedding of the endometrium when fertilization does not occur and pregnancy is not established; it has no role in triggering completion of meiosis II in an oocyte, and in fact happens only when fertilization did not occur.

preguntas.q: The first, long stage of ovarian follicle development (lasting roughly 13-50 years) involves development of which follicle type from a primordial follicle?

e.correcta: The first stage of follicular development is the slow, gonadotropin-independent growth of primordial follicles into primary follicles, characterized by the oocyte enlarging and granulosa cells transitioning from flat to cuboidal while a zona pellucida forms; this process can take 13 to 50 years because primordial follicles are recruited gradually and continuously from the fixed pool established before birth. This extended timeline is why a woman's total complement of oocytes, though fixed at birth, continues to be slowly depleted throughout her reproductive lifespan.

incorrectas.A: The Graafian follicle is the fully mature, pre-ovulatory follicle that results from the much faster second stage of folliculogenesis (about 70-85 days), not the primordial-to-primary transition described in this long first stage.
incorrectas.B: The secondary (antral) follicle forms during the second stage of development when fluid-filled antral spaces appear, which is a later and much faster process than the initial primordial-to-primary transition being asked about here.
incorrectas.D: The corpus luteum forms only after ovulation from a ruptured Graafian follicle, representing the very end of the follicular life cycle, not the initial decades-long growth stage from primordial to primary follicle.

preguntas.q: The second stage of ovarian follicle development, lasting about 70-85 days, culminates in formation of which follicle type from a primary/secondary follicle?

e.correcta: The second stage of folliculogenesis is gonadotropin-dependent and involves the primary/secondary follicle acquiring an antrum (fluid-filled cavity), proliferating granulosa and theca cells, and increasing estrogen output, culminating over about 70-85 days in the fully mature Graafian (pre-ovulatory) follicle poised to ovulate. This stage is tightly regulated by FSH and LH, and only one dominant follicle typically completes this maturation each cycle while others undergo atresia.

incorrectas.A: The primordial follicle is the earliest, quiescent stage present from before birth, representing the starting point of the entire follicular pool, not the endpoint of this second maturation stage.
incorrectas.C: The corpus albicans is the involuted scar tissue that remains after the corpus luteum regresses, occurring well after ovulation — it is the final stage of follicular fate, not the result of the pre-ovulatory maturation stage described here.
incorrectas.D: The primary follicle is actually the starting point (or an intermediate point) of this second stage, formed at the end of the first, decades-long stage — it is not the culmination of the 70-85 day maturation process being described.

preguntas.q: In the third, rapid stage of ovarian follicle development (lasting about 48 hours), a dominant graafian follicle ruptures and releases its oocyte into the peritoneal cavity via which process?

e.correcta: Ovulation is the process by which the LH surge triggers proteolytic digestion and rupture of the follicular wall and overlying ovarian surface epithelium, expelling the secondary oocyte (with its surrounding cumulus cells) into the peritoneal cavity, where it is normally captured by the fimbriae of the fallopian tube. This rapid, roughly 48-hour process from LH surge to rupture marks the transition from follicular growth to the luteal phase, and is the specific event that makes the oocyte available for fertilization.

incorrectas.A: Luteinization is the transformation of the ruptured follicle's granulosa and theca cells into the progesterone-secreting corpus luteum, which happens after ovulation, not the rupture event itself that releases the oocyte.
incorrectas.B: Atresia is the degeneration of non-dominant follicles that fail to ovulate during a cycle; it describes follicular death, not the successful rupture and release of the oocyte from the dominant follicle.
incorrectas.D: Implantation is the embedding of a blastocyst into the endometrium, occurring roughly a week after fertilization if it happens at all — it is unrelated to the mechanical rupture and release of the oocyte from the ovary.

preguntas.q: If fertilization occurs, the residual granulosa and theca cells of the ruptured ovarian follicle form which structure, which continues to secrete steroid hormones?

e.correcta: After ovulation, the residual granulosa and theca cells of the ruptured follicle undergo luteinization, transforming into the corpus luteum, which is maintained by LH (and later hCG if pregnancy occurs) and continues to secrete progesterone (and some estrogen) to support the endometrium and early pregnancy. This continued hormone secretion is critical because progesterone maintains the secretory endometrium and suppresses uterine contractions, sustaining a pregnancy until the placenta can take over steroidogenesis.

incorrectas.A: The corpus albicans is the fibrotic, hormonally inactive scar that the corpus luteum eventually becomes if it degenerates (i.e., when fertilization does not occur or after the corpus luteum of pregnancy involutes); it is not what forms immediately if fertilization occurs.
incorrectas.C: The Graafian follicle is the pre-ovulatory structure that existed before rupture; once ovulation has occurred and the follicle has ruptured, it no longer exists as a Graafian follicle — its remnant cells become the corpus luteum instead.
incorrectas.D: The primordial follicle is an early, dormant stage of a different, unrelated follicle elsewhere in the ovary; it has no connection to the fate of the cells left behind after a specific follicle ruptures and ovulates.

preguntas.q: If fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum degenerates and is replaced by which structure?

e.correcta: Without fertilization (and without hCG support), LH levels fall as the cycle progresses, and the corpus luteum loses its trophic support, undergoes progressive fibrosis, and regresses into the corpus albicans — an inactive scar of dense connective tissue that produces no hormones. This regression causes progesterone and estrogen levels to drop sharply, which withdraws hormonal support from the endometrium and precipitates menstruation, restarting the cycle.

incorrectas.A: A Graafian follicle is a pre-ovulatory structure belonging to the next developing follicle in a subsequent cycle, not something the corpus luteum itself becomes upon degeneration.
incorrectas.B: A primary follicle is an early developmental stage of an entirely different, still-immature follicle; it has no relationship to the fate of a corpus luteum that has already ovulated and is now regressing.
incorrectas.D: A theca lutein cyst is a pathological ovarian cyst usually associated with excessive hCG stimulation (e.g., molar pregnancy or multiple gestation), not the normal physiologic fate of a corpus luteum in an unfertilized cycle.

preguntas.q: In the ovaries, cholesterol desmolase activity (converting cholesterol to pregnenolone) in theca cells is primarily stimulated by which hormone, paralleling its role in the testes?

e.correcta: LH binds receptors on theca cells and stimulates cholesterol desmolase (the cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme), initiating steroidogenesis by converting cholesterol into pregnenolone, which is the same LH-driven mechanism used by Leydig cells in the testes to begin testosterone synthesis. This shared LH-cholesterol desmolase axis across theca and Leydig cells reflects the conserved two-cell, two-gonadotropin model of gonadal steroidogenesis, where LH drives the initial androgen precursor synthesis and FSH acts on the second cell type (granulosa/Sertoli) for further processing.

incorrectas.A: FSH acts primarily on granulosa cells (stimulating aromatase to convert androgens to estrogen) rather than on theca cells to initiate cholesterol conversion, so it is not the hormone driving cholesterol desmolase activity in theca cells.
incorrectas.C: GnRH acts upstream at the pituitary to stimulate LH and FSH release; it does not directly act on theca cells or directly stimulate cholesterol desmolase itself.
incorrectas.D: hCG can mimic LH action later in pregnancy (e.g., supporting the corpus luteum), but under normal physiologic ovarian cycling it is LH, not hCG, that is the primary stimulus for theca cell cholesterol desmolase activity.

preguntas.q: In the ovaries, which cell type synthesizes and secretes progesterone from pregnenolone via 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase?

e.correcta: Theca cells express 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, which converts the pregnenolone generated by LH-stimulated cholesterol desmolase into progesterone; theca cells then also convert some of this steroid pathway further into androstenedione, which diffuses to neighboring granulosa cells for aromatization into estrogen. This localization of progesterone and androgen synthesis specifically to theca cells (rather than granulosa cells) is central to the two-cell model of ovarian steroidogenesis tested throughout reproductive physiology.

incorrectas.A: Granulosa cells lack significant cholesterol desmolase and 3-beta-HSD activity of their own in this pathway and instead rely on receiving androgens from theca cells, which granulosa cells then aromatize into estrogen using FSH-stimulated aromatase — they are not the site of progesterone synthesis from pregnenolone described here.
incorrectas.C: Oocytes are the germ cells being nurtured within the follicle; they do not carry out steroidogenic enzymatic conversions like 3-beta-HSD activity, which is the job of the surrounding somatic (theca and granulosa) cells.
incorrectas.D: Corpus albicans cells are fibrotic, hormonally inert scar tissue formed after corpus luteum regression; they have no active steroidogenic enzymes and produce no progesterone.

preguntas.q: In addition to progesterone, theca cells also synthesize which androgen, which then diffuses to nearby granulosa cells for further processing?

e.correcta: Beyond progesterone, theca cells further process the steroidogenic pathway to produce androstenedione, an androgen precursor that lacks the enzymes (17-beta-HSD and aromatase) needed for its own further conversion locally, so it diffuses across the basement membrane into neighboring granulosa cells, which are equipped with those enzymes to convert it first to testosterone and then, via FSH-stimulated aromatase, into estradiol. This division of labor — theca cells make androgens, granulosa cells convert them to estrogen — is the essence of the two-cell, two-gonadotropin model of ovarian estrogen production.

incorrectas.A: Testosterone is actually produced downstream, inside granulosa cells, after they take up androstenedione from theca cells and convert it via 17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase; theca cells themselves do not primarily secrete testosterone directly.
incorrectas.B: Dihydrotestosterone requires 5-alpha-reductase activity, which is not the relevant enzyme pathway active in theca or granulosa cells during normal ovarian estrogen synthesis; DHT is not part of this ovarian steroidogenic diffusion pathway.
incorrectas.D: Estradiol is the final product formed within granulosa cells via aromatization, not something theca cells synthesize and pass along — theca cells supply the androgen precursor, not the finished estrogen.

preguntas.q: In which ovarian cell type is androstenedione converted to testosterone via 17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, before further conversion to estradiol?

e.correcta: Granulosa cells receive androstenedione diffused from adjacent theca cells and use 17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase to convert it into testosterone, which FSH-stimulated aromatase then converts into estradiol; this two-step conversion within granulosa cells completes the two-cell model of ovarian estrogen production. Because granulosa cells (not theca cells) express both 17-beta-HSD and aromatase, they are the site where the final, biologically dominant estrogen of the ovarian cycle is generated.

incorrectas.A: Theca cells are the site where cholesterol is converted through pregnenolone and progesterone to androstenedione, but they lack the 17-beta-HSD and aromatase activity needed to convert androstenedione onward to testosterone and estradiol — that conversion happens after the androgen diffuses to granulosa cells.
incorrectas.C: Corpus albicans cells are inactive scar tissue with no steroidogenic enzyme activity, so they play no role in converting androstenedione to testosterone.
incorrectas.D: Oocytes are the germ cells nurtured by the surrounding somatic cells; they do not perform steroidogenic enzymatic conversions like 17-beta-HSD-mediated androstenedione-to-testosterone conversion.

preguntas.q: In the ovaries, aromatase activity in granulosa cells is primarily stimulated by which hormone?

e.correcta: FSH binds receptors on granulosa cells and upregulates aromatase expression, enabling these cells to convert theca-derived androgens (testosterone and androstenedione) into estradiol and estrone; this FSH-driven aromatase induction is a key part of the maturing follicle's rising estrogen output that ultimately triggers the LH surge via positive feedback. This is the granulosa-cell half of the two-cell, two-gonadotropin model, complementing LH's stimulation of androgen precursor synthesis in theca cells.

incorrectas.A: LH acts primarily on theca cells to stimulate cholesterol desmolase and androgen precursor synthesis, not on granulosa cell aromatase; granulosa cells actually only acquire LH receptors later, closer to ovulation and luteinization.
incorrectas.B: GnRH acts upstream at the pituitary to stimulate FSH and LH secretion; it does not directly act on granulosa cells to induce aromatase expression.
incorrectas.D: Prolactin's main physiologic role is stimulating lactation and, when elevated pathologically, it actually suppresses GnRH and gonadotropin secretion; it is not a stimulator of granulosa cell aromatase activity.

preguntas.q: Hypothalamic control over oogenesis and ovarian progesterone/estradiol secretion is mediated through which hormone?

e.correcta: GnRH, released in a pulsatile fashion from the hypothalamus, stimulates the anterior pituitary to secrete FSH and LH, which in turn drive follicular development, oogenesis, and ovarian steroidogenesis (progesterone from theca cells, estradiol from granulosa cells). This hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis is the master regulatory pathway of the menstrual cycle, and disruption of GnRH pulsatility (e.g., from stress, extreme exercise, or low body weight) is a common cause of hypothalamic amenorrhea.

incorrectas.A: Inhibin is secreted by granulosa cells to selectively suppress FSH at the pituitary level as part of a negative feedback loop, but it is a downstream ovarian hormone, not the hypothalamic signal that initiates the axis.
incorrectas.B: Activin is also a gonadal peptide hormone that modulates FSH secretion (generally enhancing it) but, like inhibin, it acts at the pituitary/paracrine level rather than serving as the hypothalamic hormone controlling the axis.
incorrectas.D: hCG is produced by the placenta during pregnancy and mimics LH to support the corpus luteum, but it is not the normal hypothalamic hormone regulating oogenesis and ovarian steroid secretion outside of pregnancy.

preguntas.q: Ovarian granulosa cells may produce which hormone that inhibits FSH secretion from the anterior pituitary, analogous to its role in the testes?

e.correcta: Inhibin is secreted by granulosa cells (as inhibin B in the follicular phase and inhibin A in the luteal phase) and acts on the anterior pituitary to selectively suppress FSH secretion without significantly affecting LH, providing negative feedback that helps limit the number of follicles recruited each cycle. This mirrors the analogous role of inhibin secreted by Sertoli cells in the testes, which likewise selectively suppresses FSH as part of spermatogenesis regulation.

incorrectas.A: Activin is structurally related to inhibin but has the opposite effect, generally stimulating rather than inhibiting FSH secretion, so it does not match the FSH-suppressing hormone described in the question.
incorrectas.C: Estradiol does provide feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis (negative feedback at low levels, positive feedback triggering the LH surge at high levels), but it is not the granulosa-derived hormone whose specific, primary role is selectively suppressing FSH the way inhibin does.
incorrectas.D: Progesterone mainly acts on the endometrium and provides negative feedback on GnRH pulsatility during the luteal phase, but it is not the specific FSH-suppressing peptide hormone produced by granulosa cells analogous to testicular inhibin.

preguntas.q: Ovarian granulosa cells may also produce which hormone that stimulates FSH secretion from the anterior pituitary?

e.correcta: Activin, produced by granulosa cells (and by the pituitary gonadotrophs themselves), stimulates FSH synthesis and secretion, reinforcing follicular recruitment and estrogen production early in the cycle. It works in functional opposition to inhibin — both come from the same granulosa cell population but exert opposite effects on FSH, which is a classic exam pairing to memorize together.

incorrectas.A: Inhibin is also secreted by granulosa cells, but it does the opposite of what the question asks — it suppresses FSH release from the anterior pituitary as part of the negative feedback loop that limits follicular recruitment.
incorrectas.B: Progesterone is a steroid hormone from the corpus luteum (not chiefly a granulosa-cell peptide product) that acts mainly on the endometrium and hypothalamic-pituitary axis to suppress GnRH pulsatility, not to stimulate FSH release directly.
incorrectas.D: Testosterone is produced by theca cells, not granulosa cells, and serves as the aromatization substrate that granulosa cells convert to estrogen — it does not act on the pituitary to stimulate FSH secretion.

preguntas.q: Which female sex steroid is chiefly responsible for the development of the fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and upper vagina from the Mullerian ducts?

e.correcta: Estrogen drives the differentiation of the paramesonephric (Mullerian) ducts into the fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and upper vagina in the absence of Mullerian inhibitory factor (which is only produced by testes in genetic males). Because the default pathway of the undifferentiated genital tract is female, estrogen (largely of maternal/placental origin in utero) supports this development rather than actively inducing it against opposition, distinguishing it from testosterone's role in driving Wolffian duct differentiation in males.

incorrectas.A: Progesterone's major physiologic roles are maintaining the secretory endometrium and pregnancy, not directing the embryologic differentiation of the Mullerian ducts into internal genital structures.
incorrectas.B: Testosterone promotes Wolffian (mesonephric) duct development into male internal genitalia (epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles) and, via its metabolite DHT, external male genitalia — it does not build the Mullerian-derived female structures.
incorrectas.C: Inhibin regulates FSH secretion via pituitary feedback in the postnatal ovarian cycle; it is unrelated to inhibiting or promoting Mullerian duct fate (that role belongs to anti-Mullerian hormone from Sertoli cells, not inhibin).

preguntas.q: Which female sex steroid is primarily responsible for stimulating breast development at puberty?

e.correcta: Estrogen stimulates ductal proliferation and fat deposition in the breast at puberty, initiating thelarche, by acting on estrogen receptors in breast ductal epithelium and stroma. Progesterone later contributes lobuloalveolar development once ovulatory cycles begin, but the initial pubertal breast bud growth is estrogen-driven.

incorrectas.A: Progesterone promotes lobuloalveolar (glandular) development of the breast, which matters for milk-producing capacity, but it acts on a ductal system already established by estrogen and is not the primary driver of pubertal breast development.
incorrectas.C: Prolactin stimulates milk production during lactation by acting on alveolar cells, but it is not the hormone responsible for initiating breast development at puberty, which precedes any prolactin-driven lactogenesis.
incorrectas.D: Oxytocin causes myoepithelial cell contraction for milk ejection (the let-down reflex) during lactation; it plays no role in the structural growth of breast tissue at puberty.

preguntas.q: Which female sex steroid is responsible for growth of the ovarian follicle and proliferation of the endometrium during the follicular phase?

e.correcta: Estrogen, secreted by the growing granulosa cells of the developing follicle, drives both follicular maturation (via upregulation of FSH and LH receptors on granulosa/theca cells) and proliferation of the endometrial glands and stroma during the follicular (proliferative) phase, preparing the endometrium to receive a possible embryo. This is why the proliferative phase of the endometrial cycle is named for its histologic correlate to rising estrogen from the follicular phase of the ovarian cycle.

incorrectas.A: Progesterone acts later, during the luteal phase, to convert the proliferative endometrium into a secretory endometrium rather than driving proliferation or follicular growth in the follicular phase.
incorrectas.B: Inhibin from granulosa cells selectively suppresses FSH to help select the dominant follicle, but it does not itself drive endometrial proliferation — that is estrogen's job.
incorrectas.D: LH is a pituitary gonadotropin that stimulates theca cell androgen production (substrate for estrogen synthesis) and later triggers ovulation, but it is not the steroid directly responsible for endometrial proliferation.

preguntas.q: Immediately prior to delivery, which female sex steroid increases myometrial (uterine) contractility and excitability by upregulating gap junctions and oxytocin receptors?

e.correcta: Near term, estrogen levels rise relative to progesterone, and estrogen increases the number of myometrial gap junctions (connexin-43) and oxytocin receptors, which synchronizes and amplifies uterine smooth muscle contractions in preparation for labor. This estrogen-driven shift in the estrogen:progesterone ratio helps overcome progesterone's normal quiescent effect on the myometrium, contributing to the onset of coordinated labor contractions.

incorrectas.A: Progesterone does the opposite — it maintains uterine quiescence throughout pregnancy by inhibiting gap junction formation and contractility, and its relative withdrawal (rather than its action) is part of what permits labor to begin.
incorrectas.B: Relaxin softens the cervix and pelvic ligaments and inhibits myometrial contractions to prepare the birth canal, but it does not increase gap junctions or oxytocin receptor density on the myometrium.
incorrectas.D: hCG's main role is maintaining the corpus luteum's progesterone output in early pregnancy; it is not the hormone responsible for the late-pregnancy increase in myometrial excitability.

preguntas.q: Which female sex steroid is chiefly responsible for the typical female pattern of fat distribution (hips, thighs, breasts)?

e.correcta: Estrogen promotes lipoprotein lipase activity and adipocyte differentiation preferentially in gluteofemoral and breast fat depots, producing the classic gynoid (pear-shaped) fat distribution seen in women, in contrast to androgen-driven central/visceral adiposity in men. This is one of the many peripheral, non-reproductive actions of estrogen worth knowing alongside its effects on bone, lipids, and the reproductive tract.

incorrectas.A: Progesterone has minimal independent effect on body fat distribution; its major actions are on the endometrium, myometrium, and hypothalamic feedback rather than adipocyte patterning.
incorrectas.B: Testosterone (and androgens generally) promotes the opposite pattern — central, visceral fat deposition typical of male body habitus — so it works against, not for, the female fat distribution pattern.
incorrectas.C: Inhibin's role is limited to pituitary FSH feedback regulation; it has no established role in directing regional adipose tissue distribution.

preguntas.q: Estrogen exerts what effect on LH, estrogen, and progesterone receptor expression in target tissues?

o.B: No significant effect on receptor expression
o.D: Selective down-regulation of only progesterone receptors

e.correcta: Estrogen up-regulates its own receptor as well as LH and progesterone receptors in target tissues (endometrium, myometrium, ovary), amplifying tissue responsiveness to itself and priming tissues to respond to the subsequent LH surge and post-ovulatory progesterone. This positive feedback on receptor density is part of why estrogen's actions accelerate as the follicular phase progresses, culminating in the tissue sensitivity needed for ovulation and implantation.

incorrectas.A: Down-regulation is actually the effect progesterone has on estrogen receptors (a negative feedback loop), not the effect estrogen has on these receptors — the direction described here is reversed from the true relationship.
incorrectas.B: Saying there is no significant effect ignores estrogen's well-documented role as a receptor-inducing hormone across the female reproductive tract — this is a key mechanism by which estrogen amplifies its own and progesterone's downstream signaling.
incorrectas.D: Estrogen affects LH, estrogen, and progesterone receptors together (broadly up-regulating them), not selectively down-regulating only progesterone receptors while sparing the others; that selective, opposite pattern doesn't match estrogen's actual physiology.

preguntas.q: What is the effect of estrogen on prolactin secretion from the anterior pituitary?

o.D: Biphasic effect depending on cycle day

e.correcta: Estrogen stimulates lactotroph proliferation and prolactin gene transcription in the anterior pituitary, which is why prolactin levels rise during pregnancy as estrogen (mostly placental) climbs, and why pituitary lactotroph hyperplasia occurs in pregnancy. This estrogen-prolactin relationship is also relevant clinically, as estrogen-containing therapies can enlarge prolactinomas or elevate prolactin levels.

incorrectas.A: A decrease would be the opposite of estrogen's actual action — dopamine (not estrogen) is the physiologic inhibitor of prolactin secretion via D2 receptors on lactotrophs.
incorrectas.B: No effect misses the direct trophic and transcriptional stimulation estrogen exerts on lactotrophs, which is well demonstrated by the marked rise in prolactin across pregnancy as estrogen rises.
incorrectas.D: There is no clinically significant biphasic estrogen effect on prolactin tied to cycle day — estrogen's stimulatory effect on prolactin is a fairly consistent, dose-dependent relationship rather than one that reverses direction across the cycle.

preguntas.q: Which form of estrogen is the predominant one produced by the ovary in a nonpregnant woman?

e.correcta: 17β-estradiol is the most potent and most abundant estrogen produced by the ovary in a nonpregnant woman, synthesized by granulosa cells via aromatization of androgens supplied by theca cells (the two-cell, two-gonadotropin model), and it drives endometrial proliferation and feedback regulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. Its potency and central role in the menstrual cycle make it the estrogen most measured clinically to assess ovarian function.

incorrectas.A: Estrone is a weaker estrogen produced mainly by peripheral aromatization of androstenedione in adipose tissue and becomes the predominant estrogen after menopause when ovarian estradiol production declines, not the main form in a cycling nonpregnant woman.
incorrectas.B: Estriol is the weakest of the three major estrogens and is the predominant form produced by the placenta during pregnancy, making it a marker of fetoplacental health rather than the ovary's main product outside pregnancy.
incorrectas.D: Ethinyl estradiol is a synthetic estrogen used in oral contraceptives, not a naturally occurring hormone produced by the ovary.

preguntas.q: Which form of estrogen is characteristically produced by the placenta during pregnancy?

e.correcta: Estriol is the estrogen characteristically produced in large quantities by the placenta during pregnancy, synthesized from fetal adrenal DHEA-S that is sulfated and 16-hydroxylated by the fetal liver before the placenta aromatizes it into estriol — making it a marker of both fetal and placental function (historically used in the 'triple screen' for aneuploidy and to assess fetoplacental unit health). Because its production depends on an intact fetal adrenal-liver-placenta axis, abnormally low estriol can signal fetal distress, adrenal insufficiency, or placental dysfunction.

incorrectas.A: 17β-estradiol is the predominant and most potent estrogen in non-pregnant reproductive-age women, produced mainly by the ovarian granulosa cells, but during pregnancy it is estriol, not estradiol, that is characteristically produced in dramatically increased amounts by the placenta.
incorrectas.B: Estrone is the predominant estrogen in postmenopausal women, produced via peripheral aromatization of androstenedione in adipose tissue, and is not the estrogen specifically associated with placental production during pregnancy.
incorrectas.D: Estradiol valerate is a synthetic pharmaceutical ester of estradiol used in hormone therapy formulations; it is not a naturally occurring placental hormone and has no role in normal pregnancy physiology.

preguntas.q: Which form of estrogen is produced primarily in adipose tissue and becomes the main source of estrogen after menopause?

e.correcta: Estrone is produced largely by peripheral aromatization of adrenal and ovarian androstenedione in adipose tissue, and because ovarian estradiol production collapses after menopause, estrone (from continued peripheral aromatization) becomes the predominant circulating estrogen postmenopausally. This is also why obesity is associated with higher estrogen exposure and increased risk of estrogen-sensitive conditions like endometrial hyperplasia in postmenopausal women — more adipose tissue means more aromatase activity.

incorrectas.A: 17β-estradiol is the most potent estrogen and the dominant form during reproductive years, produced mainly by the ovarian granulosa cells via aromatization of theca-derived androgens — but ovarian production falls sharply after menopause, which is exactly why it is no longer the main source.
incorrectas.B: Estriol is the weakest naturally occurring estrogen and is produced in large quantities by the placenta during pregnancy (used clinically as a marker of fetoplacental well-being); it is not the postmenopausal or adipose-derived estrogen.
incorrectas.D: Progesterone is a distinct steroid class (a progestin, not an estrogen) synthesized mainly by the corpus luteum and placenta; it is not produced by adipose tissue as a form of estrogen.

preguntas.q: Which ranking correctly orders the naturally occurring estrogens from most to least potent?

e.correcta: 17β-estradiol has the highest binding affinity for the estrogen receptor and is the most biologically potent, followed by estrone (a weaker, ketone-form estrogen), with estriol being the weakest due to structural differences that reduce receptor affinity and metabolic stability. A useful mnemonic is that estradiol dominates in reproductive years, estriol dominates in pregnancy (highest quantity but lowest potency), and estrone dominates after menopause (from peripheral aromatization) — quantity and potency are not the same thing.

incorrectas.A: This puts estrone above estradiol, but estradiol is actually the more potent of the two due to its higher receptor binding affinity, even though estrone can be produced in larger amounts in certain states like menopause or obesity.
incorrectas.B: This ranks estriol as most potent, but estriol is in fact the weakest of the three despite being produced in the largest quantity during pregnancy — quantity produced does not equal receptor potency.
incorrectas.D: This ranks estriol above estradiol, but estriol's weak receptor affinity makes it the least potent of the three, not the most potent — again conflating high circulating quantity (as in pregnancy) with hormonal potency.

preguntas.q: Where are estrogen receptors located within the target cell prior to hormone binding?

o.A: Cell membrane, as a G protein-coupled receptor
o.B: Cytoplasm, translocating to the nucleus once bound by estrogen
o.D: Endoplasmic reticulum, remaining there after binding

e.correcta: Estrogen receptors are classic nuclear hormone receptors that reside in the cytoplasm (and partly in the nucleus) unbound, and upon binding lipophilic estrogen that diffuses across the plasma membrane, the receptor-hormone complex translocates to the nucleus, dimerizes, and binds estrogen response elements on DNA to regulate gene transcription. This genomic mechanism explains the relatively slow onset but long duration of estrogen's effects compared to fast membrane-receptor-mediated signaling.

incorrectas.A: Classic estrogen receptors are not G protein-coupled membrane receptors; that describes the mechanism of peptide hormones and catecholamines, whereas estrogen (a lipophilic steroid) uses an intracellular nuclear receptor mechanism (though a separate membrane-associated GPER exists, it is not the classical receptor being tested here).
incorrectas.C: Estrogen receptors are not localized to the mitochondrial membrane as their primary site of action; their canonical mechanism involves cytoplasmic/nuclear localization and direct gene transcription regulation.
incorrectas.D: The receptor does not remain fixed in the endoplasmic reticulum after binding — it translocates to the nucleus to act as a transcription factor, which is the defining feature of steroid hormone receptor signaling.

preguntas.q: What effect does estrogen have on hepatic production of sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG)?

o.D: Decreased SHBG binding affinity without change in level

e.correcta: Estrogen increases hepatic synthesis of SHBG, which binds and reduces the free (bioavailable) fraction of circulating sex steroids like testosterone and estradiol; this is part of why estrogen therapy or pregnancy (high estrogen states) raises total but not necessarily proportionally free hormone levels. This mechanism is also clinically relevant in conditions like PCOS, where low SHBG (from lower estrogen relative to androgen effect) contributes to higher free testosterone and hyperandrogenic symptoms.

incorrectas.A: A decrease in SHBG is actually more characteristic of androgen excess states or insulin resistance, not estrogen action — estrogen has the opposite, stimulatory effect on hepatic SHBG production.
incorrectas.C: No change misses estrogen's well-established transcriptional upregulation of SHBG synthesis in the liver, which is exploited clinically (e.g., oral estrogen-containing contraceptives raise SHBG).
incorrectas.D: Estrogen's effect is on the amount of SHBG synthesized, not on the binding affinity of existing SHBG molecules for their ligands — the mechanism is transcriptional induction, not an affinity change.

preguntas.q: What is the effect of estrogen on serum HDL cholesterol levels?

o.D: Increased HDL only in postmenopausal women

e.correcta: Estrogen increases hepatic synthesis of apolipoprotein A-I and upregulates HDL receptor turnover in a way that favors higher circulating HDL, while also lowering LDL, contributing to the relatively favorable lipid profile and lower cardiovascular disease risk seen in premenopausal women compared to age-matched men. This effect partly explains the rise in cardiovascular risk that follows the estrogen decline at menopause.

incorrectas.A: A decrease in HDL is not the estrogen effect — estrogen actually raises HDL as part of its generally favorable hepatic lipid effects, which is why postmenopausal estrogen loss is associated with a more atherogenic lipid profile.
incorrectas.C: No effect fails to capture estrogen's well-documented hepatic action on lipoprotein metabolism, which is a major reason cardiovascular risk profiles differ between premenopausal women and men of similar age.
incorrectas.D: The HDL-raising effect of estrogen is most relevant while estrogen is present in premenopausal (or exogenously supplemented) states, not something that appears only after menopause when endogenous estrogen actually falls.

preguntas.q: What is the effect of estrogen on serum LDL cholesterol levels?

o.D: Increased LDL only with exogenous estrogen

e.correcta: Estrogen decreases serum LDL cholesterol by up-regulating hepatic LDL receptor expression, which increases hepatic clearance of LDL particles from the circulation, while also raising HDL — this is part of the favorable lipid profile seen in premenopausal women that is thought to contribute to their relatively lower cardiovascular risk compared to age-matched men. This effect is also why LDL levels tend to rise after menopause as estrogen declines, and why exogenous estrogen (e.g., oral contraceptives, HRT) can shift lipid panels toward lower LDL.

incorrectas.A: Increased LDL is the opposite of estrogen's actual effect; estrogen enhances hepatic LDL receptor activity and clearance, lowering rather than raising circulating LDL, which is part of why LDL characteristically rises after the estrogen decline of menopause.
incorrectas.B: Estrogen does have a measurable, clinically relevant effect on LDL cholesterol via hepatic receptor up-regulation, so 'no effect' does not accurately describe its lipid-modulating action.
incorrectas.D: Estrogen's LDL-lowering effect is not exclusive to exogenous administration; endogenous estrogen in premenopausal women similarly lowers LDL, which is why LDL tends to rise after natural menopause as endogenous estrogen falls.

preguntas.q: Which female sex steroid is primarily responsible for the maintenance of pregnancy?

e.correcta: Progesterone, first from the corpus luteum and later from the placenta, maintains pregnancy by keeping the myometrium quiescent (inhibiting contractility and gap junction formation) and sustaining the secretory, decidualized endometrium needed to support implantation and continued gestation. A drop in progesterone support (whether from luteal insufficiency or antiprogestin drugs like mifepristone) can precipitate pregnancy loss or labor, underscoring its central role.

incorrectas.A: Estrogen supports endometrial proliferation and later increases myometrial excitability near term (working toward labor, not against it), so it does not serve the same pregnancy-maintaining, contraction-suppressing role that progesterone does throughout gestation.
incorrectas.C: hCG's main job is rescuing and maintaining the corpus luteum (and its progesterone output) during early pregnancy before the placenta takes over steroidogenesis; it is upstream support for progesterone production rather than the hormone directly maintaining the uterine environment.
incorrectas.D: Prolactin's primary pregnancy-related role is preparing the breast for lactation, not maintaining uterine quiescence or the endometrial lining needed to sustain the pregnancy itself.

preguntas.q: Which female sex steroid stimulates secretory activity of the endometrial glands?

e.correcta: Progesterone, secreted by the corpus luteum during the secretory (luteal) phase, converts the estrogen-primed proliferative endometrium into a secretory endometrium by stimulating glandular tortuosity and glycogen-rich secretions that prepare the uterine lining for potential blastocyst implantation. Progesterone also raises basal body temperature and thickens cervical mucus, both of which are used clinically to confirm that ovulation has occurred.

incorrectas.A: Estrogen drives the earlier proliferative phase, causing endometrial glandular and stromal proliferation, but it is progesterone that induces the subsequent secretory changes needed for implantation.
incorrectas.B: FSH acts on the ovary to stimulate follicular growth and estrogen production; it does not act directly on the endometrium to induce secretory changes.
incorrectas.D: LH triggers ovulation and supports the corpus luteum's progesterone production, but LH itself does not directly stimulate endometrial glandular secretory activity — progesterone is the downstream effector hormone that does.

preguntas.q: Which female sex steroid promotes the development of endometrial spiral arteries?

e.correcta: Progesterone, secreted by the corpus luteum during the secretory phase, promotes maturation and coiling of the endometrial spiral arteries along with glandular secretory changes, preparing the endometrium to support implantation. This vascular development is essential for adequately perfusing the secretory endometrium, and progesterone withdrawal (when implantation does not occur) causes spiral artery vasoconstriction and ischemia, triggering menstruation.

incorrectas.A: Estrogen drives the proliferative phase, stimulating endometrial glandular and stromal proliferation and thickening, but it is progesterone in the subsequent secretory phase that specifically promotes spiral artery development and coiling.
incorrectas.C: hCG maintains the corpus luteum (and thus progesterone production) in early pregnancy but does not itself directly act on the endometrium to develop spiral arteries — its role is upstream, supporting the source of progesterone.
incorrectas.D: Inhibin acts on the pituitary to suppress FSH secretion as part of ovarian hormonal feedback, and has no direct role in endometrial spiral artery development, which is a progesterone-driven local uterine effect.

preguntas.q: Which female sex steroid decreases myometrial contractility and excitability?

e.correcta: Progesterone maintains uterine quiescence during the luteal phase and pregnancy by hyperpolarizing myometrial smooth muscle cells and reducing gap junction formation between them, which decreases electrical coupling and prevents the coordinated contractions needed for labor. This is why progesterone withdrawal (or antiprogestins like mifepristone) is associated with the onset of labor, while progesterone supplementation is used clinically to help prevent preterm labor in some patients.

incorrectas.A: Estrogen has the opposite effect — it increases myometrial excitability by upregulating oxytocin receptors and promoting gap junction formation, priming the uterus for contraction rather than quieting it.
incorrectas.B: Oxytocin directly stimulates myometrial contraction by binding uterine oxytocin receptors and triggering calcium influx, making it a pro-contractile hormone, the opposite of progesterone's inhibitory role.
incorrectas.D: Prostaglandin F2α promotes myometrial contraction and is used clinically (or its analogs are) to induce labor or manage postpartum hemorrhage, functioning as a uterotonic rather than a relaxant like progesterone.

preguntas.q: Which female sex steroid produces thick cervical mucus that inhibits sperm entry into the uterus?

e.correcta: Progesterone, secreted by the corpus luteum after ovulation, transforms cervical mucus from the thin, watery, sperm-friendly consistency seen under estrogen dominance into a thick, viscous plug that physically blocks sperm and pathogen entry into the uterus. This is the same principle exploited by progestin-only contraceptives, which thicken cervical mucus as one of their contraceptive mechanisms.

incorrectas.A: Estrogen does the opposite — around ovulation, rising estrogen produces thin, clear, elastic ('spinnbarkeit') mucus that facilitates sperm penetration, which is the fertile-window pattern distinct from progesterone's post-ovulatory thickening effect.
incorrectas.C: LH triggers ovulation via a surge that stimulates the primary oocyte to complete meiosis I and release from the follicle, but LH itself does not act directly on cervical mucus consistency the way progesterone does.
incorrectas.D: FSH drives follicular growth and estrogen production earlier in the cycle, but it does not directly alter cervical mucus texture — that downstream effect is mediated through the estrogen and progesterone it induces, especially progesterone after ovulation.

preguntas.q: Which female sex steroid produces thin, watery cervical mucus that facilitates sperm entry into the uterus around ovulation?

e.correcta: Rising estrogen levels in the late follicular phase (just before ovulation) act on the cervical glands to produce abundant, thin, watery, and elastic ('spinnbarkeit') mucus with an alkaline pH, creating channels that facilitate sperm penetration and survival during the fertile window. This estrogen-driven mucus change is the physiologic basis of fertility awareness methods that track cervical mucus quality to predict ovulation.

incorrectas.A: Progesterone, dominant in the luteal phase after ovulation, makes cervical mucus thick, scant, and impenetrable to sperm — the opposite effect from the thin, sperm-friendly mucus described, and it serves to block further sperm entry once the fertile window closes.
incorrectas.C: Testosterone is the principal androgen driving male reproductive physiology and has no meaningful physiologic role in modulating cervical mucus characteristics in the female cycle.
incorrectas.D: Inhibin, secreted by granulosa cells, functions mainly in negative feedback to suppress FSH release from the pituitary and does not act on cervical gland mucus secretion.

preguntas.q: Which female sex steroid is responsible for the rise in basal body temperature seen after ovulation?

e.correcta: Progesterone, secreted by the corpus luteum after ovulation, has a thermogenic effect on the hypothalamic thermoregulatory center that raises basal body temperature by about 0.5°F, a rise that persists through the luteal phase until progesterone falls (if pregnancy does not occur) or continues to rise (if it does). This temperature shift is used clinically and by patients tracking fertility to confirm that ovulation has occurred, since the temperature rise only appears after the corpus luteum starts producing progesterone. The sustained biphasic temperature pattern across a cycle is a classic physiologic marker taught alongside the menstrual cycle hormone timeline.

incorrectas.A: Estrogen dominates the follicular phase before ovulation and does not have the same thermogenic hypothalamic effect; it is progesterone, released afterward from the corpus luteum, that produces the basal temperature rise.
incorrectas.C: FSH drives follicular development in the ovary but has no direct thermoregulatory action on the hypothalamus, so it does not explain the post-ovulatory temperature increase.
incorrectas.D: Inhibin B is secreted by granulosa cells to provide negative feedback on FSH release; it has no role in thermoregulation and does not cause the basal body temperature shift attributed to progesterone.

preguntas.q: Which female sex steroid causes uterine smooth muscle (myometrial) relaxation?

e.correcta: Progesterone relaxes uterine smooth muscle by decreasing myometrial excitability and reducing gap junction formation between myometrial cells, which prevents coordinated contractions and helps maintain pregnancy; this is why progesterone withdrawal is a key trigger for the onset of labor. Its calming effect on the myometrium contrasts directly with the contractile stimuli that eventually initiate parturition.

incorrectas.A: Estrogen increases myometrial excitability and promotes gap junction formation between smooth muscle cells, priming the uterus for coordinated contraction — essentially the opposite effect of progesterone's relaxant action.
incorrectas.B: Oxytocin directly stimulates uterine smooth muscle contraction by binding myometrial oxytocin receptors (which increase in density near term), driving labor rather than causing relaxation.
incorrectas.D: Prostaglandin E2 promotes cervical ripening and stimulates myometrial contractions, contributing to labor onset, the opposite effect of the myometrial relaxation caused by progesterone.

preguntas.q: What effect does progesterone have on estrogen receptor expression in target tissues?

o.C: No effect on estrogen receptor number
o.D: Conversion of estrogen receptors to progesterone receptors

e.correcta: Progesterone downregulates estrogen receptor expression in target tissues such as the endometrium and myometrium, which is a key negative feedback mechanism that limits continued estrogenic proliferation once ovulation has occurred and the luteal phase begins. This receptor downregulation is part of how progesterone converts the endometrium from a proliferative to a secretory, non-proliferative state and helps protect against unopposed estrogen effects like endometrial hyperplasia.

incorrectas.A: Upregulation is the opposite of what progesterone does to estrogen receptors — that direction of effect actually describes what estrogen does to its own and to progesterone receptors, not what progesterone does to estrogen receptors.
incorrectas.C: No effect misses progesterone's well-established role in downregulating estrogen receptors, a mechanism that is central to how the luteal phase counterbalances the proliferative estrogen effects of the follicular phase.
incorrectas.D: Progesterone does not convert one receptor type into another; receptors are distinct proteins whose expression levels change via transcriptional regulation, not interconversion between receptor types.

preguntas.q: Which female sex steroid protects against endometrial hyperplasia by opposing unchecked estrogen stimulation?

e.correcta: Progesterone opposes estrogen's proliferative drive on the endometrium by downregulating estrogen receptors and converting the endometrium into a differentiated, secretory (non-mitotic) state, which prevents the continued unchecked glandular proliferation that would otherwise predispose to endometrial hyperplasia and, over time, endometrial cancer. This is precisely why unopposed estrogen (e.g., in anovulatory cycles, PCOS, or estrogen-only hormone therapy without a progestin) is a recognized risk factor for endometrial hyperplasia — the balancing progesterone signal is missing.

incorrectas.A: Estrogen is the hormone that drives the proliferation being described — it stimulates endometrial gland and stroma growth, which is exactly what unchecked exposure to it (without progesterone opposition) causes to become hyperplastic, so it cannot be the protective hormone here.
incorrectas.B: Testosterone is not a physiologic regulator of the normal endometrial proliferation-secretion balance; its relevance to the endometrium is mainly as an aromatization substrate for estrogen production, not as a direct opposing hormone.
incorrectas.D: FSH acts on the ovary to drive follicular development and estrogen production; it does not act directly on the endometrium to oppose estrogen's proliferative effects the way progesterone does.

preguntas.q: Approximately how many-fold do circulating estradiol and estrone levels increase during pregnancy?

e.correcta: During pregnancy, the placenta becomes a major steroidogenic organ, converting maternal and fetal adrenal precursors (like DHEA-S) into large quantities of estrogen, causing circulating estradiol and estrone to rise roughly 50-fold above nonpregnant levels by term. This dramatic rise supports uterine growth, mammary development, and uteroplacental blood flow, and is part of why estriol (which rises even more dramatically, roughly 1000-fold, due to its dependence on fetal adrenal and liver contributions) is used as a marker of fetoplacental well-being.

incorrectas.A: A 5-fold increase substantially underestimates the true rise in estradiol and estrone during pregnancy, which is a much larger, roughly 50-fold increase driven by placental steroidogenesis.
incorrectas.C: A 200-fold increase overestimates the rise specifically for estradiol and estrone; that magnitude of increase is more characteristic of estriol, which rises far more dramatically due to its dependence on fetal adrenal precursor supply.
incorrectas.D: A 1000-fold increase describes the classic rise in estriol during pregnancy (reflecting fetal contribution to its synthesis), not estradiol or estrone, which rise to a lesser though still substantial degree.

preguntas.q: Approximately how many-fold does estriol increase during pregnancy, making it a useful indicator of fetal well-being?

e.correcta: Estriol rises approximately 1000-fold during pregnancy because it is produced through a unique fetoplacental pathway: the fetal adrenal gland and liver synthesize precursors (DHEA-S, 16-OH-DHEA-S) that the placenta then aromatizes into estriol, making maternal serum estriol a marker of both fetal and placental function. A falling or low estriol level can signal fetal distress or placental insufficiency, which is why it was historically part of the triple/quad screen.

incorrectas.A: A 50-fold rise understates the actual magnitude of estriol's increase in pregnancy, which is a defining feature distinguishing it from estrone and estradiol, whose relative rises are smaller.
incorrectas.B: 100-fold, while a large increase, still substantially underestimates the roughly 1000-fold rise that makes estriol uniquely useful as a marker requiring intact fetal adrenal/liver and placental function.
incorrectas.D: 10-fold is far too small a change to characterize estriol's dramatic pregnancy-associated rise and would not distinguish it as a clinically useful fetoplacental marker.

preguntas.q: Variability in the overall length of the menstrual cycle is mainly attributed to variation in the duration of which phase?

e.correcta: The follicular phase is variable in length because it depends on the time needed for a dominant follicle to be recruited and mature to the point of triggering the LH surge, which can vary cycle to cycle and shortens as women approach menopause; the luteal phase, by contrast, is fixed at about 14 days because it is governed by the finite, relatively constant lifespan of the corpus luteum. This is a high-yield physiology fact: total cycle length variability is essentially follicular phase variability, while luteal phase length is a much more reliable, near-constant 14 days used clinically to back-calculate ovulation timing.

incorrectas.A: The luteal phase is actually the more fixed component of the cycle (~14 days, determined by the corpus luteum's programmed lifespan), so it is not the source of the variability in total cycle length that the question is asking about.
incorrectas.C: The menstrual phase (the days of sloughing/bleeding) is a brief, relatively fixed portion at the start of the cycle and is not the major driver of overall cycle length variability between women or cycles.
incorrectas.D: The ovulatory phase refers to the brief periovulatory window itself, not an extended phase whose duration varies enough to meaningfully change total cycle length.

preguntas.q: By convention, what event marks day 0 (day 1) of the menstrual cycle?

e.correcta: By convention, day 1 of the menstrual cycle is defined as the first day of menses (the onset of endometrial shedding), because this is the only externally observable and reliably timed event in the cycle, allowing consistent staging of the follicular phase, ovulation, and luteal phase relative to it. This anchoring matters clinically for calculating expected ovulation (day 14 in a 28-day cycle), dating pregnancies, and timing fertility treatments or hormone assays. Menses itself reflects withdrawal of progesterone and estrogen support from the corpus luteum of the prior cycle, triggering endometrial breakdown.

incorrectas.A: Ovulation occurs around day 14 of a typical 28-day cycle, counted from the start of menses — it is a mid-cycle event triggered by the LH surge, not the reference point that defines day 1.
incorrectas.B: The LH surge precedes ovulation by about 36 hours and is a discrete hormonal trigger, but it occurs mid-cycle and is not used as the day 0/1 reference; it depends on the follicular phase length, which varies, unlike the fixed convention of counting from menses.
incorrectas.D: Fertilization, if it occurs, happens around the time of ovulation in the fallopian tube, an event with variable and often unknown timing that cannot serve as the fixed, observable landmark that menses provides for cycle day counting.

preguntas.q: The first phase of the menstrual cycle, lasting from approximately day 0 to day 14 and characterized histologically by straight endometrial glands with abundant mitotic figures, is called what?

e.correcta: The follicular (proliferative) phase spans roughly day 0 (start of menses) to day 14 (ovulation) and is histologically marked by straight, tubular endometrial glands with abundant mitoses, reflecting estrogen-driven regeneration and thickening of the endometrium after the prior cycle's shedding. This proliferative histology directly mirrors the ovarian follicular phase, since rising estradiol from the developing follicle is what drives this endometrial regrowth.

incorrectas.A: The secretory (luteal) phase occurs after ovulation and is marked by tortuous, coiled glands with subnuclear then luminal glycogen vacuoles under progesterone influence — the opposite histologic picture (straight glands, high mitotic activity) described here belongs to the earlier proliferative phase.
incorrectas.C: The ischemic phase refers to the brief period just before menstruation when progesterone/estrogen withdrawal causes spiral artery vasoconstriction and endometrial breakdown, not the day 0–14 window of gland regrowth and proliferation described in the question.
incorrectas.D: Menstrual phase alone typically refers only to the few days of active bleeding/shedding (roughly days 1-5), not the entire day 0-14 window of proliferative regrowth with mitotically active straight glands described in the stem.

preguntas.q: During the follicular phase, a graafian follicle develops into which structure, while neighboring follicles undergo atresia?

e.correcta: Under FSH stimulation, one follicle becomes more sensitive to gonadotropins and outpaces the others, becoming the dominant (Graafian) follicle that continues to grow, secrete rising estradiol, and eventually ovulate, while the other recruited follicles — deprived of adequate FSH support once estradiol and inhibin rise and suppress FSH — undergo atresia. This selection process ensures normally only one oocyte is ovulated per cycle in humans, and is a key concept tying together follicular recruitment, dominant follicle selection, and hormonal feedback.

incorrectas.A: The corpus luteum forms after ovulation from the ruptured follicle's remaining granulosa and theca cells, which is a later step than the dominant follicle stage being described in the question (which occurs during, not after, the follicular phase).
incorrectas.B: The corpus albicans is the fibrotic, involuted remnant of the corpus luteum after it degenerates (if no pregnancy occurs), representing an even later stage than the dominant follicle or corpus luteum.
incorrectas.D: A primordial follicle is the earliest, quiescent stage of follicular development present from birth; it precedes the antral/Graafian stages and is not the structure that a Graafian follicle develops into during selection.

preguntas.q: During most of the follicular phase, rising estradiol has what effect on FSH and LH secretion from the pituitary?

o.D: Selectively inhibits only FSH, not LH

e.correcta: During most of the follicular phase, moderately rising estradiol exerts negative feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis, suppressing GnRH pulsatility and thus FSH and LH secretion, which helps limit the number of follicles recruited and refines selection of the dominant follicle. This negative feedback relationship reverses only once estradiol reaches a sustained high threshold near mid-cycle, at which point the same hormone switches to positive feedback and triggers the LH surge — a key conceptual pivot point in the cycle.

incorrectas.A: Stimulation is the effect estradiol has only once it crosses a high, sustained threshold near mid-cycle (triggering the LH surge), not during most of the follicular phase when its rising-but-still-moderate levels are actually suppressing gonadotropins.
incorrectas.C: Saying there is no effect ignores the well-established negative feedback loop by which follicular-phase estradiol restrains FSH/LH secretion, which is central to how the body prevents multiple follicles from being recruited each cycle.
incorrectas.D: Estradiol during most of the follicular phase suppresses both FSH and LH together via negative feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis, not selectively only one of the two gonadotropins.

preguntas.q: During the follicular phase of the menstrual cycle, circulating progesterone levels are typically at what level?

e.correcta: During the follicular phase, the corpus luteum from the prior cycle has regressed and no significant progesterone-producing structure is yet present, so progesterone remains low while the developing follicle instead ramps up estrogen production, which drives endometrial proliferation and eventually triggers the LH surge. Progesterone only rises substantially after ovulation, once the corpus luteum forms and begins secreting it to support a secretory, receptive endometrium in the luteal phase.

incorrectas.A: High progesterone is characteristic of the luteal phase, when the corpus luteum is actively secreting it to maintain the endometrium in case of implantation, not the follicular phase when no corpus luteum yet exists.
incorrectas.C: A mid-phase peak is the pattern seen for estrogen (with a smaller pre-ovulatory peak) and especially for LH (the ovulatory surge), not for progesterone, which stays low throughout the follicular phase and only rises after ovulation.
incorrectas.D: Progesterone levels in the follicular phase are distinctly lower than in the luteal phase, precisely because the corpus luteum — the main source of progesterone — has not yet formed; they are not equal between the two phases.

preguntas.q: In the middle of the menstrual cycle, sustained high estradiol levels have what effect on FSH and LH secretion, producing the LH surge?

o.D: Only suppresses FSH via inhibin-like action

e.correcta: When estradiol remains high for a sustained period (roughly 36-48 hours) near mid-cycle, the hypothalamic-pituitary axis switches from negative to positive feedback, causing a surge in GnRH pulsatility and pituitary sensitivity that produces the LH surge (with a smaller accompanying FSH rise), which in turn triggers ovulation roughly 36 hours later. This switch from negative to positive feedback based on the duration and magnitude of estradiol exposure is one of the more nuanced and testable concepts in reproductive endocrinology.

incorrectas.A: Inhibition is the effect estradiol has earlier in the follicular phase at lower, less sustained levels; but once estradiol is high and sustained near mid-cycle, the feedback relationship flips to stimulatory, producing the LH surge described in the question.
incorrectas.C: No effect ignores the well-established positive feedback switch that sustained high estradiol produces at mid-cycle, which is the entire physiologic basis for the LH surge and subsequent ovulation.
