preguntas.q: A fluid-filled cavity lined with uroepithelium located between the umbilicus and the bladder describes which structure?

e.correcta: The urachus is the remnant of the allantois that normally involutes into the fibrous median umbilical ligament connecting the bladder to the umbilicus; when a segment of this tract fails to obliterate but both ends close off, uroepithelium-lined fluid can accumulate in the isolated middle segment, forming a urachal cyst located between the umbilicus and bladder. This is distinct from other urachal anomalies that depend on which portions of the tract remain patent.

incorrectas.A: A vesicourachal diverticulum results from incomplete closure of the urachus specifically at the bladder end, creating an outpouching from the bladder dome itself, rather than an isolated fluid-filled cavity in the mid-portion of the tract.
incorrectas.B: A patent urachus is a fully open connection from bladder to umbilicus, causing urine to leak from the umbilicus, which is a continuous open tract rather than an isolated, closed, fluid-filled cyst between the two ends.
incorrectas.D: An omphalomesenteric (vitelline) duct remnant arises from failure of the yolk sac connection to the midgut to obliterate, an entirely separate embryologic structure connecting bowel to umbilicus, unrelated to the urachus/bladder system.

preguntas.q: A slight, localized failure of the urachus to obliterate near the bladder produces which anomaly?

e.correcta: A vesicourachal diverticulum occurs when there is partial (localized) failure of urachal obliteration specifically at the bladder end, leaving a small outpouching of the bladder that persists as a diverticulum — a limited/segmental failure rather than a fully patent connection to the umbilicus. This reflects the general principle that urachal anomalies form a spectrum depending on which portion (or how much) of the urachus fails to close: complete failure gives a patent urachus, isolated middle segment failure gives a urachal cyst, and localized failure near the bladder gives a vesicourachal diverticulum.

incorrectas.A: Patent urachus is complete failure of urachal obliteration along its entire length, creating a continuous connection between the bladder and umbilicus that can leak urine from the umbilicus — a much more extensive defect than the localized failure described in the vignette.
incorrectas.C: A urachal cyst results from failure of obliteration in the middle segment of the urachus (both ends closed, fluid trapped in between), which is a different location of failure than the bladder-adjacent defect described here.
incorrectas.D: Bladder exstrophy is a distinct, severe anterior abdominal wall/bladder defect caused by failure of the infraumbilical mesenchyme to migrate properly, exposing the bladder mucosa — an entirely different embryologic mechanism from urachal remnant anomalies.

preguntas.q: A vesicourachal diverticulum presents as an outpouching of which structure?

e.correcta: The urachus is the remnant of the allantois connecting the fetal bladder to the umbilicus; when it fails to fully obliterate, focal outpouchings can form, and a vesicourachal diverticulum specifically represents persistent patency at the bladder end of the urachal tract, appearing as an outpouching of the bladder dome. This differs from a fully patent urachus (urine draining from the umbilicus) or a urachal cyst (an isolated fluid-filled remnant in the middle of the tract), representing a spectrum of incomplete urachal regression.

incorrectas.A: An outpouching centered at the umbilicus itself (rather than at the bladder) would be more consistent with an umbilical or urachal sinus opening at the skin surface, not the vesicourachal diverticulum, which is defined by its bladder-side location.
incorrectas.C: The ureter is a distinct embryologic structure derived from the ureteric bud, unrelated to urachal remnants, and diverticula of the ureter are a different entity from the urachal anomalies arising from incomplete allantoic regression.
incorrectas.D: The urethra develops from the urogenital sinus and is not connected embryologically to the urachus/allantois remnant, so it would not be the structure involved in a vesicourachal diverticulum.

preguntas.q: An invasive mole most commonly represents the malignant progression of which type of hydatidiform mole?

e.correcta: An invasive mole most commonly arises from a complete hydatidiform mole because complete moles are entirely paternal in origin (typically 46,XX from duplication of a single sperm's genome after fertilizing an empty egg) and show diffuse, more aggressive trophoblastic proliferation of all villi, giving them a higher propensity to invade the myometrium and persist or metastasize compared to partial moles. This is why complete moles require closer beta-hCG surveillance after evacuation — to catch invasive or (less commonly) choriocarcinomatous transformation early.

incorrectas.A: A partial mole (typically triploid, 69,XXY, from two sperm fertilizing one egg) has focal, less pronounced trophoblastic hyperplasia and carries a much lower risk of progressing to an invasive mole compared to a complete mole.
incorrectas.C: Choriocarcinoma is itself a malignant, highly invasive gestational trophoblastic neoplasm that can follow a mole (or any pregnancy), but it is a distinct, more aggressive entity than an invasive mole, not what an invasive mole itself progresses from.
incorrectas.D: Placental site trophoblastic tumor is a separate, rare gestational trophoblastic neoplasm arising from intermediate trophoblast, not a precursor-progression relationship with invasive moles, which specifically arise from complete moles.

preguntas.q: Invasive moles are diagnosed histologically by identifying chorionic villi invading which layer, typically seen on a hysterectomy specimen?

e.correcta: Invasive moles are diagnosed by finding chorionic villi that have penetrated into and through the myometrium, reflecting locally invasive trophoblastic tissue that behaves more aggressively than a simple intrauterine mole but, unlike choriocarcinoma, still retains villous structures and generally does not metastasize as readily. This myometrial invasion is why invasive moles can cause uterine perforation or hemorrhage and are sometimes only fully appreciated on a hysterectomy specimen when conservative management fails.

incorrectas.A: Endometrium only would describe a non-invasive, contained mole confined to the uterine cavity — the defining feature of an invasive mole is that it goes beyond this superficial layer into the muscular wall.
incorrectas.C: Serosal invasion would suggest a more advanced, transmural process with a higher risk of perforation and would raise concern for a more aggressive process (or misdiagnosis), whereas the classic finding for an invasive mole is myometrial, not full-thickness serosal, invasion.
incorrectas.D: Cervical stroma invasion is not the characteristic site used to define an invasive mole, which is specifically characterized by penetration into the myometrium of the uterine corpus.

preguntas.q: Which of the following is a recognized risk factor for placental abruption?

o.A: Trauma (e.g., motor vehicle accident, physical abuse)
o.C: Advanced maternal age with no other risk factors

e.correcta: Trauma, such as a motor vehicle accident or physical abuse, is a well-recognized cause of placental abruption because the shearing forces from sudden deceleration or a direct blow can separate the placenta from the decidua basalis, disrupting the maternal spiral arteries and causing retroplacental hemorrhage. This is why any pregnant trauma patient is monitored for signs of abruption (painful bleeding, uterine tenderness/rigidity, contractions) even when external injuries appear minor.

incorrectas.B: Prior cesarean section is a well-established risk factor for placenta accreta spectrum and uterine rupture (due to the myometrial scar), but it is not a classic risk factor for placental abruption, which relates more to vascular and mechanical disruption of the placental attachment itself.
incorrectas.C: Advanced maternal age is a general risk factor for various pregnancy complications, but with no other risk factors specified, it is not the primary, well-established cause of abruption the way trauma, hypertension, cocaine use, or prior abruption are.
incorrectas.D: Multiple prior vaginal deliveries alone is not an established risk factor for placental abruption; recognized risk factors instead include hypertension, trauma, smoking, cocaine use, and a history of prior abruption.

preguntas.q: A prior cesarean section increases the risk of placenta accreta primarily because it results in which uterine change?

o.B: A scar with a deficient or absent decidua basalis
o.D: Increased uterine vascularity throughout the fundus

e.correcta: A prior cesarean section leaves a scar in the lower uterine segment where normal decidua basalis formation is impaired or absent, so in a subsequent pregnancy the chorionic villi can attach directly to or invade into the myometrium at that site (rather than being limited by a healthy decidual layer), producing placenta accreta. This mechanism explains why the risk of accreta rises sharply with each additional cesarean delivery, especially when combined with placenta previa overlying the old scar.

incorrectas.A: A cesarean scar does not increase myometrial thickness — if anything, scar tissue is typically thinner and less vascularly robust than normal myometrium, which is part of why it is vulnerable to abnormal placental attachment and invasion.
incorrectas.C: Cervical incompetence refers to painless cervical dilation leading to second-trimester loss or preterm birth, a distinct entity related to cervical structural integrity, not to the decidual defect at a uterine scar that predisposes to accreta.
incorrectas.D: Increased uterine vascularity throughout the fundus is not the mechanism at play; the risk is localized to the scar itself (the deficient decidua basalis there), not a global increase in vascularity across the entire uterus.

preguntas.q: What is the standard diagnostic modality used to identify placenta previa?

e.correcta: Transvaginal or transabdominal ultrasound is the standard, safe, and highly accurate modality for diagnosing placenta previa, directly visualizing the placental edge relative to the internal cervical os without introducing risk to the pregnancy. It is used both to establish the diagnosis after painless third-trimester bleeding and to monitor for possible resolution as the lower uterine segment develops later in pregnancy.

incorrectas.A: Digital cervical examination is absolutely contraindicated when placenta previa is suspected, because probing the cervix can disrupt the previa and provoke severe hemorrhage — this is precisely why ultrasound is used first to rule out previa before any pelvic exam.
incorrectas.C: Amniocentesis involves needle sampling of amniotic fluid for genetic or fetal lung maturity testing and carries no role in visualizing placental location; performing it in the presence of an undiagnosed previa could actually be dangerous.
incorrectas.D: MRI of the pelvis can occasionally be used in complex cases (e.g., suspected placenta accreta spectrum), but it is not the standard first-line test for previa given its cost, limited availability, and the excellent accuracy of ultrasound for this purpose.

preguntas.q: A pregnant patient presents with rupture of membranes, painless vaginal bleeding, and fetal bradycardia (<110 bpm). Which diagnosis best fits this triad?

e.correcta: Vasa previa fits this triad because fetal vessels run unsupported through the membranes over the cervical os; when the membranes rupture, these exposed vessels can tear, causing painless vaginal bleeding that is actually fetal blood, and the resulting fetal blood loss produces bradycardia (or even fetal exsanguination) very rapidly — making this an obstetric emergency requiring immediate cesarean delivery. The temporal link to rupture of membranes is the key clue, since it is the membrane rupture that directly damages the aberrant vessels.

incorrectas.A: Placental abruption classically presents with painful bleeding and a tender, often rigid uterus due to retroplacental hemorrhage, not the painless bleeding tied specifically to membrane rupture described here.
incorrectas.B: Placenta previa causes painless bleeding from the low-lying placenta over the cervix, but it is not specifically triggered by rupture of membranes and does not characteristically cause the abrupt fetal bradycardia from bleeding fetal vessels the way vasa previa does.
incorrectas.D: Uterine rupture typically presents with sudden severe abdominal pain, loss of fetal station, and maternal hemodynamic instability (often in a patient with a prior uterine scar), not painless bleeding tied to membrane rupture.

preguntas.q: A pregnant woman in the third trimester presents with painless vaginal bleeding and no fetal bradycardia. Which condition is most likely responsible?

e.correcta: Placenta previa is the classic cause of painless third-trimester bleeding because the placenta implants over or near the internal cervical os, and as the lower uterine segment thins and the cervix effaces, the overlying placental tissue shears and bleeds without associated pain or uterine contraction. Because the fetal vasculature itself is not directly torn (unlike vasa previa), fetal bradycardia is not a typical accompanying feature, which is the key detail distinguishing it from vasa previa in this vignette.

incorrectas.A: Vasa previa also causes painless bleeding, but it is specifically associated with fetal bradycardia because the bleeding originates from unprotected fetal vessels — the absence of fetal bradycardia here argues against vasa previa and for placenta previa instead.
incorrectas.C: Placental abruption presents with painful bleeding and uterine tenderness/rigidity from retroplacental separation, which is inconsistent with the painless presentation described in this vignette.
incorrectas.D: Preterm labor presents with regular painful contractions and cervical change, not painless vaginal bleeding as the primary feature, making it inconsistent with this presentation.

preguntas.q: A pregnant patient has painless third-trimester bleeding accompanied by fetal bradycardia (HR <110 bpm). Which diagnosis is most consistent with this presentation?

e.correcta: Vasa previa is the diagnosis here because unprotected fetal vessels coursing through the membranes over the cervix are prone to tearing (especially with membrane rupture or cervical dilation), and because the blood lost is fetal in origin, even a small volume causes rapid fetal bradycardia or exsanguination despite painless bleeding in the mother. Recognizing this combination is critical because it demands emergent cesarean delivery to save the fetus, in contrast to previa or abruption where the timeline and management differ.

incorrectas.A: Placenta previa causes painless bleeding from the maternal placental bed itself, and because fetal vessels are not directly disrupted, it does not typically cause the acute fetal bradycardia that defines this vignette.
incorrectas.C: Placental abruption causes painful bleeding with uterine tenderness or rigidity due to retroplacental separation, which contradicts the painless presentation described here.
incorrectas.D: Chorioamnionitis presents with maternal fever, uterine tenderness, and fetal tachycardia (not bradycardia), and is an infectious process rather than a vascular one, making it inconsistent with this painless-bleeding-with-bradycardia presentation.

preguntas.q: Painful vaginal bleeding in the third trimester, often accompanied by uterine tenderness or rigidity, is most characteristic of which condition?

e.correcta: Placental abruption is characterized by painful bleeding with uterine tenderness or rigidity because the placenta separates prematurely from the decidua basalis, causing retroplacental hemorrhage that irritates and can hypertonically contract the myometrium, distinguishing it clinically from the painless bleeding seen in previa or vasa previa. Risk factors include hypertension, trauma, cocaine use, and smoking, and severe cases can progress to fetal distress, DIC, and hemorrhagic shock, making prompt recognition essential.

incorrectas.A: Vasa previa causes painless bleeding from torn fetal vessels typically after membrane rupture, and it is defined by fetal bradycardia rather than maternal uterine pain or rigidity.
incorrectas.B: Placenta previa causes painless bleeding as the lower-segment placenta shears with cervical effacement, without the uterine tenderness or rigidity that defines abruption.
incorrectas.D: Cervical insufficiency presents with painless cervical dilation and effacement leading to second-trimester pregnancy loss, not third-trimester painful bleeding with uterine tenderness.

preguntas.q: A newborn is noted to have pulmonary hypoplasia and facial/limb deformities. Prenatal ultrasounds had shown a markedly reduced amniotic fluid volume. Which amniotic fluid abnormality was present, classically associated with placental insufficiency, bilateral renal agenesis, or posterior urethral valves?

e.correcta: Oligohydramnios (reduced amniotic fluid volume) is classically associated with placental insufficiency, bilateral renal agenesis, or posterior urethral valves — all conditions that reduce fetal urine production or output, since fetal urine is the dominant source of amniotic fluid in later pregnancy. The resulting fluid deficiency compresses the fetus, restricting limb and facial development (deformities) and preventing normal lung expansion, causing pulmonary hypoplasia — collectively known as Potter sequence.

incorrectas.A: Polyhydramnios is an excess of amniotic fluid, classically from fetal inability to swallow fluid (e.g., esophageal or duodenal atresia, anencephaly) or maternal diabetes — the opposite fluid abnormality from what is described here.
incorrectas.C: Amniotic band rupture refers to fibrous bands from a ruptured amnion entangling and constricting fetal parts, causing disruptive amputations or defects, a distinct mechanical process rather than a fluid volume abnormality.
incorrectas.D: Vasa previa is a placental/vascular anomaly involving unprotected fetal vessels over the cervix, unrelated to amniotic fluid volume or the renal/pulmonary findings described in this vignette.

preguntas.q: A pregnant woman at 32 weeks with severe preeclampsia is started on a medication to prevent progression to eclamptic seizures. Which drug is used?

e.correcta: IV magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice to prevent eclamptic seizures in severe preeclampsia because it raises the seizure threshold, likely through NMDA receptor antagonism and cerebral vasodilation (reducing cerebral vasospasm/ischemia), and has been shown in trials to be more effective than phenytoin or benzodiazepines for this specific indication. It is given as a loading dose followed by continuous infusion, with the patient monitored for signs of magnesium toxicity (loss of deep tendon reflexes, respiratory depression), since calcium gluconate is the antidote if toxicity occurs.

incorrectas.A: Phenytoin is a seizure medication used for other epilepsy indications but has been shown in clinical trials to be inferior to magnesium sulfate specifically for preventing eclamptic seizures in preeclampsia, so it is not the standard of care here.
incorrectas.B: Labetalol is used to control the hypertension of severe preeclampsia itself, but it does not prevent eclamptic seizures — magnesium sulfate is given in addition to antihypertensives specifically for seizure prophylaxis.
incorrectas.D: Diazepam (a benzodiazepine) can be used to terminate an active seizure but is not the standard prophylactic agent for preventing eclamptic seizures in preeclampsia, a role reserved for magnesium sulfate.

preguntas.q: A woman develops glucose intolerance around 26 weeks of gestation. Elevated levels of which placental hormone are responsible for the increased insulin resistance underlying gestational diabetes?

e.correcta: Human placental lactogen (hPL), produced by the syncytiotrophoblast, rises progressively through pregnancy and antagonizes maternal insulin action (promoting lipolysis and decreasing peripheral glucose uptake) in order to spare glucose for the fetus; when this insulin resistance exceeds the mother's pancreatic capacity to compensate with extra insulin secretion, gestational diabetes results, which is why screening is classically performed around 24-28 weeks when hPL-driven resistance peaks. This physiologic mechanism explains why gestational diabetes tends to emerge in the second half of pregnancy rather than earlier.

incorrectas.A: Human chorionic gonadotropin's main roles are maintaining the corpus luteum early in pregnancy and serving as the basis for pregnancy testing; it is not the hormone responsible for the insulin resistance that drives gestational diabetes.
incorrectas.B: Progesterone does contribute modestly to insulin resistance and is important for maintaining uterine quiescence, but the placental hormone most directly and classically implicated in the diabetogenic insulin resistance of pregnancy is human placental lactogen, not progesterone.
incorrectas.D: Estriol is a marker of fetoplacental well-being (part of the classic triple/quad screen) reflecting fetal adrenal and hepatic function, but it is not the hormone driving maternal insulin resistance in gestational diabetes.

preguntas.q: A pregnant woman at 34 weeks has new hypertension (150/95 mmHg) on two occasions. What level of proteinuria supports the diagnosis of preeclampsia?

e.correcta: Preeclampsia is defined as new-onset hypertension (≥140/90 mmHg on two occasions ≥4 hours apart) after 20 weeks' gestation plus evidence of end-organ involvement, and proteinuria ≥300 mg over a 24-hour urine collection (or a protein/creatinine ratio ≥0.3) is the classic marker used to satisfy that criterion. The underlying mechanism is abnormal placental spiral artery remodeling leading to placental ischemia, which releases anti-angiogenic factors (like sFlt-1) that damage maternal glomerular endothelium (glomerular endotheliosis) and cause protein to leak into the urine. Note that in current guidelines proteinuria is not strictly required if other severe features (thrombocytopenia, renal/liver dysfunction, pulmonary edema, cerebral symptoms) are present, but the 300 mg/day threshold remains the classic testable cutoff.

incorrectas.A: 100 mg/day is below the diagnostic threshold and would be seen in normal pregnancy or mild physiologic proteinuria; it does not reflect the degree of glomerular endothelial injury required to support a preeclampsia diagnosis.
incorrectas.C: 1000 mg/day is well above the diagnostic cutoff — while it would certainly qualify as proteinuria, it overstates the minimum threshold that defines the condition, which is set at 300 mg/day, not 1 g/day.
incorrectas.D: 5000 mg/day (5 g/day) was an older criterion once used to define 'severe' preeclampsia in some classification schemes, but current guidelines have moved away from using a specific severe-range proteinuria cutoff and it is not the threshold used to establish the initial diagnosis.

preguntas.q: A woman has significant vaginal bleeding immediately after a vaginal delivery, and on exam the uterine fundus is soft and boggy rather than firm. What is the most likely cause of this postpartum hemorrhage?

e.correcta: Uterine atony — failure of the myometrium to contract firmly after delivery — is the most common cause of postpartum hemorrhage, and the boggy, soft fundus on exam is its hallmark finding because normal postpartum hemostasis depends on myometrial contraction compressing the spiral arteries that fed the placental bed. Risk factors include uterine overdistension (multiple gestation, polyhydramnios), prolonged labor, and multiparity, and first-line treatment is uterine massage plus uterotonics (oxytocin, methylergonovine, carboprost). The physical exam distinguishes it from the other causes of PPH, which classically present with a firm, well-contracted uterus.

incorrectas.B: Retained placental tissue also causes bleeding because the uterus cannot fully contract around retained cotyledons, but it is typically suspected when the placenta appears incomplete on inspection or ultrasound shows retained products, not primarily diagnosed by fundal tone alone, and the uterus may still feel firm in places.
incorrectas.C: Genital tract lacerations (cervical or vaginal tears) cause postpartum bleeding despite a firm, well-contracted uterus — bright red bleeding continuing with a firm fundus should prompt a search for a laceration, which is essentially the opposite exam finding from what's described here.
incorrectas.D: Coagulopathy (e.g., DIC from abruption or amniotic fluid embolism) causes diffuse oozing from IV sites, incisions, and the uterus in the setting of a normally contracted (firm) uterus and abnormal coagulation studies, not a boggy fundus.

preguntas.q: A hemodynamically stable woman is diagnosed with an unruptured ectopic pregnancy and low, declining beta-hCG levels. Which chemotherapeutic agent may be used to medically manage this pregnancy?

e.correcta: Methotrexate is a folic acid antagonist (inhibits dihydrofolate reductase) that blocks DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing trophoblastic tissue, making it effective for medically managing an unruptured ectopic pregnancy when the patient is hemodynamically stable and beta-hCG is low and declining (favorable prognostic factors for medical therapy success). It avoids the morbidity of surgery (salpingostomy/salpingectomy) in appropriately selected patients, but it is contraindicated with high hCG, cardiac activity on ultrasound, or hemodynamic instability, in which case surgery is required.

incorrectas.A: Cyclophosphamide is an alkylating agent that cross-links DNA and is used in malignancies and autoimmune disease, but it is not the drug used for ectopic pregnancy — it carries greater toxicity (hemorrhagic cystitis, myelosuppression) that is unnecessary for this indication.
incorrectas.C: Vincristine is a vinca alkaloid that disrupts microtubule/mitotic spindle formation, used in lymphomas and other cancers; it plays no role in ectopic pregnancy management and is not chosen for its reproductive tissue selectivity.
incorrectas.D: 5-Fluorouracil is a pyrimidine analog antimetabolite used mainly in solid tumor and skin cancer chemotherapy; while also antiproliferative, it is not the agent validated and used clinically for medical management of ectopic pregnancy — that role belongs specifically to methotrexate.

preguntas.q: A phenotypic male with gynecomastia, small testes, and a karyotype of 47,XXY undergoes buccal smear analysis. Is a Barr body expected to be present?

o.A: No, because only one X chromosome is present
o.B: Yes, because the extra X chromosome is inactivated
o.C: No, Barr bodies only occur in females
o.D: Yes, but only in half of cells (mosaicism)

e.correcta: A Barr body is the condensed, transcriptionally inactive X chromosome (heterochromatin) seen at the nuclear periphery in cells with more than one X chromosome, formed via X-inactivation (Lyonization) to achieve dosage compensation. Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) has two X chromosomes, so one is inactivated and appears as a single Barr body — the same number of Barr bodies as a normal 46,XX female, which is why Klinefelter patients are Barr-body positive despite having a male phenotype and testes.

incorrectas.A: This option incorrectly states only one X chromosome is present — the karyotype 47,XXY explicitly has two X chromosomes plus a Y, which is precisely why a Barr body forms in the first place (one of the two Xs is inactivated).
incorrectas.C: Barr bodies are not exclusive to females; the general rule is (number of X chromosomes) − 1 = number of Barr bodies, so any cell with ≥2 X chromosomes, including Klinefelter males, will show a Barr body.
incorrectas.D: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is a nonmosaic constitutional karyotype present in essentially all cells (barring rare mosaic variants), so a Barr body would be expected in all cells with two X chromosomes, not just half via mosaicism — mosaicism is not the mechanism being tested here.

preguntas.q: A short female with webbed neck, wide-spaced nipples, and primary amenorrhea has a karyotype of 45,X. Is a Barr body expected on buccal smear?

o.A: Yes, one Barr body is present
o.B: No, because there is only one X chromosome
o.C: Yes, two Barr bodies are present
o.D: It cannot be determined without further testing

e.correcta: Turner syndrome (45,X) has only a single X chromosome and no second X to inactivate, so by the rule (number of X chromosomes − 1 = number of Barr bodies), zero Barr bodies are seen on buccal smear. This absence of Barr bodies helps distinguish Turner syndrome from other causes of primary amenorrhea and short stature, and clinically correlates with streak ovaries, webbed neck, and wide-spaced nipples from lymphatic dysgenesis during development.

incorrectas.A: This suggests a Barr body is present, which would only be true if there were two or more X chromosomes; Turner syndrome has just one X, so no Barr body forms.
incorrectas.C: Two Barr bodies would require three X chromosomes (as in 47,XXX), not the single X chromosome found in 45,X Turner syndrome.
incorrectas.D: The karyotype 45,X is diagnostic and unambiguous for the number of X chromosomes present; a buccal smear showing zero Barr bodies is fully consistent with this and does not require further testing to determine Barr body status.

preguntas.q: Which two benign breast pathologies are characterized by proliferation primarily of the fibrous stroma rather than the glandular epithelium?

e.correcta: Fibroadenoma and phyllodes tumor both arise from proliferation of the fibrous (connective tissue) stroma of the breast, with fibroadenoma being a benign, well-circumscribed, hormonally responsive stromal-epithelial biphasic tumor common in young women, and phyllodes tumor being a stromal-predominant tumor (usually in older women) with a leaf-like architecture that can behave more aggressively and rarely become malignant. Distinguishing stromal-based from epithelial-based breast lesions matters because it changes the expected growth pattern, hormone sensitivity, and malignant potential.

incorrectas.A: Fibrocystic change involves cystic dilation of ducts and epithelial/stromal changes driven by hormonal fluctuation, and fat necrosis is a reactive inflammatory response to trauma or surgery — neither is defined by primary fibrous stromal proliferation the way fibroadenoma and phyllodes tumor are.
incorrectas.B: Intraductal papilloma is a proliferation of ductal epithelium (papillary epithelial fronds) within a duct, and ductal ectasia is dilation and inflammation of subareolar ducts — both are epithelial/ductal processes, not primarily stromal proliferations.
incorrectas.D: Sclerosing adenosis is a proliferative lesion of acini and stroma often mistaken for cancer on imaging, and mastitis is an inflammatory/infectious process (classically in breastfeeding women) — neither represents the stromal-predominant proliferation pattern characteristic of fibroadenoma/phyllodes tumor.

preguntas.q: A breast biopsy shows small, discohesive cells growing in a single-file pattern with occasional cells containing a mucin vacuole that pushes the nucleus to one side, giving a signet ring appearance. Which type of breast cancer is this?

e.correcta: Lobular carcinoma (in situ or invasive) is characteristically caused by loss of E-cadherin, a cell adhesion molecule, which explains why the malignant cells lose cohesion and grow in single-file (Indian file) rows rather than forming glands or sheets. The loss of cellular adhesion also explains the signet ring morphology, where an intracytoplasmic mucin vacuole displaces the nucleus to the periphery, and clinically, invasive lobular carcinoma is notable for being difficult to detect by palpation or mammography and having a higher rate of bilaterality/multicentricity than ductal carcinoma.

incorrectas.A: Invasive ductal carcinoma is the most common breast cancer subtype and typically forms glandular/duct-like structures or solid nests with desmoplastic stroma; it does not characteristically show E-cadherin loss or the single-file, signet ring pattern described here.
incorrectas.B: Medullary carcinoma is characterized by sheets of large, poorly differentiated cells with a prominent lymphocytic infiltrate and pushing (not infiltrative) borders — it has a distinctive syncytial growth pattern, not single-file cells with signet ring morphology.
incorrectas.D: Inflammatory breast carcinoma is a clinical diagnosis defined by dermal lymphatic invasion causing peau d'orange skin changes and erythema, not a specific cytologic growth pattern — the single-file/signet ring appearance described is specific to the loss of E-cadherin seen in lobular carcinoma.

preguntas.q: A 55-year-old man develops unilateral breast tissue enlargement. This condition results from an imbalance favoring which hormonal activity relative to androgen activity?

e.correcta: Gynecomastia results from an increased estrogen-to-androgen activity ratio in breast tissue, since estrogen (from any source — increased production, decreased clearance, or peripheral aromatization of androgens, as occurs with aging, obesity, liver disease, or certain drugs) stimulates ductal epithelial and stromal proliferation in the male breast. In an older man, this is often physiologic (age-related decline in testosterone with relatively preserved/increased peripheral aromatization) but medications, liver cirrhosis, hypogonadism, and rarely estrogen- or hCG-secreting tumors should be considered.

incorrectas.B: Prolactin stimulates milk production (galactorrhea) rather than ductal/stromal proliferation causing breast enlargement; hyperprolactinemia can secondarily cause gynecomastia by suppressing GnRH and lowering testosterone (raising the estrogen:androgen ratio indirectly), but the direct driver of gynecomastia is the estrogen effect, not prolactin itself.
incorrectas.C: Cortisol excess (Cushing syndrome) causes central obesity, striae, and hyperglycemia, but is not a classic direct mediator of gynecomastia through altering the estrogen:androgen balance in breast tissue.
incorrectas.D: Thyroid hormone excess causes hyperthyroid symptoms (weight loss, tachycardia, heat intolerance) and can increase sex hormone-binding globulin, indirectly altering free hormone levels, but it is not the primary or classically tested mechanism of gynecomastia compared to a direct increase in estrogen activity.

preguntas.q: A patient develops gynecomastia after starting a new medication regimen. Which of the following is LEAST likely to be the causative drug, based on drugs classically linked to gynecomastia (remembered by 'Some Hormones Create Knockers')?

e.correcta: Metoprolol is a beta-1 selective blocker and is not among the classic drugs causing gynecomastia; beta-blockers work by blocking sympathetic beta-adrenergic receptors and have no meaningful effect on the estrogen/androgen balance in breast tissue. The mnemonic 'Some Hormones Create Knockers' (Spironolactone, cimetidine (H2 blockers), estrogens/anabolic steroids, alcohol, some antipsychotics, ketoconazole) lists drugs known to disrupt androgen signaling or increase estrogenic activity, and metoprolol does not fit that mechanism.

incorrectas.A: Spironolactone is an aldosterone antagonist that also blocks the androgen receptor and inhibits androgen synthesis, directly shifting the estrogen:androgen ratio toward estrogen dominance and causing gynecomastia — a well-known and testable side effect.
incorrectas.B: Cimetidine (an H2 blocker, unlike other H2 blockers) has anti-androgenic activity by blocking androgen receptors, which increases the relative estrogenic effect on breast tissue and causes gynecomastia — this is a classic, distinguishing feature of cimetidine among H2 blockers.
incorrectas.C: Ketoconazole inhibits steroidogenic cytochrome P450 enzymes, blocking testosterone synthesis while also having some anti-androgen receptor activity, which shifts the estrogen:androgen ratio and produces gynecomastia — this is part of its known endocrine side effect profile.

preguntas.q: A young woman presents with an ovarian mass; on gross pathology it appears as a yellow, friable, hemorrhagic solid mass, and serum AFP is markedly elevated. Which germ cell tumor is this?

e.correcta: The yolk sac (endodermal sinus) tumor is the germ cell tumor classically associated with markedly elevated AFP, because AFP is normally produced by the fetal yolk sac and liver, and this tumor recapitulates yolk sac differentiation. Grossly it appears as a yellow, friable, hemorrhagic mass, and histologically it shows Schiller-Duval bodies (glomeruloid structures) — it is the most common germ cell tumor of the ovary/testis in children, and AFP serves as a useful tumor marker for diagnosis and monitoring treatment response.

incorrectas.A: Dysgerminoma is the ovarian counterpart of testicular seminoma, composed of sheets of uniform cells with clear cytoplasm and central nuclei; it is associated with elevated LDH and sometimes hCG (if syncytiotrophoblastic giant cells are present), but not with AFP elevation or the yellow, friable, hemorrhagic gross appearance described.
incorrectas.B: Mature (cystic) teratoma (dermoid cyst) is the most common ovarian germ cell tumor overall and contains differentiated tissue from all three germ layers (hair, teeth, sebaceous material) — it does not secrete AFP and is not classically hemorrhagic/friable on gross exam.
incorrectas.D: Choriocarcinoma is composed of syncytiotrophoblasts and cytotrophoblasts and secretes markedly elevated beta-hCG rather than AFP; it hematogenously metastasizes early (notably to lungs) but is not the tumor associated with this AFP elevation and gross appearance.

preguntas.q: A young woman is found to have an ovarian germ cell tumor with markedly elevated serum LDH. Which tumor is most classically associated with this laboratory finding?

e.correcta: Dysgerminoma is the germ cell tumor classically associated with markedly elevated serum LDH, which reflects the tumor's high glycolytic activity and large tumor cell burden — analogous to its testicular counterpart, seminoma, which also elevates LDH. Recognizing LDH elevation alongside the characteristic histology (sheets of large cells with clear cytoplasm, central nuclei, and a fibrous septa infiltrated by lymphocytes) helps identify this tumor, which is notably radiosensitive and chemosensitive with an excellent prognosis.

incorrectas.A: Yolk sac tumor is classically associated with markedly elevated AFP (reflecting its yolk sac differentiation), not LDH, and shows Schiller-Duval bodies histologically rather than the sheet-like clear cell pattern of dysgerminoma.
incorrectas.C: Choriocarcinoma is associated with markedly elevated beta-hCG from syncytiotrophoblastic cells, not LDH, and behaves aggressively with early hematogenous spread rather than the more indolent, chemosensitive course typical of dysgerminoma.
incorrectas.D: Immature teratoma contains embryonic (immature neuroectodermal) tissue and can be associated with elevated AFP in some cases, but LDH is not its classic tumor marker — LDH elevation is the hallmark of dysgerminoma.

preguntas.q: An ovarian germ cell tumor is found to secrete markedly elevated alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). Which tumor is this?

e.correcta: The yolk sac (endodermal sinus) tumor is the ovarian germ cell tumor that secretes markedly elevated AFP because it differentiates toward yolk sac structures, which normally produce AFP in the developing fetus (analogous to fetal liver production). This tumor mainly affects children and young women, shows Schiller-Duval bodies (glomeruloid structures resembling a primitive glomerulus) on histology, and AFP is used clinically both to support the diagnosis and to monitor for recurrence after treatment.

incorrectas.A: Dysgerminoma is associated with elevated LDH (and sometimes hCG), not AFP; it is composed of uniform cells resembling primordial germ cells, distinct from the yolk sac differentiation that drives AFP production.
incorrectas.C: Choriocarcinoma secretes markedly elevated beta-hCG from its syncytiotrophoblastic component, not AFP, and spreads hematogenously early, in contrast to the AFP-secreting yolk sac tumor.
incorrectas.D: Struma ovarii is a monodermal teratoma composed predominantly of thyroid tissue and can cause hyperthyroidism, but it does not secrete AFP — it is functionally and histologically unrelated to the yolk sac tumor's AFP secretion.

preguntas.q: A woman with a markedly elevated beta-hCG level (from a hydatidiform mole or choriocarcinoma) is found to have bilateral, multiloculated ovarian cysts on ultrasound. Which type of ovarian cyst is this, resulting from gonadotropin overstimulation?

e.correcta: Theca-lutein cysts form when the ovarian theca interna cells are markedly overstimulated by very high levels of beta-hCG (which shares a receptor with LH), as occurs with a hydatidiform mole, choriocarcinoma, multiple gestation, or ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, producing bilateral, multiloculated, often large ovarian cysts. Recognizing this association is clinically useful because the cysts typically regress spontaneously once the hCG-driving process (e.g., the mole) is treated, and they don't require direct surgical intervention.

incorrectas.A: Follicular cysts arise from a dominant follicle that fails to rupture or involute during a normal menstrual cycle and are usually small, unilateral, and unrelated to markedly elevated hCG states like molar pregnancy.
incorrectas.B: Corpus luteum cysts form from a corpus luteum that persists or hemorrhages after ovulation, typically unilateral and related to normal-range hormonal support of early pregnancy, not the massive gonadotropin overstimulation seen with a mole or choriocarcinoma.
incorrectas.D: Endometrioma ('chocolate cyst') results from ectopic endometrial tissue bleeding within the ovary in the context of endometriosis, unrelated to hCG level or trophoblastic disease, and is not characteristically bilateral/multiloculated in the way theca-lutein cysts are.

preguntas.q: A young woman with hyperthyroidism, exophthalmos, and a diffusely enlarged thyroid is found to carry two specific HLA alleles associated with this autoimmune disease. Which HLA alleles are classically linked to Graves disease?

e.correcta: Graves disease, an autoimmune hyperthyroidism driven by stimulating autoantibodies against the TSH receptor, is classically associated with HLA-B8 and HLA-DR3, reflecting a genetic predisposition to autoimmune thyroid disease (these alleles influence antigen presentation and T-cell selection, increasing susceptibility to breaking self-tolerance against thyroid antigens). This HLA association is a useful pattern-recognition fact linking Graves disease to other HLA-B8/DR3-associated autoimmune conditions in some classification schemes.

incorrectas.A: HLA-DR4 is associated with rheumatoid arthritis and type 1 diabetes, and HLA-DQ8 is associated with celiac disease and type 1 diabetes — neither is the classic pairing linked to Graves disease.
incorrectas.B: HLA-B27 is associated with the seronegative spondyloarthropathies (ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, IBD-associated arthritis), and HLA-DR2 is linked to conditions like Goodpasture syndrome and MS — this pairing is unrelated to Graves disease.
incorrectas.D: HLA-DR5 is associated with Hashimoto thyroiditis and pernicious anemia, and HLA-DQ2 is associated with celiac disease — these are different autoimmune associations from the HLA-B8/DR3 link classically taught for Graves disease.

preguntas.q: A woman in her first trimester of pregnancy is diagnosed with Graves disease requiring thionamide therapy. Which drug is preferred during the first trimester due to a lower teratogenic risk than its alternative?

e.correcta: Propylthiouracil (PTU) is preferred in the first trimester of pregnancy because methimazole is associated with a rare but specific embryopathy (aplasia cutis congenita, choanal/esophageal atresia) when used during early organogenesis, whereas PTU carries a lower (though not zero) teratogenic risk during this critical window. Both drugs inhibit thyroid peroxidase to block synthesis of new thyroid hormone, but PTU has the added mechanism of inhibiting peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion; the tradeoff is that PTU carries a black box warning for hepatotoxicity, which is why it is switched to methimazole after the first trimester.

incorrectas.A: Methimazole is generally preferred outside of pregnancy and after the first trimester due to its more favorable side effect profile (once-daily dosing, lower hepatotoxicity risk), but during the first trimester it is avoided because of its association with methimazole embryopathy (aplasia cutis, choanal atresia).
incorrectas.C: Levothyroxine is used to treat hypothyroidism, not hyperthyroidism — giving additional thyroid hormone to a patient with Graves disease (who already has excess thyroid hormone) would worsen thyrotoxicosis rather than treat it.
incorrectas.D: Radioactive iodine ablates the thyroid gland by concentrating in thyroid follicular cells and destroying them with beta radiation, but it is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy because it crosses the placenta and can destroy the fetal thyroid or cause other fetal harm.

preguntas.q: A pregnant woman with Graves disease is now in her second trimester. Which thionamide becomes the preferred agent at this point in pregnancy, given PTU's own toxicity profile?

e.correcta: Methimazole becomes preferred in the second and third trimesters because PTU carries a risk of severe hepatotoxicity (including fulminant liver failure) with more prolonged use, so the drug most associated with teratogenic risk (methimazole) is used only briefly during the vulnerable first-trimester organogenesis window, after which the safer long-term hepatic profile of methimazole outweighs its by-then-diminished teratogenic risk (since major organogenesis is complete). This practical trade-off — teratogenicity risk in trimester 1 vs. hepatotoxicity risk with prolonged use — is why clinicians switch thionamides partway through pregnancy.

incorrectas.A: PTU is preferred specifically during the first trimester due to its lower teratogenic risk during organogenesis, but continuing it through the rest of pregnancy increases cumulative exposure to its hepatotoxicity risk, which is why the switch to methimazole happens after the first trimester.
incorrectas.C: Iodide (Lugol's solution) is used short-term for thyroid storm or preoperative preparation (via the Wolff-Chaikoff effect) to acutely reduce hormone release, not as a first-line chronic thionamide replacement during pregnancy.
incorrectas.D: Propranolol is used for symptomatic control of adrenergic symptoms (tachycardia, tremor) in hyperthyroidism/thyroid storm, but it does not inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis and is not a substitute thionamide for definitive Graves disease management.

preguntas.q: A healthcare worker presents with symptoms of hyperthyroidism, recent unexplained weight loss, and low radioactive iodine uptake on thyroid scan. Which cause of hyperthyroidism is most consistent with this presentation?

e.correcta: Factitious thyrotoxicosis from exogenous thyroid hormone ingestion (e.g., a healthcare worker with access to thyroid medication) causes hyperthyroid symptoms and weight loss along with low radioactive iodine uptake, because the excess circulating hormone suppresses TSH, which in turn suppresses the thyroid gland's own iodine trapping and hormone synthesis — the gland itself is quiescent, not overactive. Low RAIU is the key distinguishing lab finding that separates thyrotoxicosis without true thyroid gland hyperfunction (factitious ingestion, subacute thyroiditis) from thyrotoxicosis due to gland overactivity (Graves disease, toxic nodules), which show high RAIU.

incorrectas.A: Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis also causes low RAIU (due to follicular destruction releasing preformed hormone) and can cause transient hyperthyroid symptoms, but it classically presents with a painful, tender thyroid gland and often a preceding viral illness — not the profile of a healthcare worker with access to thyroid hormone, which points more directly to factitious use.
incorrectas.C: Toxic multinodular goiter causes hyperthyroidism due to autonomously functioning nodules that actively take up iodine, so RAIU would be increased (patchy) rather than low, distinguishing it from this presentation.
incorrectas.D: A TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma causes hyperthyroidism with elevated (not suppressed) TSH driving the thyroid to overproduce hormone, which would show increased RAIU due to genuine gland hyperactivity, unlike the low RAIU described here.

preguntas.q: A patient taking a thionamide for hyperthyroidism develops a new skin eruption. Which of the following is a well-known possible skin complication common to both propylthiouracil and methimazole?

e.correcta: Rash (skin eruption/pruritus) is a common and well-recognized adverse effect shared by both propylthiouracil and methimazole, thought to reflect a hypersensitivity-type reaction to the thionamide class itself rather than to either drug's unique structural feature; it is usually mild and can sometimes be managed by switching to the other agent within the class rather than stopping thionamide therapy altogether. More severe but rarer shared reactions include agranulocytosis, which requires distinguishing from simple rash since agranulocytosis needs urgent drug discontinuation and workup (fever, sore throat, CBC).

incorrectas.B: Aplasia cutis congenita is a fetal malformation (scalp skin defect) associated specifically with methimazole exposure during early pregnancy (methimazole embryopathy), not a skin complication seen in the general patient taking either drug, and it does not occur in PTU.
incorrectas.C: Hyperpigmentation is not a characteristic side effect of thionamides; it is more classically associated with conditions of ACTH excess (e.g., Addison disease, Nelson syndrome) or certain other drugs, not with PTU or methimazole.
incorrectas.D: Photosensitivity with bullae is characteristic of drugs like tetracyclines, amiodarone, or certain diuretics (pseudoporphyria), not a recognized shared toxicity of the thionamides used for hyperthyroidism.

preguntas.q: A patient with hypothyroidism and myxedema is started on a synthetic hormone analog structurally identical to T4. Which drug is this?

e.correcta: Levothyroxine is a synthetic form of T4 (thyroxine), structurally identical to endogenous T4, and is the standard long-term replacement therapy for hypothyroidism because it provides a stable prohormone that peripheral tissues (via deiodinases) convert to the active T3 as needed, giving smooth, sustained hormone levels with once-daily dosing. This makes it ideal for chronic maintenance therapy, including in severe hypothyroidism/myxedema, where it corrects the underlying deficiency driving the myxedematous changes (non-pitting edema from glycosaminoglycan accumulation, cold intolerance, bradycardia).

incorrectas.A: Triiodothyronine (liothyronine) is synthetic T3, the more potent and rapidly acting but shorter half-life active hormone, generally reserved for situations needing fast onset (e.g., myxedema coma) rather than routine chronic maintenance, unlike the T4 analog levothyroxine.
incorrectas.C: Propylthiouracil is a thionamide used to treat hyperthyroidism by blocking thyroid hormone synthesis and peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion — giving it to a hypothyroid patient would worsen, not correct, the hormone deficiency.
incorrectas.D: Methimazole is likewise an antithyroid thionamide used for hyperthyroidism, working by inhibiting thyroid peroxidase-mediated hormone synthesis; it has the opposite therapeutic purpose from what is needed in a hypothyroid, myxedematous patient.

preguntas.q: A patient in myxedema coma is given a fast-acting synthetic thyroid hormone identical to T3 for rapid effect. Which drug is this?

e.correcta: Triiodothyronine (liothyronine) is synthetic T3, the biologically active thyroid hormone with a faster onset of action and higher potency than T4, making it the preferred choice in myxedema coma where rapid restoration of thyroid hormone activity is needed to reverse life-threatening hypothyroid physiology (hypothermia, hypotension, altered mental status, hypoventilation). Because T3 does not require peripheral deiodinase conversion (which may be impaired in severe illness), it acts more quickly than levothyroxine (T4) in this emergency setting.

incorrectas.A: Levothyroxine (T4) is the standard chronic maintenance therapy for hypothyroidism but has a slower onset since it must be peripherally converted to active T3, making it less ideal alone for the acute, rapid correction needed in myxedema coma (though it may be given alongside T3 in practice).
incorrectas.C: Cinacalcet is a calcimimetic that increases the sensitivity of the calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid cells, used to treat secondary hyperparathyroidism or parathyroid carcinoma — it has no role in thyroid hormone replacement.
incorrectas.D: Fludrocortisone is a synthetic mineralocorticoid used for adrenal insufficiency (aldosterone replacement) — it addresses a completely different endocrine axis and has no thyroid hormone activity relevant to myxedema coma.

preguntas.q: Beyond treating hypothyroidism, thyroid hormone replacement drugs like levothyroxine and triiodothyronine are sometimes misused off-label for which purpose?

o.D: Blood pressure lowering in hypertensive emergencies

e.correcta: Thyroid hormone increases basal metabolic rate by upregulating Na+/K+-ATPase activity and mitochondrial oxidative metabolism across tissues, which is why supratherapeutic or misused thyroid hormone (levothyroxine or triiodothyronine) is sometimes abused off-label as a weight-loss aid, exploiting this thermogenic/metabolic effect to burn calories faster. This is dangerous because it induces an iatrogenic thyrotoxic state with tachycardia, arrhythmias, bone loss, and muscle wasting without providing sustainable or safe weight loss, and thyroid hormone should never be used in euthyroid individuals for this purpose.

incorrectas.B: Thyroid hormone excess actually tends to increase appetite (alongside increased metabolic rate) in classic hyperthyroidism, rather than being used deliberately as an appetite stimulant — its off-label misuse is specifically for weight loss via increased metabolism, not for stimulating hunger.
incorrectas.C: Thyroid hormone is stimulatory, not sedating — excess thyroid hormone causes anxiety, tremor, and insomnia, the opposite of a sedative effect, so it would not be misused for sedation.
incorrectas.D: Thyroid hormone excess causes tachycardia and widened pulse pressure, not therapeutic blood pressure lowering; it is not used to manage hypertensive emergencies, and doing so would be inappropriate and dangerous given its cardiostimulatory effects.

preguntas.q: A patient on levothyroxine for hypothyroidism is inadvertently overdosed and develops palpitations on ECG monitoring. Which cardiac adverse effects are classically associated with excess thyroid hormone replacement?

e.correcta: Excess thyroid hormone increases the density and sensitivity of beta-adrenergic receptors in the myocardium and directly increases heart rate and contractility, so overdose classically produces tachycardia and can precipitate arrhythmias, particularly atrial fibrillation, especially in older patients or those with underlying cardiac disease. This cardiostimulatory effect is why thyroid function should be monitored and doses titrated carefully, and why beta-blockers are often used adjunctively in overt thyrotoxicosis to control the adrenergic symptoms.

incorrectas.A: Bradycardia and heart block are features of hypothyroidism (insufficient thyroid hormone slowing metabolic and cardiac activity), the opposite physiologic direction from what occurs with thyroid hormone excess/overdose.
incorrectas.C: Pericardial effusion is a recognized finding in hypothyroidism (due to myxedematous fluid accumulation and reduced cardiac output), not a complication of thyroid hormone overdose, which instead produces a hyperdynamic, tachycardic state.
incorrectas.D: Orthostatic hypotension is more typical of hypothyroidism or autonomic dysfunction, whereas thyroid hormone excess increases cardiac output and heart rate, more often associated with palpitations and sometimes even mild systolic hypertension rather than orthostatic drops.

preguntas.q: A woman at term is being induced for labor. Which posterior pituitary hormone is administered to stimulate uterine contractions?

e.correcta: Oxytocin is the posterior pituitary hormone (synthesized in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary) that binds oxytocin receptors on myometrial smooth muscle to stimulate rhythmic uterine contractions, making it the standard agent used for labor induction and augmentation as well as for controlling postpartum hemorrhage via its uterotonic effect. Its release is also central to the milk let-down reflex (via contraction of myoepithelial cells in the breast) in a classic positive feedback loop with nipple stimulation.

incorrectas.A: Vasopressin (ADH) is also released from the posterior pituitary but acts on renal V2 receptors to promote water reabsorption (antidiuresis) and V1 receptors to cause vasoconstriction — it has no meaningful role in stimulating uterine contractions during labor.
incorrectas.C: Prolactin is an anterior pituitary hormone that stimulates milk production by mammary glandular tissue, not uterine muscle contraction, so it plays no direct role in labor induction.
incorrectas.D: Follicle-stimulating hormone is an anterior pituitary gonadotropin that drives follicular development and spermatogenesis, entirely unrelated to myometrial contraction or labor induction.

preguntas.q: A patient with primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) requires replacement of deficient mineralocorticoid activity in addition to glucocorticoid replacement. Which drug, an aldosterone analog, is used for this purpose?

e.correcta: Fludrocortisone is a synthetic mineralocorticoid analog with potent activity at the aldosterone receptor in the renal distal tubule and collecting duct, promoting sodium (and water) reabsorption and potassium/hydrogen excretion — replacing the mineralocorticoid deficiency in primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), where the adrenal cortex fails to produce both cortisol and aldosterone. It is given alongside a glucocorticoid (typically hydrocortisone) because glucocorticoid replacement alone does not adequately replace the mineralocorticoid axis needed to prevent hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypotension.

incorrectas.A: Hydrocortisone is a glucocorticoid with some intrinsic mineralocorticoid activity, used to replace the missing cortisol, but it is not potent or selective enough as a mineralocorticoid to be relied upon alone — fludrocortisone is added specifically to cover the mineralocorticoid deficiency.
incorrectas.C: Spironolactone is a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (aldosterone blocker) used to treat conditions of aldosterone excess (e.g., hyperaldosteronism, heart failure) — it does the opposite of what's needed in adrenal insufficiency, where mineralocorticoid activity is deficient, not excessive.
incorrectas.D: Cinacalcet is a calcimimetic used in secondary hyperparathyroidism or parathyroid carcinoma to lower PTH and calcium levels; it has no mineralocorticoid activity and no role in adrenal insufficiency management.

preguntas.q: A patient on fludrocortisone for adrenal insufficiency develops darkened patches of skin. Which skin complication is associated with this drug?

e.correcta: Fludrocortisone (and glucocorticoid dosing in general) is associated with hyperpigmentation in this clinical setting largely because patients on replacement for primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) already have markedly elevated ACTH/POMC-derived peptides (from loss of cortisol negative feedback), and melanocyte-stimulating hormone activity from POMC cleavage products drives increased melanin production in skin, especially at pressure points, palmar creases, and mucous membranes. While hyperpigmentation is primarily a feature of the underlying disease (elevated ACTH) rather than a direct pharmacologic toxicity of fludrocortisone itself, it is the skin finding classically linked to this clinical context and is often incompletely reversed even with adequate replacement therapy.

incorrectas.A: Vitiligo is a separate autoimmune process involving destruction of melanocytes leading to depigmented patches, and while it can co-occur with autoimmune Addison disease (both being autoimmune conditions), it is not the darkening pigmentation change directly linked to the ACTH/MSH pathway described here.
incorrectas.C: Erythema nodosum is a panniculitis presenting as tender red nodules, typically associated with infections, sarcoidosis, or inflammatory bowel disease, not with adrenal insufficiency or fludrocortisone therapy.
incorrectas.D: Acanthosis nigricans is a velvety, hyperpigmented skin thickening classically associated with insulin resistance (e.g., type 2 diabetes, obesity) or occasionally paraneoplastic syndromes, not with adrenal insufficiency or mineralocorticoid replacement therapy.

preguntas.q: A patient on fludrocortisone develops peripheral edema and worsening dyspnea on exertion. Which underlying condition is being exacerbated by this aldosterone analog's sodium and water retention?

e.correcta: Fludrocortisone is a synthetic mineralocorticoid that acts on the principal cells of the renal collecting duct to upregulate ENaC and Na+/K+-ATPase, driving sodium reabsorption with obligate water retention and potassium/hydrogen secretion. In a patient with underlying heart failure, the expanded plasma volume increases venous return and left ventricular preload beyond what the already-compromised myocardium can handle, precipitating pulmonary congestion (dyspnea) and peripheral edema. This is why mineralocorticoid excess (endogenous or iatrogenic) is a classic precipitant of decompensated heart failure and why aldosterone antagonists, not agonists, are used therapeutically in HF.

incorrectas.B: Chronic kidney disease impairs sodium and water excretion through reduced GFR and nephron mass, but the vignette specifically invokes the drug's aldosterone-like action driving volume overload, which manifests as cardiac decompensation (dyspnea, edema from elevated filling pressures) rather than being a primary renal filtration problem.
incorrectas.C: Cirrhosis causes edema and ascites primarily through portal hypertension, hypoalbuminemia, and secondary hyperaldosteronism from decreased effective arterial volume, not through exogenous mineralocorticoid receptor stimulation as the direct culprit; the question is testing the direct cardiac consequence of added sodium/water retention.
incorrectas.D: Hypothyroidism can cause a form of edema (myxedema, which is due to glycosaminoglycan deposition, not fluid overload) and is unrelated to mineralocorticoid receptor activity, so it does not explain worsening dyspnea and true peripheral edema from volume expansion.

preguntas.q: A patient with secondary hyperparathyroidism from chronic kidney disease is started on a drug that increases the sensitivity of calcium-sensing receptors in the parathyroid gland. Which drug is this?

e.correcta: Cinacalcet is a calcimimetic that allosterically increases the sensitivity of the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) on chief cells of the parathyroid gland, making the receptor 'think' serum calcium is higher than it actually is. This tricks the gland into suppressing PTH secretion, which is useful in secondary hyperparathyroidism from CKD where chronically low calcium and elevated phosphate would otherwise drive persistent PTH overproduction and renal osteodystrophy. Because the effect is receptor sensitization rather than direct calcium supplementation, cinacalcet lowers both PTH and serum calcium simultaneously.

incorrectas.A: Teriparatide is recombinant PTH (1-34) given intermittently to stimulate osteoblastic bone formation in osteoporosis; it works oppositely to what's needed here, activating rather than suppressing the PTH axis, and has no CaSR-sensitizing mechanism.
incorrectas.C: Sevelamer is a non-absorbed phosphate binder that reduces intestinal phosphate absorption in CKD, indirectly helping control secondary hyperparathyroidism by lowering phosphate, but it does not act on calcium-sensing receptors at all.
incorrectas.D: Calcitriol (active vitamin D) suppresses PTH by directly binding vitamin D receptors on parathyroid cells and raising serum calcium via increased gut absorption; this is a distinct mechanism from CaSR sensitization and carries a greater risk of hypercalcemia.

preguntas.q: A patient started on cinacalcet for secondary hyperparathyroidism develops perioral numbness and tingling in the fingertips. Which adverse effect explains these symptoms?

e.correcta: By sensitizing the parathyroid CaSR, cinacalcet suppresses PTH secretion, and since PTH is the principal hormone maintaining serum calcium (via bone resorption, renal calcium reabsorption, and activation of vitamin D), a drop in PTH leads to hypocalcemia. The perioral numbness and fingertip tingling are classic neuromuscular signs of hypocalcemia, reflecting increased neuronal membrane excitability when extracellular calcium falls (calcium normally stabilizes voltage-gated sodium channels).

incorrectas.A: Hypercalcemia would be the expected effect of increased or unregulated PTH activity, the opposite of what cinacalcet produces, and clinically causes lethargy, constipation, and bone pain rather than perioral paresthesias.
incorrectas.C: Hyperkalemia is not a known direct effect of cinacalcet, which acts specifically on the parathyroid CaSR and calcium homeostasis, not on renal potassium handling; it also does not produce the classic circumoral/digital tingling described here.
incorrectas.D: Hypermagnesemia is unrelated to cinacalcet's mechanism and would more typically cause decreased reflexes and lethargy rather than the excitatory paresthesias seen with low calcium.

preguntas.q: A patient using an antacid regularly for dyspepsia develops muscle weakness, and labs reveal a common electrolyte abnormality shared by essentially all antacids. Which adverse effect is this?

e.correcta: All antacids can cause hypokalemia through a shared mechanism: by raising gastric and systemic pH, they promote a shift of potassium into cells in exchange for hydrogen ions leaving (to buffer the alkalosis), and antacid-induced alkalinization also increases distal renal tubular potassium secretion. This is why hypokalemia, manifesting as muscle weakness, is described as a common denominator adverse effect across the whole antacid class regardless of the specific cation (aluminum, magnesium, or calcium) used.

incorrectas.A: Hyperkalemia is the opposite of what alkalosis produces; alkalemia drives potassium into cells and increases renal potassium wasting, so antacids characteristically lower serum potassium rather than raise it.
incorrectas.C: Hypernatremia is not a shared class effect of antacids; sodium bicarbonate specifically can cause sodium loading, but this is not the property common to all antacids that the question is asking about, and it does not cause muscle weakness through this mechanism.
incorrectas.D: Hyponatremia is not a general antacid effect either; the classic shared electrolyte disturbance across the antacid class relates to potassium handling from the alkalotic milieu, not sodium.

preguntas.q: A patient who has been overusing an antacid for chronic heartburn develops significant constipation. Which antacid, remembered by the mnemonic 'aluminimum amount of feces,' is most associated with this side effect?

e.correcta: Aluminum hydroxide causes constipation because aluminum ions relax gastrointestinal smooth muscle and slow motility, reducing bowel transit time; the mnemonic 'aluminimum amount of feces' captures both the reduced stool output and helps distinguish it from magnesium's opposite effect. This is clinically useful because aluminum- and magnesium-containing antacids are often combined in a single formulation specifically to offset each other's bowel effects (constipation versus diarrhea).

incorrectas.A: Magnesium hydroxide causes diarrhea, not constipation, because unabsorbed magnesium ions osmotically draw water into the gut lumen and also stimulate motility, making it essentially the pharmacologic opposite of aluminum in this respect.
incorrectas.B: Calcium carbonate can cause constipation to a lesser degree but is more classically associated with milk-alkali syndrome (hypercalcemia, alkalosis, renal insufficiency) with chronic overuse; it is not the antacid captured by the 'aluminimum' mnemonic.
incorrectas.D: Sodium bicarbonate is a systemically absorbed antacid known for causing metabolic alkalosis and sodium loading, not constipation, and is not associated with the mnemonic device referenced in the question.

preguntas.q: A patient on long-term high-dose antacid therapy develops bone pain and is found to have low serum phosphate along with radiographic evidence of osteodystrophy. Which antacid is most likely responsible?

e.correcta: Aluminum hydroxide binds dietary phosphate in the gut lumen, forming insoluble aluminum phosphate that is excreted in stool rather than absorbed; with chronic high-dose use this can drive serum phosphate low enough to trigger phosphate depletion, which impairs bone mineralization and produces osteomalacia/osteodystrophy along with bone pain. This is precisely why aluminum-based binders must be used cautiously and phosphate levels monitored in patients on long-term antacid therapy.

incorrectas.A: Calcium carbonate does not deplete phosphate through gut binding in the same way and is more associated with hypercalcemia and milk-alkali syndrome with overuse, not hypophosphatemic osteodystrophy.
incorrectas.B: Magnesium hydroxide's main clinically significant adverse effect is osmotic diarrhea, not phosphate binding or bone demineralization; it doesn't share aluminum's phosphate-chelating property to a clinically significant degree.
incorrectas.D: Sodium bicarbonate is systemically absorbed and causes metabolic alkalosis, not gut phosphate binding, so it does not produce hypophosphatemic bone disease.

preguntas.q: A patient using large amounts of an antacid for dyspepsia develops hypercalcemia, metabolic alkalosis, and renal insufficiency (milk-alkali syndrome), along with rebound acid hypersecretion. Which antacid is responsible?

e.correcta: Calcium carbonate is both an antacid and a calcium source; when taken in large amounts it is absorbed systemically and can raise serum calcium directly, and the calcium plus the alkalinizing effect of the carbonate together produce hypercalcemia, metabolic alkalosis, and renal insufficiency, the classic triad of milk-alkali syndrome. It also causes rebound acid hypersecretion because the transient buffering of gastric acid triggers gastrin release once the drug wears off, stimulating even more acid production, a problem particular to calcium-containing antacids among the major classes.

incorrectas.A: Aluminum hydroxide does not add a calcium load and is instead associated with constipation and, with chronic use, phosphate depletion/osteodystrophy — a very different toxicity profile from milk-alkali syndrome.
incorrectas.B: Magnesium hydroxide is not systemically absorbed to a significant degree in patients with normal renal function and its dominant adverse effect is osmotic diarrhea, not hypercalcemia or alkalosis from calcium loading.
incorrectas.D: Sodium bicarbonate does cause metabolic alkalosis but does not provide a calcium load, so it does not reproduce the full milk-alkali triad; its systemic absorption instead risks sodium overload and alkalosis without the calcium component.

preguntas.q: By altering gastric and urinary pH, antacids can affect which pharmacokinetic property of other co-administered drugs?

e.correcta: Antacids raise gastric pH, which can alter the ionization state and dissolution of weakly acidic or basic drugs taken concurrently, changing how much of the co-administered drug is absorbed across the gut mucosa; they can also alter urinary pH, changing renal reabsorption/excretion of ionizable drugs. Both effects converge on altering how much active drug actually reaches the systemic circulation, i.e., its bioavailability, which is why clinicians are taught to separate antacid dosing from other oral medications by several hours.

incorrectas.B: Protein binding is determined by a drug's affinity for plasma proteins like albumin and is not altered by gastric or urinary pH changes from antacids; this is a distinct pharmacokinetic parameter unaffected by luminal pH shifts.
incorrectas.C: Volume of distribution reflects how a drug partitions between plasma and tissues based on lipophilicity and protein/tissue binding, not on gastric or urinary pH, so antacids do not directly change this parameter.
incorrectas.D: Hepatic clearance depends on hepatic blood flow and enzymatic metabolism (e.g., CYP450 activity), which is not mechanistically linked to gastric or urinary pH changes caused by antacids.

preguntas.q: Which class of GI drugs works by binding directly to the ulcer base to form a physical barrier, allowing HCO3- secretion to reestablish the mucosal pH gradient?

e.correcta: Bismuth and sucralfate work by a cytoprotective, non-acid-suppressing mechanism: in the acidic environment of the stomach, sucralfate polymerizes and binds selectively to the proteinaceous exudate at the base of an ulcer crater, forming a physical gel-like barrier that shields the mucosa from acid, pepsin, and bile while allowing the underlying epithelium to secrete bicarbonate and heal. This distinguishes them fundamentally from drugs that reduce acid secretion, since their benefit comes from local mechanical protection rather than altering gastric pH.

incorrectas.A: Proton pump inhibitors irreversibly inhibit the H+/K+-ATPase in parietal cells, reducing acid secretion at its source; they do not form a physical barrier over the ulcer, which is the specific mechanism the question describes.
incorrectas.B: H2 receptor antagonists block histamine-mediated stimulation of parietal cell acid secretion, again reducing acid production rather than physically coating and protecting the ulcer base.
incorrectas.D: Prostaglandin analogs (e.g., misoprostol) work by stimulating mucus and bicarbonate secretion and maintaining mucosal blood flow, which is cytoprotective but through a different pathway than physically adhering to the ulcer crater as a barrier.

preguntas.q: Bismuth and sucralfate are used clinically to increase the rate of which process?

e.correcta: Bismuth subsalicylate and sucralfate both act locally within the GI lumen to promote ulcer healing: sucralfate binds to the ulcer base in an acidic environment forming a protective polymerized barrier that shields the mucosa from acid, pepsin, and bile, while bismuth compounds coat the ulcer surface, inhibit pepsin activity, and have some direct antibacterial effect against H. pylori. Both agents work by protecting and promoting repair of the damaged mucosa rather than by altering acid secretion itself, which is why they are classified as mucosal protective agents used adjunctively in peptic ulcer disease.

incorrectas.A: Gastric emptying is regulated by prokinetic agents like metoclopramide, not by bismuth or sucralfate, which act locally on the mucosal surface rather than on gastric motility.
incorrectas.C: Gastric acid secretion is reduced by agents like proton pump inhibitors and H2 blockers; bismuth and sucralfate do not significantly suppress acid production, instead they act as physical/protective barriers on already-acidic mucosa.
incorrectas.D: Intestinal motility is not a target of bismuth or sucralfate's mechanism — these drugs act locally on the gastric/duodenal mucosal surface to protect and heal ulcers, not on peristalsis or transit time.

preguntas.q: In addition to promoting ulcer healing, bismuth and sucralfate can also be used to treat which condition?

e.correcta: Bismuth subsalicylate has direct antimicrobial and antisecretory properties that make it effective against traveler's diarrhea, commonly caused by enterotoxigenic E. coli, in addition to its mucosal-protective, ulcer-healing role (often paired with sucralfate as part of quadruple therapy for H. pylori). This dual utility—protecting the gastric mucosa while also treating infectious diarrhea—is why bismuth compounds appear in over-the-counter antidiarrheal products like Pepto-Bismol.

incorrectas.B: Clostridioides difficile colitis is treated with agents like vancomycin or fidaxomicin that directly target C. diff; bismuth and sucralfate are not standard therapies for this specific infection despite bismuth's general antidiarrheal reputation.
incorrectas.C: Gastroparesis is a motility disorder treated with prokinetic agents (e.g., metoclopramide, erythromycin), not with mucosal-protective agents like bismuth or sucralfate, which do not address the underlying delayed gastric emptying.
incorrectas.D: Achalasia is an esophageal motility disorder caused by loss of inhibitory neurons in the myenteric plexus, treated with pneumatic dilation, myotomy, or botulinum toxin—mechanisms entirely unrelated to bismuth or sucralfate's mucosal-coating action.

preguntas.q: Which drug used in inflammatory bowel disease is a combination of an antibacterial sulfapyridine moiety and the anti-inflammatory agent 5-aminosalicylic acid?

e.correcta: Sulfasalazine is a prodrug composed of sulfapyridine (an antibacterial sulfa moiety) linked by an azo bond to 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA, mesalamine), the actual anti-inflammatory component active in the colon. This combination allows the drug to survive transit through the upper GI tract largely intact and deliver its anti-inflammatory payload locally to the colon in inflammatory bowel disease, while the sulfapyridine portion is largely responsible for many of the drug's characteristic adverse effects (hypersensitivity reactions, oligospermia).

incorrectas.A: Mesalamine is the 5-ASA anti-inflammatory moiety alone, without the sulfapyridine carrier, and is used when patients cannot tolerate the sulfa component of sulfasalazine; it is not a combination drug.
incorrectas.C: Infliximab is a monoclonal antibody against TNF-alpha used in IBD, structurally and mechanistically unrelated to the sulfapyridine/5-ASA combination described.
incorrectas.D: Balsalazide is another prodrug that releases 5-ASA in the colon, but its carrier moiety is an inert compound, not the antibacterial sulfapyridine that defines sulfasalazine specifically.

preguntas.q: Sulfasalazine requires activation of its 5-aminosalicylic acid component by which process?
