incorrectas.A: 20 is the number of standard amino acids used in protein synthesis, a completely different quantity from the number of possible 3-base combinations; the mapping of 64 codons onto only 20 amino acids is exactly what produces degeneracy.
incorrectas.D: 4 is simply the number of distinct nucleotide bases available at any single codon position, not the number of ways they can be combined across all three positions of a codon.

preguntas.q: Of the 64 possible mRNA codons, how many actually encode an amino acid (sense codons) rather than serving as a stop signal?

e.correcta: Of the 64 total triplet combinations, 3 (UAA, UAG, UGA) function as stop codons that terminate translation rather than coding for an amino acid, leaving 61 sense codons that are read by aminoacyl-tRNAs and incorporated into the growing polypeptide. Because there are only 20 amino acids to distribute among these 61 sense codons, most amino acids are specified by multiple synonymous codons (degeneracy), with methionine and tryptophan being the rare single-codon exceptions.

incorrectas.A: 64 is the total number of possible codons before removing the 3 stop codons; it does not represent the number that actually code for amino acids, since it still includes the non-coding stop signals.
incorrectas.B: 58 is not a meaningful figure here — subtracting the 3 stop codons from 64 correctly yields 61, not 58, so this undercounts the sense codons by including an incorrect subtraction.
incorrectas.C: 20 is the number of distinct amino acids used in proteins, not the number of codons — this number reflects how many synonymous codons on average map to each amino acid (61 codons / ~20 amino acids), not a codon count itself.

preguntas.q: The 61 sense codons out of the 64 possible triplet combinations collectively encode how many standard amino acids used in human protein synthesis?

e.correcta: There are 20 standard amino acids that make up human proteins, and they are collectively encoded by the 61 sense codons — since 61 codons must specify only 20 amino acids, most amino acids have multiple synonymous codons (this redundancy is the property called degeneracy). This mismatch in numbers (61 codons vs. 20 amino acids) is precisely why the code is described as degenerate rather than one-to-one in that direction.

incorrectas.B: 64 is the total number of possible codon combinations (4^3), including the 3 stop codons that do not encode any amino acid, so it overcounts relative to the actual number of amino acids specified.
incorrectas.A: 61 is the number of sense codons that do the encoding, not the number of distinct amino acids they encode — multiple codons converge on the same amino acid, so the codon count is larger than the amino acid count.
incorrectas.D: 23 is not the standard amino acid count for translation; 20 are the canonical proteinogenic amino acids encoded by the standard genetic code (selenocysteine and pyrrolysine are rare special-case additions incorporated via unique mechanisms, not part of this basic count).

preguntas.q: Which mRNA triplet functions as the start codon that establishes the reading frame and typically encodes methionine?

e.correcta: AUG is the near-universal start codon in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes; it is recognized by the initiator tRNA (charged with methionine in eukaryotes, or N-formylmethionine in bacteria) as part of the ribosomal initiation complex, and its position sets the reading frame for every downstream codon read in nonoverlapping triplets. Because AUG also appears internally within coding sequences, initiation depends on additional context (like the Kozak sequence in eukaryotes or Shine-Dalgarno sequence in prokaryotes) to correctly identify the true start site.

incorrectas.A: GUG is a rare alternative start codon, used occasionally (especially in some bacteria) but far less commonly than AUG, and when GUG does serve as a start codon it is still translated to initiate with methionine (or fMet) rather than valine, its usual amino acid — but it is not the standard/typical start codon being described here.
incorrectas.B: UAG is one of the three stop codons, signaling the ribosome to terminate translation and release the polypeptide — the functional opposite of a start codon.
incorrectas.D: UGA is likewise a stop codon (also notable as the codon reassigned to tryptophan in human mitochondria and to selenocysteine in special contexts), not a codon used to initiate translation.

preguntas.q: In eukaryotic translation, the start codon AUG is recognized by the initiator tRNA charged with which amino acid?

e.correcta: In eukaryotes, AUG is recognized by an initiator methionyl-tRNA carrying unmodified methionine, which is loaded into the ribosomal P site during formation of the 43S/48S preinitiation complex before the large subunit joins to form a functional ribosome. This is distinct from prokaryotic initiation, where the initiator tRNA carries a formylated methionine (N-formylmethionine) instead, one of several differences between eukaryotic and bacterial translation machinery that antibiotics can selectively exploit.

incorrectas.B: N-formylmethionine (fMet) is the initiator amino acid used in prokaryotic (and mitochondrial/chloroplast) translation, not cytoplasmic eukaryotic translation — eukaryotic ribosomes lack the enzyme needed to formylate the initiator methionine.
incorrectas.A: Valine is the amino acid normally encoded by GUG when it functions as a sense codon, but the initiator tRNA loaded onto a start codon is charged with methionine regardless of whether that start codon happens to be an alternative like GUG — the initiator amino acid itself is still methionine (or fMet), not valine.
incorrectas.C: Glycine is unrelated to start codon recognition; it is coded by GGN codons and has no special initiator role in eukaryotic translation.

preguntas.q: In prokaryotic translation, the AUG start codon is recognized by an initiator tRNA charged with which modified amino acid, which also acts as a chemotactic signal for neutrophils when released from bacteria?

e.correcta: In prokaryotes, the initiator tRNA carries N-formylmethionine (fMet), in which a formyl group has been added to methionine's amino group by transformylase before it is loaded onto the start codon — this formylated residue is characteristic of bacterial (and mitochondrial) translation initiation. Clinically, fMet peptides released from lysed or dying bacteria are potent chemoattractants recognized by neutrophil formyl peptide receptors, helping explain why bacterial infections rapidly recruit neutrophils to the site of infection.

incorrectas.A: Plain methionine (without the formyl modification) is the initiator amino acid used in eukaryotic cytoplasmic translation, not in prokaryotes — the formyl group is specifically added in bacteria and is what differentiates prokaryotic from eukaryotic initiation.
incorrectas.B: Formylglycine is not a real initiator species used in translation; glycine is not the amino acid loaded onto the initiator tRNA in any organism.
incorrectas.D: N-acetylmethionine describes acetylation, a different chemical modification (removal of the N-terminal formyl/methionine and addition of an acetyl group can occur post-translationally in some proteins), not the formylation reaction that defines the bacterial initiator tRNA-methionine species.

preguntas.q: Which three mRNA codons signal the ribosome to terminate translation (stop codons)?

e.correcta: UAA, UAG, and UGA are the three stop codons; they are not recognized by any tRNA anticodon but instead by release factors that bind the ribosomal A site and trigger hydrolysis of the completed polypeptide from the P-site tRNA, ending translation. The mnemonic "U Go Away, U Are Away, U Are Gone" helps encode all three, and clinically, a point mutation that converts a sense codon into one of these three (a nonsense mutation) causes premature truncation of the protein.

incorrectas.A: AUG is the start codon (coding for methionine/fMet), and GUG/UUG are occasional alternative start codons in some bacterial contexts — none of these three terminate translation, they are all associated with initiation rather than termination.
incorrectas.C: UCA and UCG code for serine, and UGG is the sole codon for tryptophan (the other single-codon amino acid besides methionine) — none of these are stop signals; UGG in particular is easy to confuse with the stop codon UGA due to their similarity, but differs by one base and has an entirely different meaning.
incorrectas.D: AAA (lysine), GGG (glycine), and CCC (proline) are ordinary sense codons encoding amino acids, with no role in translation termination.

preguntas.q: What term describes the specific consensus DNA sequence in a genome at which DNA replication begins?

e.correcta: The origin of replication is a defined consensus sequence, typically AT-rich, that is recognized by initiator proteins which recruit helicase and the rest of the replication machinery to begin unwinding and copying the DNA. Prokaryotes (e.g., E. coli) have a single origin (oriC) given their smaller circular genome, allowing replication to complete quickly, whereas eukaryotic chromosomes are far larger and use multiple origins firing simultaneously so the entire genome can be copied within the S phase timeframe.

incorrectas.A: The replication fork is the Y-shaped structure that forms after replication has already begun at the origin, where the two template strands are actively being separated and copied — it is the site of ongoing synthesis, not the sequence that marks where synthesis starts.
incorrectas.C: Telomeres are repetitive nucleotide sequences (TTAGGG in humans) at chromosome ends that protect against degradation and are extended by telomerase; they are unrelated to marking where bidirectional replication initiates internally.
incorrectas.D: Okazaki fragments are the short, discontinuous segments synthesized on the lagging strand during replication, a downstream consequence of the antiparallel nature of DNA synthesis at the fork, not a sequence associated with initiating replication.

preguntas.q: Origins of replication and promoter regions are characteristically enriched in which type of base pair, facilitating strand separation?

e.correcta: AT-rich sequences are found at origins of replication and in promoters because adenine-thymine base pairs are held together by only 2 hydrogen bonds, compared to the 3 hydrogen bonds of guanine-cytosine pairs, making AT-rich DNA easier to melt (denature) locally. This lower energy requirement allows helicase (at origins) or the transcription machinery (at promoters) to more easily separate the two strands to expose the template for replication or transcription initiation.

incorrectas.A: GC-rich sequences form 3 hydrogen bonds per base pair, making them more thermodynamically stable and harder to melt — the opposite of what is needed at a site where strand separation must be initiated efficiently, which is why GC-rich regions are not favored at origins or promoters.
incorrectas.C: CpG methylation is an epigenetic modification associated with gene silencing (commonly at CpG islands in promoters), not a description of the base composition that facilitates strand separation at origins of replication.
incorrectas.D: Purine content (A and G together) is not the relevant distinguishing feature here; what matters for ease of strand separation is the AT versus GC hydrogen-bonding difference, not whether a base is a purine or pyrimidine.

preguntas.q: What is the name for the Y-shaped region of DNA where the double helix is unwound and the leading and lagging strands are actively synthesized?

e.correcta: The replication fork is the actively moving Y-shaped junction where the parental double helix separates into two single-stranded templates, each being copied by DNA polymerase — one continuously (leading strand) and one discontinuously in Okazaki fragments (lagging strand) due to the 5' to 3' directionality constraint of polymerases. Two replication forks move outward in opposite directions from each origin, and in eukaryotes many origins fire so that forks eventually meet and fuse to complete replication of the whole chromosome efficiently.

incorrectas.B: The origin of replication is the fixed starting sequence where forks are first established, not the actively moving Y-shaped structure itself — the origin is a location, while the fork is the dynamic structure that moves away from it.
incorrectas.C: The replisome is the multiprotein machine (helicase, primase, polymerase, clamp proteins, etc.) that operates at the fork, but the term "replication fork" refers specifically to the geometric Y-shaped DNA structure, not the protein complex driving it, so equating the two conflates structure with machinery.
incorrectas.D: A Holliday junction is a cross-shaped DNA intermediate formed during homologous recombination (e.g., in meiotic crossing over or DNA repair), structurally different from and unrelated to the replication fork of normal DNA synthesis.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme unwinds the double-stranded DNA template ahead of the replication fork, breaking the hydrogen bonds between base pairs?

e.correcta: Helicase is an ATP-dependent motor enzyme that translocates along the DNA and unwinds the double helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs, generating the two single-stranded templates needed for polymerase to act on at the replication fork. Because unwinding ahead of the fork introduces positive supercoiling downstream, helicase's action is functionally coupled to topoisomerase, which relieves that torsional strain so the fork can keep advancing.

incorrectas.A: Topoisomerase relieves the supercoiling/torsional stress created ahead of the fork by helicase's unwinding, by making transient strand breaks — it does not itself separate the two strands of the double helix at the fork.
incorrectas.B: Primase synthesizes short RNA primers that provide a free 3'-OH group for DNA polymerase to begin elongation; it acts downstream of unwinding and does not break the hydrogen bonds holding the double helix together.
incorrectas.D: DNA ligase seals nicks in the sugar-phosphate backbone, such as joining Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand, which is a late step in replication unrelated to the initial unwinding of the double helix.

preguntas.q: Which proteins coat the separated single-stranded DNA template during replication to prevent the strands from reannealing?

e.correcta: Single-stranded binding (SSB) proteins coat the exposed single-stranded DNA immediately after helicase unwinds the duplex, physically preventing the complementary strands from reannealing (re-forming base pairs) and protecting the fragile single-stranded template from nuclease degradation until polymerase can synthesize the new complementary strand. Without SSB proteins, the two strands would tend to snap back together due to their complementary base pairing, stalling replication.

incorrectas.A: Histones are proteins around which eukaryotic DNA is wound to form nucleosomes for chromatin packaging; they do not function at the replication fork to stabilize single-stranded template DNA against reannealing.
incorrectas.C: Sliding clamp proteins (like PCNA in eukaryotes or the beta clamp in prokaryotes) encircle the DNA to increase DNA polymerase's processivity, keeping it attached to the template, but this is a different function from preventing the two separated strands from re-pairing with each other.
incorrectas.D: Topoisomerase manages supercoiling tension generated ahead of the fork by cutting and resealing the DNA backbone; it has no role in stabilizing already-separated single strands against reannealing.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme relieves torsional strain in the DNA helix by creating transient single- or double-stranded breaks to add or remove supercoils?

e.correcta: Topoisomerases relieve the positive supercoiling that builds up ahead of the replication fork (a direct consequence of helicase unwinding the double helix) by transiently cutting one strand (type I) or both strands (type II) of the DNA, allowing controlled rotation before resealing the break. This is clinically important because bacterial topoisomerase II (DNA gyrase) and topoisomerase IV are targeted by fluoroquinolone antibiotics, while eukaryotic topoisomerase II is targeted by chemotherapeutics like etoposide and teniposide.

incorrectas.A: Helicase unwinds the double helix by breaking hydrogen bonds between base pairs, which is actually the cause of the downstream supercoiling problem that topoisomerase must then resolve — helicase does not itself cut the DNA backbone to relieve strain.
incorrectas.C: DNA ligase seals nicks in the phosphodiester backbone, such as joining Okazaki fragments together on the lagging strand or sealing the final nick after topoisomerase's strand-passage reaction, but it does not create the strategic breaks used to relieve supercoiling in the first place.
incorrectas.D: Primase synthesizes short RNA primers to give DNA polymerase a starting point for elongation; it has no role in managing helical tension or supercoiling.

preguntas.q: What is the alternate name for prokaryotic topoisomerase II, the enzyme targeted by fluoroquinolone antibiotics?

e.correcta: DNA gyrase is the prokaryotic name for topoisomerase II; it introduces negative supercoils ahead of the replication fork by making transient double-stranded breaks and passing DNA through them, counteracting the positive supercoiling generated by helicase unwinding. Because gyrase is essential for bacterial DNA replication and is structurally distinct from human topoisomerases, it is a selective target for fluoroquinolone antibiotics (e.g., ciprofloxacin), which trap the gyrase-DNA cleavage complex and cause lethal double-strand breaks in the bacterial genome.

incorrectas.A: Topoisomerase IV is a separate bacterial enzyme, related to gyrase but functioning primarily to decatenate (separate) interlinked daughter chromosomes after replication, rather than being another name for topoisomerase II itself — both are fluoroquinolone targets but they are distinct enzymes with distinct primary roles.
incorrectas.C: Primase is the enzyme that synthesizes RNA primers for DNA polymerase and has no relationship to supercoiling management or to being an alternate name for topoisomerase II.
incorrectas.D: Reverse transcriptase synthesizes DNA from an RNA template (used by retroviruses) and is functionally and structurally unrelated to topoisomerase's strand-breaking, supercoil-relieving activity.

preguntas.q: Which class of antibiotics acts by inhibiting bacterial topoisomerase II (DNA gyrase) and topoisomerase IV?

e.correcta: Fluoroquinolones (e.g., ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV, trapping the DNA-enzyme cleavage complex mid-reaction and causing irreversible double-strand breaks that are lethal to the bacterium. Because these bacterial topoisomerases are structurally distinct from human topoisomerases, fluoroquinolones achieve selective toxicity against bacteria, though they carry notable toxicities including tendinopathy/tendon rupture and are generally avoided in pregnancy and children due to cartilage effects.

incorrectas.B: Macrolides (e.g., azithromycin, erythromycin) inhibit bacterial protein synthesis by binding the 50S ribosomal subunit and blocking translocation, a completely different mechanism from interfering with DNA topology enzymes.
incorrectas.C: Aminoglycosides (e.g., gentamicin) bind the 30S ribosomal subunit, causing misreading of mRNA and inhibiting initiation of protein synthesis — they target translation, not DNA gyrase or topoisomerase IV.
incorrectas.D: Rifamycins (e.g., rifampin) inhibit bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, blocking transcription, which is mechanistically distinct from blocking the strand-cutting/resealing activity of topoisomerases during replication.

preguntas.q: Which two chemotherapeutic agents act by inhibiting eukaryotic topoisomerase II?

e.correcta: Etoposide and teniposide are epipodophyllotoxins that inhibit human topoisomerase II, stabilizing the transient double-strand break intermediate the enzyme normally forms and reseals, thereby causing an accumulation of DNA strand breaks that trigger apoptosis in rapidly dividing cancer cells. This mirrors how fluoroquinolones target the bacterial version of topoisomerase II, but etoposide/teniposide instead target the human enzyme, making them useful in cancers like small cell lung cancer and testicular cancer, with myelosuppression and secondary leukemias as notable toxicities.

incorrectas.A: Vincristine and vinblastine are vinca alkaloids that bind tubulin and inhibit microtubule polymerization, arresting cells in metaphase — a mechanism targeting the mitotic spindle rather than DNA topoisomerase.
incorrectas.C: Doxorubicin does inhibit topoisomerase II as one of its mechanisms (along with intercalating DNA and generating free radicals), but bleomycin instead works by generating free radicals that cause DNA strand breaks directly; this combination is not the classic paired answer for topoisomerase II inhibitors taught alongside etoposide/teniposide.
incorrectas.D: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, blocking folate-dependent nucleotide synthesis, while 5-fluorouracil inhibits thymidylate synthase — both target nucleotide synthesis pathways, not topoisomerase II enzymatic activity.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme synthesizes the short RNA primer that provides the free 3'-OH group needed for DNA polymerase III to begin replication in prokaryotes?

e.correcta: Primase is an RNA polymerase that synthesizes a short RNA primer complementary to the single-stranded DNA template, providing the free 3'-hydroxyl group that DNA polymerase III requires to begin adding nucleotides, since DNA polymerases cannot initiate synthesis de novo. Each Okazaki fragment on the lagging strand requires its own new primer, whereas the leading strand needs only one primer at the origin, which is why lagging strand synthesis is discontinuous and more primer-dependent.

incorrectas.A: Helicase unwinds the double helix ahead of the fork to expose single-stranded template, a necessary prior step, but it does not synthesize any nucleic acid primer for polymerase to extend from.
incorrectas.B: Topoisomerase relieves supercoiling tension generated by helicase's unwinding activity; it has no role in generating a starting primer for polymerase.
incorrectas.D: DNA ligase seals the nicks between adjacent DNA fragments (such as joining Okazaki fragments after the RNA primers are removed and replaced with DNA), acting at a later step than primer synthesis, not providing the initial 3'-OH itself.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme is primarily responsible for elongating the new DNA strand by adding nucleotides during replication?

o.B: DNA polymerase (DNA polymerase III in prokaryotes)

e.correcta: DNA polymerase (DNA polymerase III in prokaryotes) is the main enzyme responsible for elongating the new DNA strand, adding deoxynucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) complementary to the template strand onto the free 3'-OH group established by the RNA primer. Each nucleotide addition releases inorganic pyrophosphate (PPi), and its subsequent hydrolysis helps drive the reaction thermodynamically forward; polymerase III also has proofreading (3' to 5' exonuclease) activity that helps maintain replication fidelity.

incorrectas.A: Primase synthesizes only a short RNA primer to establish a starting 3'-OH group; it lacks the processive elongation activity and proofreading function that make DNA polymerase III suited to synthesizing the bulk of the new strand.
incorrectas.C: Helicase's job is to unwind the parental double helix ahead of the fork, exposing single-stranded template — it does not add nucleotides to a growing strand.
incorrectas.D: Topoisomerase manages supercoiling by cutting and resealing the DNA backbone to relieve torsional stress; it plays no role in the actual polymerization/elongation of the new DNA strand.

preguntas.q: DNA and RNA polymerases move along the template strand in which direction as they synthesize new nucleic acid?

o.C: Either direction depending on the strand

e.correcta: Polymerases read the template strand in the 3' to 5' direction, which is the mechanistic reason the newly synthesized strand is built in the complementary 5' to 3' direction — the enzyme adds each incoming nucleotide's 5' phosphate onto the free 3'-OH of the growing strand while moving along the template from its 3' end toward its 5' end. This fixed template-reading directionality is why one strand (leading) can be synthesized continuously toward the fork while the other (lagging) must be synthesized discontinuously in fragments moving away from the fork.

incorrectas.A: 5' to 3' describes the direction in which the new strand is synthesized (built), not the direction in which the template strand itself is being read by the polymerase — these are complementary, opposite directions relative to each other on the same molecule.
incorrectas.C: Polymerases do not switch reading direction depending on the strand; the 3' to 5' template-reading rule (and correspondingly 5' to 3' synthesis) is a fixed, universal feature of all known DNA and RNA polymerases, on both leading and lagging strands.
incorrectas.D: Polymerases absolutely have a fixed directionality — the requirement to read template 3' to 5' and synthesize new strand 5' to 3' is a defining, invariant biochemical property of these enzymes, not an arbitrary or variable one.

preguntas.q: DNA and RNA polymerases synthesize (build) the new nucleic acid strand in which direction?

e.correcta: Polymerases always synthesize new DNA or RNA strands in the 5' to 3' direction, adding each incoming nucleoside triphosphate's alpha-phosphate to the free 3'-hydroxyl group of the growing chain's last nucleotide. This fixed synthesis direction, combined with the antiparallel nature of the double helix, is why the leading strand is made continuously toward the fork while the lagging strand must be synthesized discontinuously as Okazaki fragments, each still built 5' to 3' but overall moving away from the fork.

incorrectas.A: 3' to 5' is the direction in which the polymerase reads the template strand, not the direction in which it builds the new strand — the new strand's synthesis direction is the complementary opposite, 5' to 3'.
incorrectas.C: Synthesis is not random; polymerase always adds nucleotides in a strict 5' to 3' order determined by the chemistry of the enzyme's active site (attack of the 3'-OH on the incoming nucleotide's alpha-phosphate) — ligase's role is simply to seal remaining nicks between fragments, not to correct directionality.
incorrectas.D: There is a strict, invariant directionality to nucleic acid synthesis — 5' to 3' — used by every known DNA and RNA polymerase, so this option incorrectly denies a fundamental and consistent biochemical rule.

preguntas.q: DNA polymerase pauses periodically during replication to check the newly added base for correct pairing. Which enzymatic activity performs this proofreading function?

e.correcta: DNA polymerase's 3' -> 5' exonuclease activity backs up and excises a mismatched nucleotide it just added, working in the direction opposite to synthesis (5' -> 3'), before resuming polymerization. This proofreading step is what gives DNA replication its very high fidelity (error rate around 10^-9 to 10^-10 per base), far lower than would be achieved by base-pairing selectivity alone. Loss of this function (or of mismatch repair afterward) leads to accumulation of point mutations, as seen in some cancer-predisposition syndromes.

incorrectas.A: 5' -> 3' exonuclease activity is used by DNA polymerase I (in prokaryotes) to remove RNA primers ahead of the polymerase, not to proofread newly synthesized bases; it degrades in the same direction as synthesis rather than backtracking to check the last-added nucleotide.
incorrectas.C: Helicase unwinds the double helix ahead of the replication fork by breaking hydrogen bonds between base pairs; it has no role in checking base-pairing accuracy after a nucleotide has been incorporated.
incorrectas.D: Primase synthesizes the short RNA primer that gives DNA polymerase a 3'-OH to extend from; it initiates synthesis but has no exonuclease or error-checking capability.

preguntas.q: Compared to RNA synthesis, DNA synthesis is best described as having which level of fidelity?

o.A: Low fidelity, due to lack of a primer
o.B: Moderate fidelity, similar to RNA synthesis
o.C: High fidelity, due to proofreading exonuclease activity
o.D: Fidelity cannot be compared between DNA and RNA synthesis

e.correcta: DNA synthesis is high fidelity because DNA polymerase possesses 3' -> 5' exonuclease proofreading activity that detects and removes mismatched bases immediately after they are added, and this is further backed up by post-replication mismatch repair. This layered error-correction system is essential because DNA is the permanent genetic archive of the cell and must be copied with extremely low error rates to prevent mutation accumulation across generations of cell division.

incorrectas.A: Both DNA and RNA synthesis require a primer (RNA polymerase is the exception that does not, but that is a different distinguishing feature), so lack of a primer is not what determines fidelity here, and DNA synthesis in fact uses an RNA primer during replication.
incorrectas.B: DNA and RNA synthesis are not similar in fidelity — RNA polymerase lacks proofreading exonuclease activity, making RNA synthesis considerably less accurate than DNA synthesis, which is corrected in real time by DNA polymerase's exonuclease function.
incorrectas.D: Fidelity is a well-defined, measurable property (errors per base incorporated) and is a classic point of contrast tested between DNA and RNA polymerases, so this comparison is both possible and clinically relevant.

preguntas.q: In eukaryotic DNA replication, which enzymes are responsible for removing the RNA primers laid down by primase?

o.A: DNA polymerase I and DNA ligase
o.D: DNA polymerase δ and DNA polymerase ε

e.correcta: In eukaryotes, RNase H degrades most of the RNA primer, and FEN-1 (flap endonuclease-1) removes the remaining RNA-DNA junction fragment by cleaving the displaced 5' flap created as the adjacent Okazaki fragment is extended. Once the primer is fully excised, DNA polymerase δ fills in the resulting gap with DNA, and DNA ligase seals the remaining nick — this multi-step handoff is necessary because eukaryotes lack the single bifunctional polymerase that prokaryotes use for this job.

incorrectas.A: DNA polymerase I is the prokaryotic enzyme that combines 5'->3' exonuclease (primer removal) and polymerase (gap-filling) activities in one protein; eukaryotes do not have an equivalent single enzyme and instead rely on RNase H plus FEN-1 for primer removal.
incorrectas.C: Helicase unwinds the DNA duplex ahead of the fork and topoisomerase relieves the resulting supercoiling stress; neither enzyme processes RNA primers or has any role in excising them from Okazaki fragments.
incorrectas.D: DNA polymerase δ fills the gap left behind after primer removal (and polymerase ε is largely leading-strand focused), but neither of these polymerases performs the actual excision of the RNA primer — that job belongs to RNase H and FEN-1.

preguntas.q: Which enzyme catalyzes formation of the phosphodiester bond that joins adjacent Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand?

e.correcta: DNA ligase seals the nick between adjacent Okazaki fragments by catalyzing formation of a phosphodiester bond between the 3'-OH of one fragment and the 5'-phosphate of the next, using ATP (or NAD+ in some bacteria) as an energy source. This step is required specifically on the lagging strand, which is synthesized discontinuously in short fragments moving away from the replication fork, in contrast to the continuous leading strand; without ligase, the lagging strand would remain a series of unlinked fragments.

incorrectas.A: Primase synthesizes the short RNA primers that initiate each Okazaki fragment, providing the 3'-OH needed for DNA polymerase to begin extension, but it does not join fragments together — that final sealing step is ligase's job.
incorrectas.B: DNA polymerase δ extends DNA from the primer and fills the gap left after RNA primer removal, but it stops short of the adjacent fragment and cannot form the final phosphodiester bond closing the nick; that catalytic step requires ligase.
incorrectas.D: Topoisomerase II (or gyrase in bacteria) relieves torsional strain by cutting and rejoining DNA strands ahead of the replication fork to prevent supercoiling, an entirely separate function from joining Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand.

preguntas.q: Which human replication enzyme functions as an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase, making it a major endogenous example of reverse transcriptase activity?

e.correcta: Telomerase carries its own RNA template and uses it to synthesize new telomeric DNA repeats (TTAGGG in humans) onto the 3' end of chromosomes, meaning it copies RNA into DNA — the defining feature of reverse transcriptase activity. It is expressed in cells that must divide indefinitely, such as germ cells and certain stem cells, allowing them to counteract the progressive telomere shortening that otherwise occurs with each round of replication due to the end-replication problem.

incorrectas.A: DNA polymerase α initiates nuclear DNA replication by synthesizing a short RNA-DNA primer, but it uses a DNA template for its polymerase activity in the elongation phase and does not carry or rely on an internal RNA template for chromosome-wide synthesis.
incorrectas.B: Primase synthesizes short RNA primers to give DNA polymerases a 3'-OH starting point, which technically makes it RNA-synthesizing, but this is RNA-dependent RNA-like priming rather than the RNA-templated DNA synthesis that defines reverse transcriptase activity.
incorrectas.D: DNA ligase seals nicks between DNA fragments by forming phosphodiester bonds; it has no template-directed polymerization activity at all, let alone the RNA-to-DNA conversion characteristic of telomerase.

preguntas.q: Telomerase is notable because it exhibits which enzymatic activity that rarely occurs endogenously in normal human cells?

e.correcta: Telomerase is a ribonucleoprotein that carries its own RNA template and uses it to synthesize DNA repeats at chromosome ends, which is precisely the definition of reverse transcriptase activity (RNA-templated DNA synthesis). Aside from telomerase, this activity in humans is essentially restricted to pathologic contexts like retroviral infection (e.g., HIV) or retrotransposon activity, making telomerase a notable physiologic exception found only in eukaryotic cells that need to replicate indefinitely.

incorrectas.A: DNA-dependent RNA polymerase activity describes conventional transcription, where RNA polymerase reads a DNA template to synthesize RNA — the reverse informational direction of what telomerase does when it reads its RNA template to make DNA.
incorrectas.C: 3' -> 5' exonuclease activity is the proofreading function of replicative DNA polymerases like DNA polymerase ε and δ, unrelated to telomerase's template-copying mechanism and not a feature telomerase possesses.
incorrectas.D: Topoisomerase activity relieves supercoiling by transiently cutting and resealing DNA strands during replication and transcription; it has nothing to do with using an RNA template to synthesize DNA, which is telomerase's defining function.

preguntas.q: Increased telomerase activity, allowing cells to bypass normal replicative senescence, is most characteristically associated with which pathologic process?

e.correcta: More than 90% of cancer cells show increased telomerase activity, which maintains telomere length despite repeated division and allows cells to bypass the normal Hayflick limit and the senescence/apoptosis signals triggered by critically short telomeres. This effectively grants malignant cells a form of replicative immortality, making telomerase reactivation one of the recognized hallmarks of cancer and a target of ongoing anticancer drug development.

incorrectas.B: Progeria is a premature aging syndrome linked to decreased or dysfunctional telomere maintenance (and defective lamin A processing in classic Hutchinson-Gilford progeria), the opposite scenario from the telomerase upregulation seen in cancer.
incorrectas.C: Down syndrome results from trisomy 21, a chromosomal number abnormality unrelated to telomerase activity or telomere length regulation.
incorrectas.D: Werner syndrome is a premature aging disorder caused by a WRN helicase mutation leading to genomic instability, and it is associated with accelerated telomere shortening rather than the increased telomerase activity characteristic of cancer cells.

preguntas.q: Decreased telomerase activity, leading to accelerated telomere shortening, is most characteristically associated with which condition?

e.correcta: Progeria is characterized by decreased telomerase activity and accelerated telomere attrition, which pushes cells toward premature senescence and contributes to the accelerated aging phenotype seen in affected patients. This is the inverse of what happens in most cancers, where telomerase is upregulated to prevent senescence — illustrating how the same enzyme's activity level can drive opposite pathologic extremes (premature aging versus unchecked proliferation).

incorrectas.B: Cancer is associated with increased, not decreased, telomerase activity — over 90% of tumors upregulate telomerase to escape the senescence that would otherwise be triggered by telomere shortening, the opposite of the progeria mechanism.
incorrectas.C: Chronic myeloid leukemia is defined by the BCR-ABL fusion from the t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome translocation, a specific oncogenic driver unrelated to telomerase deficiency.
incorrectas.D: Li-Fraumeni syndrome is caused by germline TP53 mutations leading to loss of tumor suppressor function and a high lifetime cancer risk, not by decreased telomerase activity or premature telomere shortening.

preguntas.q: Unlike DNA polymerase, which enzyme can begin synthesis directly at a promoter without requiring a primer?

e.correcta: RNA polymerase does not need a pre-existing primer to begin synthesis; instead it binds directly to promoter regions with the help of transcription factors and initiates RNA synthesis de novo. This is a fundamental mechanistic difference from DNA polymerase, which can only extend an existing 3'-OH group and therefore always requires a primer (RNA, laid down by primase) to get started.

incorrectas.B: DNA polymerase δ is a replicative DNA polymerase that strictly requires a primer with a free 3'-OH to extend from; it cannot initiate synthesis de novo on a bare template the way RNA polymerase can.
incorrectas.C: Primase itself is the enzyme that generates the RNA primer needed by DNA polymerases — its existence underscores that DNA synthesis requires a primer, which is exactly the requirement RNA polymerase lacks.
incorrectas.D: Telomerase extends the 3' end of existing telomeric DNA using its internal RNA template; it still acts on a pre-existing DNA end rather than initiating a wholly new strand the way RNA polymerase initiates transcription at a promoter.

preguntas.q: Does RNA polymerase possess 3' -> 5' exonuclease proofreading activity during transcription?

o.D: Yes, but only for the first 10 nucleotides synthesized

e.correcta: RNA polymerase lacks 3' -> 5' exonuclease proofreading activity, so it cannot backtrack and remove a misincorporated ribonucleotide the way DNA polymerase corrects mismatched deoxyribonucleotides. This is biologically acceptable because RNA transcripts are transient, are produced in many copies, and are degraded and replaced, so occasional transcription errors have far less lasting impact than an uncorrected error in the permanent DNA genome would.

incorrectas.A: RNA polymerase does not have proofreading exonuclease activity at all, so it is not identical to DNA polymerase in this regard — this lack of proofreading is precisely why RNA synthesis has a much higher error rate than DNA synthesis.
incorrectas.B: The absence of significant 3'->5' exonuclease proofreading is a general feature of RNA polymerases and is not something gained specifically in eukaryotes; both prokaryotic and eukaryotic RNA polymerases lack the robust proofreading seen in replicative DNA polymerases.
incorrectas.D: There is no mechanism by which RNA polymerase proofreads only an initial stretch of nucleotides before losing that capacity; it simply does not have this exonuclease function at any point during transcription.

preguntas.q: Compared to DNA synthesis, RNA synthesis by RNA polymerase is best described as having which level of fidelity?

o.A: High fidelity, comparable to DNA synthesis
o.B: Low fidelity, due to absence of proofreading
o.C: Fidelity is not applicable to RNA synthesis
o.D: Moderate fidelity, intermediate between DNA and protein synthesis

e.correcta: RNA synthesis is low fidelity because RNA polymerase lacks the 3' -> 5' exonuclease proofreading activity that DNA polymerase uses to catch and correct mismatches as they occur. The resulting higher error rate is tolerated biologically since RNA transcripts are short-lived, present in many redundant copies, and continuously turned over, so an occasional faulty transcript is inconsequential compared to a permanent mutation in the DNA template itself.

incorrectas.A: RNA synthesis fidelity is not comparable to DNA synthesis fidelity — DNA polymerase's proofreading exonuclease activity gives it an error rate several orders of magnitude lower than RNA polymerase, which lacks this correction mechanism entirely.
incorrectas.C: Fidelity is absolutely applicable to and measurable in RNA synthesis; it is simply lower than DNA synthesis fidelity because RNA polymerase cannot proofread, not because the concept doesn't apply.
incorrectas.D: RNA synthesis fidelity is not an intermediate value between DNA and protein synthesis in any standard classification — the key testable point is the binary contrast between DNA polymerase's proofreading (high fidelity) and RNA polymerase's lack thereof (low fidelity).

preguntas.q: Which type of DNA point mutation causes the least severe functional consequence?

e.correcta: A silent mutation changes a nucleotide but, due to the degeneracy of the genetic code, still codes for the same amino acid — most often because the change occurs at the third ("wobble") position of a codon. Because the resulting protein sequence is completely unchanged, silent mutations are generally the least consequential type of point mutation, forming the low end of the severity spectrum: silent << missense < nonsense < frameshift.

incorrectas.A: A frameshift mutation results from insertion or deletion of a number of nucleotides not divisible by three, shifting the reading frame for every downstream codon and typically producing a completely garbled, nonfunctional protein — this makes it the most severe category, not the least.
incorrectas.B: A nonsense mutation converts a codon into a premature stop codon, truncating the protein and usually destroying its function; this is far more disruptive than a silent mutation, which leaves the protein sequence entirely intact.
incorrectas.D: A missense mutation changes a codon so it specifies a different amino acid, which can alter protein structure and function (as in sickle cell disease); this is more consequential than a silent mutation because the protein sequence itself is changed, even if function is sometimes preserved.

preguntas.q: Which type of DNA mutation typically causes the most severe damage to the resulting protein?

e.correcta: A frameshift mutation occurs when an insertion or deletion of nucleotides not in multiples of three shifts the reading frame for every codon downstream of the mutation site, scrambling the entire amino acid sequence from that point forward and usually introducing a premature stop codon. Because it corrupts the whole downstream protein rather than a single residue, it is generally considered the most severe class of point-level DNA mutation on the spectrum silent << missense < nonsense < frameshift.

incorrectas.A: A silent mutation changes a nucleotide without altering the encoded amino acid, so the protein product is unaffected — this places it at the mildest end of the severity spectrum, the opposite of what this question asks for.
incorrectas.B: A missense mutation swaps in a single different amino acid at one position, which can be harmful (e.g., sickle cell disease) but affects only that one residue rather than corrupting the entire downstream reading frame the way a frameshift mutation does.
incorrectas.D: A nonsense mutation introduces a single premature stop codon, truncating the protein at that point; while often damaging, it does not scramble the sequence of every downstream codon the way a frameshift mutation does, making frameshift the more severe category overall.

preguntas.q: A DNA mutation involving a single nucleotide base change is classified under which general category?

e.correcta: A point mutation is defined as a change involving a single nucleotide, which can then be further subclassified by its consequence as silent, missense, or nonsense depending on how it affects the resulting codon and amino acid sequence. This single-nucleotide scope distinguishes point mutations from insertions/deletions and larger structural rearrangements, and understanding this category is the necessary first step before classifying the specific downstream effect.

incorrectas.A: A frameshift mutation results from insertion or deletion of nucleotides (not a substitution of one base for another) in a number not divisible by three, which shifts the reading frame — a fundamentally different mechanism from the single base substitution that defines a point mutation.
incorrectas.C: A chromosomal translocation involves the exchange of large segments between (or within) chromosomes, a structural rearrangement at a much larger scale than a single nucleotide change, as seen in conditions like CML's Philadelphia chromosome.
incorrectas.D: A trinucleotide repeat expansion involves abnormal amplification of a repeating three-nucleotide sequence (as in Huntington disease or fragile X syndrome), which is a distinct category of mutation from a single-nucleotide substitution.

preguntas.q: A DNA point mutation in which a purine is replaced by another purine, or a pyrimidine by another pyrimidine, is termed which type of substitution?

e.correcta: A transition is a substitution that swaps one purine for the other purine (adenine <-> guanine) or one pyrimidine for the other pyrimidine (cytosine <-> thymine), preserving the general ring-structure class of the base at that position. Transitions occur more commonly than transversions in nature and are a classic mechanism behind mutations induced by deaminating agents and certain mutagens, making the transition/transversion distinction a frequently tested contrast on Step 1.

incorrectas.A: A transversion is the opposite type of substitution — a purine is replaced by a pyrimidine or vice versa, changing the base's structural class entirely rather than staying within the same purine or pyrimidine family.
incorrectas.C: A frameshift mutation results from insertion or deletion of nucleotides that shifts the reading frame, an entirely different mechanism from a single-base substitution that swaps one purine or pyrimidine for another of the same class.
incorrectas.D: A nonsense mutation is defined by its functional consequence — creation of a premature stop codon — rather than by the chemical relationship (purine-to-purine vs. purine-to-pyrimidine) between the original and substituted bases.

preguntas.q: A DNA point mutation in which a purine is replaced by a pyrimidine, or vice versa, is termed which type of substitution?

e.correcta: A transversion is a base substitution that exchanges a purine for a pyrimidine or a pyrimidine for a purine, crossing between the two structurally distinct base classes. Because this swap changes the base's ring structure (two-ring purine versus one-ring pyrimidine), transversions are chemically more disruptive to base pairing geometry and occur less frequently than transitions, which stay within the same base class.

incorrectas.A: A transition keeps the substitution within the same base class — purine for purine or pyrimidine for pyrimidine — which is the opposite of the cross-class purine-to-pyrimidine swap that defines a transversion.
incorrectas.B: A silent mutation is categorized by its effect on the encoded amino acid (no change), not by the chemical relationship between the original and substituted nucleotide bases, so it is an orthogonal classification to transition/transversion.
incorrectas.D: A splice site mutation disrupts the sequences recognized by the spliceosome at intron-exon boundaries, leading to intron retention or exon skipping; it is defined by its location and functional consequence, not by whether a purine or pyrimidine was substituted.

preguntas.q: A nucleotide substitution that still codes for the same amino acid, most often due to a change at the third (wobble) position of a codon, is called which type of mutation?

e.correcta: A silent mutation is a nucleotide substitution that does not change the encoded amino acid, which happens frequently because of the degeneracy of the genetic code — multiple codons can specify the same amino acid, especially when they differ only at the third ("wobble") position where the tRNA anticodon pairing is more permissive. Because the protein sequence is unaffected, silent mutations are typically phenotypically silent and represent the mildest category of point mutation.

incorrectas.A: A missense mutation changes the codon so that it specifies a different amino acid, altering the protein sequence (as in sickle cell disease), which is the opposite of a silent mutation where the amino acid stays the same despite the nucleotide change.
incorrectas.B: A nonsense mutation converts a codon into a premature stop codon, halting translation early and truncating the protein, a far more disruptive outcome than a silent mutation's unchanged amino acid sequence.
incorrectas.D: A splice site mutation disrupts intron-exon boundary recognition, causing intron retention or exon skipping in the mRNA; this operates at the level of pre-mRNA processing rather than at the level of a single codon's amino acid assignment, which is what defines silent mutations.

preguntas.q: A nucleotide substitution that causes a codon to specify a different amino acid, such as the glutamic acid to valine change in sickle cell disease, is classified as which type of mutation?

e.correcta: A missense mutation is a nucleotide substitution that changes the codon so it now encodes a different amino acid, altering the primary protein sequence at that single position. The classic example is sickle cell disease, where a single base change converts a glutamic acid codon to a valine codon in the beta-globin chain, producing HbS, which polymerizes under hypoxic conditions and distorts red cell shape — illustrating how even one amino acid substitution can have major clinical consequences.

incorrectas.A: A silent mutation also involves a nucleotide substitution, but the resulting codon still specifies the identical amino acid due to genetic code degeneracy, so the protein sequence is unchanged — unlike the sickle cell example, where the amino acid actually changes.
incorrectas.B: A nonsense mutation converts a codon into a premature stop codon rather than into a codon for a different amino acid, halting translation early instead of simply substituting one residue for another.
incorrectas.C: A frameshift mutation arises from insertion or deletion of nucleotides that shifts the reading frame for all downstream codons, a fundamentally different mechanism from the single-codon amino acid substitution seen in a missense mutation like the sickle cell mutation.

preguntas.q: A nucleotide substitution that converts a codon into a premature stop codon, usually producing a nonfunctional truncated protein, is called which type of mutation?

e.correcta: A nonsense mutation changes a codon into one of the three stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA), causing translation to terminate prematurely and producing a truncated protein that usually lacks normal function. Because everything downstream of the mutation site is lost from the protein product, nonsense mutations are typically more damaging than missense mutations affecting a single residue, though generally less catastrophic than frameshift mutations that also scramble the remaining downstream sequence.

incorrectas.A: A missense mutation results in a codon for a different amino acid, not a stop codon, so translation continues to completion — this preserves the protein's overall length even though one residue is altered, unlike a nonsense mutation's premature truncation.
incorrectas.B: A silent mutation leaves the encoded amino acid unchanged entirely, producing a completely normal protein, in stark contrast to a nonsense mutation, which introduces a premature stop and truncates the protein.
incorrectas.C: A transition describes the chemical relationship between the original and substituted base (purine-to-purine or pyrimidine-to-pyrimidine), which is an orthogonal classification from the functional consequence (creating a stop codon) that defines a nonsense mutation — a transition can itself be silent, missense, or nonsense depending on which codon results.

preguntas.q: A mutation at which sequence element results in a retained intron within the mature mRNA, producing a protein with impaired or altered function?

e.correcta: A splice site mutation disrupts the consensus sequences at intron-exon boundaries that the spliceosome recognizes to excise introns during pre-mRNA processing, causing an intron to be retained in the mature mRNA (or, alternatively, an exon to be skipped). Because retained introns often shift the reading frame or introduce premature stop codons, this class of mutation is a recognized, if less common, cause of cancers, dementia, epilepsy, and some forms of beta-thalassemia.

incorrectas.A: A promoter mutation affects the DNA sequence where RNA polymerase and transcription factors bind to initiate transcription, altering how much mRNA is made overall, but it does not affect intron removal during subsequent RNA splicing.
incorrectas.C: A poly-A signal mutation disrupts proper 3' end cleavage and polyadenylation of the mRNA transcript, affecting mRNA stability and export, which is a distinct step in mRNA processing from intron excision at splice sites.
incorrectas.D: The Shine-Dalgarno sequence is a prokaryotic ribosome-binding site upstream of the start codon that helps position the ribosome for translation initiation; it has no counterpart role in eukaryotic splicing, and eukaryotic mRNA (which undergoes splicing) does not use this bacterial translation-initiation element.

preguntas.q: In the lac operon, increased cAMP levels that occur during low glucose conditions activate which protein, which then binds upstream of the promoter to increase transcription?

e.correcta: When glucose is low, adenylate cyclase activity rises, increasing intracellular cAMP, which binds and activates catabolite activator protein (CAP). Activated CAP binds a site upstream of the lac promoter and recruits RNA polymerase more efficiently, boosting transcription of the lac operon so the cell can use lactose as an alternative energy source when its preferred fuel (glucose) is scarce — this is the mechanism of positive control layered on top of the operon's repressor-based negative control.

incorrectas.A: The lac repressor is a separate, negative regulator that binds the operator and blocks transcription when lactose is absent; it is released by allolactose binding, not by cAMP, and its regulation is independent of the CAP/cAMP glucose-sensing system.
incorrectas.C: Sigma factor is a bacterial RNA polymerase subunit that helps the core enzyme recognize and bind promoter sequences generally, but it is not the specific cAMP-activated protein that binds upstream of the lac promoter in response to low glucose.
incorrectas.D: Beta-galactosidase is one of the enzymes encoded BY the lac operon (it cleaves lactose into glucose and galactose); it is a downstream gene product, not the upstream regulatory protein activated by cAMP that controls the operon's transcription rate.

preguntas.q: In the lac operon, what is the expression level of the lac genes when glucose is low and lactose is available?

o.D: Expression only of the repressor gene

e.correcta: When glucose is low and lactose is present, both regulatory conditions favor transcription: low glucose raises cAMP, which activates CAP to enhance RNA polymerase binding at the promoter, while the presence of lactose (via its metabolite allolactose) inactivates the lac repressor, releasing it from the operator. With positive control (CAP) engaged and negative control (repressor) relieved simultaneously, the lac operon reaches its strongest level of expression — logically reflecting that the cell most needs to make lactose-metabolizing enzymes exactly when glucose is scarce and lactose is available as an alternative fuel.

incorrectas.A: No expression occurs when lactose is absent (repressor bound to the operator blocking transcription regardless of glucose/cAMP status), which is the opposite of this scenario where lactose is available and the repressor is inactivated.
incorrectas.B: Low (basal) expression occurs when glucose is high and lactose is available — CAP is inactive due to low cAMP, so transcription proceeds only at a baseline level even though the repressor is released; this differs from the strong expression seen when glucose is also low.
incorrectas.D: The repressor gene (lacI) is expressed constitutively at a low, steady level regardless of glucose or lactose conditions, and is not the regulated readout being asked about — the question concerns expression of the lac operon's structural genes (lacZ, lacY, lacA).

preguntas.q: In the lac operon, what is the expression level of the lac genes when glucose is high and lactose is unavailable?

e.correcta: With glucose high and lactose absent, both regulatory signals point toward silencing the operon: high glucose keeps cAMP levels low so CAP remains inactive and cannot enhance RNA polymerase binding, and the absence of lactose means no allolactose is present to inactivate the lac repressor, which therefore stays bound to the operator and blocks transcription. This double-negative condition (no positive activation and active repression) results in no expression of the lac operon, which makes physiologic sense since the cell has no need to metabolize a sugar that isn't even present.

incorrectas.A: Strong expression occurs only when glucose is low AND lactose is available, since that is the one condition where CAP is active and the repressor is simultaneously released — the opposite combination from high glucose and absent lactose.
incorrectas.B: Low (basal) expression occurs when glucose is high but lactose IS available — the repressor is released by allolactose even though CAP remains inactive due to high glucose; this differs from the complete repression seen when lactose is entirely absent.
incorrectas.D: There is no constitutive maximal expression state built into the lac operon's regulation; expression is tightly modulated by both the repressor and CAP systems depending on glucose and lactose levels, and here both signals actively suppress transcription.

preguntas.q: In the lac operon, what is the expression level of the lac genes when glucose is low but lactose is unavailable?

e.correcta: Even though low glucose raises cAMP and activates CAP to promote RNA polymerase binding, the absence of lactose means there is no allolactose to inactivate the lac repressor, which remains bound to the operator and physically blocks transcription. This illustrates that the repressor's negative control is dominant — CAP activation alone cannot drive expression if the repressor is still clamped onto the operator, so the net result is no expression despite favorable cAMP conditions.

incorrectas.A: Strong expression requires both low glucose (active CAP) AND lactose availability (inactivated repressor) simultaneously; here lactose is absent, so the repressor still blocks transcription regardless of CAP's activation state.
incorrectas.B: Low (basal) expression describes the high glucose/lactose available scenario, where the repressor is released but CAP is inactive; this is different from the current scenario where the repressor itself is still bound and blocking transcription entirely.
incorrectas.D: Expression is not simply proportional to cAMP/CAP activity alone — the lac repressor exerts an independent, dominant block on transcription when lactose is absent, meaning CAP activation cannot overcome the repressor's blockade by itself.

preguntas.q: In the lac operon, what is the expression level of the lac genes when glucose is high but lactose is available?

o.D: Expression is repressed to zero regardless of lactose

e.correcta: When lactose is present, allolactose binds and inactivates the lac repressor, releasing it from the operator so transcription is no longer blocked; however, because glucose is high, cAMP levels stay low and CAP remains inactive, so RNA polymerase does not get the positive boost needed for strong transcription. The net effect is a low, basal level of expression — enough to reflect that lactose is available, but far less than the strong expression seen when glucose is also scarce and CAP is fully engaged.

incorrectas.A: No expression describes the scenario where lactose is entirely absent and the repressor remains bound to the operator; here lactose IS available, so the repressor is inactivated and some transcription does occur, just at a low level.
incorrectas.B: Strong expression requires low glucose (to activate CAP) in addition to available lactose (to inactivate the repressor); here glucose is high, so CAP stays inactive and the operon cannot reach its strong-expression state.
incorrectas.D: Expression is not repressed to zero here — the presence of lactose inactivates the repressor and permits some baseline transcription, distinguishing this state from the true full repression seen when lactose is unavailable.

preguntas.q: A patient develops multiple skin cancers after chronic sun exposure. Which type of DNA mutation is characteristically induced by UV radiation and underlies this risk?

e.correcta: UV radiation is absorbed by adjacent pyrimidine bases (most classically two thymines), causing them to covalently cross-link into a thymine (pyrimidine) dimer. This bulky lesion distorts the DNA helix and blocks normal replication and transcription unless removed, which is why UV-damaged skin cells rely on nucleotide excision repair to excise the dimer before division. Clinically, this is the basis for UV-induced skin cancers and for xeroderma pigmentosum, in which defective repair of these dimers leads to marked photosensitivity and skin malignancies.

incorrectas.B: Cytosine deamination to uracil is a spontaneous or heat/nitrite-driven hydrolytic reaction that converts cytosine to uracil, a base not normally found in DNA; it is repaired by base excision repair, not by UV light, and does not create the helix-distorting bulky lesion that pyrimidine dimers do.
incorrectas.C: Depurination is the spontaneous loss of a purine base (adenine or guanine) from the deoxyribose backbone, leaving an abasic site; it occurs due to hydrolysis of the N-glycosidic bond, not UV absorption, and is also handled by base excision repair.
incorrectas.D: Single-strand mismatches arise when DNA polymerase incorporates an incorrect base during replication, a proofreading failure unrelated to UV exposure; these are corrected by mismatch repair, which recognizes strand discontinuities rather than helix-distorting photoproducts.

preguntas.q: Which DNA repair pathway is responsible for correcting the pyrimidine dimers caused by UV radiation exposure?

e.correcta: Nucleotide excision repair (NER) is specialized for bulky, helix-distorting lesions such as UV-induced pyrimidine dimers. Excision endonucleases recognize the distortion, cleave the DNA backbone on both sides of the lesion, and remove a short oligonucleotide segment containing the damage; DNA polymerase then fills the gap using the intact strand as template, and DNA ligase seals the remaining nick. This pathway operates in the G1 phase of the cell cycle, and its failure (as in xeroderma pigmentosum) leads to accumulation of UV damage and skin cancer.

incorrectas.A: Base excision repair removes small, non-helix-distorting base modifications like deaminated or oxidized bases using a glycosylase to flip out the damaged base, not the bulky covalent dimers produced by UV light, which require the wider excision tract of NER.
incorrectas.B: Mismatch repair corrects base-pair mismatches and small insertion/deletion loops that slip past DNA polymerase proofreading during replication; it acts on newly synthesized strands via strand-discrimination signals, not on UV-induced structural distortions of the helix.
incorrectas.D: Homologous recombination repairs double-strand breaks by using the sister chromatid as a template for accurate repair; pyrimidine dimers are single-strand, helix-distorting lesions, not double-strand breaks, so this pathway is not the relevant mechanism here.

preguntas.q: In nucleotide excision repair, which enzyme recognizes and excises the pyrimidine dimer lesion from the DNA strand?

e.correcta: Excision endonuclease is the enzyme complex that scans DNA for the helical distortion caused by a bulky lesion like a pyrimidine dimer, then makes incisions in the phosphodiester backbone on both the 5' and 3' sides of the damage. This releases an oligonucleotide fragment containing the dimer, creating a gap that DNA polymerase and DNA ligase subsequently fill and seal. Mutations in the genes encoding this excision machinery (the XP genes) cause xeroderma pigmentosum.

incorrectas.A: AP-endonuclease acts in base excision repair, cleaving the DNA backbone at an abasic (apurinic/apyrimidinic) site that has already been created by a glycosylase — it does not recognize bulky helix-distorting dimers, which are the substrate of nucleotide excision repair instead.
incorrectas.C: DNA helicase unwinds double-stranded DNA by breaking hydrogen bonds between base pairs, a function used broadly in replication and repair to expose single strands, but it does not itself recognize or excise damaged bases.
incorrectas.D: Topoisomerase relieves torsional strain (supercoiling) ahead of replication forks or transcription complexes by transiently cutting and resealing DNA strands; it has no role in recognizing or removing pyrimidine dimers.

preguntas.q: After excision endonuclease removes a pyrimidine dimer-containing oligonucleotide during nucleotide excision repair, which two enzymes complete the repair by filling and sealing the gap?

e.correcta: Once excision endonuclease removes the damaged oligonucleotide containing the pyrimidine dimer, DNA polymerase synthesizes new DNA to fill the resulting gap using the undamaged complementary strand as a template. DNA ligase then forms the final phosphodiester bond, sealing the nick and restoring an intact double helix. This same two-enzyme finishing step (polymerase then ligase) is common to nearly all excision-based repair pathways, though the specific isoforms used can differ.

incorrectas.A: Primase synthesizes short RNA primers to initiate DNA replication at origins or Okazaki fragments; it is not involved in filling a gap created during nucleotide excision repair, where DNA polymerase directly extends from the existing 3' end.
incorrectas.C: Reverse transcriptase synthesizes DNA from an RNA template and is used by retroviruses (and telomerase), not by nuclear DNA repair machinery; helicase unwinds DNA but does not synthesize or seal it, so neither functions in this gap-filling step.
incorrectas.D: RNA polymerase transcribes DNA into RNA and has no role in DNA gap-filling; topoisomerase manages supercoiling tension rather than closing nicks, so neither enzyme performs the finishing steps of nucleotide excision repair.

preguntas.q: Nucleotide excision repair of pyrimidine dimers characteristically takes place during which phase of the cell cycle?

e.correcta: Nucleotide excision repair predominantly occurs during G1, before the cell commits to DNA synthesis, allowing bulky lesions like pyrimidine dimers to be cleared prior to replication so that the damaged template is not copied inaccurately. This timing fits into the broader logic of cell-cycle checkpoints, which pause the cycle to allow repair of different lesion types before they can be propagated or become double-strand breaks. Contrast this with mismatch repair, which acts predominantly in S phase since it corrects errors made during ongoing replication.

incorrectas.A: S phase is when DNA replication itself occurs, and it is the phase in which mismatch repair mainly operates (correcting replication errors as they arise), not the phase primarily associated with nucleotide excision repair of pre-existing bulky lesions.
incorrectas.B: G2 phase is a checkpoint before mitosis that primarily screens for DNA damage and ensures replication is complete, but it is not the phase classically identified with nucleotide excision repair activity in First Aid-level teaching.
incorrectas.D: M phase is when the cell undergoes mitosis and chromosome segregation; active DNA repair synthesis does not occur during this phase, since the priority is faithful segregation of already-replicated and repaired chromosomes.

preguntas.q: A child with extreme photosensitivity and early-onset skin cancers is found to have an autosomal recessive defect diagnosed by measuring DNA repair activity in white blood cells. Which repair pathway is defective in this condition (xeroderma pigmentosum)?

e.correcta: Xeroderma pigmentosum results from an inherited (autosomal recessive) defect in nucleotide excision repair, most often due to mutations in the XP genes encoding components of the excision endonuclease complex. Without functional NER, UV-induced pyrimidine dimers accumulate unrepaired, leading to extreme photosensitivity, marked freckling, and a dramatically increased risk of basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and melanoma at a young age. Diagnosis can be supported by measuring the DNA repair capacity of a patient's white blood cells after UV exposure in vitro.

incorrectas.A: Mismatch repair defects (e.g., in MLH1 or MSH2) cause Lynch syndrome/HNPCC, presenting with microsatellite instability and early colorectal and endometrial cancer, not the sun-induced skin cancers and photosensitivity typical of xeroderma pigmentosum.
incorrectas.B: Base excision repair handles small base lesions from deamination or oxidation throughout the cell cycle; a defect here is not the classic cause of xeroderma pigmentosum, whose hallmark defect is specifically in the pathway that removes bulky UV-induced dimers.
incorrectas.D: Non-homologous end joining repairs double-strand DNA breaks and its dysfunction is linked to conditions like severe combined immunodeficiency (Artemis defects), not to the single-strand, UV-induced dimer lesions characteristic of xeroderma pigmentosum.

preguntas.q: Errors that occur during DNA replication, when an incorrect nucleotide is incorporated and escapes proofreading, most directly result in which type of DNA mutation?

e.correcta: When DNA polymerase inserts an incorrect nucleotide during replication and its intrinsic proofreading (3'-to-5' exonuclease) activity fails to catch the error, the result is a mismatched base pair in the newly synthesized strand. These mismatches are recognized and corrected by the mismatch repair system, which distinguishes the new (error-containing) strand from the template strand and excises and resynthesizes the incorrect segment. Persistent mismatch repair deficiency allows these replication errors to accumulate, notably causing microsatellite instability.

incorrectas.A: Pyrimidine dimers form from UV light causing covalent cross-linking between adjacent pyrimidines on the same strand; they are an environmentally induced lesion, not a byproduct of polymerase misincorporation during replication.
incorrectas.B: Base deamination is a spontaneous or chemically induced hydrolytic conversion of one base to another (e.g., cytosine to uracil) that can happen independent of replication, rather than a direct consequence of the polymerase inserting the wrong nucleotide.
incorrectas.D: Double-strand breaks involve severing of both DNA strands, typically from ionizing radiation or replication fork collapse, and require repair via homologous recombination or non-homologous end joining — a fundamentally different type of damage than a simple base-pairing error.

preguntas.q: Which DNA repair pathway is responsible for correcting base-pair mismatches that arise from errors during DNA replication?

e.correcta: Mismatch repair identifies and corrects mispaired bases that slip through DNA polymerase's proofreading during replication, using strand-discrimination cues to selectively excise and resynthesize the newly made (incorrect) strand rather than the template. This system is especially important at microsatellite (short tandem repeat) sequences, where DNA polymerase is prone to slippage; loss of mismatch repair genes (like MLH1 or MSH2) produces microsatellite instability and underlies Lynch syndrome, with a markedly increased risk of colorectal and endometrial cancer.

incorrectas.A: Nucleotide excision repair targets bulky, helix-distorting lesions such as UV-induced pyrimidine dimers, acting in G1, rather than the simple base-pairing errors generated during replication that mismatch repair specifically addresses.
incorrectas.B: Base excision repair removes small chemically altered bases (e.g., deaminated or oxidized bases) via a glycosylase-initiated mechanism operating throughout the cell cycle, not the polymerase-generated mismatches that occur specifically during replication.
incorrectas.C: Non-homologous end joining repairs double-strand breaks by directly ligating broken DNA ends, often with some loss of nucleotides, which is a different category of damage entirely from a single mismatched base pair on an otherwise intact double helix.

preguntas.q: After the mismatch repair system excises a segment of DNA containing a mispaired base, which two enzymes carry out the final steps of filling the gap and sealing the nick?

e.correcta: Just as in nucleotide excision repair, once the mismatch repair machinery excises the erroneous stretch of the newly synthesized strand, DNA polymerase resynthesizes the correct sequence using the template strand as a guide, and DNA ligase seals the remaining nick by forming the final phosphodiester bond. This shared 'excise-fill-seal' logic across DNA repair pathways is a useful pattern to remember: different recognition/excision enzymes feed into the same universal finishing enzymes.

incorrectas.A: Primase lays down RNA primers to initiate new strands during replication, and helicase unwinds the double helix — neither actually synthesizes the replacement DNA sequence or seals the final nick needed to complete mismatch repair.
incorrectas.C: Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from an RNA template (relevant to retroviruses and telomerase) and RNA polymerase transcribes RNA from DNA; neither is involved in synthesizing replacement DNA or ligating a repaired DNA strand.
incorrectas.D: Topoisomerase relieves supercoiling tension, and AP-endonuclease specifically cleaves at abasic sites generated in base excision repair — neither is the enzyme pair responsible for finishing mismatch repair.

preguntas.q: A patient develops colorectal cancer with microsatellite instability due to an inherited deficiency of the enzymes responsible for correcting DNA replication mismatches. Which syndrome does this describe?

e.correcta: Lynch syndrome (hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer) results from autosomal dominant germline mutations in mismatch repair genes such as MLH1 and MSH2. Because mismatch repair normally corrects replication slippage at repetitive microsatellite sequences, its loss allows these repeats to expand or contract unchecked, producing microsatellite instability, which drives accelerated carcinogenesis, particularly right-sided colorectal cancer as well as endometrial cancer, typically without the numerous colonic polyps seen in polyposis syndromes.

incorrectas.A: Familial adenomatous polyposis is caused by APC gene mutations leading to hundreds to thousands of colonic adenomatous polyps and eventual cancer; it is a Wnt-signaling/tumor-suppressor pathway problem, not a defect in mismatch repair or microsatellite stability.
incorrectas.B: Xeroderma pigmentosum results from defective nucleotide excision repair of UV-induced pyrimidine dimers, causing severe photosensitivity and skin cancers; it has no direct relationship to colorectal cancer or microsatellite instability.
incorrectas.D: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is caused by STK11 (LKB1) mutations, producing hamartomatous GI polyps and mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation, with increased cancer risk from a distinct mechanism unrelated to mismatch repair deficiency.

preguntas.q: Repair of DNA base mismatches generated during replication predominantly occurs in which phase of the cell cycle?

e.correcta: Mismatch repair occurs predominantly during S phase (with some activity extending into G2), because this is when DNA polymerase is actively synthesizing new strands and mismatches are actually being generated. Repairing errors close to the time and location they occur allows the repair machinery to use strand-discrimination cues (e.g. lack of methylation or nicks on the newly made strand) to know which strand to correct. This contrasts with nucleotide excision repair, which mainly occurs in G1 on pre-existing lesions, and base excision repair, which can occur throughout the cell cycle.

incorrectas.A: G1 phase is when nucleotide excision repair predominantly clears bulky lesions like pyrimidine dimers before replication begins, not when replication-associated mismatches (which haven't occurred yet) are corrected.
incorrectas.C: M phase is devoted to chromosome segregation during mitosis; active DNA synthesis and the ongoing generation of replication mismatches have already concluded by this point, so mismatch repair is not characteristically occurring here.
incorrectas.D: G0 phase is a quiescent, non-dividing state in which cells are not replicating their DNA at all, so there is no active DNA synthesis generating new mismatches for the mismatch repair system to correct.

preguntas.q: Spontaneous hydrolytic loss of an amino group from cytosine, converting it to uracil, is an example of which type of DNA mutation, which can also be induced by heat or nitrates?
