It undergoes extensive post-translational modification — hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues, glycosylation, and disulfide bond formation — before its triple helix can assemble, which is why vitamin C deficiency (needed for hydroxylation) directly disrupts collagen integrity.

incorrectas.B: Elastin is an abundant connective tissue protein that confers stretch and recoil to tissues like large arteries and lungs, but it is far less abundant overall than collagen and is not the single most abundant protein in the body.
incorrectas.C: Actin is one of the most abundant intracellular proteins, critical for the cytoskeleton and muscle contraction, but intracellular actin does not approach the total body mass contributed by extracellular collagen.
incorrectas.D: Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein, important for oncotic pressure and drug transport, but it is a small fraction of total body protein compared to the structural collagen found throughout connective tissue.

preguntas.q: The primary structural function of collagen is to organize and strengthen which cellular compartment?

e.correcta: Collagen is secreted by fibroblasts (and other cells) into the extracellular space, where its triple-helical fibrils cross-link to form a durable scaffold that organizes and mechanically strengthens the extracellular matrix. This scaffold gives tensile strength to tissues like skin, tendon, and bone and provides the framework onto which other matrix components (proteoglycans, elastin, laminin) are organized.

incorrectas.B: The nuclear envelope is supported by nuclear lamins, intermediate filament proteins inside the nucleus, not by extracellular collagen fibrils.
incorrectas.C: The mitochondrial matrix is the interior compartment where the citric acid cycle occurs; it is bounded by mitochondrial membranes and has no structural relationship to collagen.
incorrectas.D: The Golgi apparatus is an intracellular organelle involved in protein modification and trafficking (including further processing of procollagen), but it is not itself organized or strengthened by collagen.

preguntas.q: Which collagen type accounts for roughly 90% of total body collagen and is found in bone, skin, tendon, ligaments, dentin, and fascia?

e.correcta: Type I collagen is the most abundant collagen type, making up about 90% of the body's collagen and forming the thick, tensile-strength fibrils found in bone, skin, tendon, ligaments, dentin, and fascia. Its predominance in osteoid is why defects in type I collagen genes (COL1A1/COL1A2) cause osteogenesis imperfecta, the classic 'brittle bone' disease tested on Step 1.

incorrectas.A: Type II collagen is found in cartilage, the vitreous body, and the nucleus pulposus — it supports compressive, cushioning tissues rather than the tensile structural tissues (bone, tendon, skin) that type I dominates.
incorrectas.C: Type III collagen forms the more pliable reticular fibers found in skin, blood vessels, and granulation tissue, and is defective in vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, but it is not the majority collagen type in the body.
incorrectas.D: Type IV collagen forms a meshwork (not fibrils) in basement membranes and the lens capsule; it lacks the tensile fibrillar structure of type I and is a distinct minority collagen type by mass.

preguntas.q: Which collagen type predominates in bone, skin, and tendon, and is defective in osteogenesis imperfecta?

e.correcta: Type I collagen is the major structural collagen of bone, skin, and tendon (also dentin, fascia, cornea, and late-stage wound repair scar tissue). Because it is the predominant collagen in osteoid, mutations in COL1A1/COL1A2 that impair type I collagen assembly cause osteogenesis imperfecta, producing weak, fracture-prone bones.

incorrectas.A: Type III collagen forms the fine reticular fibers of skin, blood vessels, and granulation tissue; it is defective in vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, not osteogenesis imperfecta, and is not the primary bone/tendon collagen.
incorrectas.B: Type IV collagen forms basement membranes and the lens, a nonfibrillar meshwork structure, and is defective in Alport syndrome — it is not found in bone or tendon.
incorrectas.D: Type II collagen is the major collagen of cartilage and the vitreous body, providing compressive support rather than the tensile strength needed in bone and tendon.

preguntas.q: Autoantibodies against which collagen type are seen in relapsing polychondritis, and where is this collagen type normally found?

o.B: Type I, in bone and tendon

e.correcta: Type II collagen is the major structural collagen of cartilage, as well as the vitreous body, pubic symphysis, and nucleus pulposus. In relapsing polychondritis, autoantibodies target type II collagen, producing recurrent inflammation and destruction of cartilaginous structures such as the ear, nose, and tracheobronchial tree — a classic autoimmune-collagenopathy link tested on Step 1.

incorrectas.A: Type IV collagen forms basement membranes and is the target of autoantibodies in Goodpasture syndrome (anti-GBM disease), not relapsing polychondritis.
incorrectas.B: Type I collagen is the dominant collagen of bone and tendon; genetic defects in it cause osteogenesis imperfecta, but it is not the autoantibody target in relapsing polychondritis.
incorrectas.D: Type III collagen forms reticular fibers in skin and blood vessels and is defective in vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome; it is not the antigen implicated in relapsing polychondritis.

preguntas.q: Which collagen type makes up skin and blood vessels and is defective in vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome?

e.correcta: Type III collagen forms thinner, more pliable fibrils found in skin, blood vessels, the uterus, fetal tissue, and granulation tissue — tissues that require some degree of elasticity and stretch. A defect in type III collagen (COL3A1) causes vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, which predisposes to arterial rupture, uterine rupture, and organ perforation because these tissues lose their normal tensile support.

incorrectas.A: Type I collagen is the dominant, more rigid collagen of bone, tendon, and most of the dermis; its defects cause osteogenesis imperfecta and classical (not vascular) Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, which is distinct from the vascular subtype.
incorrectas.B: Type IV collagen forms the nonfibrillar basement membrane network (and lens capsule); its defect causes Alport syndrome, not the vascular fragility of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Type II collagen supports cartilage and the vitreous body; it is not implicated in skin or vascular integrity and is unrelated to Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

preguntas.q: Reticulin fibers, known for their pliability and fine meshwork structure, are composed of which collagen type?

e.correcta: Type III collagen forms the thin, highly pliable reticular fibers seen in organs like lymph nodes, spleen, liver, and bone marrow, as well as in skin, blood vessels, and granulation tissue. Its flexibility comes from a finer fibril architecture than type I collagen, which is optimized for high tensile strength rather than pliability.

incorrectas.A: Type II collagen is found in cartilage and the vitreous body, providing compressive resistance rather than the fine, pliable meshwork characteristic of reticulin fibers.
incorrectas.C: Type I collagen forms thick, strong fibrils in bone, tendon, and skin, structurally different from the delicate reticular network formed by type III collagen.
incorrectas.D: Type IV collagen forms a sheet-like meshwork specifically in basement membranes, distinct in both location and structure from the reticulin fibers of type III collagen.

preguntas.q: Which collagen type forms the basement membrane and lens, and is the target of autoantibodies in Goodpasture syndrome?

e.correcta: Type IV collagen assembles into a nonfibrillar, sheet-like network rather than rope-like fibrils, forming the basement membrane, basal lamina, and lens capsule. This network provides a filtration scaffold in the glomerular basement membrane and cochlea, which is why mutations (Alport syndrome) or autoantibodies (Goodpasture syndrome) against type IV collagen cause combined renal, ocular, and/or pulmonary disease.

incorrectas.A: Type III collagen forms reticular fibers in skin, blood vessels, and granulation tissue — a fibrillar structure, unlike the meshwork architecture of basement membrane collagen.
incorrectas.B: Type I collagen is the dominant fibrillar collagen of bone, tendon, and skin; it does not form basement membranes and is unrelated to Alport or Goodpasture syndromes.
incorrectas.C: Type II collagen supports cartilage and the vitreous body; it is a fibrillar collagen distinct from the basement-membrane-forming type IV collagen.

preguntas.q: In osteogenesis imperfecta type I, which collagen type is present in normal structure but produced in decreased quantity?

e.correcta: Osteogenesis imperfecta type I, the mildest and most common form, results from a quantitative defect: type I collagen is structurally normal but produced in reduced amounts (often due to a null COL1A1 allele), leading to decreased osteoid and fragile bones. Because type I collagen is the predominant collagen in osteoid, even a modest reduction in its quantity compromises bone strength, producing recurrent fractures, blue sclerae, and hearing loss.

incorrectas.A: Type III collagen forms reticular fibers in skin and vessels; it is not the collagen implicated in osteogenesis imperfecta, which specifically involves the bone-forming type I collagen.
incorrectas.B: Type II collagen supports cartilage, not the mineralized osteoid matrix affected in osteogenesis imperfecta.
incorrectas.C: Type IV collagen forms basement membranes and is unrelated to the osteoid defect seen in osteogenesis imperfecta.

preguntas.q: A young patient presents with hematuria, sensorineural hearing loss, and anterior lens dislocation ('can't see, can't pee, can't hear a bee'). Defective synthesis of which collagen type is responsible for this syndrome?

e.correcta: This presentation describes Alport syndrome, caused by mutations (often X-linked) in genes encoding type IV collagen, the key structural component of the glomerular basement membrane, cochlea, and ocular lens capsule. Defective type IV collagen produces a thinned, split, 'basket-weave' glomerular basement membrane leading to hematuria and progressive renal failure, along with sensorineural hearing loss and lens dislocation — remembered as 'can't see, can't pee, can't hear a bee.'

incorrectas.A: Type I collagen defects cause osteogenesis imperfecta (bone fragility) and classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, not the renal-ocular-auditory triad of Alport syndrome.
incorrectas.C: Type II collagen defects affect cartilage and cause chondrodysplasias; they do not produce the basement membrane pathology seen in Alport syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Type III collagen defects cause vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome with vessel and organ fragility, a different clinical picture from the glomerular basement membrane defect of Alport syndrome.

preguntas.q: Collagen alpha chains, synthesized by fibroblasts, consist of a repeating tripeptide sequence. What is this pattern?

e.correcta: Collagen alpha chains are built from a repeating Gly-X-Y tripeptide motif, where X and Y are frequently proline or hydroxylated proline/lysine. Glycine's small side chain (a single hydrogen) is essential because it must occupy every third position to fit into the tightly wound core of the triple helix without steric clash — substituting glycine with a bulkier residue, as occurs in osteogenesis imperfecta, disrupts helix formation.

incorrectas.A: Alanine has a small side chain (methyl group) but is still bulkier than glycine's hydrogen; it is not the repeating residue required at every third position of the collagen triple helix.
incorrectas.B: Cysteine has a bulky, reactive sulfhydryl-containing side chain; a glycine-sized residue is required in this repeating position, not cysteine, making this pattern chemically incompatible with tight helix packing.
incorrectas.D: Serine has a hydroxymethyl side chain that is far bulkier than glycine's hydrogen; it does not fit the steric requirements of the tightly coiled collagen triple helix core.

preguntas.q: Roughly one-third of the amino acid residues in a collagen strand consist of which amino acid, essential for triple helix formation?

e.correcta: Glycine makes up about one-third of collagen's amino acids because it occupies every third position in the repeating Gly-X-Y motif. Its side chain is just a single hydrogen atom, the smallest possible, which is exactly what is needed to allow three polypeptide chains to twist together tightly into the collagen triple helix without steric hindrance from bulkier side chains.

incorrectas.A: Proline is common in the X and Y positions of the Gly-X-Y repeat and its rigid ring structure helps stabilize the helix, but it is not the residue that must occupy one-third of all positions — that role belongs to glycine.
incorrectas.B: Lysine occupies X or Y positions and undergoes hydroxylation and cross-linking, contributing to collagen strength, but like proline it is not the invariant one-third glycine residue.
incorrectas.C: Alanine is not a characteristic component of the collagen repeat; its side chain, while small, is still larger than glycine's and would introduce steric hindrance if substituted into the required position.

preguntas.q: In the first step of collagen synthesis, translation of collagen alpha chain mRNA in the rough ER produces what initial polypeptide product?

e.correcta: Collagen synthesis begins when mRNA for the collagen alpha chains is translated on ribosomes of the rough ER, producing preprocollagen, which contains an N-terminal signal peptide that directs the nascent chain into the ER lumen. Once the signal sequence is cleaved, the polypeptide is termed a pro-alpha chain and undergoes further modification (hydroxylation, glycosylation) before triple helix assembly.

incorrectas.A: Tropocollagen is the triple-helical molecule formed in the extracellular space after procollagen has its terminal propeptides cleaved by procollagen peptidase — a much later step than initial translation.
incorrectas.B: Procollagen is the triple-helical molecule assembled inside the rough ER/Golgi after hydroxylation, glycosylation, and disulfide bond formation, several steps downstream of the initial translation product.
incorrectas.D: Collagen fibrils form last, in the extracellular space, when tropocollagen molecules are cross-linked by lysyl oxidase — this is the final stage, not the product of the first translational step.

preguntas.q: Hydroxylation of specific proline and lysine residues during collagen synthesis requires which vitamin as a cofactor?

e.correcta: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is a required cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase, the enzymes that hydroxylate specific proline and lysine residues on pro-alpha chains in the rough ER. Hydroxylation stabilizes the collagen triple helix through additional hydrogen bonding; without vitamin C, as in scurvy, the pro-alpha chains cannot form a stable helix and are instead degraded intracellularly rather than secreted, leading to poor wound healing, bleeding gums, and weakened vasculature.

incorrectas.A: Vitamin A is important for vision (retinal), immune function, and epithelial cell differentiation, but it is not a cofactor for the hydroxylase enzymes involved in collagen synthesis.
incorrectas.C: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) is a cofactor for transamination and decarboxylation reactions in amino acid metabolism, not for prolyl/lysyl hydroxylation in collagen synthesis.
incorrectas.D: Vitamin D regulates calcium and phosphate homeostasis and bone mineralization, but it does not participate in the hydroxylation reactions that stabilize the collagen triple helix.

preguntas.q: After hydroxylation and glycosylation of pro-alpha chains, hydrogen bonds and disulfide bonds drive the formation of what structure, called procollagen?

e.correcta: After hydroxylation and glycosylation, three pro-alpha chains associate via hydrogen bonding and disulfide bonds at their C-terminal propeptides to twist into a triple helix, forming procollagen within the rough ER and Golgi. Proper helix formation depends on glycine occupying every third position (Gly-X-Y); if glycine is replaced by a bulkier amino acid, as in osteogenesis imperfecta, steric hindrance prevents correct triple helix assembly, producing structurally faulty collagen.

incorrectas.A: A beta-pleated sheet is a secondary structure stabilized by hydrogen bonds between adjacent strands, characteristic of proteins like fibroin or amyloid, not the triple-helical architecture of procollagen.
incorrectas.B: An alpha helix is a single-chain coiled secondary structure found in many proteins (e.g., keratin), distinct from the three-chain intertwined helix that defines collagen's structure.
incorrectas.D: A random coil describes an unstructured polypeptide lacking defined secondary structure, the opposite of the highly ordered, tightly wound triple helix that collagen chains form.

preguntas.q: After the collagen triple helix (procollagen) is assembled in the fibroblast, by what process is it released into the extracellular space?

o.C: Active transport via a membrane pump

e.correcta: Once procollagen's triple helix has formed in the rough ER and been packaged through the Golgi, it is released from the fibroblast into the extracellular space via exocytosis, the standard vesicular secretory pathway used for large, membrane-impermeant molecules. Once extracellular, procollagen peptidase cleaves the terminal propeptides to yield tropocollagen, which then self-assembles and is cross-linked by lysyl oxidase into mature collagen fibrils.

incorrectas.A: Simple diffusion across the plasma membrane is reserved for small, nonpolar molecules; a large triple-helical procollagen molecule cannot cross the lipid bilayer this way and requires vesicular exocytosis.
incorrectas.C: Active transport via a membrane pump moves small ions or solutes directly through transporter proteins, a mechanism incompatible with exporting a bulky, folded triple-helical macromolecule like procollagen.
incorrectas.D: Pinocytosis is a form of endocytosis by which cells take up extracellular fluid and solutes, the opposite direction of procollagen secretion, so it cannot describe how procollagen exits the cell.

preguntas.q: Synthesis, hydroxylation, and glycosylation of preprocollagen occur in which cellular location?

e.correcta: The rough endoplasmic reticulum is where collagen mRNA is translated into preprocollagen, the signal peptide is cleaved, and the resulting pro-alpha chains undergo hydroxylation of proline/lysine residues and glycosylation before assembling into the triple helix of procollagen. This heavy reliance on the RER's ribosomes and lumenal enzymes explains why fibroblasts (which are rich in RER) are the primary collagen-producing cells.

incorrectas.A: The Golgi apparatus further modifies and packages procollagen for secretion after it leaves the RER, but the initial synthesis, hydroxylation, and glycosylation steps occur earlier, in the RER.
incorrectas.B: The cytosol is where free ribosomes translate proteins destined to stay in the cytoplasm or nucleus; collagen synthesis instead uses membrane-bound ribosomes on the RER because of its N-terminal signal sequence directing it into the secretory pathway.
incorrectas.D: The extracellular space is where later steps occur — cleavage of procollagen to tropocollagen and cross-linking into fibrils — not the initial synthesis and modification of preprocollagen.

preguntas.q: Formation of lysine-hydroxylysine cross-linkages during collagen maturation requires which trace metal and which enzyme?

e.correcta: Lysyl oxidase, a copper-dependent enzyme, oxidatively deaminates lysine and hydroxylysine residues on tropocollagen molecules in the extracellular space, generating reactive aldehydes that spontaneously form covalent cross-links between adjacent collagen (and elastin) molecules. These cross-links give mature collagen fibrils their tensile strength; copper deficiency, as in Menkes disease, impairs lysyl oxidase activity and leads to weak connective tissue.

incorrectas.A: Matrix metalloproteinases are zinc-dependent enzymes that degrade extracellular matrix components (including collagen) during remodeling, the opposite function of forming cross-links.
incorrectas.B: Prolyl hydroxylase requires vitamin C (not iron as its defining cofactor, though it does use iron in its catalytic mechanism) and acts earlier, hydroxylating proline residues in the RER — it does not create the cross-links described here.
incorrectas.D: Collagenase degrades collagen and is not involved in forming cross-links; manganese is not the key trace metal for collagen cross-linking, which specifically depends on copper-dependent lysyl oxidase.

preguntas.q: The final assembly of tropocollagen into mature collagen fibrils occurs in which location?

e.correcta: After procollagen is secreted from the fibroblast, procollagen peptidase cleaves its terminal propeptides in the extracellular space to yield tropocollagen. Tropocollagen molecules then self-assemble in a staggered array and are covalently cross-linked by copper-dependent lysyl oxidase, forming the mature collagen fibrils that give connective tissue its tensile strength — all of this final assembly happening outside the cell.

incorrectas.A: The rough endoplasmic reticulum is where earlier steps occur — translation, hydroxylation, and glycosylation of pro-alpha chains — not the final fibril assembly, which requires extracellular cleavage and cross-linking.
incorrectas.B: The Golgi apparatus packages procollagen for secretion after RER processing, but tropocollagen formation and fibril cross-linking happen only after the molecule has left the cell.
incorrectas.C: The cytosol is not involved in collagen processing at all, since collagen synthesis occurs via the RER/Golgi secretory pathway, not free cytosolic ribosomes.

preguntas.q: Which two disorders are associated with defective collagen cross-linking rather than defective triple helix formation?

e.correcta: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (classic form) results from deficient procollagen peptidase activity, which prevents cleavage of procollagen's terminal propeptides and blocks formation of the insoluble tropocollagen substrate needed for cross-linking. Menkes disease results from a copper transport defect that leaves lysyl oxidase (a copper-dependent enzyme) dysfunctional, so tropocollagen molecules cannot be cross-linked into mature fibrils — both disorders therefore disrupt the cross-linking stage rather than the earlier triple helix assembly.

incorrectas.A: Osteogenesis imperfecta and scurvy both disrupt triple helix formation — osteogenesis imperfecta via glycine substitutions causing steric hindrance, and scurvy via failed prolyl/lysyl hydroxylation from vitamin C deficiency — not the later cross-linking step.
incorrectas.B: Marfan syndrome involves a fibrillin-1 defect affecting elastic fiber microfibrils, and homocystinuria involves defective methionine metabolism causing connective tissue and vascular abnormalities; neither is a classic collagen cross-linking disorder.
incorrectas.D: Alport syndrome and Goodpasture syndrome both involve type IV collagen of the basement membrane — one genetic, one autoimmune — but neither is characterized as a cross-linking defect; they reflect structural or antigenic problems with type IV collagen itself.

preguntas.q: Which two conditions are associated with defective formation of the collagen triple helix, as opposed to defective cross-linking?

e.correcta: In osteogenesis imperfecta, mutant type I collagen substitutes glycine for a bulkier amino acid at the essential Gly-X-Y position, creating steric hindrance that prevents the three pro-alpha chains from properly winding into a triple helix — the faulty collagen is often degraded intracellularly or incorporated into bone as weak, brittle matrix. In scurvy, vitamin C deficiency prevents hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues, which destabilizes the nascent helix so severely that it cannot form properly and the unhydroxylated pro-alpha chains are degraded before secretion, causing poor wound healing and connective tissue fragility.

incorrectas.A: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (deficient procollagen peptidase) and Menkes disease (defective copper-dependent lysyl oxidase) both impair the later cross-linking of tropocollagen into fibrils, a step downstream of triple helix formation, not the helix assembly itself.
incorrectas.B: Alport syndrome involves a structural defect in type IV collagen affecting basement membranes, and Marfan syndrome involves fibrillin-1 for elastic fiber microfibrils — neither centers on defective collagen triple helix assembly in the way osteogenesis imperfecta and scurvy do.
incorrectas.D: Homocystinuria involves defective methionine/homocysteine metabolism causing connective tissue and vascular abnormalities by a different mechanism, and Menkes disease affects cross-linking (via copper-dependent lysyl oxidase), not triple helix formation.

preguntas.q: Which genetic bone disorder, caused by defective type I collagen, is also known as 'brittle bone disease'?

e.correcta: Osteogenesis imperfecta, nicknamed 'brittle bone disease,' is most often caused by autosomal dominant mutations in COL1A1 or COL1A2 that impair type I collagen quantity or structure. Because type I collagen is the predominant collagen in osteoid, patients suffer recurrent fractures with minimal trauma, along with characteristic findings such as blue sclerae (thin sclera revealing underlying choroidal veins), hearing loss, and dental imperfections.

incorrectas.A: Achondroplasia is caused by an activating mutation in FGFR3 that impairs cartilage proliferation at the growth plate, causing short-limbed dwarfism — it is unrelated to collagen defects and does not cause bone fragility.
incorrectas.B: Osteopetrosis results from defective osteoclast function (e.g., carbonic anhydrase II deficiency), causing overly dense, brittle bone due to failure of bone resorption, a very different mechanism from the collagen quantity/quality defect in osteogenesis imperfecta.
incorrectas.D: Osteomalacia is a defect in bone mineralization typically due to vitamin D deficiency, causing soft, understructured bone in adults, rather than a primary defect in collagen synthesis.

preguntas.q: Osteogenesis imperfecta is most commonly caused by mutations in which two genes?

e.correcta: COL1A1 and COL1A2 encode the two distinct pro-alpha chains that combine to form type I procollagen, and mutations in these genes are the most common cause of osteogenesis imperfecta. Because type I collagen is the predominant collagen in osteoid, defects (often glycine substitutions causing steric hindrance in the triple helix, or reduced quantity of otherwise normal collagen) compromise bone's ability to stay flexible while maintaining strength, resulting in the classic fragile, fracture-prone bones of this disease.

incorrectas.A: FBN1 (fibrillin-1) mutations cause Marfan syndrome, and TGFBR2 mutations cause Loeys-Dietz syndrome — both connective tissue disorders, but neither involves type I collagen or produces the bone fragility of osteogenesis imperfecta.
incorrectas.C: COL4A3 and COL4A5 encode type IV collagen chains and are mutated in Alport syndrome, affecting basement membranes in the kidney, ear, and eye rather than bone.
incorrectas.D: COL3A1 encodes type III collagen (mutated in vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome), and LOX encodes lysyl oxidase (implicated in cross-linking defects like those seen with copper deficiency) — neither is the primary gene defect in osteogenesis imperfecta.

preguntas.q: A young child presents with multiple long-bone fractures from minimal trauma, blue sclerae, and a family history of similar fractures in a parent. What is the inheritance pattern of the most common form of osteogenesis imperfecta?

e.correcta: The most common form of osteogenesis imperfecta (type I) is autosomal dominant, typically caused by a mutation in COL1A1 or COL1A2 that reduces the quantity of otherwise structurally normal type I collagen rather than producing abnormal collagen. Because one functional allele still makes normal collagen, this milder quantitative defect is compatible with a dominant pattern and a relatively mild phenotype (blue sclerae, fractures, sometimes hearing loss), unlike the more severe types with qualitative collagen defects.

incorrectas.A: Autosomal recessive inheritance is seen in some of the rarer, more severe forms of osteogenesis imperfecta (e.g., due to defects in collagen-processing proteins like CRTAP or P3H1), but the classic, most common presentation taught for Step 1 is autosomal dominant type I disease.
incorrectas.C: X-linked recessive inheritance is the pattern for Menkes disease (ATP7A mutation), a distinct connective tissue disorder of copper transport, not for osteogenesis imperfecta.
incorrectas.D: Mitochondrial inheritance applies to disorders of mitochondrial DNA (e.g., MELAS, Leber hereditary optic neuropathy) and has no role in osteogenesis imperfecta, which is a nuclear-gene collagen disorder.

preguntas.q: An infant is brought to the emergency department with multiple fractures at different stages of healing but no bruising or soft tissue injury. Blue sclerae are noted on exam. This presentation is most likely to be mistaken for which condition?

e.correcta: Osteogenesis imperfecta classically mimics non-accidental trauma (child abuse) because both present with multiple fractures, sometimes at different stages of healing, in a young child. The key distinguishing clues favoring osteogenesis imperfecta are blue sclerae (thin sclera revealing underlying choroidal veins), a family history of fragility fractures, and the absence of bruising or other soft-tissue findings typical of inflicted trauma, so clinicians must carefully differentiate the two to avoid a wrongful abuse accusation.

incorrectas.A: Rickets results from vitamin D deficiency causing impaired bone mineralization, presenting with bowing of the long bones, growth delay, and craniotabes rather than the recurrent fragility fractures and blue sclerae of osteogenesis imperfecta, and it is not the classic diagnosis confused with abuse.
incorrectas.C: Osteoporosis is a disease of reduced bone density typically affecting older adults (or occurring secondarily to other conditions), not the classic pediatric mimicker of child abuse; osteogenesis imperfecta is the collagen disorder specifically associated with that diagnostic dilemma.
incorrectas.D: Achondroplasia is a disorder of defective endochondral ossification causing short-limb dwarfism due to FGFR3 mutations; it causes disproportionate short stature, not recurrent fractures, and is not confused with abuse.

preguntas.q: A toddler with blue sclerae is noted to have sustained several bone injuries over the past year despite only minor falls. Which finding is most characteristic of this connective tissue disorder?

o.A: Multiple recurrent fractures with minimal trauma

e.correcta: Osteogenesis imperfecta is defined by bones that fracture with minimal or trivial trauma because decreased or abnormal type I collagen weakens the organic matrix that normally gives bone its tensile strength, so even routine handling (including during birth) can cause fractures. These can occur at multiple sites and stages of healing, and unlike abuse, there is no accompanying bruising, which is treated with bisphosphonates to reduce fracture frequency by inhibiting osteoclast-mediated resorption.

incorrectas.B: Progressive proximal muscle weakness is characteristic of muscular dystrophies or myopathies, which involve defects in muscle fibers or their membrane proteins (e.g., dystrophin), not the collagen matrix defect that makes bones brittle in osteogenesis imperfecta.
incorrectas.C: Recurrent joint dislocations without fractures are more characteristic of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, in which lax, hyperextensible joints from abnormal collagen cross-linking cause instability, whereas osteogenesis imperfecta primarily weakens bone itself, producing fractures rather than dislocations.
incorrectas.D: Symmetric polyarthritis with morning stiffness describes inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis, an autoimmune synovial process entirely distinct from the structural collagen defect of osteogenesis imperfecta.

preguntas.q: A patient with osteogenesis imperfecta develops progressive hearing loss. What is the most likely underlying mechanism?

o.A: Sensorineural damage from cochlear hair cell degeneration
o.B: Abnormal ossicles due to defective type I collagen
o.C: Chronic otitis media from eustachian tube dysfunction
o.D: Cranial nerve VIII compression by a vestibular schwannoma

e.correcta: The tiny bones of the middle ear (malleus, incus, stapes) are composed largely of type I collagen, so the same defect that makes long bones fragile in osteogenesis imperfecta also weakens the ossicles, making them prone to fracture and abnormal remodeling. This produces a conductive hearing loss because sound transmission through the ossicular chain to the oval window is impaired, distinct from a sensory or neural cause of deafness.

incorrectas.A: Sensorineural hearing loss from cochlear hair cell damage is typically caused by noise exposure, ototoxic drugs, or presbycusis, mechanisms unrelated to the collagen matrix defect of osteogenesis imperfecta, which instead disrupts the bony ossicles.
incorrectas.C: Chronic otitis media relates to recurrent middle ear infections and eustachian tube dysfunction, an infectious/anatomic process rather than the intrinsic collagen fragility of the ossicles seen in osteogenesis imperfecta.
incorrectas.D: Vestibular schwannoma is a tumor of Schwann cells on CN VIII that causes sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus through nerve compression, an entirely separate neoplastic mechanism unrelated to bone collagen defects.

preguntas.q: A child with osteogenesis imperfecta has teeth that appear opalescent and wear down rapidly. This dental abnormality (dentinogenesis imperfecta) results from a defect in which tooth component?

e.correcta: Dentinogenesis imperfecta, seen in some forms of osteogenesis imperfecta, results from defective type I collagen within dentin, the mineralized tissue that forms the bulk of the tooth beneath the enamel and provides structural support. Because dentin is weakened, the overlying enamel loses its foundation and chips or wears away easily, giving the teeth a translucent, opalescent, blue-gray appearance and making them prone to rapid attrition.

incorrectas.A: Enamel is the hardest, most mineralized outer layer of the tooth, composed mainly of hydroxyapatite with minimal collagen; it is secondarily affected because it rests on abnormal dentin, but the primary genetic defect in dentinogenesis imperfecta lies in dentin, not enamel itself.
incorrectas.B: Cementum covers the tooth root and anchors periodontal ligament fibers; it is not the site of collagen defect responsible for the opalescent, easily worn appearance characteristic of dentinogenesis imperfecta.
incorrectas.D: Pulp is the innermost soft tissue containing nerves and blood vessels; it does not provide structural mineralized support to the tooth crown and is not the tissue whose collagen defect produces the opalescent enamel appearance.

preguntas.q: A young woman presents with generalized joint hypermobility, recurrent joint dislocations, and mildly hyperextensible skin, with no history of vascular rupture. Which type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is most likely, given that it is the most common subtype?

e.correcta: The hypermobility type (formerly EDS type 3) is the most common form of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and is characterized predominantly by joint instability, hypermobility, and recurrent dislocations, with skin changes present but generally milder than in the classical type. Unlike the vascular type, it carries a much lower risk of arterial or organ rupture, making joint-centered symptoms the dominant clinical feature to recognize.

incorrectas.A: The vascular type is a more dangerous but less common subtype caused by COL3A1 mutations affecting type III collagen, leading to fragile blood vessels and organs prone to rupture (e.g., aortic dissection, bowel perforation), a far more severe and distinct presentation than isolated joint laxity.
incorrectas.B: The kyphoscoliotic type is a rare subtype caused by lysyl hydroxylase deficiency, presenting with severe scoliosis, muscle hypotonia, and ocular fragility; it is much less common than the hypermobility type and has a distinct skeletal/ocular phenotype.
incorrectas.D: The classical type, caused by COL5A1/COL5A2 mutations, features more prominent skin hyperextensibility, atrophic scarring, and easy bruising alongside joint hypermobility, but it is less common overall than the hypermobility type.

preguntas.q: A patient with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome has skin that can be stretched far beyond normal limits before returning to its original position. This finding results from faulty synthesis of which protein?

e.correcta: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome arises from defective synthesis or structure of collagen (commonly type V, or type III in the vascular form), the primary structural protein providing tensile strength to skin, ligaments, and blood vessels. Abnormal collagen cross-linking or structure allows the skin to be pulled well beyond its normal range and yet spring back due to preserved elastin, producing the classic hyperextensible skin along with joint laxity and easy bruising.

incorrectas.A: Elastin is the protein responsible for the skin's ability to recoil after stretching, and its dysfunction (as in cutis laxa) causes loose, sagging skin that does not spring back, which is a different phenotype from the hyperextensible-but-recoiling skin of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome caused by collagen defects.
incorrectas.C: Fibrillin forms the microfibrillar scaffold that anchors elastin and is defective in Marfan syndrome, producing tall stature, lens dislocation, and aortic root dilation, a distinct connective tissue disorder rather than the collagen defect underlying Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Keratin is a structural protein of epidermal cells and hair/nails, and its mutations cause disorders like epidermolysis bullosa simplex; it is unrelated to the dermal collagen defect responsible for skin hyperextensibility in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

preguntas.q: A patient with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome can hyperextend her fingers and thumb well beyond normal range and has a history of recurrent joint dislocations. This joint finding is a direct consequence of faulty synthesis of which protein?

e.correcta: Collagen provides the tensile strength that normally limits how far ligaments and joint capsules can stretch; when its structure or cross-linking is abnormal, as in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, the connective tissue supporting joints becomes lax, permitting hypermobility and predisposing to recurrent subluxations and dislocations. This joint laxity, together with skin hyperextensibility and easy bruising, forms the classic clinical triad used to recognize the disease.

incorrectas.A: Fibrillin forms the scaffold for elastic fibers and is defective in Marfan syndrome, which causes joint hypermobility as a minor feature but is primarily distinguished by aortic root dilation and lens subluxation, not the primary joint pathology driven by collagen defects in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
incorrectas.B: Elastin confers recoil/stretch-and-return properties to tissues like skin, lungs, and arteries, but joint stability is chiefly governed by collagen in ligaments and capsules, so elastin dysfunction is not the mechanism behind the hypermobile joints of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Dystrophin is a cytoskeletal protein linking the muscle cell membrane to the extracellular matrix, and its absence causes Duchenne muscular dystrophy with progressive muscle weakness, an entirely different mechanism from the connective tissue collagen defect causing joint laxity in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

preguntas.q: A patient with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome presents with easy bruising and a history of prolonged bleeding after minor cuts, despite normal platelet counts and coagulation studies. What best explains this bleeding tendency?

o.A: Fragility of blood vessel walls due to defective collagen support
o.D: Vitamin K deficiency impairing clotting factor synthesis

e.correcta: In Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, defective collagen weakens the perivascular connective tissue that normally supports and reinforces blood vessel walls, making capillaries and small vessels more fragile and prone to rupture with minor trauma. This produces easy bruising and a bleeding tendency that is mechanical/structural in origin rather than due to a true defect in the platelet or coagulation cascade, which is why standard coagulation studies are typically normal.

incorrectas.B: Acquired factor VIII deficiency would cause a coagulation factor-based bleeding disorder with prolonged PTT, as seen in acquired hemophilia, not the structural vessel fragility seen in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and would show abnormal coagulation studies.
incorrectas.C: Qualitative platelet dysfunction (as in disorders like Bernard-Soulier or Glanzmann thrombasthenia) would cause mucocutaneous bleeding due to abnormal platelet adhesion/aggregation, which would be reflected in abnormal platelet function testing, unlike the normal platelet studies typical of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Vitamin K deficiency impairs synthesis of factors II, VII, IX, and X, prolonging PT/INR, a distinct mechanism from the structural vessel wall weakness caused by abnormal collagen in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

preguntas.q: The classical and vascular forms of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, which involve defects in structural collagen proteins, are inherited in which pattern?

e.correcta: The classical (type V collagen, COL5A1/COL5A2) and vascular (type III collagen, COL3A1) forms of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome are inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, since these genes encode structural collagen proteins where even a single mutant allele can disrupt the normal collagen fibril assembly (a dominant-negative effect), unlike enzyme deficiencies where a recessive pattern is more typical. Other, rarer EDS subtypes involving defects in collagen-processing enzymes can instead be autosomal recessive, so subtype matters when predicting inheritance.

incorrectas.A: X-linked dominant inheritance is not the pattern for any major Ehlers-Danlos subtype; this pattern is classically associated with conditions like hypophosphatemic rickets, not connective tissue collagen structural disorders.
incorrectas.B: Autosomal recessive inheritance applies to some rarer EDS subtypes that involve enzymatic defects in collagen processing (e.g., kyphoscoliotic type from lysyl hydroxylase deficiency), but not to the classical and vascular types, which involve structural collagen genes and are dominant.
incorrectas.C: Mitochondrial inheritance applies to disorders of the mitochondrial genome and has no relevance to Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, which results from nuclear gene mutations in structural collagen or collagen-processing enzymes.

preguntas.q: A male infant presents with kinky, brittle hair, growth failure, and hypotonia. Laboratory studies reveal low serum copper and ceruloplasmin. What is the inheritance pattern of this disorder?

e.correcta: Menkes disease is inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern due to mutations in ATP7A, which impairs intestinal copper absorption and copper delivery to enzymes throughout the body, leading to functional copper deficiency. Because the gene is on the X chromosome, affected males (hemizygous) manifest the full disease, while carrier females are typically asymptomatic — a useful mnemonic is that 'Menkes' affects 'Men' more.

incorrectas.A: Autosomal dominant inheritance would affect both sexes roughly equally and would not require an X-linked carrier state; Menkes disease instead shows the male-predominant pattern characteristic of X-linked recessive disease.
incorrectas.B: Autosomal recessive inheritance also affects both sexes similarly when homozygous, unlike Menkes disease, which almost exclusively affects males because the defective ATP7A gene is X-linked rather than autosomal.
incorrectas.D: Mitochondrial inheritance is transmitted only through the maternal line to all offspring irrespective of sex, a pattern distinctly different from the male-predominant transmission seen with the X-linked ATP7A mutation in Menkes disease.

preguntas.q: A male infant with kinky brittle hair, hypotonia, and low serum copper is diagnosed with a disorder of copper transport. Which gene is defective in this condition?

e.correcta: Menkes disease is caused by mutations in ATP7A, a copper-transporting ATPase needed for intestinal absorption of dietary copper and for delivering copper to enzymes in the trans-Golgi network. Loss of function leads to systemic copper deficiency, which impairs copper-dependent enzymes such as lysyl oxidase, causing the connective tissue and neurologic abnormalities (kinky hair, hypotonia, growth failure) seen in affected infants.

incorrectas.A: ATP7B is the copper-transporting ATPase defective in Wilson disease, which causes copper accumulation (not deficiency) in the liver, brain, and cornea; it is easy to confuse with ATP7A due to the similar name, but the two diseases have opposite copper phenotypes and different inheritance implications for management.
incorrectas.C: COL1A1 encodes a chain of type I collagen and is mutated in osteogenesis imperfecta, a distinct connective tissue disorder involving bone fragility rather than a defect in copper transport.
incorrectas.D: NPC1 is mutated in Niemann-Pick disease type C, a lysosomal cholesterol trafficking disorder causing neurodegeneration and hepatosplenomegaly, unrelated to copper transport or Menkes disease.

preguntas.q: An infant with Menkes disease has impaired connective tissue and vascular integrity. Decreased activity of which copper-dependent enzyme, needed for collagen and elastin cross-linking, best explains this finding?

e.correcta: Lysyl oxidase is a copper-dependent enzyme that oxidatively deaminates lysine and hydroxylysine residues in collagen and elastin, enabling the covalent cross-links that give these fibers their tensile strength and elasticity. Because Menkes disease causes systemic copper deficiency via defective ATP7A transport, lysyl oxidase activity falls, weakening connective tissue and vessel walls and contributing to the vascular tortuosity, aneurysms, and lax skin seen in affected infants.

incorrectas.A: Prolyl hydroxylase requires vitamin C (not copper) as a cofactor to hydroxylate proline residues in procollagen, a step whose failure causes scurvy rather than the copper-deficiency phenotype of Menkes disease.
incorrectas.C: Procollagen peptidase cleaves terminal propeptides from procollagen to allow fibril assembly, but it is not copper-dependent; its dysfunction is implicated in a form of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (dermatosparaxis type), not Menkes disease.
incorrectas.D: Glycosyltransferases add glycosyl groups to hydroxylysine residues during collagen synthesis but do not depend on copper, so they are not the enzyme impaired by the ATP7A defect in Menkes disease.

preguntas.q: Which stretchy connective tissue protein is the dominant elastic component of the large arteries, ligamentum flava, and vocal cords, allowing these structures to stretch and recoil?

e.correcta: Elastin is the dominant elastic protein in tissues that must stretch and recoil, making up roughly half of aortic wall tissue and providing the ligamentum flavum with the ability to allow spinal flexion and then return the vertebral column to its resting conformation. Its unique, largely non-hydroxylated amino acid composition and random-coil structure after cross-linking give it rubber-like elastic properties distinct from the tensile-strength role of collagen.

incorrectas.A: Fibrillin forms the microfibrillar scaffold that organizes and anchors elastin during elastic fiber assembly, but it is not itself the stretchy component; fibrillin defects (Marfan syndrome) disrupt elastic fiber integrity indirectly rather than eliminating elasticity directly.
incorrectas.B: Type I collagen is the predominant structural protein providing tensile strength in bone, skin, and tendons, but it is relatively inextensible and rigid compared to elastin, and is not the protein responsible for the stretch-and-recoil property described.
incorrectas.D: Keratin is a structural intermediate filament protein found in epidermis, hair, and nails that provides mechanical toughness and barrier function, not the elasticity found in arteries, vocal cords, or ligamentum flava.

preguntas.q: Compared to collagen, which of the following best describes the amino acid composition of elastin?

o.A: Rich in hydroxylysine with extensive glycosylation
o.B: Rich in non-hydroxylated proline, glycine, and lysine
o.C: Composed mainly of cysteine-rich disulfide-bonded domains
o.D: Predominantly hydroxyproline with a triple-helical repeating Gly-X-Y motif

e.correcta: Elastin is rich in proline, glycine, and lysine residues that are largely non-hydroxylated, in contrast to collagen's extensively hydroxylated proline and lysine residues. This distinct composition, combined with elastin's lack of glycosylation and unique tropoelastin backbone, allows it to form random coils upon cross-linking that confer the rubber-like elasticity needed in arteries, lungs, and skin.

incorrectas.A: Extensive hydroxylysine and glycosylation are hallmark features of collagen, which uses these modifications to help stabilize its triple helix and enable interchain cross-linking; elastin instead has only sparse hydroxyproline, no hydroxylysine, and no surrounding glycosylation.
incorrectas.C: Elastin is not characterized by cysteine-rich disulfide bonding; that description better fits proteins like fibrillin microfibrils (which do contain many cysteine residues forming disulfide bonds) rather than elastin itself.
incorrectas.D: A triple-helical structure with repeating Gly-X-Y motifs and abundant hydroxyproline is the defining architecture of collagen, not elastin, which lacks a triple helix and instead adopts a random-coil conformation after cross-linking.

preguntas.q: Elastin fibers in the extracellular matrix are organized around a scaffold of which glycoprotein, which is defective in Marfan syndrome?

e.correcta: Elastin is secreted as tropoelastin and assembled onto a scaffold of fibrillin microfibrils, which organize and template proper elastic fiber formation before tropoelastin molecules are cross-linked into mature elastin. This structural relationship explains why fibrillin mutations in Marfan syndrome secondarily disrupt elastic fiber integrity in the aorta and other elastin-rich tissues, contributing to aortic root dilation and dissection risk.

incorrectas.A: Fibronectin is a glycoprotein that mediates cell adhesion to the extracellular matrix and plays a role in wound healing and cell migration, but it is not the scaffold protein that organizes tropoelastin into elastic fibers.
incorrectas.B: Laminin is a major component of the basement membrane that helps anchor epithelial cells, distinct from the fibrillin microfibril scaffold specifically required for elastic fiber assembly.
incorrectas.D: Perlecan is a heparan sulfate proteoglycan found in basement membranes that contributes to filtration barriers (e.g., in the glomerulus), not to the organization of elastin fibers in elastic connective tissue.

preguntas.q: Elastin fibers can stretch to several times their original length and then recoil once the stretching force is released. What structural feature is primarily responsible for this rubber-like elastic property?

o.A: Cross-linking of tropoelastin via desmosine bonds
o.C: Formation of a rigid triple helix
o.D: Covalent attachment of glycosaminoglycan side chains

e.correcta: Lysyl oxidase deaminates lysine residues on tropoelastin molecules, allowing them to form desmosine cross-links between adjacent tropoelastin chains. These cross-links lock the otherwise randomly coiled tropoelastin backbone into a network that can be stretched under tension and then snaps back to its original random-coil conformation once the force is released, giving elastin its signature rubber-like recoil.

incorrectas.B: Extensive proline hydroxylation is a feature of collagen synthesis (via prolyl hydroxylase, using vitamin C) that stabilizes the collagen triple helix, but elastin is largely non-hydroxylated, and this modification is not what confers elastin's stretch-recoil property.
incorrectas.C: A rigid triple helix is the hallmark structural motif of collagen, which provides tensile strength but not elasticity; elastin instead adopts a flexible random-coil structure, which is the opposite of a rigid helix.
incorrectas.D: Glycosaminoglycan side chains are found on proteoglycans (like those in cartilage) and contribute to compressive resistance and hydration, not to the desmosine-mediated cross-linking that gives elastin its elastic recoil.

preguntas.q: Cross-linking of tropoelastin molecules by lysyl oxidase, which generates mature elastin fibers, occurs in which cellular location?

e.correcta: Tropoelastin is secreted from the cell into the extracellular space, where it associates with the fibrillin microfibril scaffold and is cross-linked by lysyl oxidase to form mature, functional elastin fibers. This mirrors the general pattern for extracellular matrix proteins like collagen, whose final cross-linking and fibril assembly steps also occur outside the cell after secretion, rather than intracellularly.

incorrectas.A: The rough endoplasmic reticulum is where tropoelastin (like other secretory proteins) is synthesized and undergoes initial folding, but the actual cross-linking that produces mature elastic fibers happens later, after secretion into the extracellular space.
incorrectas.B: The Golgi apparatus is involved in further processing, packaging, and secretion of tropoelastin, but lysyl oxidase-mediated cross-linking into desmosine bonds occurs after the protein has left the cell, not within the Golgi.
incorrectas.D: The cytoplasm is where translation and initial intracellular trafficking occur, but tropoelastin must be secreted before final extracellular assembly and cross-linking into mature elastin fibers takes place.

preguntas.q: A researcher inserts a human insulin gene into a bacterial plasmid vector to produce insulin in bacteria. What term describes the resulting DNA molecule, which is spliced together from two different sources?

e.correcta: Recombinant DNA is DNA formed by joining fragments from two different sources, typically a gene of interest (such as human insulin) and a vector such as a bacterial plasmid, allowing foreign genes to be propagated and expressed in a host organism. This technique underlies biotechnology applications like production of recombinant human insulin, growth hormone, and vaccines, and requires restriction enzymes to cut both the insert and vector at compatible palindromic sites before ligation.

incorrectas.A: Complementary DNA (cDNA) is synthesized from mRNA using reverse transcriptase and therefore lacks introns; it may serve as the insert used to create recombinant DNA, but the cDNA itself is not defined by being 'spliced together from two sources' the way recombinant DNA is.
incorrectas.C: Genomic DNA refers to the native, complete DNA of an organism as found in its chromosomes, including introns and regulatory regions; it is the source material sometimes used to obtain genes, but it is not itself a construct combining sequences from two different organisms.
incorrectas.D: Satellite DNA refers to highly repetitive, non-coding DNA sequences often found near centromeres and telomeres, a structural genomic feature unrelated to laboratory splicing of DNA from two different sources.

preguntas.q: A restriction endonuclease such as EcoRI recognizes and cleaves a specific 6-base-pair DNA sequence that reads identically on both strands when read 5' to 3'. What is this type of sequence called?

e.correcta: A palindrome in molecular biology is a DNA sequence (usually 4 or 6 base pairs) that reads the same on both strands when each is read in the 5' to 3' direction, creating a symmetric site that restriction endonucleases like EcoRI recognize and cleave. This symmetry allows the enzyme's two identical subunits to bind and cut both strands at matching positions, often producing sticky ends useful for cloning.

incorrectas.B: A consensus sequence is the most commonly observed nucleotide sequence at a given functional site (such as a promoter or splice site) across many genes, describing sequence conservation rather than the strand symmetry that defines a palindrome.
incorrectas.C: A tandem repeat is a sequence of nucleotides repeated consecutively multiple times in the genome (relevant to trinucleotide repeat expansion diseases), which is a different structural feature from a palindromic sequence recognized by restriction enzymes.
incorrectas.D: An origin of replication is a specific genomic locus where DNA replication initiates, unrelated to the symmetric, restriction-enzyme-recognized palindromic sequences used in molecular cloning.

preguntas.q: Which class of enzymes cleaves nucleotides specifically from the ends of a DNA strand, playing a role in processes like proofreading during replication?

e.correcta: Exonucleases cleave nucleotides one at a time from the free ends (5' or 3') of a DNA strand, a mechanism exploited by DNA polymerase's proofreading (3' to 5' exonuclease) activity to remove mismatched nucleotides during replication, as well as in RNA primer removal. This end-directed action distinguishes them from enzymes that cut internally within a strand.

incorrectas.A: Endonucleases cleave phosphodiester bonds within the interior of a DNA strand rather than at its ends, a distinction used, for example, by restriction endonucleases that recognize internal palindromic sequences to cut DNA at specific internal sites.
incorrectas.B: Ligases catalyze the formation of phosphodiester bonds to join DNA fragments together (e.g., sealing Okazaki fragments or joining vector and insert DNA in cloning), which is the opposite function of cleaving nucleotides.
incorrectas.D: Helicases unwind the DNA double helix by breaking hydrogen bonds between base pairs, enabling replication or transcription machinery access, but they do not cleave the phosphodiester backbone as exonucleases do.

preguntas.q: A restriction enzyme cleaves a DNA strand at an internal palindromic recognition site rather than at the strand's terminus. What class of enzyme does this describe?

e.correcta: Endonucleases cleave phosphodiester bonds at internal sites within a DNA strand rather than only at its ends, and restriction endonucleases exemplify this by recognizing specific internal palindromic sequences and cutting the DNA there, a property essential to molecular cloning for generating fragments with defined ends for ligation into vectors.

incorrectas.A: Exonucleases remove nucleotides sequentially from the free ends of a DNA strand rather than cutting internally, which is the opposite mechanism from the internal, sequence-specific cleavage performed by endonucleases like restriction enzymes.
incorrectas.C: Topoisomerases relieve supercoiling by transiently cutting and rejoining one or both DNA strands during replication or transcription, a function related to DNA topology management rather than sequence-specific palindrome recognition and cleavage.
incorrectas.D: DNA polymerases synthesize new DNA strands by adding nucleotides complementary to a template, and while some possess exonuclease proofreading activity, their primary role is synthesis, not internal sequence-specific cleavage like an endonuclease.

preguntas.q: What term describes the process of producing a self-perpetuating recombinant DNA molecule, typically by inserting a gene of interest into a vector that replicates within a host cell?

e.correcta: Cloning is the process by which a recombinant DNA molecule — formed by inserting a gene or cDNA of interest into a vector such as a plasmid — is introduced into a host cell (commonly bacteria) so that it replicates alongside the host genome, producing many self-perpetuating copies of the inserted sequence. This is the foundational technique enabling downstream applications like protein expression, genetic analysis, and gene therapy vector production.

incorrectas.B: Transcription is the process of synthesizing RNA from a DNA template within a cell, a step in gene expression rather than the laboratory process of constructing and propagating a self-replicating recombinant DNA molecule.
incorrectas.C: Translation is the process of synthesizing protein from an mRNA template at the ribosome, a downstream step in gene expression distinct from the DNA-level process of cloning a recombinant molecule.
incorrectas.D: Gel electrophoresis is a laboratory technique used to separate DNA, RNA, or protein fragments by size using an electric field, useful for analyzing cloning products but not itself the process of creating a self-perpetuating recombinant molecule.

preguntas.q: In molecular cloning of a eukaryotic gene, what is typically isolated first as starting material for generating complementary DNA?

e.correcta: The first step in cloning a eukaryotic gene is to isolate the mature mRNA of interest, because mRNA has already had its introns removed by splicing and represents the coding sequence actually expressed as protein. This mRNA then serves as the template for reverse transcriptase to synthesize complementary DNA (cDNA), which lacks introns and can be inserted into an expression vector for use in prokaryotic hosts that cannot splice pre-mRNA.

incorrectas.A: Genomic DNA contains the full gene sequence including introns and regulatory regions, but using it directly to clone a eukaryotic gene into bacteria would be problematic since bacteria cannot splice out introns, which is precisely why mRNA (via cDNA) is used instead as the starting material.
incorrectas.C: tRNA functions in translation by carrying amino acids to the ribosome and is not used as a template for generating a coding sequence to be cloned; it plays no role as starting material in this cloning workflow.
incorrectas.D: A restriction fragment is a piece of DNA generated after restriction endonuclease digestion, a step that occurs later in the cloning process (often on cDNA or vector DNA), not the very first material isolated when cloning a eukaryotic gene.

preguntas.q: After isolating eukaryotic mRNA of interest for cloning, the mRNA is exposed to reverse transcriptase to produce which product, which lacks introns?

e.correcta: Reverse transcriptase synthesizes a DNA strand complementary to the mRNA template, generating complementary DNA (cDNA); because it is made from mature, spliced mRNA, cDNA lacks introns and represents only the coding sequence of the gene. This intron-free cDNA can then be inserted into an expression vector and used in bacterial hosts, which lack the splicing machinery needed to remove introns from genomic DNA.

incorrectas.A: Genomic DNA is the native chromosomal DNA containing both exons and introns; it is not the product of reverse transcriptase acting on mRNA, and using genomic DNA directly in bacterial expression systems would be problematic due to unspliced introns.
incorrectas.C: A restriction fragment results from cutting DNA with a restriction endonuclease at specific recognition sites, a distinct downstream step from the reverse-transcriptase-mediated synthesis of cDNA from mRNA.
incorrectas.D: Pre-mRNA is the initial, unspliced transcript produced by RNA polymerase II that still contains introns; it is the precursor to mature mRNA, not the DNA product generated by reverse transcriptase.

preguntas.q: After a recombinant plasmid carrying a gene of interest has been assembled, into what host is it transformed to produce cloned copies of the DNA?

e.correcta: In molecular cloning, the recombinant plasmid (vector + insert) is transformed into bacteria (classically E. coli), which have been made competent to take up foreign DNA. Bacteria that have successfully taken up the plasmid carry an antibiotic resistance gene on the vector, so plating on antibiotic-containing medium selects only the transformed colonies, which then replicate the plasmid (and the cloned cDNA insert) as they divide, yielding large quantities of identical DNA.

incorrectas.A: Yeast can be used as a eukaryotic expression host in some cloning systems (e.g., for proteins requiring eukaryotic post-translational modification), but the classic, fast, and cheap step of amplifying a recombinant plasmid described here uses bacterial transformation, not yeast protoplast uptake.
incorrectas.C: Mammalian cell transfection is used later in a workflow when eukaryotic expression of the cloned gene is the goal, but it is slower, more expensive, and not the standard first step for amplifying recombinant plasmid DNA itself.
incorrectas.D: Bacteriophages can serve as cloning vectors themselves (e.g., lambda phage vectors) and infect bacteria rather than being introduced into another host, which is a distinct strategy from transforming a plasmid directly into bacterial cells.

preguntas.q: Before Southern blot analysis, DNA must first undergo which processing step that is not required for RNA (Northern blot) or protein (Western blot) samples?

e.correcta: Genomic DNA is enormous and exists as long continuous molecules, so it must first be cut into manageable fragments using restriction endonucleases before it can be separated by gel electrophoresis and analyzed in a Southern blot. RNA transcripts and proteins are already naturally sized as discrete, analyzable units (individual mRNAs or polypeptides), so they can be loaded onto a gel and probed directly without an enzymatic fragmentation step.

incorrectas.A: Denaturation into single strands is actually a shared step across blotting techniques (DNA and RNA must be single-stranded to hybridize with a probe), so it does not distinguish DNA processing from RNA or protein processing.
incorrectas.C: Labeling is applied to the probe (or sometimes the antibody in a Western blot), not as a preparatory step unique to the DNA sample itself, so it doesn't explain why only DNA needs extra handling before electrophoresis.
incorrectas.D: Transfer to a membrane occurs in all blotting procedures after gel electrophoresis, regardless of whether the target is DNA, RNA, or protein, so it is a shared downstream step rather than the DNA-specific requirement being tested.

preguntas.q: What is the net charge of essentially all RNA and DNA molecules?

e.correcta: Nucleic acids are uniformly negatively charged because each nucleotide contributes a phosphate group in the sugar-phosphate backbone, and each phosphodiester linkage carries a negative charge at physiologic pH. This uniform negative charge is exactly what allows gel electrophoresis to work as a size-based separation: since charge density is constant per unit length, all fragments migrate toward the anode at a rate determined by size (and gel pore size) rather than by charge differences.

incorrectas.B: If nucleic acids were neutral they would not migrate in an electric field at all, which would make electrophoretic separation impossible; the consistent negative backbone charge is precisely what drives their migration toward the positive electrode.
incorrectas.A: Positively charged molecules would migrate toward the cathode, the opposite of what is observed for DNA/RNA in a gel; the phosphate backbone is acidic and deprotonated at physiologic pH, giving nucleic acids a negative, not positive, charge.
incorrectas.D: The charge does not vary with base sequence because the charge comes from the invariant phosphate backbone shared by every nucleotide, not from the bases themselves — this is why size, not sequence-dependent charge, determines migration in electrophoresis.

preguntas.q: Most proteins carry what net charge, an important exception being histones?

e.correcta: Most proteins are net negatively charged at physiologic pH because they contain a preponderance of acidic (aspartate, glutamate) side chains relative to basic ones, allowing them to migrate toward the anode during native or SDS-PAGE electrophoresis. Histones are a key exception: they are rich in lysine and arginine residues, giving them a strongly positive charge that lets them bind tightly to the negatively charged DNA phosphate backbone and package it into nucleosomes.

incorrectas.A: If proteins were neutral overall, native gel electrophoresis based on intrinsic charge would not separate them at all; most proteins in fact carry a net negative charge from their amino acid composition, which is why they migrate in an electric field.
incorrectas.C: Positively charged proteins are the exception rather than the rule; histones are the classic example because their high lysine/arginine content lets them electrostatically bind DNA, but most cellular proteins do not share this feature.
incorrectas.D: While individual proteins do differ, the point being tested is the general rule that most proteins skew negative overall due to acidic residue content, with histones being the specific, well-known exception — not that charge is unpredictable across the proteome.

preguntas.q: Gel electrophoresis separates DNA, RNA, or protein fragments primarily on the basis of which property?

e.correcta: In gel electrophoresis, an electric field drives negatively charged nucleic acid or SDS-coated protein fragments through a porous gel matrix toward the anode; because all fragments carry a comparable charge density, smaller fragments thread through the gel pores faster than larger ones, so migration distance is inversely related to fragment size. This lets investigators compare an unknown sample against a DNA/protein ladder of known sizes to estimate fragment length.

incorrectas.A: Isoelectric focusing (a related but distinct technique) separates proteins by isoelectric point along a pH gradient, but standard gel electrophoresis used in blotting workflows separates fragments by size, not by pI.
incorrectas.C: Overall net charge is intentionally made uniform (all nucleic acid fragments are negatively charged via the phosphate backbone, and SDS coats proteins with a proportional negative charge) precisely so that charge does not confound the separation — the whole point is to isolate size as the separating variable.
incorrectas.D: Sequence is not what the gel resolves; two fragments of identical length but different sequence migrate identically, since migration depends on molecular size (and shape) moving through the gel matrix, not on the specific base or amino acid composition.

preguntas.q: In a blotting procedure (Southern, Northern, or Western), what determines which specific sequences or proteins are detected on the membrane?

o.A: The pore size of the electrophoresis gel
o.B: The type of membrane used for transfer

e.correcta: After DNA, RNA, or protein has been separated by size and transferred to a membrane, it is the probe — a labeled single-stranded DNA/RNA oligonucleotide complementary to the target sequence in a Southern or Northern blot, or a labeled antibody in a Western blot — that determines what gets visualized. Only membrane-bound material that hybridizes (or binds, for antibodies) with the probe will produce a detectable signal, so choosing a different probe changes what target is being interrogated even though the same gel and membrane could be used.

incorrectas.A: Gel pore size affects how fragments are separated by size during electrophoresis, but it does not determine specificity for a particular sequence or protein — that selectivity comes entirely from the probe used afterward.
incorrectas.B: The membrane (typically nitrocellulose or nylon) serves as a passive solid support that immobilizes the transferred material so it can be probed; it does not confer any sequence- or protein-specific detection itself.
incorrectas.D: Voltage influences the rate and pattern of migration during electrophoresis, affecting resolution and run time, but it has no role in determining which specific sequence or protein is subsequently detected by the probe.

preguntas.q: Does a Southern blot require gel electrophoresis as a step prior to probing and analysis?

o.A: No, DNA is probed directly without any separation step
o.D: Only for samples larger than 10 kb

e.correcta: A Southern blot analyzes DNA that has first been cut into fragments by restriction enzymes, then separated by size using gel electrophoresis, and finally transferred onto a membrane before being hybridized with a labeled probe. Gel electrophoresis is an essential intermediate step because it resolves the complex mixture of DNA fragments by size, which is what allows the technique to reveal information such as restriction fragment length differences (e.g., RFLP analysis).

incorrectas.A: Skipping electrophoresis would defeat the purpose of the Southern blot's size-based analysis (such as detecting RFLPs), and is instead more characteristic of a dot/slot blot, which applies sample directly to a membrane without separation.
incorrectas.C: RNA contamination is not the reason electrophoresis is performed; electrophoresis is required to size-separate the DNA fragments themselves so meaningful size-based patterns can be visualized after probing.
incorrectas.D: There is no size cutoff below which electrophoresis becomes optional — the Southern blot protocol always includes electrophoresis as a core step regardless of fragment size.

preguntas.q: Does a Northern blot require gel electrophoresis prior to probing and analysis of the RNA sample?

o.B: No, RNA is spotted directly onto the membrane
o.C: Only if the RNA is degraded

e.correcta: Like the Southern blot, a Northern blot requires that RNA first be separated by size via gel electrophoresis before being transferred to a membrane and hybridized with a labeled probe. This size separation lets investigators confirm transcript length and assess relative abundance of specific mRNA species, which is the whole point of using a Northern blot to study gene expression.

incorrectas.B: Spotting sample directly onto a membrane without electrophoresis describes a dot/slot blot, not a Northern blot; the Northern blot's defining feature is that it resolves RNA by size on a gel first.
incorrectas.C: RNA integrity (degradation) is a quality-control concern that can complicate interpretation of a Northern blot, but electrophoresis is performed regardless of RNA quality — it's a required step in the protocol, not a conditional one.
incorrectas.D: The requirement for gel electrophoresis applies to standard Northern blotting for mRNA transcripts in general; specialized microRNA detection may use variant protocols, but this does not change the fact that standard Northern blotting always includes an electrophoresis step.

preguntas.q: A Northern blot is most useful for studying which aspect of a gene?

e.correcta: A Northern blot detects and quantifies specific mRNA transcripts, making it a direct readout of gene expression — whether and how much a given gene is being transcribed in a tissue or under a given condition. Because RNA levels reflect active transcription rather than the underlying gene sequence itself, Northern blotting is the classic technique for studying differential expression, unlike Southern blotting which examines the DNA sequence/structure itself.

incorrectas.A: Chromosomal location of a gene is typically assessed with techniques like fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), which localizes DNA sequences on chromosomes, not with a Northern blot, which examines RNA transcripts rather than chromosomal positioning.
incorrectas.C: Detecting germline DNA mutations is the domain of Southern blotting or PCR-based sequencing/RFLP analysis on genomic DNA, since a Northern blot probes RNA and does not directly reveal DNA sequence variants.
incorrectas.D: Copy number variation (duplications/deletions of DNA segments) is assessed by techniques that examine genomic DNA dosage, such as Southern blot or microarray/FISH-based comparative genomic hybridization, not by measuring RNA transcript levels.

preguntas.q: In a Western blot, what type of probe is used to detect the target protein after it has been separated by gel electrophoresis and transferred to a membrane?

e.correcta: A Western blot uses a labeled antibody as the probe, which binds specifically to the protein of interest via antigen-antibody recognition (often using a primary antibody against the target followed by a labeled secondary antibody for signal amplification). This antibody-based detection is what distinguishes protein blotting from nucleic acid blotting, where hybridization between complementary nucleic acid strands is used instead of antigen-antibody binding.

incorrectas.A: A labeled single-stranded DNA or RNA oligonucleotide probe is used in Southern and Northern blots, where detection relies on complementary base pairing (hybridization) with a DNA or RNA target, a mechanism that does not apply to protein detection.
incorrectas.B: Fluorescently tagged dNTPs are incorporated into newly synthesized DNA strands during processes like PCR or sequencing, not used as a standalone detection probe in Western blotting.
incorrectas.D: Restriction endonucleases are enzymes used earlier in molecular biology workflows to cut DNA at specific sequences (e.g., before Southern blotting or cloning), and play no role in detecting protein on a membrane.

preguntas.q: In Southern and Northern blotting, what type of probe is used to detect the target DNA or RNA sequence?

o.D: Fluorescently labeled dye that binds double-stranded DNA nonspecifically

e.correcta: Southern and Northern blots use a labeled single-stranded DNA or RNA oligonucleotide probe that is complementary in sequence to the target of interest; the probe finds and hybridizes specifically to its matching sequence on the membrane via Watson-Crick base pairing. The probe can be labeled radioactively (historically with 32P) or with a fluorescent tag, allowing the specific bands of interest to be visualized against the background of all the other separated fragments on the membrane.

incorrectas.A: A labeled antibody is the detection reagent used in Western blotting for protein targets, relying on antigen-antibody binding rather than nucleic acid base pairing, so it is not applicable to detecting DNA or RNA sequences.
incorrectas.C: Restriction enzymes are used earlier in sample preparation to cut genomic DNA into fragments before electrophoresis; they are not conjugated as detection probes and have no sequence-hybridization detection role.
incorrectas.D: A nonspecific dsDNA-binding dye (like ethidium bromide) stains all double-stranded DNA in a gel regardless of sequence, which is useful for visualizing total DNA but cannot selectively identify one particular gene sequence the way a complementary probe can.
