The Prader-Willi/Angelman region on chromosome 15q11-13 is the classic example: certain genes there are normally expressed only from the paternal allele, while others are expressed only from the maternal allele. Because only one functional allele is normally active at an imprinted locus, losing that single active allele (whether by deletion or uniparental disomy) causes disease even though the "silent" allele's sequence is perfectly intact.

incorrectas.B: Codominance describes simultaneous expression of both alleles in a heterozygote (like ABO blood groups), which is essentially the opposite of imprinting, where by design only one parental allele is ever transcribed.
incorrectas.C: Uniparental disomy is a chromosomal transmission event (inheriting both copies of a chromosome from one parent) that can unmask an imprinting disorder, but it is not itself the normal biological process of parent-of-origin gene silencing.
incorrectas.D: Loss of heterozygosity refers to losing the remaining functional allele of a tumor suppressor gene in carcinogenesis, an oncogenic mechanism distinct from the normal developmental process of imprinting.

preguntas.q: Both Prader-Willi syndrome and Angelman syndrome arise from abnormalities affecting imprinted genes located on which chromosome?

e.correcta: Both Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes map to the same imprinted region on chromosome 15q11-13, which contains a cluster of genes whose expression differs depending on parental origin. When the paternally active genes in this region are lost (by deletion or maternal uniparental disomy), Prader-Willi syndrome results; when the maternally active UBE3A gene in this same region is lost (by deletion or paternal uniparental disomy), Angelman syndrome results. This single chromosomal region producing two clinically distinct syndromes, depending on which parental allele is missing, is a classic illustration of genomic imprinting.

incorrectas.B: Chromosome 21 is best known for trisomy 21 (Down syndrome), a numerical chromosomal abnormality, not the imprinted region implicated in Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes.
incorrectas.C: Chromosome 7 harbors the CFTR gene responsible for cystic fibrosis and is also associated with Williams syndrome (7q11.23 microdeletion), not the imprinting disorders in question.
incorrectas.D: Chromosome 11 contains the WT1 and other genes associated with Wilms tumor and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (itself another imprinting disorder), but it is not the locus for Prader-Willi or Angelman syndrome.

preguntas.q: In about 25% of cases, Prader-Willi syndrome results from a child inheriting both copies of chromosome 15 from a single parent, with no paternal contribution at that locus. Which parent's uniparental disomy accounts for this subset of cases?

e.correcta: About 25% of Prader-Willi syndrome cases arise from maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15, in which the child receives two maternal copies and no paternal copy of chromosome 15. Because the Prader-Willi critical region is normally expressed only from the paternal allele (the maternal copy is imprinted/silenced), having only maternal chromosome 15 material means there is no active copy of these genes at all, producing the Prader-Willi phenotype. A helpful mnemonic is that "moms have no willis" — maternal disomy means no paternal (active) Prader-Willi genes are present.

incorrectas.B: Paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15 instead causes Angelman syndrome, because it deprives the child of the maternally active UBE3A gene, the opposite parental deficiency from what causes Prader-Willi syndrome.
incorrectas.C: The parent of origin is not interchangeable here — because the genes in this region are imprinted, only maternal uniparental disomy (missing the paternal contribution) produces Prader-Willi syndrome, while paternal disomy produces the entirely different Angelman phenotype.
incorrectas.D: Uniparental disomy is defined relative to the immediate parents contributing gametes at conception; grandparental origin of the disomic chromosome may be traced molecularly but is not how this mechanism is classified or named.

preguntas.q: About 5% of Angelman syndrome cases occur when a child inherits both copies of chromosome 15 from a single parent with no maternal contribution at that locus. Which parent's uniparental disomy explains these cases, and why is this less common than the analogous mechanism in Prader-Willi syndrome?

o.A: Paternal uniparental disomy; less common because meiotic nondisjunction leading to trisomy rescue occurs more often in oocytes than sperm
o.B: Maternal uniparental disomy; less common because sperm undergo nondisjunction more often than oocytes
o.C: Paternal uniparental disomy; equally common as maternal disomy in Prader-Willi syndrome
o.D: Maternal uniparental disomy; occurs due to imprinting of the SNRPN gene

e.correcta: Angelman syndrome from uniparental disomy requires paternal uniparental disomy — two paternal copies of chromosome 15 and no maternal copy — because the maternally active UBE3A gene at that locus is completely absent when there is no maternal contribution. This mechanism is rarer (about 5% of Angelman cases) than the analogous maternal uniparental disomy seen in roughly 25% of Prader-Willi cases, largely because meiotic nondisjunction errors that set up trisomy rescue occur more frequently during the prolonged, decades-long arrest of oocyte meiosis than during the comparatively rapid, continuously renewing process of spermatogenesis. A useful mnemonic is that "snow angels are imprints of men" — paternal disomy underlies Angelman syndrome.

incorrectas.B: This reverses the correct parent of origin — Angelman syndrome results from paternal (not maternal) uniparental disomy, and it is oocyte nondisjunction, not sperm nondisjunction, that occurs more frequently and explains the relative rarity of this route to Angelman syndrome.
incorrectas.C: Paternal uniparental disomy causing Angelman syndrome (about 5% of cases) is actually less common than maternal uniparental disomy causing Prader-Willi syndrome (about 25% of cases), reflecting the higher rate of nondisjunction events during oogenesis compared with spermatogenesis.
incorrectas.D: The parent of origin identified is correct in direction only by coincidence in this option's phrasing, but the explanation is wrong — the mechanism relates to which parental copy is missing (maternal, i.e., no active UBE3A), not to imprinting of SNRPN, which is instead the gene implicated in Prader-Willi syndrome.

preguntas.q: A child presents with insatiable appetite and obesity, hypotonia, intellectual disability, and hypogonadism, and is found to have a deletion of paternally-derived genes on chromosome 15. Which syndrome does this presentation describe?

e.correcta: Prader-Willi syndrome results from loss of the paternally-expressed genes in the imprinted region of chromosome 15q11-13 (via deletion, maternal uniparental disomy, or an imprinting defect), and classically presents with neonatal hypotonia, followed later by hyperphagia and obesity, intellectual disability, and hypogonadism. The hyperphagia arises from hypothalamic dysfunction affecting satiety signaling, which is why weight gain becomes a major management issue as these children grow. Because the maternal allele at this locus is normally imprinted (silenced), losing the only active (paternal) copy leaves no functional gene product at all.

incorrectas.B: Angelman syndrome arises from loss of the maternally-expressed UBE3A gene at this same chromosome 15 locus, but presents very differently — with inappropriate laughter, seizures, ataxia, and severe intellectual disability — rather than hyperphagia and hypogonadism.
incorrectas.C: Williams syndrome is caused by a microdeletion at 7q11.23 (affecting the elastin gene, among others) and presents with a distinctive "elfin" facies, cardiovascular abnormalities (like supravalvular aortic stenosis), and an unusually friendly personality — a completely different genetic locus and phenotype from Prader-Willi syndrome.
incorrectas.D: DiGeorge syndrome results from a 22q11.2 microdeletion affecting third and fourth pharyngeal pouch development, causing thymic aplasia, hypocalcemia, and cardiac defects, none of which overlaps with the chromosome 15 imprinting mechanism or hyperphagia/hypogonadism phenotype of Prader-Willi syndrome.

preguntas.q: A child presents with inappropriate bouts of laughter, seizures, ataxia, and severe intellectual disability, and is found to have loss of the maternally-derived UBE3A gene on chromosome 15. Which syndrome does this presentation describe?

e.correcta: Angelman syndrome results from loss of the maternally-expressed UBE3A gene in the imprinted chromosome 15q11-13 region (via deletion, paternal uniparental disomy, or an imprinting defect), producing a phenotype of severe intellectual disability, ataxic gait, seizures, and characteristic paroxysms of inappropriate laughter, which together have earned it the nickname "happy puppet" syndrome. Because the paternal allele at this locus is normally imprinted (silenced), losing the only active maternal copy leaves the UBE3A gene product entirely absent in affected neurons.

incorrectas.B: Prader-Willi syndrome results from the opposite parental deficiency — loss of paternally-expressed genes at this same chromosome 15 locus — and presents with hyperphagia, obesity, and hypogonadism rather than the seizures and inappropriate laughter characteristic of Angelman syndrome.
incorrectas.C: Fragile X syndrome is caused by CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome, presenting with intellectual disability, a long face with large ears, and macroorchidism — a completely different genetic mechanism and phenotype from the chromosome 15 imprinting defect in Angelman syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Rett syndrome is caused by mutations in the X-linked MECP2 gene, predominantly affecting girls with regression of developmental milestones and stereotyped hand-wringing movements, which is mechanistically and phenotypically distinct from the chromosome 15 imprinting abnormality of Angelman syndrome.

preguntas.q: Which chromosome 15 imprinting disorder, characterized by seizures, ataxia, and inappropriate laughter, is also historically referred to as "happy puppet" syndrome?

e.correcta: Angelman syndrome earned the older nickname "happy puppet" syndrome because affected children display a characteristic ataxic, jerky gait along with unprovoked bouts of laughter and a generally happy demeanor, resembling a marionette's movements. The underlying defect is loss of the maternally-active UBE3A gene on chromosome 15q11-13, which functions in the brain as part of the ubiquitin-proteasome system important for synaptic development. The nickname has fallen out of favor clinically as potentially stigmatizing, but it remains a useful memory aid for board exams.

incorrectas.B: Prader-Willi syndrome shares the same chromosome 15 region but stems from loss of paternally-active genes rather than the maternal UBE3A gene, and its clinical picture (hyperphagia, obesity, hypogonadism) is entirely different from the seizures and laughter of "happy puppet" syndrome.
incorrectas.C: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is an imprinting disorder involving chromosome 11p15, causing macrosomia, macroglossia, omphalocele, and a predisposition to Wilms tumor — a different chromosome and phenotype from Angelman syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Cri-du-chat syndrome results from a deletion on chromosome 5p, causing a distinctive high-pitched, cat-like cry in infancy along with intellectual disability and microcephaly, and is unrelated to chromosome 15 imprinting or the "happy puppet" nickname.

preguntas.q: For both Angelman syndrome and Prader-Willi syndrome, what is the most common underlying molecular abnormality at the chromosome 15q11-13 locus?

o.A: Deletion of the active parental allele
o.B: Point mutation in the imprinted allele itself

e.correcta: The most common cause of both Angelman and Prader-Willi syndrome is a deletion of the normally active (non-imprinted) parental allele at chromosome 15q11-13 — deletion of the paternal allele (removing SNRPN/necdin, among others) causes Prader-Willi syndrome, while deletion of the maternal allele (removing UBE3A) causes Angelman syndrome. In both cases, the imprinting process itself is entirely normal — the silenced allele from the other parent is still appropriately imprinted — the disease results because the one allele that should be active is physically missing. Uniparental disomy is a less common alternative route to the same phenotypes, produced by inheriting both copies from the parent whose allele would normally be silenced.

incorrectas.B: A point mutation directly in the imprinted (silenced) allele would have no clinical effect, since that allele is not transcribed anyway — the disease-causing lesion needs to affect the active allele, and the imprinting mechanism itself is not disrupted in typical cases, ruling out this option as the most common mechanism.
incorrectas.C: Trisomy of chromosome 15 is a distinct and generally more severe chromosomal abnormality involving an extra whole chromosome copy, not the microdeletion at 15q11-13 that is actually most commonly responsible for these two imprinting syndromes.
incorrectas.D: A balanced translocation would redistribute genetic material without a net loss of DNA and would not, by itself, typically cause Prader-Willi or Angelman syndrome, whereas the classic and most common mechanism is an actual microdeletion removing the active allele's genes.

preguntas.q: In the Hardy-Weinberg equation p + q = 1, what do the variables p and q represent?

e.correcta: In Hardy-Weinberg population genetics, p and q represent the frequencies of the two alleles at a given locus in the gene pool (for example, the frequency of the normal allele versus the frequency of the disease allele), and by definition they must sum to 1 since together they account for all alleles at that locus. This is the foundation for deriving genotype frequencies (p², 2pq, q²) and is used clinically to estimate carrier frequency or disease prevalence in a population assumed to be in genetic equilibrium (no mutation, migration, selection, or non-random mating).

incorrectas.B: Genotype frequencies are represented by the expanded terms p², 2pq, and q² (homozygous dominant, heterozygous, and homozygous recessive, respectively), not by p and q themselves, which represent the underlying allele frequencies that generate those genotype proportions.
incorrectas.C: Disease incidence and prevalence are epidemiologic measures of new and existing cases in a population over time, concepts distinct from the allele frequency variables used in the Hardy-Weinberg equation.
incorrectas.D: Carrier and affected proportions are specific genotype categories (2pq for heterozygous carriers, q² for homozygous affected individuals) derived from the Hardy-Weinberg genotype equation, not the raw allele frequency terms p and q themselves.

preguntas.q: In the Hardy-Weinberg equation p² + 2pq + q² = 1, what do the terms p², 2pq, and q² represent?

e.correcta: The expanded Hardy-Weinberg equation p² + 2pq + q² = 1 describes genotype frequencies in a population at equilibrium: p² is the frequency of homozygous dominant individuals, 2pq is the frequency of heterozygous carriers, and q² is the frequency of homozygous recessive (often affected) individuals, and these three genotype categories together account for the entire population. This equation is derived directly from the allele frequency equation (p + q = 1) by squaring it, and it lets clinicians estimate, for instance, carrier frequency (2pq) for a recessive disease from the observed frequency of affected individuals (q²).

incorrectas.B: Allele frequencies are represented by the simpler terms p and q alone (from p + q = 1), not by the squared and cross-multiplied terms p², 2pq, and q², which instead describe how those allele frequencies combine into genotypes.
incorrectas.C: Mutation rates are a separate population genetics parameter describing how quickly new alleles arise, and one of the assumptions of Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium is actually that mutation rate is negligible — it is not represented by any term in this equation.
incorrectas.D: Selection coefficients quantify the relative fitness disadvantage of a genotype and, like mutation rate, are assumed to be absent (no selection) for a population to remain in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium; they are not represented by the p², 2pq, or q² terms.

preguntas.q: Which equation is used to calculate allele frequencies under Hardy-Weinberg population genetics assumptions?

e.correcta: The equation p + q = 1 calculates allele frequencies, where p represents the frequency of one allele (often the normal/dominant allele) and q represents the frequency of the alternative allele (often the disease/recessive allele) at a given locus, and since these are the only two alleles being considered, their frequencies must sum to 1. This simple relationship is the starting point for Hardy-Weinberg analysis and allows calculation of q (disease allele frequency) directly from the square root of the observed disease prevalence, then solving for p.

incorrectas.B: p² + 2pq + q² = 1 calculates genotype frequencies (homozygous dominant, heterozygous, homozygous recessive), which is a downstream application built on top of the allele frequency equation, not the allele frequency equation itself.
incorrectas.C: p² = q² is not a valid Hardy-Weinberg relationship at all; it would only be true in the special case where p and q happen to be numerically equal, and it does not represent any general principle for calculating allele or genotype frequencies.
incorrectas.D: 2p + 2q = 1 is mathematically inconsistent with the true relationship p + q = 1 (it would actually imply p + q = 0.5), and does not correspond to any standard Hardy-Weinberg formula used to calculate allele frequencies.

preguntas.q: Which equation is used to calculate genotype frequencies under Hardy-Weinberg population genetics assumptions?

e.correcta: The equation p² + 2pq + q² = 1 calculates genotype frequencies in a population at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium: p² is the frequency of individuals homozygous for one allele, q² is the frequency of individuals homozygous for the other allele, and 2pq is the frequency of heterozygotes, together accounting for the whole population. This equation is derived by squaring the allele frequency equation (p + q = 1), and it is the practical formula clinicians use to estimate the number of carriers (2pq) in a population once the frequency of affected homozygotes (q²) is known, such as from disease incidence data.

incorrectas.B: p + q = 1 calculates allele frequencies (the frequency of each individual allele in the gene pool), which is the simpler precursor equation, not the expanded genotype frequency formula that includes the p², 2pq, and q² terms.
incorrectas.C: p x q = 1 is not a valid Hardy-Weinberg relationship; multiplying p and q together does not yield any meaningful population genetics quantity and is inconsistent with the actual derivation of genotype frequencies from squaring p + q.
incorrectas.D: p2 - q2 = 1 is not a Hardy-Weinberg formula; subtracting these squared terms has no biological meaning in population genetics and does not correspond to the correct algebraic expansion of (p + q)2, which instead yields p2 + 2pq + q2.

preguntas.q: Under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of an X-linked recessive disease in males is best represented by which term?

e.correcta: Males are hemizygous for X-linked genes (only one X chromosome), so a single recessive allele is sufficient to produce the phenotype — there is no second allele to mask it. Therefore the disease frequency in males equals the allele frequency itself, q, rather than a squared or cross term as in autosomal genetics. This is why X-linked recessive conditions like hemophilia or G6PD deficiency are so much more common in males than females for the same allele frequency.

incorrectas.A: p² represents the frequency of the homozygous dominant genotype in standard autosomal Hardy-Weinberg math, but males only have one X allele, so genotype frequencies for X-linked traits don't follow the p² + 2pq + q² = 1 framework the way autosomal traits do.
incorrectas.C: 2pq is the frequency of heterozygous carriers in autosomal inheritance, a concept that doesn't apply to males for X-linked genes since they have only a single X allele and cannot be heterozygous at that locus.
incorrectas.D: q² is the frequency of the affected homozygous recessive genotype for autosomal traits (requiring two copies of the recessive allele), but this is the formula used for the disease frequency in females, who have two X chromosomes, not males.

preguntas.q: Under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of an X-linked recessive disease in females is best represented by which term?

e.correcta: Females have two X chromosomes, so for an X-linked recessive disease to manifest, a female must inherit the recessive allele on both X chromosomes, just as with autosomal recessive inheritance. This genotype frequency is q², the product of independently inheriting the recessive allele from each parent. Because q² is much smaller than q (since q is a fraction), X-linked recessive diseases are dramatically rarer in females than in males, who need only one copy (frequency q).

incorrectas.A: q is simply the allele frequency of the recessive allele in the population and, by itself, is the disease frequency in hemizygous males — not in females, who require two copies to be affected.
incorrectas.B: 2pq is the frequency of heterozygous carrier females, who carry one normal and one recessive allele; these women are typically unaffected carriers, not diseased, since the normal allele is expressed.
incorrectas.D: p² is the frequency of females who are homozygous for the normal dominant allele — the unaffected, non-carrier group — which is the opposite of what the question is asking about.

preguntas.q: In Hardy-Weinberg population genetics for an autosomal recessive condition, which term represents the frequency of unaffected heterozygous carriers?

e.correcta: The Hardy-Weinberg equation p² + 2pq + q² = 1 partitions the population into homozygous dominant (p²), heterozygous (2pq), and homozygous recessive (q²) genotypes. The 2pq term captures heterozygous carriers because there are two ways to be heterozygous — inheriting the dominant allele from the mother and recessive from the father, or vice versa — hence the factor of 2. This is clinically important because carrier frequency (2pq) is often far higher than disease frequency (q²) for rare recessive conditions, which is why carrier screening matters even in unaffected-looking couples.

incorrectas.A: q² is the frequency of homozygous recessive individuals who actually manifest the disease, not carriers — carriers by definition have only one recessive allele and are phenotypically normal.
incorrectas.C: p² is the frequency of homozygous dominant individuals who carry two normal alleles and are neither carriers nor affected, representing the unaffected non-carrier portion of the population.
incorrectas.D: q is just the allele frequency of the recessive allele itself, not a genotype frequency; it must be combined with p (2pq) to yield the proportion of the population that is heterozygous.

preguntas.q: Which of the following is a required assumption for a population to remain in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?

o.A: High rate of mutation at the locus
o.B: No net migration into or out of the population
o.C: Strong natural selection favoring one allele

e.correcta: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium models an idealized population where allele frequencies stay constant across generations, which requires no gene flow — that is, no net migration bringing in or removing alleles from the gene pool. If individuals with different allele frequencies migrate in or out, the population's allele frequencies shift, violating equilibrium. This assumption, along with no mutation, no selection, random mating, and a large population size (no genetic drift), forms the complete list of conditions Step 1 expects you to recognize.

incorrectas.A: A high mutation rate would introduce new alleles or convert existing ones, changing allele frequencies over time — this is the opposite of what equilibrium requires, which is essentially zero net mutation at the locus.
incorrectas.C: Strong natural selection would preferentially increase or decrease the frequency of certain alleles because they confer a survival or reproductive advantage or disadvantage, actively driving the population away from equilibrium rather than maintaining it.
incorrectas.D: Non-random (assortative) mating, where individuals preferentially mate with those of similar phenotype, skews genotype frequencies (increasing homozygosity) even if allele frequencies stay the same, whereas equilibrium requires completely random mating.

preguntas.q: Which of the following mating patterns is required for a population to satisfy Hardy-Weinberg assumptions?

e.correcta: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium assumes that individuals pair up without regard to genotype at the locus in question — completely random mating. This ensures that allele combinations in offspring reflect only the allele frequencies in the gene pool (p and q), which is what allows the p² + 2pq + q² genotype distribution to hold. Any deviation from random mating, such as choosing partners based on a trait linked to that gene, restructures genotype frequencies without necessarily changing allele frequencies.

incorrectas.B: Restricting mating to small subpopulations promotes genetic drift and can lead to founder effects, both of which alter allele frequencies through chance events in violation of the large, freely-interbreeding population assumed by Hardy-Weinberg.
incorrectas.A: Assortative mating means individuals choose mates based on shared phenotypic traits (e.g., height, or in genetics terms, choosing similar genotypes), which increases homozygosity in the population and disrupts the equilibrium's random pairing assumption.
incorrectas.D: Preferential mating among relatives (inbreeding) increases the probability that offspring inherit two copies of the same allele from a shared ancestor, again raising homozygosity beyond what random mating alone would produce.

preguntas.q: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium assumes that a population is not evolving, meaning which process must be absent at the locus of interest?

o.B: Genetic drift only in large populations

e.correcta: Natural selection changes allele frequencies over generations by favoring genotypes that confer a survival or reproductive advantage, which is the very definition of evolution at a locus. Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium is essentially a null model describing a population that is NOT evolving, so the absence of selection (along with no mutation, migration, or drift, and random mating) is required for allele and genotype frequencies to stay stable across generations. This is why the Hardy-Weinberg equation is often used as a baseline to detect whether evolution is occurring by comparing observed genotype frequencies to expected ones.

incorrectas.A: Random mating is itself one of the assumptions that must be present (not absent) for equilibrium, since non-random mating patterns like assortative mating would disturb genotype (though not necessarily allele) frequencies.
incorrectas.B: Large population size limiting genetic drift is indeed an assumption of equilibrium, but the question specifically asks about the process related to "the population is not evolving," which classically refers to the absence of natural selection, not drift.
incorrectas.D: Meiotic recombination (crossing over) shuffles alleles between homologous chromosomes during gamete formation but does not, by itself, change allele frequencies in the population, so it is not one of the five classic violations of Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.

preguntas.q: For a population to satisfy Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, no new alleles can arise at the locus, meaning which event must not occur?

e.correcta: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium assumes allele frequencies remain fixed generation to generation, which requires that no new alleles are introduced or lost through mutation at the locus being studied. Even a low but nonzero mutation rate will, over many generations, gradually shift the balance between p and q, so the model technically requires a mutation rate of essentially zero. This is one of the five classic conditions (alongside no selection, no migration, random mating, and infinite/large population size) tested on Step 1.

incorrectas.A: Independent assortment refers to the random distribution of chromosomes from different homologous pairs into gametes during meiosis I; it reshuffles existing alleles into new combinations but does not create new alleles or alter their frequencies.
incorrectas.C: Nondisjunction is the failure of chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate properly during meiosis, producing aneuploid gametes (like trisomies), which is a distinct phenomenon from single-locus mutation and not one of the classic Hardy-Weinberg assumptions.
incorrectas.D: Genetic recombination (crossing over) exchanges segments between homologous chromosomes, creating new allele combinations along a chromosome, but it does not generate new alleles at a single locus or change that locus's allele frequency.

preguntas.q: At the end of S phase of the cell cycle, sister chromatids remain physically joined at which structure?

e.correcta: During S phase, each chromosome is replicated to form two identical sister chromatids, and cohesin protein complexes hold these chromatids together at the centromere, the constricted region of the chromosome. This centromeric attachment persists through G2 and into mitosis until anaphase, when cohesin is cleaved by separase, allowing sister chromatids to be pulled apart to opposite poles. Understanding this is key to understanding nondisjunction, since failure of proper centromeric cohesion or its premature or delayed resolution can cause chromosomes to segregate incorrectly.

incorrectas.A: Telomeres are the repetitive nucleotide sequences (TTAGGG in humans) capping the ends of chromosomes that protect against degradation and end-to-end fusion; they are not the site of sister chromatid attachment.
incorrectas.B: Kinetochores are protein complexes that assemble ON the centromere and serve as the attachment point for spindle microtubules during mitosis, but the kinetochore is a structure built upon the centromere, not the site where sister chromatids are joined to each other.
incorrectas.D: The nucleolus organizer region contains the rDNA genes that form the nucleolus and is located on the short arms of acrocentric chromosomes; it has no role in holding sister chromatids together.

preguntas.q: On a standard chromosome diagram, the short arm is designated by which letter?

e.correcta: The short arm of a chromosome is labeled "p," from the French word "petit" meaning small, while the long arm is labeled "q" (simply the next letter in the alphabet, with no special meaning). This nomenclature is essential for interpreting cytogenetic notation, such as describing a deletion (e.g., 5p- in cri-du-chat syndrome, a deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5) or a duplication/translocation breakpoint.

incorrectas.A: "q" designates the long arm of the chromosome, the arm opposite to the one being asked about here; mixing these up is a common point of confusion on cytogenetic nomenclature questions.
incorrectas.B: "s" is not standard chromosome arm nomenclature at all — despite seeming like an intuitive abbreviation for "short," the accepted convention uses "p" (from "petit").
incorrectas.D: "c" is not used to denote a chromosome arm in standard karyotype nomenclature; only p (short) and q (long) are the recognized designations.

preguntas.q: Chromosomes with a very short p arm relative to the q arm, such as chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21, and 22, are classified as which type?

e.correcta: Acrocentric chromosomes have their centromere positioned very close to one end, resulting in a very short (often genetically sparse) p arm and a long q arm carrying most of the genetic material. In humans, chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21, and 22 are acrocentric, and their short arms contain repetitive rDNA sequences (satellite stalks) rather than essential protein-coding genes. This matters clinically because these five chromosomes are the ones most prone to Robertsonian translocations, since losing their p arms causes no significant genetic consequence.

incorrectas.A: Metacentric chromosomes have the centromere roughly in the middle, giving p and q arms of similar length — the opposite of the markedly asymmetric arm lengths that define acrocentric chromosomes.
incorrectas.B: Submetacentric chromosomes have a centromere slightly off-center, producing one arm modestly longer than the other, but not to the extreme degree seen in acrocentric chromosomes where the p arm is minimal.
incorrectas.C: Telocentric chromosomes have the centromere essentially at the very tip, with no appreciable p arm at all; humans do not normally have telocentric chromosomes, distinguishing this from the acrocentric chromosomes that do retain a small but present p arm.

preguntas.q: Which set of human chromosomes are classified as acrocentric, making them prone to Robertsonian translocations?

e.correcta: Chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21, and 22 are the human acrocentric chromosomes, meaning their centromeres sit near one end, leaving a very short p arm that carries only redundant rDNA repeats rather than essential genes. Because losing the p arm causes no meaningful loss of genetic material, these five chromosomes are the ones that can fuse at the centromere (losing their short arms) to form Robertsonian translocations without necessarily causing a phenotype in the carrier. This is why balanced Robertsonian translocation carriers are usually phenotypically normal but at risk of producing unbalanced gametes, such as those causing Down syndrome (translocation type) or Patau syndrome.

incorrectas.A: Chromosomes 1, 2, 3, 16, and 19 are metacentric or submetacentric with centromeres closer to the middle, so they have substantial p arms containing essential genes and are not typically involved in Robertsonian translocations.
incorrectas.B: Chromosomes 6 through 10 are also submetacentric to metacentric with significant short arms carrying important genes, making them structurally different from the acrocentric group and not the chromosomes classically tested for Robertsonian translocation risk.
incorrectas.D: Chromosomes 4, 5, 12, 17, and 18 have p arms of meaningful length and genetic content (chromosome 5's short arm deletion, for example, causes cri-du-chat syndrome), unlike the genetically sparse p arms of the true acrocentric chromosomes.

preguntas.q: What is the most common mechanism by which chromosomal aneuploidy (such as trisomy) arises?

e.correcta: Meiotic nondisjunction — the failure of homologous chromosomes to separate during meiosis I, or sister chromatids to separate during meiosis II — is the most common cause of aneuploidy such as trisomy 21 (Down syndrome), trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome), and trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome). This failure produces a gamete with either an extra or a missing chromosome, which upon fertilization with a normal gamete yields a trisomic or monosomic zygote in every cell of the resulting individual. The risk of meiotic nondisjunction (particularly in meiosis I) increases significantly with advanced maternal age, which is why maternal age is the classic risk factor tested for trisomy 21.

incorrectas.A: Mitotic nondisjunction occurs after fertilization, in a somatic cell during embryonic development, producing a mosaic pattern of aneuploid and normal cell lines rather than uniform aneuploidy in every cell, and it is a less common cause of aneuploidy overall compared to meiotic nondisjunction.
incorrectas.B: Robertsonian translocation is a structural rearrangement where two acrocentric chromosomes fuse, and while unbalanced segregation of a Robertsonian translocation can cause trisomy in offspring, this is a much less common route to aneuploidy than straightforward meiotic nondisjunction of normal chromosomes.
incorrectas.D: Chromosomal deletion refers to the loss of a segment of a chromosome (as in cri-du-chat syndrome), which is a distinct category of structural chromosomal abnormality and does not produce aneuploidy (an abnormal chromosome number).

preguntas.q: What term describes the presence of two or more genetically distinct cell lines derived from a single fertilized egg within the same individual?

e.correcta: Mosaicism describes the coexistence of two or more genetically distinct cell populations within a single individual, all derived from one fertilized zygote, typically arising from a mitotic error (such as nondisjunction or a new mutation) occurring after fertilization during embryonic development. Depending on when in development the error occurs, the proportion of abnormal cells and which tissues are affected can vary widely, explaining why mosaic conditions often have milder or more variable phenotypes than their non-mosaic counterparts (e.g., mosaic Turner syndrome or mosaic McCune-Albright syndrome).

incorrectas.A: Chimerism refers to an individual composed of cells derived from two different zygotes (for example, from fusion of two fertilized eggs or from twin-to-twin blood cell exchange in utero), which is fundamentally different from mosaicism's single-zygote origin.
incorrectas.C: Heteroplasmy specifically refers to having a mixture of normal and mutated mitochondrial DNA within the same cell or individual, a concept tied to mitochondrial inheritance rather than to genetically distinct nuclear cell lineages from a single zygote.
incorrectas.D: Genomic imprinting is an epigenetic phenomenon where gene expression depends on the parent of origin (only the maternal or only the paternal allele is expressed), which is unrelated to having multiple genetically distinct cell lines in one individual.

preguntas.q: A mutation that is present only in the egg or sperm cells of a parent, without affecting the parent's other tissues, is best described as which type of mosaicism?

e.correcta: Gonadal mosaicism occurs when a mutation arises during early development and becomes restricted to the germ cell line (the cells that give rise to eggs or sperm), while the rest of the parent's body remains genetically normal. Because the parent's other tissues are unaffected, the parent appears clinically normal and shows no signs of the disease, yet the mutation can still be transmitted to offspring, who will then carry the mutation in every cell of their body. This explains the classically tested scenario of two unaffected parents having more than one child with a seemingly "new" autosomal dominant mutation (like osteogenesis imperfecta), which is otherwise puzzling if you assume all new mutations are random single events.

incorrectas.A: Somatic mosaicism refers to a mutation confined to non-reproductive (somatic) tissues, which can cause patchy findings in the affected individual (like the café-au-lait patches of McCune-Albright syndrome) but, unlike gonadal mosaicism, is not transmitted to offspring since the germ cells are unaffected.
incorrectas.B: Confined placental mosaicism describes a discordance between the chromosomal makeup of the placenta and the fetus, relevant to prenatal genetic testing interpretation, but it does not describe a mutation isolated to the parent's germ cells.
incorrectas.D: Germline chimerism is not a standard genetics term for this scenario; chimerism describes two genetically distinct cell populations from separate zygotes coexisting in one individual, which is a different phenomenon from a single-lineage mutation confined to germ cells.

preguntas.q: McCune-Albright syndrome is typically lethal if the causative mutation occurs before fertilization and affects every cell, but is survivable when the individual instead has which condition?

e.correcta: McCune-Albright syndrome is caused by an activating postzygotic somatic mutation in the GNAS gene, and because the mutation arises after fertilization rather than in the germline, only a subset of cells carry it — this is mosaicism. If the same mutation were present in every single cell from the moment of conception (i.e., non-mosaic, constitutional), it is thought to be incompatible with life, which is why all surviving patients with this syndrome are mosaic, showing patchy features like irregular café-au-lait ("coast of Maine") spots, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, and precocious puberty limited to certain tissues.

incorrectas.B: Uniparental disomy occurs when both copies of a chromosome (or chromosome pair) are inherited from a single parent instead of one from each; this is a distinct mechanism from postzygotic mosaicism and is not what allows survival in McCune-Albright syndrome.
incorrectas.C: Genomic imprinting refers to parent-of-origin-specific gene expression (e.g., in Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes) and has no role in explaining why McCune-Albright syndrome is survivable only in its mosaic form.
incorrectas.D: Anticipation describes a phenomenon in trinucleotide repeat disorders where disease severity worsens and age of onset decreases in successive generations; it is unrelated to the mosaic distribution of a somatic GNAS mutation.

preguntas.q: McCune-Albright syndrome results from a somatic mutation affecting which signaling component?

e.correcta: McCune-Albright syndrome is caused by an activating mutation in the GNAS gene, which encodes the alpha subunit of the stimulatory G protein (Gsα). This mutation locks Gsα in its active, GTP-bound state, causing constitutive activation of adenylate cyclase and excess cAMP production independent of normal receptor-ligand signaling. This unregulated signaling in affected tissues explains the classic triad: polyostotic fibrous dysplasia (bone), café-au-lait skin macules, and autonomous endocrine hyperfunction such as precocious puberty or hyperthyroidism.

incorrectas.A: Receptor tyrosine kinases (like RET or FGFR) transduce signals through intrinsic kinase activity and downstream cascades like RAS-MAPK, but mutations in these receptors cause different syndromes (e.g., MEN2, achondroplasia) rather than McCune-Albright syndrome.
incorrectas.C: The JAK-STAT pathway is used by cytokine and growth hormone receptors that lack intrinsic kinase activity, relying on associated Janus kinases; this pathway is not the one dysregulated in McCune-Albright syndrome, which specifically involves the Gsα subunit.
incorrectas.D: Nuclear hormone receptors (like the glucocorticoid or thyroid hormone receptor) act as ligand-activated transcription factors in the nucleus, a fundamentally different signaling mode from the plasma-membrane G-protein/adenylate cyclase pathway disrupted in McCune-Albright syndrome.

preguntas.q: What term describes the chromosomal rearrangement in which homologous chromosomes exchange segments during meiosis?

e.correcta: Crossover (crossing over) is the physical exchange of DNA segments between homologous chromosomes during prophase I of meiosis, occurring at sites called chiasmata. This process is a normal and essential part of meiosis that increases genetic diversity in gametes and is the biological basis for genetic linkage and recombination frequency, which geneticists use to map gene distances on a chromosome (the closer two genes are, the less likely a crossover will occur between them).

incorrectas.A: Translocation is the transfer of a chromosome segment to a nonhomologous chromosome (or a Robertsonian fusion between two acrocentric chromosomes), which is a structural chromosomal abnormality rather than the normal, homologous-chromosome exchange process of meiotic crossover.
incorrectas.B: Inversion occurs when a single chromosome segment is excised, flipped 180 degrees, and reinserted, altering gene orientation without exchanging material with another chromosome — a fundamentally different (and often pathologic) event from crossover between homologs.
incorrectas.D: Duplication refers to a chromosome segment being copied so it appears twice, increasing the copy number of that region; this is a type of structural variant, not the reciprocal exchange of segments between homologous chromosomes that defines crossover.

preguntas.q: Which type of chromosome is most commonly involved in a Robertsonian translocation?

e.correcta: Acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21, and 22 in humans) have their centromeres located very close to one end, giving them very short p arms that contain only redundant rDNA repeats and no essential genes. This makes them uniquely suited to Robertsonian translocation, in which the long (q) arms of two acrocentric chromosomes fuse at or near the centromere and the two short arms are lost, without meaningful loss of genetic material — which is why balanced carriers are typically phenotypically normal.

incorrectas.A: Metacentric chromosomes have centromeres near the middle with substantial p and q arms of similar length, both carrying essential genes, so losing either arm (as would happen in a Robertsonian-type fusion) would cause significant genetic loss, making this type unsuitable for such translocations.
incorrectas.B: Telocentric chromosomes have centromeres at the very tip with essentially no p arm at all; humans do not normally have telocentric chromosomes, so this is not a relevant category for human Robertsonian translocations.
incorrectas.C: Submetacentric chromosomes have centromeres slightly off-center but still retain p arms with meaningful genetic content, unlike the genetically sparse p arms of acrocentric chromosomes that can be safely lost in a Robertsonian translocation.

preguntas.q: Which chromosomal rearrangement occurs when the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes fuse at the centromere while both short arms are lost?

e.correcta: A Robertsonian translocation is the fusion of the long (q) arms of two acrocentric chromosomes at or near the centromere, with loss of both short (p) arms. Because the p arms of acrocentric chromosomes carry only redundant rDNA and no essential genes, this loss is typically inconsequential, so carriers usually have only 45 chromosomes but a normal, balanced phenotype. The clinical significance emerges in the carrier's offspring, who may inherit an unbalanced chromosome complement (e.g., a gamete carrying the fused chromosome plus a normal copy of one of the involved chromosomes), producing conditions like translocation Down syndrome.

incorrectas.A: A reciprocal translocation involves the exchange of segments between two nonhomologous chromosomes (breaking at points along their arms, not necessarily at the centromere), and unlike a Robertsonian translocation, it does not specifically involve fusion of two acrocentric chromosomes with loss of both short arms.
incorrectas.B: Isochromosome formation occurs when a chromosome divides transversely through the centromere rather than longitudinally, producing a chromosome with two identical arms (either two p arms or two q arms) instead of a fusion between two different chromosomes.
incorrectas.D: Ring chromosome formation occurs when a single chromosome breaks at both ends and the broken ends fuse into a circular structure, a very different mechanism from the centromeric fusion of two separate acrocentric chromosomes seen in Robertsonian translocation.

preguntas.q: A phenotypically normal carrier of a balanced Robertsonian translocation involving chromosomes 14 and 21 has an unaffected daughter. What is the most likely mechanism by which this translocation could still cause chromosomal imbalance in future offspring?

o.A: Somatic mosaicism developing in the carrier's own tissues over time
o.B: A gamete carrying the fused translocation chromosome, t(14;21), being passed on to offspring
o.C: Spontaneous reversal of the translocation during oogenesis

e.correcta: During meiosis in a balanced Robertsonian translocation carrier, the fused t(14;21) chromosome must segregate along with the remaining normal chromosomes 14 and 21, but this segregation is prone to producing unbalanced gametes. If a gamete inherits the t(14;21) fusion chromosome plus a normal chromosome 21 (in addition to a normal 14 from the other parent), the resulting offspring effectively has three functional copies of chromosome 21 material — causing translocation-type Down syndrome — even though the parent themselves is a completely healthy, balanced carrier with a normal phenotype.

incorrectas.A: Somatic mosaicism refers to a mutation confined to certain body tissues from a postzygotic event; it is unrelated to how a germline-transmitted balanced translocation causes imbalance through abnormal gamete segregation.
incorrectas.C: Spontaneous reversal of a translocation back to normal chromosomes essentially does not occur biologically; translocations are stable structural rearrangements, and the risk to offspring comes from unbalanced segregation, not reversal.
incorrectas.D: X-inactivation skewing pertains to the random or non-random silencing of one X chromosome in females and has no relevance to autosomal Robertsonian translocations involving chromosomes 14 and 21.

preguntas.q: An individual is found to carry a Robertsonian translocation between chromosomes 13 and 14. What is the most likely clinical consequence for this individual?

o.A: Intellectual disability from loss of essential genes on the lost short arms
o.B: No pathology, since it is usually a balanced translocation
o.C: Infertility due to loss of chromosome 13 and 14 genetic material

e.correcta: Because a Robertsonian translocation fuses the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes and discards only the short arms — which carry solely redundant rDNA sequences and no essential protein-coding genes — the carrier retains a full, balanced complement of essential genetic material despite having only 45 chromosomes. As a result, the carrier is typically phenotypically completely normal and unaware of the translocation unless it is discovered incidentally or through recurrent miscarriages or an affected child, since the real risk of pathology falls on their offspring rather than themselves.

incorrectas.A: Intellectual disability would only be expected if essential genes were lost, but the short arms of acrocentric chromosomes lost in a Robertsonian translocation contain only repetitive rDNA, not genes required for normal development, so this outcome does not occur in balanced carriers.
incorrectas.C: Infertility is not a typical direct consequence of carrying a balanced Robertsonian translocation; while carriers may have increased rates of miscarriage due to unbalanced gametes, the carrier's own genetic material is complete and balanced.
incorrectas.D: A Patau syndrome-like phenotype would require the individual themselves to have three functional copies of chromosome 13 material (trisomy 13), which describes an affected offspring of a translocation carrier, not the balanced carrier itself.

preguntas.q: An infant presents with microcephaly, severe intellectual disability, and a distinctive high-pitched, cat-like cry. Which genetic syndrome is most consistent with this presentation?

e.correcta: Cri-du-chat syndrome is caused by a deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p-) and classically presents with microcephaly, significant intellectual disability, and the pathognomonic high-pitched, cat-like cry in infancy that gives the syndrome its name (French for "cry of the cat"). Additional features can include epicanthal folds and congenital cardiac defects such as ventricular septal defects, reflecting the broader developmental impact of losing genes on the 5p segment.

incorrectas.A: Williams syndrome results from a microdeletion on chromosome 7 (region containing the elastin gene) and presents with "elfin" facies, intellectual disability, and unusually friendly/sociable personality with strangers, along with cardiovascular problems and hypercalcemia — a distinct constellation that does not include the characteristic cat-like cry.
incorrectas.C: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11 deletion) presents with the classic CATCH-22 features (cardiac defects, abnormal facies, thymic aplasia causing T-cell deficiency, cleft palate, hypocalcemia), none of which include the specific high-pitched cry described in this vignette.
incorrectas.D: Prader-Willi syndrome results from loss of paternal gene expression at chromosome 15q11-13 (via deletion or maternal uniparental disomy) and presents with hyperphagia, obesity, hypotonia, and intellectual disability, a very different phenotype from the cat-cry and microcephaly of cri-du-chat syndrome.

preguntas.q: A child has distinctive "elfin" facial features, intellectual disability, and an unusually friendly, uninhibited demeanor toward strangers. Which genetic syndrome does this describe?

e.correcta: Williams syndrome is caused by a microdeletion on chromosome 7q11.23 that includes the elastin gene, producing the classic triad of "elfin" facies (upturned nose, wide mouth, full cheeks), intellectual disability, and a hallmark hypersocial, overly friendly personality even with unfamiliar people. The elastin gene deletion also explains the cardiovascular abnormalities seen in this syndrome (such as supravalvular aortic stenosis) and contributes to the hypercalcemia caused by increased sensitivity to vitamin D.

incorrectas.B: Angelman syndrome results from loss of the maternal UBE3A gene copy at 15q11-13 and presents with severe intellectual disability, ataxic movements, inappropriate laughter, and seizures — a happy demeanor is present but the facial features and overall presentation ("happy puppet" with ataxia) differ from the elfin facies and hypersociability specifically described in Williams syndrome.
incorrectas.C: Cri-du-chat syndrome (5p deletion) presents with microcephaly, intellectual disability, and a characteristic high-pitched cat-like cry, not the elfin facial features or hypersocial personality that define Williams syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Smith-Magenis syndrome (17p11.2 deletion) presents with intellectual disability, sleep disturbances, and self-injurious behavior, a very different behavioral and physical profile from the friendly demeanor and elfin facies of Williams syndrome.

preguntas.q: An isochromosome involving the X chromosome, denoted 46,X,i(Xq), is most classically associated with which condition?

e.correcta: An isochromosome forms when a chromosome divides transversely through the centromere instead of longitudinally, producing a chromosome with two identical arms — in this case, i(Xq) means the resulting isochromosome consists of two copies of the X long arm and lacks the short arm entirely. This effectively deletes genes on Xp (including the SHOX gene important for growth) while duplicating Xq, and is one of several structural X abnormalities that produce the Turner syndrome phenotype (short stature, gonadal dysgenesis, webbed neck) even though the overall chromosome count may appear as 46 rather than the classic 45,X.

incorrectas.A: Klinefelter syndrome is characterized by an extra X chromosome in a male (47,XXY), a difference in chromosome number rather than the abnormal isochromosome structure of a single X chromosome described here.
incorrectas.C: Triple X syndrome (47,XXX) involves an extra complete X chromosome in a female, again a numerical chromosomal abnormality rather than the structural isochromosome rearrangement described by the i(Xq) notation.
incorrectas.D: Fragile X syndrome is caused by a CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome, a molecular/sequence-level mutation entirely distinct from the gross structural chromosomal rearrangement of isochromosome formation.

preguntas.q: What term describes the tendency of alleles at two loci on the same chromosome to be inherited together more or less often than would be expected by chance alone?

e.correcta: Linkage disequilibrium refers to the observed deviation from the expected random inheritance of two alleles based purely on their individual population allele frequencies, whether they are physically linked or not. While physical proximity on a chromosome (linkage) makes recombination between two loci less likely and thus tends to produce linkage disequilibrium, disequilibrium can also arise from population-level factors like recent admixture or genetic drift, so the two concepts, while related, are not identical. The closer two loci are physically, the lower the recombination frequency between them and the stronger the linkage disequilibrium tends to be.

incorrectas.A: Genetic linkage is the tendency of alleles at two loci to be inherited together, often attributed to their physical proximity on a chromosome, but this term refers to the physical relationship itself, whereas linkage disequilibrium refers to the statistical, population-level observation of non-random co-inheritance (which is not always due to physical linkage).
incorrectas.C: Pleiotropy describes a single gene influencing multiple, seemingly unrelated phenotypic traits (e.g., a single mutation causing effects on connective tissue, eyes, and the cardiovascular system in Marfan syndrome), which is unrelated to the joint inheritance pattern of alleles at two separate loci.
incorrectas.D: Epistasis occurs when the effect of one gene is modified or masked by one or more other genes at a different locus (e.g., the effect of one gene depends on the genotype at another gene), a concept about gene interaction and expression rather than about co-inheritance frequency of alleles.

preguntas.q: Linkage disequilibrium is a phenomenon that must be measured at which level, rather than within a single family?

e.correcta: Linkage disequilibrium describes the non-random association of alleles at two loci across a population, and it can only be detected by looking at allele frequencies in many unrelated individuals, not within one family. This is because seeing a recombination event between two very close loci is rare, so an unfeasibly large number of meioses (far more than any single family provides) is needed to observe deviations from the expected independent assortment, which is why population-level haplotype data is required.

incorrectas.B: A nuclear family provides far too few meioses to detect the rare recombination events that reveal linkage; recombination frequency between closely linked loci is low, so you need the pooled meioses of a large population sample, not a handful of siblings, to estimate it reliably.
incorrectas.C: Even an extended three-generation pedigree only captures a limited number of meiotic events, which is still generally insufficient to detect small deviations in allele co-inheritance; linkage disequilibrium is a population genetics measure, not a pedigree-based one like classic linkage analysis (LOD scores) which does use families.
incorrectas.D: A single somatic cell line reflects one individual's genotype and has no meiotic recombination events to sample at all, so it cannot be used to assess whether alleles at two loci co-segregate more or less often than expected by chance.

preguntas.q: When alleles at two different loci are inherited together exactly as often as would be predicted by random chance, the loci are said to be in what state?

e.correcta: Linkage equilibrium is present when the observed frequency of a particular allele combination (haplotype) equals the product of the individual allele frequencies, meaning the two loci assort independently in the population, just as unlinked genes would. This is the null/expected state; deviation from it, where certain allele combinations appear together more or less often than chance predicts, defines linkage disequilibrium instead.

incorrectas.B: Linkage disequilibrium is the opposite state, where alleles at two loci are inherited together more or less frequently than random chance would predict, often because the loci are physically close on a chromosome and recombination between them is rare.
incorrectas.C: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium describes stability of allele and genotype frequencies at a single locus across generations in a non-evolving population, which is a distinct concept from the joint inheritance of alleles at two separate loci.
incorrectas.D: Genetic drift refers to random fluctuations in allele frequencies over generations due to chance sampling of gametes, particularly in small populations, and is unrelated to whether two loci co-segregate as expected by chance.

preguntas.q: As the recombination frequency between two loci approaches which value, the physical distance between the alleles in a haplotype is understood to be smaller?

e.correcta: Recombination frequency reflects how often crossing over separates two alleles during meiosis, and the closer two loci are on a chromosome, the less physical space (and fewer potential crossover points) lies between them, so recombination happens less often. A recombination frequency approaching 0% therefore indicates the loci are very tightly linked and physically close together, while a frequency of 50% indicates the loci assort independently, as if unlinked.

incorrectas.B: A recombination frequency of 25% would indicate loci that are linked but separated by a moderate distance, with crossovers occurring in a quarter of meioses — this is neither the tightest linkage nor equivalent to independent assortment.
incorrectas.C: A recombination frequency of 50% is the value expected for genes on different chromosomes or very far apart on the same chromosome, since it matches the frequency of independent assortment, the opposite extreme from tight physical proximity.
incorrectas.D: A recombination frequency of 100% is not a biologically meaningful steady-state value for linkage analysis; observed recombination frequencies plateau at 50% once loci are far enough apart or unlinked, they do not approach 100%.

preguntas.q: Two linked genes have a recombination frequency of 15%. Approximately how far apart are these genes on the chromosome?

e.correcta: By convention, 1% recombination frequency is approximately equal to 1 centiMorgan (cM) of genetic map distance, a unit that reflects physical distance in terms of crossover likelihood rather than a fixed number of base pairs (roughly 1 cM corresponds to about 1 million base pairs, though this varies by chromosomal region). A 15% recombination frequency therefore translates directly to approximately 15 cM of separation between the two loci.

incorrectas.A: 1.5 cM would correspond to a recombination frequency of only about 1.5%, representing loci that are much more tightly linked (and physically closer) than the 15% recombination frequency given in this scenario.
incorrectas.C: 150 cM would correspond to a recombination frequency far exceeding the maximum meaningful value of 50% for linked loci, since recombination frequency plateaus at 50% once genes are unlinked or very far apart, making this figure inconsistent with the 1% ≈ 1 cM relationship.
incorrectas.D: 1500 cM is an even larger overestimate and is inconsistent with how genetic map distance is derived from recombination frequency; such a value would imply recombination frequencies vastly beyond the 50% ceiling seen for unlinked genes.

preguntas.q: Which statistical measure is calculated to determine the probability that two genetic loci are linked (i.e., in linkage disequilibrium)?

e.correcta: The LOD (logarithm of the odds) score is a statistical test used in linkage analysis that compares the likelihood of obtaining the observed pedigree data if two loci are linked at a given recombination frequency versus the likelihood if they are unlinked (assorting independently). A sufficiently high LOD score provides statistical support that two loci are physically linked on the same chromosome rather than assorting independently.

incorrectas.B: An odds ratio is a measure used in case-control studies to compare the odds of an exposure between diseased and non-diseased groups; it is not the specialized likelihood-ratio statistic used to establish genetic linkage between loci.
incorrectas.C: Relative risk compares the incidence of an outcome between an exposed and unexposed cohort in a study design, a concept from epidemiology rather than from pedigree-based linkage analysis.
incorrectas.D: The chi-squared statistic tests for association between categorical variables (such as observed versus expected genotype counts) but is not the specific logarithmic likelihood-ratio method used to calculate linkage probability across a pedigree.

preguntas.q: An LOD score greater than which threshold value is considered evidence that two loci are linked?

e.correcta: By convention, an LOD score greater than 3 indicates that the odds favoring linkage between two loci are at least 1000 to 1 (since LOD is a base-10 logarithm of the odds ratio), which is accepted as statistically significant evidence of linkage in a pedigree. In this context, a LOD score of 3 roughly corresponds to a recombination frequency around 10%, and because of linkage disequilibrium effects, recombination frequencies lower than that tend to produce even higher (more significant) LOD scores.

incorrectas.A: A LOD score of 1 would correspond to odds of only 10 to 1 favoring linkage, which is far below the conventional threshold needed to confidently conclude that two loci are linked rather than assorting independently by chance.
incorrectas.B: A LOD score of 2 corresponds to odds of 100 to 1, still short of the accepted cutoff of 3 (1000 to 1) that geneticists use to declare significant linkage between two loci.
incorrectas.D: A LOD score of 5 would actually exceed the minimum threshold and would still indicate linkage, but 3 is the standard minimum cutoff value used to define significant linkage, not 5.

preguntas.q: An LOD score less than which value indicates that two loci are not linked?

e.correcta: An LOD score less than -2 is the conventional cutoff used to statistically exclude linkage between two loci, corresponding to odds against linkage that are strong enough to conclude the loci assort independently (roughly consistent with a recombination frequency near 50%, the value expected for unlinked genes). This threshold is the mirror-image counterpart of the +3 cutoff used to establish that linkage is present.

incorrectas.A: A LOD score of 0 simply means the data are equally consistent with linkage and non-linkage (odds of 1:1); it does not represent the accepted statistical threshold for excluding linkage, which requires stronger negative evidence.
incorrectas.B: A LOD score of -1 reflects modest evidence against linkage but is not negative enough to meet the conventional -2 cutoff used to definitively rule out linkage between the two loci.
incorrectas.D: A LOD score of -5 would still fall below the -2 threshold and technically also excludes linkage, but -2 (not -5) is the standard minimum cutoff value conventionally used to declare loci unlinked.

preguntas.q: Which connective tissue protein, which normally acts as a scaffold for elastin, is defective in Marfan syndrome?

e.correcta: Marfan syndrome results from mutations in the FBN1 gene encoding fibrillin-1, a glycoprotein that forms microfibrils providing a structural scaffold onto which elastin is deposited in connective tissue. Loss of normal fibrillin-1 destabilizes elastic fibers throughout the body, explaining the skeletal, ocular, and especially cardiovascular findings (aortic root dilation and dissection) that make Marfan syndrome high-yield.

incorrectas.A: Collagen type I is the major structural collagen of bone, skin, and tendon, and defects in it cause osteogenesis imperfecta, not Marfan syndrome; it does not serve as the elastin scaffold protein implicated here.
incorrectas.C: Elastin is the protein that actually provides tissue elasticity, but in Marfan syndrome elastin itself is not mutated — rather, the fibrillin-1 scaffold it depends on is defective, leading to disorganized, fragile elastic fibers.
incorrectas.D: Collagen type III is found in blood vessels, skin, and hollow organs, and its deficiency causes vascular (type IV) Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, a distinct connective tissue disorder from Marfan syndrome.

preguntas.q: A tall patient presents with long, tapering fingers and toes (arachnodactyly) and bilateral upward lens subluxation. Which condition is most consistent with this presentation?

e.correcta: Marfan syndrome, caused by fibrillin-1 mutations, classically presents with a tall stature with long extremities, arachnodactyly, hypermobile joints, pectus deformities, and characteristic upward and temporal lens subluxation (ectopia lentis) due to weakened zonular fibers. The combination of skeletal habitus plus this specific direction of lens subluxation is a key exam distinguisher from other connective tissue and metabolic disorders.

incorrectas.A: Homocystinuria also causes marfanoid habitus and lens subluxation, but classically the lens dislocates downward and inward, along with intellectual disability, thrombosis, and megaloblastic changes from impaired cystathionine synthase or related enzyme activity — a different mechanism and direction of subluxation.
incorrectas.B: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, from collagen defects, causes hyperextensible skin and joint hypermobility with easy bruising, but it is not classically associated with arachnodactyly or lens subluxation, which are distinguishing features of fibrillin-related disease.
incorrectas.D: Osteogenesis imperfecta results from type I collagen defects and presents with bone fragility, fractures, blue sclerae, and hearing loss, not with arachnodactyly or lens dislocation.

preguntas.q: In Marfan syndrome, in which direction does subluxation of the lens classically occur?

e.correcta: In Marfan syndrome, weakened zonular fibers (due to defective fibrillin-1 microfibrils) cause the lens to sublux upward and temporally, a pattern useful for distinguishing it from other causes of ectopia lentis on exam questions. Remembering this specific directionality helps differentiate Marfan syndrome from homocystinuria at the bedside even before genetic or biochemical testing is available.

incorrectas.A: Downward and inward lens subluxation is the classic pattern seen in homocystinuria, not Marfan syndrome, reflecting a different underlying defect (impaired methionine metabolism causing connective tissue and vascular damage) rather than a primary fibrillin scaffold problem.
incorrectas.C: Downward and temporal displacement is not the classic direction described for either Marfan syndrome or homocystinuria; the classically tested directions are upward/temporal for Marfan and downward/inward for homocystinuria.
incorrectas.D: Upward and nasal displacement is not the pattern taught for Marfan syndrome; the temporal (not nasal) direction is the specific detail tested alongside the upward displacement.

preguntas.q: Marfan syndrome is classically associated with a floppy, prolapsing valve involving which cardiac structure?

e.correcta: In Marfan syndrome, defective fibrillin-1 weakens the connective tissue support of the mitral valve leaflets and chordae, leading to a floppy, myxomatous mitral valve that prolapses into the left atrium during systole, often producing a mid-systolic click and late systolic murmur. This mitral valve prolapse occurs alongside the more life-threatening aortic root dilation and risk of dissection that also stem from weakened elastic/connective tissue in the aortic wall.

incorrectas.A: The tricuspid valve is not the classically emphasized valve in Marfan syndrome; connective tissue weakness in this condition preferentially manifests as mitral valve prolapse and aortic root pathology rather than tricuspid valve disease.
incorrectas.B: The aortic valve itself is not typically described as "floppy" in Marfan syndrome — instead, the aortic root and ascending aorta dilate (from cystic medial necrosis), which can secondarily cause aortic regurgitation, distinct from the floppy mitral valve finding.
incorrectas.D: The pulmonic valve is not a characteristic site of pathology in Marfan syndrome; the disease's valvular hallmark is mitral valve prolapse, reflecting the specific tissues most affected by fibrillin dysfunction.

preguntas.q: What is the mode of inheritance of Fragile X syndrome?

e.correcta: Fragile X syndrome is inherited in an X-linked dominant pattern due to a CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome, which leads to hypermethylation and transcriptional silencing of FMR1. Because the phenotype can manifest even with only one abnormal X allele, and the repeat tends to expand further with each generation (anticipation), both males and, to a variable and often milder degree, some female carriers can be affected.

incorrectas.A: Autosomal dominant inheritance involves a gene on a non-sex chromosome, but FMR1 is located on the X chromosome, so Fragile X syndrome's transmission pattern (with typically more severely affected males) is not consistent with a classic autosomal dominant pedigree.
incorrectas.B: Autosomal recessive conditions require two mutant alleles on a non-sex chromosome and typically skip generations, unlike Fragile X syndrome, which is X-linked and often shows a pattern of anticipation with increasing severity across generations due to repeat expansion.
incorrectas.D: X-linked recessive conditions typically require two mutant alleles in females to manifest disease, with carrier females usually asymptomatic; however, in Fragile X syndrome, some carrier females do show a phenotype because of unfavorable X-inactivation patterns, which is why it is classified as X-linked dominant rather than recessive.

preguntas.q: Fragile X syndrome belongs to which broader class of genetic diseases?

e.correcta: Fragile X syndrome is a trinucleotide repeat expansion disease, caused by an expanded CGG repeat in the 5' untranslated region of the FMR1 gene, which leads to hypermethylation and gene silencing. This class of disease is characterized by repeat sequences that can expand further with each generation (genetic anticipation), a feature shared with other members of this disease family such as Huntington disease, myotonic dystrophy, and Friedreich ataxia.

incorrectas.B: Mitochondrial DNA point mutation diseases (such as MELAS or Leber hereditary optic neuropathy) arise from single-nucleotide changes in mitochondrial DNA and follow maternal inheritance, an entirely different molecular mechanism from repeat expansion within a nuclear gene.
incorrectas.C: Imprinting disorders, such as Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes, result from parent-of-origin-specific gene silencing via epigenetic marks on specific chromosomal regions, not from an expanding repetitive DNA sequence like the CGG repeat in FMR1.
incorrectas.D: Chromosomal nondisjunction disorders, like Down syndrome (trisomy 21), result from failure of chromosomes to separate properly during meiosis, producing an abnormal chromosome number, which is mechanistically distinct from a repeat expansion within a single gene.

preguntas.q: A young boy presents with an elongated face, enlarged jaw, prominent ears, and macroorchidism. Which condition is most likely?

e.correcta: Fragile X syndrome, from CGG repeat expansion silencing FMR1, produces a characteristic phenotype of a long face, large everted ears, an enlarged jaw (macrognathia), and macroorchidism (enlarged testes) after puberty, along with intellectual disability and autism spectrum features. This is the second most common cause of genetic intellectual disability after Down syndrome, and the physical features combined with developmental delay should trigger consideration of FMR1 repeat testing.

incorrectas.A: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) presents with tall stature, gynecomastia, small firm testes, and infertility, which is essentially the opposite testicular finding (small, not enlarged) compared to the macroorchidism seen in Fragile X syndrome.
incorrectas.C: Prader-Willi syndrome, from loss of paternal genes on chromosome 15q11-13, presents with hypotonia, hyperphagia with obesity, and hypogonadism, not the long face, large jaw, and macroorchidism pattern seen in Fragile X syndrome.
incorrectas.D: Noonan syndrome presents with a webbed neck, short stature, and pulmonic stenosis (a "male Turner phenotype" with normal karyotype), a distinct constellation of features unrelated to the FMR1 trinucleotide repeat expansion causing Fragile X syndrome.

preguntas.q: Which trinucleotide sequence is expanded in the FMR1 gene in Fragile X syndrome?

e.correcta: Fragile X syndrome results from expansion of a CGG trinucleotide repeat in the 5' untranslated region of the FMR1 gene, and once the repeat count crosses a critical threshold, the region becomes hypermethylated, silencing FMR1 transcription and causing loss of FMRP protein, which is needed for normal neuronal synaptic function. A useful mnemonic is 'X-Girlfriend's First Aid Helped Ace My Test' — pointing to the X chromosome and the sequence spelled by the repeat and downstream genetics facts.

incorrectas.A: CAG repeat expansion is the hallmark of Huntington disease, occurring in the HTT gene and causing a toxic gain-of-function polyglutamine protein, a completely different gene and disease mechanism from the FMR1 silencing seen in Fragile X syndrome.
incorrectas.C: CTG repeat expansion is characteristic of myotonic dystrophy, located in the DMPK gene, leading to myotonia and muscle wasting rather than the FMR1-related intellectual disability phenotype of Fragile X syndrome.
incorrectas.D: GAA repeat expansion is the trinucleotide repeat found in Friedreich ataxia, located within the FXN (frataxin) gene, causing impaired mitochondrial iron handling and neurodegeneration, distinct from the CGG repeat and FMR1 silencing of Fragile X syndrome.

preguntas.q: What is the second most common genetic cause of intellectual disability, after Down syndrome?

e.correcta: Fragile X syndrome, caused by CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion silencing FMR1, is the second most common identifiable genetic cause of intellectual disability overall, trailing only Down syndrome (trisomy 21), and is in fact the most common inherited (as opposed to sporadic chromosomal) cause of intellectual disability. It is also strongly associated with autism spectrum disorder, making early recognition important for genetic counseling and family planning.

incorrectas.B: Turner syndrome (45,X) is characterized by short stature, ovarian dysgenesis, and webbed neck, but affected individuals typically have normal intelligence, so it is not ranked among the leading genetic causes of intellectual disability.
incorrectas.C: Prader-Willi syndrome causes intellectual disability and hyperphagia due to loss of paternally expressed genes on chromosome 15, but it is considerably less common than Fragile X syndrome as a cause of intellectual disability overall.
incorrectas.D: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is usually associated with normal to mildly reduced intelligence and learning difficulties rather than significant intellectual disability, and it is not the second most common genetic cause of intellectual disability.
