This allows ions to flow directly from cell to cell, so the action potential spreads rapidly across the myocardium as if it were a single functional unit (a functional syncytium), enabling coordinated, near-simultaneous contraction of the atria and then the ventricles rather than a slow cell-by-cell spread.

incorrectas.A: Desmosomes are also found within intercalated discs, but they provide mechanical adhesion between cells (anchoring intermediate filaments) to withstand the mechanical stress of contraction — they do not conduct electrical current between cells the way gap junctions do.
incorrectas.C: Tight junctions seal the space between epithelial cells to prevent paracellular movement of molecules (e.g., in the gut or blood-brain barrier); they are not a feature of cardiac intercalated discs and do not mediate electrical coupling.
incorrectas.D: Focal adhesions anchor cells to the extracellular matrix via integrins, providing structural attachment to the matrix rather than electrical or mechanical connection between two adjacent cardiac cells.

preguntas.q: What term refers to the intrinsic ability of myocardial cells to develop force at a given muscle fiber length?

e.correcta: Inotropism, or contractility, describes the intrinsic strength of contraction generated by myocardial cells independent of preload (fiber stretch) — it reflects the cell's calcium-handling efficiency and cross-bridge cycling capacity. Contractility is modulated by autonomic tone (β1 stimulation increases it), heart rate (positive staircase/Bowditch effect), and drugs (digoxin, catecholamines increase it; beta-blockers decrease it), and it is a key determinant of stroke volume independent of the Frank-Starling (preload) mechanism.

incorrectas.A: Chronotropism refers to changes in heart rate (SA node firing frequency), a distinct property from the force-generating capacity of the myocardium at a given fiber length.
incorrectas.B: Dromotropism refers to changes in conduction velocity through cardiac tissue (especially the AV node), which concerns how fast an impulse travels, not how forcefully the muscle contracts.
incorrectas.D: Lusitropism refers to the rate and completeness of myocardial relaxation during diastole, governed by calcium reuptake into the SR — this is the inverse/complementary property to contraction force, not the force-generating property itself.

preguntas.q: What effect does a positive inotropic agent have on heart contractility?

o.D: Increases only heart rate, not contractility

e.correcta: A positive inotropic effect increases the force of myocardial contraction at any given fiber length, typically by raising intracellular Ca2+ availability to the contractile apparatus. Agents like catecholamines (via β1-cAMP-PKA, which phosphorylates L-type channels and phospholamban) and digoxin (via Na+/K+-ATPase inhibition, raising intracellular Na+ and secondarily reducing Ca2+ extrusion via NCX) both increase contractility this way, shifting the Frank-Starling curve upward and increasing stroke volume for a given preload.

incorrectas.A: Decreased contractility describes a negative inotropic effect (e.g., from beta-blockers or non-dihydropyridine CCBs), the opposite of what a positive inotrope produces.
incorrectas.C: By definition, an inotropic effect (positive or negative) changes contractility; stating there is no change contradicts the premise that a positive inotropic effect is present.
incorrectas.D: Heart rate is a chronotropic property, separate from inotropy; a positive inotrope specifically affects contractile force and may or may not affect heart rate depending on the specific agent's other properties (e.g., pure inotropes can increase force without increasing rate).

preguntas.q: What effect does a negative inotropic agent have on heart contractility?

e.correcta: A negative inotropic effect decreases the force of myocardial contraction. This typically occurs when intracellular Ca2+ availability to the contractile apparatus is reduced — beta-blockers reduce β1-mediated Ca2+ channel phosphorylation, and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers directly block L-type Ca2+ channels, both lowering the calcium transient that drives cross-bridge cycling and shifting the Frank-Starling curve downward, reducing stroke volume for a given preload.

incorrectas.A: Increased contractility describes a positive inotropic effect, produced by agents like catecholamines or digoxin — the opposite of the negative inotropic effect being asked about here.
incorrectas.C: An inotropic effect by definition changes contractility; "no change" is inconsistent with the premise that a negative inotropic effect is occurring.
incorrectas.D: Conduction velocity is a dromotropic property, separate from contractility (inotropy); a negative inotrope's defining feature is reduced force of contraction, not a change in impulse conduction speed (though some drugs, like beta-blockers, do have both negative inotropic and negative dromotropic effects).

preguntas.q: Cardiac contractility correlates directly with the concentration of which intracellular ion?

e.correcta: Cardiac contractility rises and falls in direct proportion to intracellular Ca2+ concentration, since Ca2+ binding to troponin C is the molecular trigger that permits actin-myosin cross-bridge cycling. Any intervention that raises the cytosolic calcium transient — increased extracellular Ca2+ entry through L-type channels, enhanced SR calcium release via ryanodine receptors, or reduced calcium extrusion — increases the force generated per contraction, which is the physiologic basis for how catecholamines and cardiac glycosides enhance contractility.

incorrectas.A: Intracellular K+ primarily sets the resting membrane potential and drives repolarization through outward currents; it does not bind the troponin-tropomyosin complex and therefore does not directly determine contractile force the way calcium does.
incorrectas.C: Intracellular Cl- concentration influences membrane potential in some tissues (via Cl- channels) but has no established direct role in activating the cardiac contractile apparatus.
incorrectas.D: Intracellular HCO3- is primarily involved in acid-base buffering and pH regulation within the cell, not in the calcium-troponin interaction that governs the strength of myocardial contraction.

preguntas.q: Sympathetic stimulation increases myocardial contractility primarily via which receptor?

e.correcta: Sympathetic stimulation increases myocardial contractility mainly through β1 receptors on cardiac myocytes, which are Gs-coupled and activate adenylyl cyclase to raise intracellular cAMP. This activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates L-type calcium channels (increasing Ca2+ influx) and phospholamban (relieving its inhibition of SERCA2a, speeding SR calcium reuptake and relaxation) — the net effect is both a stronger contraction and a faster relaxation, matched to increased heart rate during sympathetic activation.

incorrectas.A: α1 receptors are Gq-coupled and mediate vascular smooth muscle contraction (vasoconstriction) as their predominant cardiovascular effect; they are not the primary receptor responsible for the positive inotropic effect on cardiac myocytes.
incorrectas.B: M2 muscarinic receptors are the parasympathetic (vagal) receptor subtype in the heart, coupled to Gi, and they decrease heart rate and AV conduction — this is the opposite autonomic arm from the sympathetic stimulation described in the question.
incorrectas.D: β2 receptors are present in the heart to a lesser extent and are more important in vascular and bronchial smooth muscle relaxation; while they can contribute modestly to cardiac effects, β1 receptors are the dominant subtype mediating the sympathetic increase in myocardial contractility.

preguntas.q: What effect does an increased heart rate have on cardiac contractility (the force-frequency relationship)?

o.B: Increases contractility, to an extent (positive staircase)

e.correcta: Increased heart rate increases contractility up to a point, a phenomenon known as the positive staircase (Treppe) or Bowditch effect. As heart rate rises, there is less time between beats for Ca2+ to be extruded from the cytosol, so intracellular Ca2+ accumulates progressively with each successive beat, and each subsequent contraction becomes stronger until a new steady state is reached. This force-frequency relationship is one reason tachycardia can transiently augment cardiac output, though at very high rates diastolic filling time becomes so limited that output eventually falls.

incorrectas.A: Progressively decreasing contractility with increased rate describes the opposite (negative staircase) relationship, which is not the normal physiologic response in healthy myocardium — the normal Bowditch effect is a positive, not negative, staircase.
incorrectas.C: Heart rate and contractility are physiologically linked through calcium accumulation kinetics; stating there is no relationship ignores the well-established force-frequency (Treppe) phenomenon.
incorrectas.D: The force-frequency (staircase) relationship and the Frank-Starling (length-tension) relationship are distinct but coexisting mechanisms that both regulate stroke work — increased heart rate does not eliminate or override the preload-dependent Frank-Starling mechanism.

preguntas.q: What effect does a decreased heart rate have on cardiac contractility?

e.correcta: Decreased heart rate decreases contractility, the mirror image of the positive staircase (Treppe/Bowditch) effect seen with tachycardia. With a slower rate, there is more time between beats for intracellular Ca2+ to be extruded via the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger and taken back up into the SR, so less calcium accumulates in the cytosol from beat to beat, and the force generated by each contraction is correspondingly lower. This force-frequency relationship illustrates that heart rate itself is a determinant of contractile strength, separate from autonomic inotropic signaling.

incorrectas.A: Increased contractility with a slower rate would describe a negative staircase relationship, which is not the typical physiologic pattern — normal myocardium shows a positive relationship between rate and force (more beats per minute means more calcium accumulation and more force, up to a point).
incorrectas.C: Heart rate and contractility are mechanistically linked via calcium accumulation kinetics (the force-frequency relationship), so a change in rate is expected to produce a real, measurable change in contractility, not none.
incorrectas.D: Contractility fundamentally depends on intracellular calcium binding to troponin C to permit cross-bridge cycling; it never becomes calcium-independent, regardless of heart rate.

preguntas.q: Cardiac contractility increases with which change in circulating catecholamine levels?

o.C: Catecholamines have no effect on contractility
o.D: Only epinephrine, not norepinephrine, affects contractility

e.correcta: Increased circulating catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine) raise cardiac contractility by binding β1 receptors on myocytes, activating the Gs-adenylyl cyclase-cAMP-PKA cascade. PKA phosphorylates L-type Ca2+ channels (increasing Ca2+ influx during the plateau) and phospholamban (accelerating SR Ca2+ reuptake via SERCA2a), together producing a stronger and faster contraction-relaxation cycle — this is the physiologic mechanism behind the fight-or-flight increase in cardiac performance and the therapeutic rationale for using catecholamine infusions (e.g., dobutamine, epinephrine) in cardiogenic shock.

incorrectas.A: Decreased catecholamines would reduce β1 receptor stimulation and lower cAMP-PKA signaling, thereby decreasing, not increasing, contractility — this is the opposite of the relationship being asked about.
incorrectas.C: Catecholamines have a well-established, clinically significant positive inotropic effect through β1 receptor signaling; stating they have no effect ignores this core physiologic mechanism.
incorrectas.D: Both epinephrine and norepinephrine act on β1 receptors in the heart and increase contractility; norepinephrine is in fact the primary sympathetic neurotransmitter released at cardiac sympathetic nerve terminals, so excluding it from having cardiac inotropic effects is incorrect.

preguntas.q: Cardiac contractility increases with which change in intracellular Ca2+?

o.C: Intracellular Ca2+ has no bearing on contractility
o.D: Only extracellular, not intracellular, Ca2+ matters

e.correcta: Cardiac contractility increases with increased intracellular Ca2+, because Ca2+ is the direct trigger that binds troponin C on the thin filament, displacing tropomyosin and exposing myosin-binding sites on actin to permit cross-bridge cycling. More available calcium means more troponin sites occupied and more cross-bridges cycling per unit time, producing greater force — this is the shared final common pathway by which catecholamines, digoxin, and increased heart rate (via the force-frequency relationship) all enhance contractility.

incorrectas.A: Decreased intracellular Ca2+ would reduce troponin C occupancy and cross-bridge formation, decreasing (not increasing) contractility — this is the opposite of the relationship being described.
incorrectas.C: Intracellular Ca2+ is the central second messenger of excitation-contraction coupling; it has a direct, well-established, dose-dependent relationship with contractile force, not none.
incorrectas.D: While extracellular Ca2+ entering through L-type channels is the initial trigger, it works precisely by raising intracellular Ca2+ (both directly and via triggering SR release) — it is the resulting intracellular calcium level that troponin C actually senses to produce contraction, so intracellular calcium is very much the relevant variable.

preguntas.q: A decrease in extracellular Na+ concentration has what effect on cardiac contractility, and why?

o.A: Increased contractility, because a lower transmembrane Na+ gradient reduces Na+/Ca2+ exchanger activity
o.B: Decreased contractility, because low extracellular Na+ impairs the fast Na+ channels responsible for phase 0 depolarization
o.C: No change, because contractility is independent of extracellular ion concentrations
o.D: Decreased contractility, because the Na+/K+ ATPase becomes hyperactive and hyperpolarizes the myocyte

e.correcta: The cardiac Na+/Ca2+ exchanger (NCX) normally uses the inward Na+ gradient to drive Ca2+ out of the myocyte. When extracellular Na+ falls, the transmembrane Na+ gradient shrinks, so NCX-mediated Ca2+ extrusion slows down. The resulting rise in intracellular Ca2+ increases the amount of Ca2+ available to bind troponin C during systole, boosting contractility — the same end result produced by digoxin, which works indirectly by raising intracellular Na+ instead of lowering extracellular Na+.

incorrectas.B: Fast voltage-gated Na+ channels drive phase 0 upstroke velocity and conduction, not steady-state contractility, and modest reductions in extracellular Na+ used in this context are not primarily testing channel excitability — the tested mechanism is the NCX-mediated calcium effect, which increases (not decreases) contractility.
incorrectas.C: Contractility is highly sensitive to the transmembrane Na+ gradient because that gradient is what powers the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger; changing extracellular Na+ directly changes how much Ca2+ the exchanger can remove from the cytoplasm each cycle.
incorrectas.D: The Na+/K+ ATPase activity is governed by intracellular Na+ and ATP availability, not primarily by extracellular Na+ concentration in this scenario, and its activity does not directly cause hyperpolarization-mediated contractility changes — the key player here is the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, not the Na+/K+ pump.

preguntas.q: What is the overall effect of cardiac glycosides (e.g., digoxin) on myocardial contractility?

o.C: No effect on contractility, only on heart rate
o.D: Biphasic effect — initial decrease followed by delayed increase

e.correcta: Cardiac glycosides are positive inotropes: by inhibiting the Na+/K+ ATPase, they raise intracellular Na+, which in turn slows the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger and raises intracellular Ca2+ available for excitation-contraction coupling. This makes digoxin useful in systolic heart failure, where it improves cardiac output and symptoms, though it does not reduce mortality — it is prescribed for symptom control.

incorrectas.A: A decrease in contractility would be the effect of a negative inotrope (such as a beta-blocker or non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker), which is the opposite of how digoxin works — digoxin raises, not lowers, intracellular calcium available to the contractile apparatus.
incorrectas.C: Digoxin does slow heart rate (via increased vagal tone and slowed AV conduction), but its clinically important cardiac effect on the ventricular myocardium itself is a positive inotropic (contractility-boosting) action, not merely a rate effect.
incorrectas.D: Digoxin's inotropic effect is not classically biphasic — the drug produces a sustained increase in contractility as long as Na+/K+ ATPase remains inhibited and intracellular Ca2+ stays elevated; a biphasic pattern is not the mechanism tested here.

preguntas.q: Cardiac glycosides such as digoxin and ouabain exert their inotropic effect via direct inhibition of which membrane transporter?

e.correcta: Digoxin and ouabain bind to and directly inhibit the Na+-K+ ATPase on the cardiac myocyte membrane, the pump that normally extrudes 3 Na+ in exchange for 2 K+ using ATP hydrolysis. Blocking this pump causes intracellular Na+ to accumulate, which secondarily slows the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger and raises intracellular Ca2+, producing the positive inotropic effect that makes these drugs useful in heart failure and atrial fibrillation rate control.

incorrectas.A: The Na+/Ca2+ exchanger is affected only indirectly — its reduced activity is the downstream consequence of the rising intracellular Na+ caused by Na+-K+ ATPase inhibition, not the direct target of the drug itself.
incorrectas.C: SERCA pumps Ca2+ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum during diastole and is not directly inhibited by cardiac glycosides; the glycoside-induced calcium rise instead comes from reduced NCX-mediated calcium efflux across the plasma membrane.
incorrectas.D: L-type calcium channels mediate calcium influx during the plateau phase of the cardiac action potential and are the target of calcium channel blockers, not cardiac glycosides, which act on the Na+-K+ ATPase instead.

preguntas.q: What happens to intracellular Na+ concentration in cardiac myocytes after treatment with a cardiac glycoside?

o.A: Decreased, due to enhanced Na+-K+ ATPase activity
o.B: Unchanged, since glycosides act only on calcium channels
o.C: Increased, due to inhibition of the Na+-K+ ATPase
o.D: Decreased, due to compensatory upregulation of the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger

e.correcta: Because cardiac glycosides directly inhibit the Na+-K+ ATPase, the pump can no longer efficiently extrude Na+ from the cell, so intracellular Na+ accumulates. This rise in intracellular Na+ is the pivotal first step in the cascade that ultimately increases intracellular Ca2+ and boosts contractility, since a smaller Na+ gradient across the membrane slows the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger that normally removes calcium from the cytoplasm.

incorrectas.A: Enhanced Na+-K+ ATPase activity would lower, not raise, intracellular Na+ — this is the opposite of what cardiac glycosides do, since they inhibit rather than activate this pump.
incorrectas.B: Cardiac glycosides act primarily on the Na+-K+ ATPase, not directly on calcium channels; the rise in intracellular calcium is a downstream consequence of altered sodium handling, not a direct channel effect.
incorrectas.D: The Na+/Ca2+ exchanger is not upregulated by glycosides — instead its activity is functionally reduced because the Na+ gradient it depends on is diminished by Na+-K+ ATPase inhibition, and intracellular Na+ rises rather than falls.

preguntas.q: An increase in intracellular Na+ concentration in cardiac myocytes (e.g., from cardiac glycoside use) directly decreases the activity of which transporter?

e.correcta: The Ca2+-Na+ exchanger (NCX) uses the inward electrochemical gradient for Na+ to power the outward extrusion of Ca2+ from the myocyte. When intracellular Na+ rises (as with digoxin-induced Na+-K+ ATPase inhibition), the Na+ gradient across the membrane shrinks, so NCX has less driving force and extrudes calcium less efficiently — leading to a buildup of intracellular Ca2+ that enhances contractility.

incorrectas.A: SERCA actively pumps cytosolic Ca2+ into the sarcoplasmic reticulum using ATP, a process driven by ATP hydrolysis rather than the Na+ gradient, so a rise in intracellular Na+ does not directly impair SERCA function the way it impairs NCX.
incorrectas.C: The Na+-K+ ATPase is the pump being inhibited by the glycoside in the first place (the cause of the elevated intracellular Na+), not a transporter whose activity changes as a downstream consequence of the Na+ rise itself.
incorrectas.D: The ryanodine receptor releases Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum in response to calcium-induced calcium release and is triggered by L-type calcium channel opening, not by the transmembrane Na+ gradient that governs NCX.

preguntas.q: Decreased activity of the Ca2+-Na+ exchanger (e.g., due to cardiac glycoside therapy) has what effect on intracellular Ca2+ concentration?

o.A: Decreased intracellular Ca2+, because the exchanger normally imports calcium
o.B: No change, since the exchanger does not handle calcium transport
o.C: Increased intracellular Ca2+, because less calcium is extruded from the cell
o.D: Increased intracellular Ca2+, because the exchanger begins pumping calcium in exchange for potassium

e.correcta: The Na+-Ca2+ exchanger's normal job is to extrude calcium from the cytoplasm in exchange for incoming Na+, using the Na+ gradient as its energy source. If this exchanger's activity falls, calcium extrusion slows, so more Ca2+ remains in the cytosol and accumulates in the sarcoplasmic reticulum for release with each beat — this is precisely the mechanism by which digoxin increases contractility (more Ca2+ available to bind troponin C).

incorrectas.A: The exchanger normally removes calcium from the cell, not imports it, so reduced exchanger activity causes calcium to build up inside the cell rather than be depleted.
incorrectas.B: The Na+-Ca2+ exchanger is precisely the transporter responsible for extruding calcium from cardiac myocytes; it is central to calcium handling, not unrelated to it.
incorrectas.D: The exchanger works by swapping Ca2+ for Na+, not potassium, and its direction is normally calcium-out/sodium-in; it does not switch to a calcium-importing, potassium-linked mode when its activity decreases.

preguntas.q: The velocity of cardiac muscle fiber shortening is maximal under which afterload condition?

o.B: When afterload is at its physiologic maximum
o.D: When afterload equals mean arterial pressure

e.correcta: In the force-velocity relationship of cardiac muscle, shortening velocity is inversely related to the load the muscle must overcome — the fiber contracts fastest when it has no resistance to work against. At zero afterload, all of the energy of contraction goes into rapid shortening rather than generating pressure, so velocity is at its theoretical maximum (Vmax), a concept tested alongside the fact that increasing afterload progressively slows the rate of shortening.

incorrectas.A: Preload determines the resting sarcomere length and the force of the subsequent contraction via the Frank-Starling mechanism, but matching preload and afterload does not produce maximal shortening velocity — the relevant variable for velocity is the load being worked against, which is minimized (not balanced) at zero.
incorrectas.B: Shortening velocity is inversely, not directly, related to afterload — as afterload rises toward its physiologic maximum, the muscle shortens more slowly because more of its force is dedicated to overcoming resistance rather than moving quickly.
incorrectas.D: Afterload approximates the pressure the ventricle must generate to eject blood (related to aortic/arterial pressure), and setting afterload equal to mean arterial pressure represents a physiologic, nonzero load — velocity is maximal only when this load is eliminated entirely, not matched to a specific pressure value.

preguntas.q: As afterload on cardiac muscle increases, what happens to the velocity of muscle fiber shortening?

o.C: It remains constant regardless of afterload

e.correcta: The force-velocity relationship describes an inverse curve: as the load the sarcomere must overcome (afterload) increases, the muscle fiber shortens more slowly because a larger fraction of the cross-bridge cycling force is used to generate tension rather than to produce rapid movement. Clinically, this is why conditions that raise afterload (e.g., severe aortic stenosis or hypertension) reduce the rate and extent of ventricular ejection, contributing to reduced stroke volume if contractility cannot compensate.

incorrectas.A: Velocity moves inversely, not directly, with afterload — increasing the load a muscle fiber must contract against slows its shortening rather than speeding it up, the opposite of what this option describes.
incorrectas.C: Shortening velocity is highly sensitive to afterload; it is only at the theoretical extreme of zero afterload that velocity reaches its maximum, and it falls progressively as load increases, so it is not independent of afterload.
incorrectas.D: There is no initial rise in shortening velocity as afterload increases — the relationship is monotonically decreasing across the physiologic range, unlike some other curves in physiology (e.g., length-tension) that do show non-monotonic behavior.

preguntas.q: Which cardiac output variable is defined as the volume of blood ejected by the ventricle during one contraction?

e.correcta: Stroke volume (SV) is the volume of blood ejected from the ventricle with each heartbeat, calculated as end-diastolic volume (EDV) minus end-systolic volume (ESV). It is one of the two determinants of cardiac output (CO = SV x HR) and is influenced by preload, afterload, and contractility — making it central to understanding how conditions like heart failure or valvular disease alter forward blood flow.

incorrectas.A: Cardiac output is the total volume of blood pumped by the heart per minute (SV x HR), a broader measure that incorporates stroke volume along with heart rate, rather than the volume ejected in a single beat.
incorrectas.B: Ejection fraction is the fraction (percentage) of the end-diastolic volume that is ejected as stroke volume (SV/EDV), a ratio rather than an absolute volume, and is used clinically to assess systolic function.
incorrectas.D: End-diastolic volume is the total volume of blood in the ventricle just before contraction begins (representing preload), not the volume that is actually ejected during the subsequent contraction.

preguntas.q: Which cardiac parameter is defined as the fraction of end-diastolic volume that is ejected with each stroke volume?

e.correcta: Ejection fraction (EF = SV/EDV) expresses stroke volume as a proportion of the total blood volume present in the ventricle at the end of diastole, normally 55-70%. It is the single most widely used clinical index of systolic function, and a reduced EF (e.g., <40%) defines heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, correlating with impaired contractile performance of the myocardium.

incorrectas.A: Stroke volume is the absolute volume of blood ejected per beat (EDV minus ESV), not a fraction or ratio — ejection fraction normalizes stroke volume to ventricular size, which stroke volume alone does not do.
incorrectas.B: Cardiac index normalizes cardiac output to body surface area (CO/BSA) to allow comparison across patients of different sizes; it is not a measure of what fraction of ventricular volume is ejected.
incorrectas.D: Fractional shortening is an echocardiographic measure of the percent change in ventricular diameter (not volume) between diastole and systole, a related but distinct index from the volume-based ejection fraction.

preguntas.q: Which equation correctly calculates stroke volume?

e.correcta: Stroke volume is the difference between the volume in the ventricle just before contraction (end-diastolic volume, EDV) and the volume remaining just after contraction (end-systolic volume, ESV): SV = EDV - ESV. This subtraction reflects exactly how much blood was physically ejected during systole, and it is the numerator used to calculate ejection fraction (SV/EDV).

incorrectas.A: Adding EDV and ESV would not represent a physiologically meaningful quantity — stroke volume specifically reflects the blood that leaves the ventricle, which requires subtracting the residual (end-systolic) volume from the starting (end-diastolic) volume, not summing them.
incorrectas.C: Dividing EDV by ESV produces a dimensionless ratio, not a volume, and does not correspond to any standard cardiac output variable; stroke volume must be expressed as a volume (mL), which requires subtraction rather than division.
incorrectas.D: SV = CO/HR is actually an alternative, algebraically valid way to derive stroke volume once cardiac output and heart rate are known (rearranging CO = SV x HR), but it is not the definitional equation relating stroke volume to ventricular volumes as tested here.

preguntas.q: Which equation is used to calculate ejection fraction?

e.correcta: Ejection fraction is calculated as stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume (EF = SV/EDV), expressing what fraction of the blood present before contraction is actually ejected. Since SV = EDV - ESV, this ratio directly reflects systolic pumping efficiency, and a normal EF (55-70%) confirms adequate systolic function, while a low EF signals systolic heart failure.

incorrectas.A: Inverting the ratio (EDV/SV) would produce a number greater than 1 in normal physiology, which does not match the definition of ejection fraction as a percentage of blood ejected relative to the starting volume.
incorrectas.C: CO/HR actually equals stroke volume itself (since CO = SV x HR), not ejection fraction — this expression gives an absolute volume, not the fractional relationship between SV and EDV.
incorrectas.D: ESV/EDV represents the fraction of blood remaining in the ventricle after systole, which is the complement of ejection fraction (roughly 1 - EF), not ejection fraction itself.

preguntas.q: A normal ejection fraction is typically greater than what percentage?

e.correcta: Normal ejection fraction is generally defined as greater than 55% (with a typical range of 55-70%), reflecting a ventricle that ejects the majority of its end-diastolic volume with each beat. This threshold matters clinically because an EF below roughly 40% defines heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, while an EF in the 41-49% range is considered borderline/mildly reduced.

incorrectas.A: An EF of 40% or below is the threshold used to diagnose heart failure with reduced ejection fraction — it is well below the normal range, not the lower limit of normal.
incorrectas.B: 45% falls within the borderline/mildly reduced EF category used in some heart failure classifications, still below the accepted lower limit of normal ejection fraction.
incorrectas.D: 70% is within (near the upper end of) the normal EF range, but it is not the standard lower cutoff quoted for normal ejection fraction — 55% is the typically cited threshold.

preguntas.q: Which equation is used to calculate cardiac output from a patient's stroke volume and heart rate?

e.correcta: Cardiac output equals stroke volume multiplied by heart rate (CO = SV x HR), reflecting the total volume of blood the heart pumps per minute as the product of how much blood is ejected per beat and how many beats occur per minute. This relationship explains why both bradycardia (low HR) and reduced stroke volume (e.g., from systolic dysfunction or hypovolemia) can each independently lower cardiac output and blood pressure.

incorrectas.A: Dividing stroke volume by heart rate does not correspond to any standard hemodynamic variable and would actually shrink as heart rate rises, which is the opposite of how cardiac output behaves with a rising heart rate (up to a point).
incorrectas.C: CO = MAP/TPR is a rearrangement of the relationship MAP = CO x TPR, which relates cardiac output to blood pressure and resistance — a valid but different equation from the one relating CO directly to stroke volume and heart rate.
incorrectas.D: Subtracting heart rate from stroke volume mixes two variables with different units (mL vs beats/min) in a way that has no physiologic meaning; cardiac output must be derived by multiplication, not subtraction, of these two variables.

preguntas.q: What effect does increased venous return have on ventricular end-diastolic volume (EDV)?

o.A: Decreased EDV, due to reflex tachycardia shortening diastolic filling time
o.C: No change, since EDV is fixed by ventricular compliance alone
o.D: Decreased EDV, due to increased atrial natriuretic peptide release

e.correcta: Venous return delivers blood back to the right heart and, ultimately, fills the ventricles during diastole; more venous return means more blood accumulates in the ventricle before the next contraction, directly raising EDV. Because EDV is the physiologic correlate of preload, this is the mechanistic basis of the Frank-Starling law — increased venous return stretches the sarcomeres further, which (within physiologic limits) increases stroke volume as well.

incorrectas.A: While very high venous return can sometimes coincide with tachycardia in certain states, the direct and tested relationship here is that more blood returning to the heart increases the volume available to fill the ventricle, raising rather than lowering EDV.
incorrectas.C: Ventricular compliance affects how much the ventricle's pressure rises for a given increase in volume, but EDV itself is not fixed — it varies directly with how much blood is delivered to the ventricle via venous return during diastole.
incorrectas.D: Atrial natriuretic peptide is released in response to atrial stretch and promotes natriuresis and vasodilation to reduce volume over time, but it does not acutely prevent the immediate rise in EDV that results from increased venous return filling the ventricle.

preguntas.q: An increase in cardiac contractility (e.g., from catecholamines or digoxin) shifts the Frank-Starling curve in which direction?

o.C: It flattens the curve without shifting it
o.D: Downward only, without a horizontal shift

e.correcta: Positive inotropes such as catecholamines and digoxin increase the force generated at any given preload, which shifts the entire Frank-Starling (cardiac function) curve upward — meaning more stroke volume/cardiac output is produced for the same EDV — and slightly to the left, since a greater fraction of blood is now ejected at any given filling volume. This upward shift is the graphical representation of enhanced contractility independent of preload changes.

incorrectas.A: A downward and rightward shift is the pattern seen with decreased contractility (e.g., heart failure), the opposite direction from what increased contractility produces — this describes a failing heart producing less output for a given preload.
incorrectas.C: The Starling curve does not simply flatten with increased contractility; it is displaced as a whole (upward/leftward), preserving its general shape but showing greater output at every preload value.
incorrectas.D: Increased contractility does not shift the curve downward at all, and describing it as a purely vertical change without any horizontal component misses the leftward shift that also occurs with enhanced inotropy.

preguntas.q: A decrease in cardiac contractility, such as occurs in heart failure, shifts the Frank-Starling curve in which direction?

o.B: It has no effect on the curve, only on heart rate
o.D: Rightward only, with the same peak height

e.correcta: In heart failure, the failing myocardium generates less stroke volume/cardiac output for any given end-diastolic volume, which shifts the Frank-Starling curve downward. This is why patients with systolic heart failure can develop fluid overload (high EDV from venous congestion) yet still have a reduced cardiac output — they sit on a lower, flatter curve where increasing preload further yields diminishing returns and worsening pulmonary/systemic congestion.

incorrectas.A: An upward and leftward shift is characteristic of increased contractility (e.g., catecholamines or digoxin), the opposite of the depressed pump function seen in heart failure.
incorrectas.B: Decreased contractility directly alters the pressure-volume relationship captured by the Starling curve itself (independent of heart rate); heart rate changes are a separate compensatory mechanism, not the reason the curve shifts.
incorrectas.D: The curve in heart failure does not merely shift rightward while preserving peak output — it drops downward in peak height and plateaus earlier, showing that the heart cannot generate a normal stroke volume even at higher preloads.

preguntas.q: During exercise, sympathetic stimulation shifts the cardiac (Frank-Starling) function curve in which direction?

o.C: There is no shift; only heart rate changes during exercise
o.D: Downward, due to increased afterload from vasoconstriction

e.correcta: Exercise increases sympathetic outflow and circulating catecholamines, which enhance myocardial contractility. Like other positive inotropic states, this shifts the Starling curve upward (and slightly leftward), allowing the heart to generate a greater stroke volume/cardiac output at any given preload — a key adaptation that, together with increased heart rate and venous return, allows cardiac output to rise several-fold during exercise.

incorrectas.A: A downward and rightward shift describes worsening pump function (e.g., heart failure), the opposite of what happens physiologically during exercise when contractility is enhanced by sympathetic drive.
incorrectas.C: While heart rate does rise substantially during exercise, contractility also increases due to sympathetic stimulation of the myocardium itself, and this is represented graphically as an upward shift of the Starling curve, not merely a rate change.
incorrectas.D: Exercise causes skeletal muscle vasodilation (via local metabolites and beta-2 effects) that lowers, rather than raises, total peripheral resistance/afterload in the exercising vascular beds, and increased contractility—not increased afterload—is what shifts the curve upward.

preguntas.q: Which phase of the cardiac cycle occurs between mitral valve closure and aortic valve opening, and represents the first phase of the cycle?

e.correcta: Isovolumetric contraction begins immediately after the mitral valve closes (marking the start of systole, S1) and ends when the aortic valve opens. During this phase both the mitral and aortic valves are closed, so ventricular pressure rises steeply as the myocardium contracts around a fixed volume of blood — no ejection occurs until ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure and forces the aortic valve open.

incorrectas.A: Isovolumetric relaxation is the mirror-image phase occurring later in the cycle, between aortic valve closure and mitral valve opening, when the ventricle relaxes at constant volume before diastolic filling resumes — not the phase right after mitral closure.
incorrectas.B: Rapid ventricular filling occurs during diastole, just after the mitral valve opens, when blood rushes into the relaxed ventricle — this is a filling phase with the mitral valve open, unlike isovolumetric contraction where both valves are shut.
incorrectas.D: Ventricular ejection is the phase that follows isovolumetric contraction, occurring once the aortic valve has opened and blood is actively being pumped out of the ventricle — it comes after, not during, the interval between mitral closure and aortic opening.

preguntas.q: Which phase of the cardiac cycle occurs between aortic valve opening and aortic valve closing, representing the second phase of the cycle?

e.correcta: Ventricular ejection is the phase during which the aortic valve is open and blood is actively expelled from the left ventricle into the aorta, beginning once ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure and ending when ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure, closing the aortic valve (contributing to S2). This phase can be subdivided into rapid and reduced ejection and is the phase during which stroke volume is actually delivered to the systemic circulation.

incorrectas.A: Isovolumetric contraction precedes ejection — it is the period with both valves closed while ventricular pressure builds, ending exactly when the aortic valve opens and ejection (this phase) begins.
incorrectas.C: Reduced filling (diastasis) is a late diastolic phase where ventricular filling slows before atrial contraction, occurring well after ejection has ended and the ventricle has already relaxed and refilled.
incorrectas.D: Isovolumetric relaxation occurs immediately after aortic valve closure, when the ventricle relaxes with both valves shut — this comes right after ejection ends, not during the ejection phase itself.

preguntas.q: Which phase of the cardiac cycle occurs between aortic valve closing and mitral valve opening, representing the third phase of the cycle?

e.correcta: Isovolumetric relaxation begins right after the aortic valve closes (generating S2) and continues until ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure, at which point the mitral valve opens. During this interval both valves are closed and ventricular volume stays constant while the myocardium relaxes and pressure drops rapidly, setting the stage for the mitral valve to open and diastolic filling to begin.

incorrectas.A: Isovolumetric contraction is the analogous early-systolic phase (both valves closed, volume constant) but it occurs between mitral closure and aortic opening — the opposite end of the cardiac cycle from isovolumetric relaxation.
incorrectas.B: Rapid ventricular filling occurs immediately after the mitral valve opens, once isovolumetric relaxation has ended, so it comes after (not during) the isovolumetric relaxation phase.
incorrectas.D: Reduced filling (diastasis) is a later diastolic phase, occurring after rapid filling has already slowed, well past the isovolumetric relaxation period that precedes mitral valve opening.

preguntas.q: Which phase of the cardiac cycle occurs just after mitral valve opening, representing the fourth phase of the cycle?

e.correcta: Rapid ventricular filling begins as soon as the mitral valve opens, when the pressure gradient between the relaxed, low-pressure left atrium and ventricle is greatest, allowing blood to rush passively into the ventricle. This phase accounts for the majority of ventricular filling in a normal heart and corresponds to the rapid rise seen early in the ventricular volume tracing of the cardiac cycle diagram.

incorrectas.A: Reduced filling (diastasis) is the phase that follows rapid filling, once the atrioventricular pressure gradient has largely equalized and filling slows to a trickle — it comes later in diastole, not immediately after mitral valve opening.
incorrectas.C: Isovolumetric relaxation is the phase that precedes mitral valve opening (both valves still closed), ending exactly when the valve opens and rapid filling (this phase) begins.
incorrectas.D: Atrial systole is the final phase of ventricular filling, occurring at the end of diastole to deliver the last portion of blood ('atrial kick'), well after rapid filling and diastasis have already occurred.

preguntas.q: Which phase of the cardiac cycle occurs just before mitral valve closure, representing the fifth phase of the cycle?

e.correcta: Reduced filling (diastasis) follows the initial burst of rapid ventricular filling, once atrial and ventricular pressures have largely equalized so blood continues to enter the ventricle only slowly. It is the longest phase of diastole at slow heart rates and ends when the mitral valve closes as ventricular contraction begins (often aided by the atrial kick immediately beforehand) — reduced filling is markedly shortened during tachycardia, which is part of why fast heart rates impair ventricular filling.

incorrectas.A: Rapid ventricular filling is the phase immediately preceding diastasis, characterized by a fast influx of blood right after mitral valve opening — it occurs earlier in diastole, not right before mitral valve closure.
incorrectas.B: Isovolumetric contraction occurs after mitral valve closure, not before it — it is the systolic phase where the ventricle contracts with both valves shut, following (not preceding) the point at which the mitral valve actually closes.
incorrectas.D: Ventricular ejection is a systolic phase that occurs later in the cycle, after isovolumetric contraction and aortic valve opening — it is far removed in time from the diastolic phase just before mitral valve closure.

preguntas.q: Preload on the ventricle is best approximated by which physiologic parameter?

e.correcta: Preload refers to the degree of ventricular wall stretch before contraction, which is directly related to the volume of blood filling the ventricle at the end of diastole — hence EDV serves as its clinical and physiologic proxy. Because the Frank-Starling law states that increased sarcomere stretch (higher EDV) leads to a stronger subsequent contraction, EDV is the variable used to plot preload on the x-axis of the cardiac function curve.

incorrectas.A: Mean arterial pressure reflects the pressure the ventricle must pump against during ejection and is more closely tied to afterload, not the stretch of the ventricular wall before contraction.
incorrectas.B: End-systolic volume is the blood remaining in the ventricle after contraction has already occurred, so it reflects how completely the heart emptied — it is not the measure of stretch before the contraction begins, which is what preload describes.
incorrectas.D: Total peripheral resistance is a determinant of afterload (the resistance the ventricle must overcome to eject blood), not a measure of ventricular filling or wall stretch before systole.

preguntas.q: What effect does increased venous return have on ventricular preload?

o.A: Decreased preload, due to baroreceptor-mediated vasodilation
o.B: No effect, since preload depends only on afterload
o.D: Decreased preload, due to reduced time for diastolic filling

e.correcta: Since preload is approximated by ventricular end-diastolic volume, and venous return is what fills the ventricle during diastole, more venous return directly increases the volume (and thus the stretch) present in the ventricle before contraction — increasing preload. This is the basis of the Frank-Starling mechanism, in which increased venous return (e.g., with fluid administration or exercise) raises preload and, up to a physiologic limit, boosts stroke volume.

incorrectas.A: Baroreceptor reflexes respond to changes in blood pressure and can influence heart rate and vascular tone, but the direct, mechanical effect of increased venous return on the ventricle is to increase its filling volume, not decrease it via a reflex vasodilatory pathway.
incorrectas.B: Preload is determined by ventricular filling (venous return), while afterload is a separate variable related to the resistance against which the ventricle ejects blood — the two are physiologically distinct, and preload is not dependent on afterload.
incorrectas.D: Increased venous return does not shorten diastolic filling time; if anything, more blood returning to the heart simply means more volume is delivered during the same diastolic interval, increasing rather than decreasing the resulting EDV/preload.

preguntas.q: Afterload on the left ventricle is most closely approximated clinically by which of the following?

e.correcta: Afterload is the wall stress (tension) the ventricle must generate to eject blood, and by the Law of Laplace it scales with the pressure the ventricle must overcome to open the aortic valve and push blood forward. Because that pressure is set largely by the resistance and pressure in the systemic arterial system, mean arterial pressure serves as a practical clinical proxy for afterload — an acutely hypertensive patient effectively hands the left ventricle a higher afterload to work against.

incorrectas.A: Left atrial pressure reflects the pressure the left ventricle experiences during diastolic filling (contributing to preload, not the resistance it ejects against), so it does not approximate afterload.
incorrectas.C: Central venous pressure reflects right atrial/venous filling pressure and is used as a surrogate for right ventricular preload, not left ventricular afterload.
incorrectas.D: Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is used to estimate left atrial pressure (and thus LV preload) via a catheter wedged in a pulmonary artery branch — it is a preload measure, not an afterload measure.

preguntas.q: A patient develops acute severe hypertension with a markedly elevated aortic pressure. What is the expected effect on left ventricular afterload?

e.correcta: Afterload is the resistance (pressure) the ventricle must overcome to eject blood into the aorta; when aortic pressure rises, the ventricle must generate more wall tension/pressure before the aortic valve opens and throughout ejection, so afterload increases. On a pressure-volume loop this manifests as a higher aortic valve opening point and a steeper, taller ejection line, which — all else equal — reduces stroke volume for a given contractility and preload.

incorrectas.A: Decreased afterload would occur with a fall in aortic/systemic vascular resistance (e.g., vasodilator therapy or septic shock), the opposite of what happens when aortic pressure rises.
incorrectas.B: Afterload is directly defined by the pressure the ventricle must overcome, so a rise in aortic pressure necessarily changes afterload rather than leaving it unaffected.
incorrectas.D: Afterload remains a well-defined, quantifiable parameter (approximated by mean arterial/aortic pressure) regardless of how high it climbs; it does not become 'undefined' with hypertension.

preguntas.q: Per the Frank-Starling mechanism, what happens to stroke volume when ventricular preload increases?

o.D: Stroke volume becomes independent of contractility

e.correcta: Increased preload stretches cardiac sarcomeres toward their optimal length, increasing the sensitivity of troponin C for calcium and the number of effective actin-myosin cross-bridges formed, which increases the force of contraction — the Frank-Starling law. On a pressure-volume loop, higher preload shifts the end-diastolic volume rightward, and with afterload and contractility held constant, the ventricle ejects a larger stroke volume.

incorrectas.A: A decrease in stroke volume with rising preload would violate the Frank-Starling relationship and is instead what happens when afterload rises or contractility falls, not when preload increases.
incorrectas.C: Stroke volume is not preload-independent — that description would apply to a purely rate-limited or fixed-output state, which does not reflect normal ventricular physiology governed by the length-tension relationship.
incorrectas.D: Stroke volume actually depends on the interplay of preload, afterload, and contractility together; preload does not make stroke volume independent of contractility, it interacts with it through the same length-tension mechanism.

preguntas.q: If afterload increases while preload and contractility remain constant, what happens to stroke volume?

o.D: Stroke volume becomes equal to end-diastolic volume

e.correcta: Increased afterload means the ventricle must generate more pressure before the aortic valve opens, leaving less of the contractile energy available to eject volume before the myocardium reaches its limit of shortening. On a pressure-volume loop, a higher afterload raises the pressure at which ejection begins and shifts the end-systolic pressure-volume relationship point up and to the right, leaving a larger end-systolic volume and therefore a smaller stroke volume for a given end-diastolic volume.

incorrectas.A: Stroke volume increasing with higher afterload would require either more preload or greater contractility to compensate; by itself, isolated afterload elevation reduces stroke volume, the classic principle exploited when vasodilators like ACE inhibitors reduce afterload to improve forward flow in heart failure.
incorrectas.B: Stroke volume is not independent of afterload — it is one of the three major determinants (preload, afterload, contractility), and holding the other two fixed while raising afterload measurably lowers stroke volume.
incorrectas.D: Stroke volume equaling end-diastolic volume would imply an ejection fraction of 100% (no residual end-systolic volume), which is physiologically impossible and the opposite of what increased afterload produces (it increases end-systolic volume).

preguntas.q: What effect does an acute increase in afterload have on left ventricular end-systolic volume?

e.correcta: With higher afterload, the ventricle must eject against greater resistance, so it cannot shorten as much before intraventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure and the aortic valve closes, leaving more blood behind at the end of systole. This is reflected on the pressure-volume loop as the ejection phase terminating at a higher volume along the end-systolic pressure-volume relationship, directly producing the fall in stroke volume seen with increased afterload.

incorrectas.A: A decrease in end-systolic volume would occur with increased contractility (which shifts the end-systolic pressure-volume relationship line leftward, allowing more complete emptying), the opposite mechanism from an afterload increase.
incorrectas.C: End-systolic volume is directly tied to how far the ventricle can eject against resistance, so it is not unaffected by afterload — afterload is one of its principal determinants along with contractility.
incorrectas.D: Ventricular volume cannot be negative; end-systolic volume is always a positive residual volume of blood remaining in the ventricle after ejection, even when contractility is very high.

preguntas.q: A positive inotropic agent increases myocardial contractility. What is the expected effect on left ventricular end-systolic volume?

e.correcta: Increased contractility enhances calcium-troponin C interaction and cross-bridge cycling independent of fiber length, allowing the ventricle to generate more force and shorten further for a given afterload. This shifts the end-systolic pressure-volume relationship leftward (steeper slope), meaning the ventricle empties to a smaller residual volume — this is precisely why inotropes like dobutamine or digoxin increase stroke volume and ejection fraction in heart failure.

incorrectas.A: An increase in end-systolic volume is what happens with increased afterload or decreased contractility (e.g., in systolic heart failure), the opposite effect of a positive inotrope.
incorrectas.B: End-systolic volume is not independent of contractility — it is one of the two major determinants of ESV (along with afterload), and the entire clinical rationale for inotropic drugs is to reduce it and improve emptying.
incorrectas.D: End-systolic volume equaling end-diastolic volume would mean zero stroke volume and 0% ejection fraction, the opposite of what a contractility increase produces — greater contractility improves, not abolishes, ejection.

preguntas.q: An increase in myocardial contractility (e.g., from sympathetic stimulation) has what effect on stroke volume, assuming preload and afterload are unchanged?

e.correcta: Increased contractility (e.g., via beta-1 adrenergic stimulation increasing intracellular calcium influx and calcium-induced calcium release) lets the ventricle generate more force and shorten more completely at any given preload and afterload. This lowers end-systolic volume while end-diastolic volume stays the same, so the difference between them — stroke volume — rises, along with ejection fraction.

incorrectas.A: A fall in stroke volume with increased contractility would be paradoxical; decreased stroke volume instead results from reduced contractility (e.g., in systolic heart failure) or increased afterload, not from a positive inotropic state.
incorrectas.C: Stroke volume is not contractility-independent; contractility is one of the three principal determinants of stroke volume (along with preload and afterload), so changing it changes stroke volume when the others are fixed.
incorrectas.D: Stroke volume falling to zero would imply cardiac arrest or complete outflow obstruction, essentially the opposite of what enhanced contractility produces, since enhanced contractility improves ejection.

preguntas.q: What is the effect of increased preload on ejection fraction, assuming contractility and afterload remain constant?

e.correcta: Increased preload stretches the sarcomeres and, via the Frank-Starling mechanism, increases the force of contraction, so stroke volume rises more than proportionally to the rise in end-diastolic volume when afterload and contractility are fixed. Since ejection fraction = stroke volume / end-diastolic volume, this proportionally larger stroke volume increase translates into a modest increase in ejection fraction — a distinct point from stroke volume itself, which behaves this way primarily due to length-dependent activation.

incorrectas.A: A fall in ejection fraction with rising preload would suggest impaired systolic function (as in dilated cardiomyopathy where the ventricle cannot generate proportionally more force despite stretch), not the normal Frank-Starling response being tested here.
incorrectas.B: Ejection fraction is not preload-independent in the normal heart; because the Frank-Starling mechanism boosts contractile force with greater stretch, ejection fraction actually rises slightly rather than staying flat as preload increases.
incorrectas.D: Ejection fraction cannot exceed 100%, since stroke volume can never surpass the total end-diastolic volume available to eject; even maximal contractile enhancement only approaches, not exceeds, complete emptying.

preguntas.q: Myocardial oxygen consumption is highest during which phase of the cardiac cycle?

e.correcta: Isovolumetric contraction is the phase in which the ventricle develops maximal tension and pressure while both valves are closed and volume does not change, meaning essentially all the metabolic energy is converted into generating wall tension rather than external mechanical work of ejection. Because myocardial O2 consumption correlates most strongly with wall tension (afterload) developed rather than the work of moving blood, this isovolumetric, high-tension, no-flow phase carries the greatest oxygen demand — clinically relevant because ischemia is worsened by anything that raises this tension (e.g., hypertension, tachycardia).

incorrectas.A: Isovolumetric relaxation is when the ventricle is relaxing with both valves closed and pressure falling rapidly; energy demand here is lower than during active tension generation in isovolumetric contraction.
incorrectas.B: Rapid ventricular filling is a passive, largely energy-cheap phase driven by the pressure gradient between atrium and relaxed ventricle, not one of active tension generation, so it has comparatively low oxygen demand.
incorrectas.D: Diastasis is the slow, passive filling period in mid-diastole with minimal pressure change and low myocardial workload, making it one of the lowest oxygen-demand phases of the cycle.

preguntas.q: According to the Law of Laplace, cardiac wall stress is best represented by which formula?

e.correcta: The Law of Laplace for a thick-walled sphere states wall stress equals pressure times radius divided by twice the wall thickness (P×r / 2H): rising intracavitary pressure or chamber radius increases the tension the wall must bear, while greater wall thickness distributes that tension over more muscle mass and reduces stress per unit area. This relationship explains why a dilated, thin-walled ventricle (large r, small H) is mechanically disadvantaged compared to a concentrically hypertrophied one facing the same pressure.

incorrectas.A: Adding pressure and radius rather than multiplying them, and omitting the factor of 2, does not correspond to any recognized form of the Laplace relationship and would not correctly predict how stress scales with chamber dilation or pressure overload.
incorrectas.C: Inverting the relationship so that stress is proportional to 1/(r×H) misrepresents the physics — increasing radius should raise wall stress (as more surface area must contain the same pressure), not lower it as this formula implies.
incorrectas.D: This puts wall thickness in the numerator and pressure/radius in the denominator, effectively reversing the true relationship in which greater thickness protects against (reduces) wall stress rather than being what stress is proportional to.

preguntas.q: Myocardial oxygen consumption correlates most directly with which of the following ventricular properties?

o.C: Tension (wall stress) developed by the ventricle

e.correcta: Cardiac myocytes consume ATP mainly to generate cross-bridge cycling and force (tension), so the greater the wall tension the ventricle must develop — determined by intraventricular pressure and chamber radius via the Law of Laplace — the more oxygen it consumes, largely independent of how much external stroke work is actually produced. This is why isovolumetric contraction (high tension, no ejection) is so oxygen-costly, and why conditions raising wall tension, such as hypertension or ventricular dilation, increase myocardial O2 demand and predispose to ischemia.

incorrectas.A: Ejection fraction reflects how effectively the ventricle empties relative to its filled volume, but it is a downstream index of pump performance, not the direct driver of oxygen consumption the way developed tension is.
incorrectas.B: Heart rate variability reflects autonomic balance and beat-to-beat timing, not the mechanical tension the myocardium generates, so it is not the parameter that tracks with oxygen demand in this context.
incorrectas.D: Diastolic filling time affects how much preload the ventricle receives before the next contraction, but oxygen consumption is driven by the tension generated during contraction, not by how long filling takes.

preguntas.q: A patient with poorly controlled hypertension has chronically elevated aortic pressure (afterload). What effect does this have on myocardial O2 consumption?

o.D: O2 consumption becomes independent of pressure

e.correcta: By the Law of Laplace, higher aortic pressure requires the ventricle to generate greater wall tension to overcome it and open the aortic valve, and because myocardial oxygen consumption tracks closely with developed tension, chronically elevated afterload raises O2 demand. This is a key reason uncontrolled hypertension predisposes to demand ischemia and, over time, drives compensatory ventricular hypertrophy that itself carries further metabolic cost.

incorrectas.A: A fall in O2 consumption would be expected with afterload reduction (e.g., vasodilator or ACE inhibitor therapy), the opposite physiologic direction from a rise in aortic pressure.
incorrectas.B: Oxygen consumption is not insensitive to afterload — wall tension (a primary driver of O2 demand) is directly proportional to intraventricular pressure via the Laplace relationship, so raising aortic pressure necessarily raises consumption.
incorrectas.D: Myocardial oxygen consumption remains pressure-dependent at essentially all physiologic and pathologic pressures; it does not become decoupled from afterload even with chronic hypertension.

preguntas.q: A dilated cardiomyopathy patient has an enlarged left ventricular chamber (increased radius). How does this affect myocardial O2 consumption?

o.C: O2 consumption is unaffected by chamber size
o.D: O2 consumption depends only on heart rate

e.correcta: By the Law of Laplace (wall stress = P × r / 2H), an increase in ventricular radius directly raises wall tension for any given intraventricular pressure and wall thickness, and because myocardial oxygen consumption tracks with tension developed, a dilated ventricle needs more oxygen to generate the same pressure than a normal-sized one. This is part of why ventricular dilation in heart failure is self-perpetuating — the dilated, thin-walled chamber is less energy-efficient and more prone to ongoing ischemic stress.

incorrectas.A: A decrease in O2 consumption would require either a smaller radius or a thicker wall (both reducing wall stress), the opposite of what happens with chamber dilation, which increases the radius term in the Laplace equation.
incorrectas.C: Chamber size is a direct variable in the Laplace relationship, so it is not irrelevant to oxygen demand — a larger radius mechanically forces the ventricle to generate more tension (and consume more O2) to reach the same pressure.
incorrectas.D: While heart rate is also an important determinant of myocardial oxygen demand, it is not the only factor — wall tension from radius and pressure contributes independently, so consumption cannot be said to depend only on rate.

preguntas.q: A patient is started on a positive inotropic agent to improve cardiac contractility. What effect does this have on myocardial oxygen consumption?

o.D: O2 consumption depends solely on preload

e.correcta: Increased contractility requires more calcium cycling and cross-bridge formation per beat to generate greater force, and this added ATP-dependent cross-bridge activity increases myocardial oxygen consumption even at a fixed heart rate, preload, and afterload. This is clinically important because inotropes, while improving cardiac output, can worsen ischemia in patients with limited coronary reserve by raising the heart's oxygen demand.

incorrectas.A: A decrease in oxygen consumption would be expected with negative inotropes (e.g., beta-blockers) that reduce contractile force and thus cross-bridge cycling, the opposite of what a positive inotrope produces.
incorrectas.C: Contractility is one of the major independent determinants of myocardial O2 demand (along with heart rate and wall tension), so enhancing it changes — rather than leaves unchanged — total oxygen consumption.
incorrectas.D: Myocardial oxygen consumption is multifactorial, driven by heart rate, wall tension (from preload and afterload), and contractility together; it is not determined by preload alone, and here the change in contractility itself is what drives the shift in demand.

preguntas.q: A patient develops sinus tachycardia. What effect does the increased heart rate have on myocardial oxygen consumption?

o.C: O2 consumption is unaffected by rate
o.D: O2 consumption depends only on stroke volume

e.correcta: Heart rate is one of the three principal determinants of myocardial oxygen consumption (along with wall tension and contractility); more beats per minute means more cycles of cross-bridge formation and calcium cycling per unit time, directly raising total ATP and O2 demand. This is precisely why beta-blockers, which slow heart rate, are protective in ischemic heart disease — they reduce myocardial oxygen demand and lengthen diastolic coronary filling time.

incorrectas.A: A decrease in oxygen consumption with a faster heart rate would be physiologically backwards; oxygen demand rises, not falls, with tachycardia because more contractile cycles occur per minute.
incorrectas.C: Heart rate is not irrelevant to oxygen demand — it multiplies the oxygen cost of each individual beat by the number of beats per minute, making it one of the most clinically manipulable determinants of myocardial O2 consumption.
incorrectas.D: Oxygen consumption depends on heart rate, wall tension, and contractility together, not stroke volume alone; even if stroke volume were unchanged, a faster rate alone increases total oxygen consumption.

preguntas.q: In a patient with chronic systemic hypertension, concentric left ventricular hypertrophy develops as a compensatory response. What is the primary mechanism by which this hypertrophy helps the ventricle cope with the pressure overload?

o.A: Increased wall thickness decreases wall stress by offsetting increased wall tension
o.B: Increased chamber radius decreases wall stress
o.C: Decreased wall thickness reduces the energy cost of contraction
o.D: Increased heart rate reduces wall tension

e.correcta: By the Law of Laplace (wall stress = pressure × radius / 2 × wall thickness), chronic hypertension raises intraventricular pressure and thus wall tension; the myocardium compensates by adding sarcomeres in parallel to thicken the wall, which increases the denominator of the equation and normalizes wall stress despite the higher pressure. This concentric hypertrophy also allows the ventricle to generate the higher pressures needed to overcome elevated aortic pressure, though over time it can impair diastolic compliance and eventually progress to heart failure.

incorrectas.B: An increased chamber radius would actually increase, not decrease, wall stress according to the Laplace relationship (radius is in the numerator); this describes eccentric dilation, which is a maladaptive response to volume overload, not the concentric hypertrophic response to pressure overload.
incorrectas.C: Decreasing wall thickness would raise wall stress per the Laplace equation (thickness is in the denominator), the opposite of the protective adaptation seen in concentric hypertrophy, and it would not by itself reduce contractile energy cost.
incorrectas.D: Heart rate is not a variable in the Laplace wall stress equation; while it affects overall myocardial oxygen consumption, it does not mechanically offset the increased wall tension from elevated pressure the way increased wall thickness does.

preguntas.q: In response to chronically increased afterload from hypertension, the left ventricle undergoes which structural change to reduce wall tension?

e.correcta: By the Law of Laplace (T = P × r / 2H), the ventricle can offset a chronic rise in pressure by increasing wall thickness (H), which lowers wall tension for any given pressure and radius; this concentric hypertrophy is the heart's structural adaptation to sustained pressure overload such as poorly controlled hypertension or aortic stenosis. While protective in reducing wall stress, the thickened, stiffer wall also impairs diastolic relaxation, which is why chronic pressure-overload hypertrophy can eventually progress to diastolic heart failure.

incorrectas.A: Chamber dilation increases the radius term in the Laplace equation, which would raise wall tension rather than lower it — dilation is instead the characteristic response to chronic volume overload (e.g., valvular regurgitation), not pressure overload.
incorrectas.B: Wall thinning would decrease the denominator in the Laplace equation and increase wall tension, the opposite of the adaptive response needed to cope with elevated afterload.
incorrectas.D: Valve annular dilation refers to stretching of a valve ring (as can occur secondarily in a failing, dilated ventricle) and is not a compensatory mechanism for reducing ventricular wall tension in response to afterload.

preguntas.q: An acute rise in aortic pressure (afterload) has what immediate effect on cardiac wall stress?

o.C: Wall stress remains constant due to autoregulation
o.D: Wall stress depends only on heart rate

e.correcta: By the Law of Laplace (wall stress = P × r / 2H), an acute increase in aortic pressure directly raises the pressure term, and since wall thickness cannot change acutely to compensate, wall stress (and wall tension) rises immediately. This acute increase in wall stress is also what drives the immediate rise in myocardial oxygen consumption seen with sudden increases in afterload, before any compensatory hypertrophy has time to develop.

incorrectas.A: A decrease in wall stress would require a fall in pressure, an increase in wall thickness, or a decrease in radius; acutely rising aortic pressure moves the equation in the opposite direction, raising rather than lowering wall stress.
incorrectas.C: There is no acute autoregulatory mechanism that instantaneously normalizes wall stress against a sudden pressure rise; the only long-term compensation is structural hypertrophy, which takes weeks and is not available acutely.
incorrectas.D: Wall stress by the Laplace relationship depends on pressure, radius, and wall thickness, not heart rate; heart rate influences myocardial oxygen consumption but is not a term in the wall stress equation itself.

preguntas.q: Per Poiseuille's equation, vascular resistance (R) is calculated using which formula?

e.correcta: Poiseuille's equation states resistance R = 8ηl / πr⁴, where η is blood viscosity, l is vessel length, and r is vessel radius raised to the fourth power. Because radius is in the denominator and raised to the fourth power, small changes in vessel diameter (as with arteriolar vasoconstriction/vasodilation) produce enormous changes in resistance, which is why the arterioles — not large arteries — are the primary site of regulating total peripheral resistance and blood pressure.

incorrectas.A: This inverts the true relationship by putting r⁴ in the numerator, which would mean resistance increases with vessel radius — the opposite of reality, where wider vessels have dramatically lower resistance.
incorrectas.C: Placing r⁴ in the numerator alongside viscosity, while moving length to the denominator, misrepresents both relationships: resistance should rise with vessel length and fall steeply with vessel radius, not vice versa.
incorrectas.D: Adding an extra π to the numerator and misplacing the terms does not correspond to the Poiseuille relationship; the correct form keeps viscosity and length in the numerator and radius to the fourth power in the denominator, scaled by 8/π.

preguntas.q: The likelihood of turbulent blood flow is predicted using Reynolds number (NR), which is calculated by which formula?

e.correcta: Reynolds number equals the density of blood (ρ) times vessel diameter (d) times velocity (v), divided by viscosity (η): NR = ρdv/η. A higher Reynolds number (from increased velocity or diameter, or decreased viscosity, as in anemia) favors turbulent rather than laminar flow, which is why conditions like anemia, valve stenosis, or high cardiac output states produce audible turbulence (murmurs or bruits).

incorrectas.A: Inverting the ratio so viscosity is in the numerator would mean turbulence increases with viscosity, which is backwards — higher viscosity (as in polycythemia) actually stabilizes laminar flow and reduces the tendency toward turbulence.
incorrectas.C: Placing density and viscosity together in the numerator while diameter and velocity sit in the denominator scrambles the true relationship; turbulence should increase with vessel diameter and flow velocity, not decrease as this formula implies.
incorrectas.D: This formula omits density from the numerator terms it should be paired with and misplaces viscosity; the correct relationship keeps density, diameter, and velocity together in the numerator over viscosity in the denominator.

preguntas.q: The dominant cardiac pacemaker is located in the wall of the right atrium near the orifice of which structure?

e.correcta: The sinoatrial (SA) node, the heart's primary pacemaker, sits in the wall of the right atrium at the junction with the superior vena cava (the crista terminalis region), where its cells spontaneously depolarize faster than any other cardiac tissue (funny current, If, driving the fastest phase 4 slope) and thus set the heart rate under normal conditions. Its impulse then spreads through the atria to the AV node, making the SA node's anatomic location clinically relevant for understanding sinus arrhythmias and surgical/catheter approaches near the cavoatrial junction.

incorrectas.B: The coronary sinus, which drains venous blood from the myocardium into the right atrium, is located near the AV node region (relevant to slow pathway/AV nodal reentry anatomy), not the SA node.
incorrectas.C: The inferior vena cava enters the right atrium near the eustachian valve, a different anatomic landmark than the SA node, which sits at the superior vena cava-right atrial junction.
incorrectas.D: Pulmonary veins drain oxygenated blood into the left atrium, not the right atrium, and have no anatomic relationship with the SA node's location — though ectopic pacemaker foci near the pulmonary veins are a well-known trigger for atrial fibrillation.

preguntas.q: The first heart sound (S1) is produced by closure of which valves?

e.correcta: S1 marks the onset of ventricular systole and is generated by the closure of the atrioventricular valves — the mitral and tricuspid valves — as ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure, snapping the leaflets shut and preventing backflow into the atria. This is the sound heard at the start of isovolumetric contraction and is best appreciated at the mitral and tricuspid auscultation areas, marking the sound clinicians use to identify systole at the bedside.

incorrectas.A: Aortic and pulmonic valve closure produces S2, which marks the end of systole/onset of diastole, not S1, and reflects semilunar rather than atrioventricular valve function.
incorrectas.C: Mixing one AV valve (mitral) with one semilunar valve (aortic) does not correspond to any single physiologic heart sound; S1 and S2 are each generated by a matched pair of valves closing together (AV pair for S1, semilunar pair for S2).
incorrectas.D: Tricuspid and pulmonic valves are on opposite sides of the closure pairing used to generate heart sounds; S1 requires both AV valves (mitral and tricuspid) closing together, not an AV valve paired with a semilunar valve.

preguntas.q: The heart sound S1 is normally loudest when auscultated over which cardiac area?

e.correcta: S1, produced by mitral and tricuspid valve closure, is loudest at the mitral (apical) auscultation area near the cardiac apex, because the mitral valve's larger muscle mass and its proximity to the chest wall at the apex make its closure sound most prominent there. This is why auscultating at the apex (5th intercostal space, midclavicular line) is the standard way to assess S1 and detect abnormalities like a loud S1 in mitral stenosis.

incorrectas.A: The aortic area (2nd right intercostal space) is where aortic valve closure sounds (contributing to S2) and aortic murmurs are best heard, not where S1 is loudest.
incorrectas.B: The pulmonic area (2nd left intercostal space) is used to assess pulmonic valve closure (also part of S2) and pulmonic flow murmurs, not S1.
incorrectas.D: Erb's point (3rd left intercostal space) is a location where both S1 and S2 can often be heard and is useful for detecting some murmurs (e.g., aortic regurgitation), but it is not the site where S1 is characteristically loudest — that is the mitral area.

preguntas.q: The heart sound S2 is normally loudest when auscultated over which location?
